# Flui Assistant — identity & guardrails

> Hand-authored, canonical. This is the assistant's system contract. It is injected
> ahead of the knowledge corpus and the version manifest. Keep it short, explicit, and
> human-reviewable — changes here change the assistant's behavior.

## Identity

You are the **Flui Assistant**, the built-in assistant for Flui — an open source platform
for running applications on top of a user's own cloud provider. You help people understand
and operate Flui: its concepts, its CLI, the `flui.yaml` manifest, the catalog, and
troubleshooting — especially the first-run operations (installing the platform, creating the
first cluster/environment, the first deploy).

You are not a general-purpose chatbot. You are a domain assistant for Flui.

## Scope (what you help with)

- Flui concepts (clusters, nodes, environments, applications, catalog, observability, DNS,
  TLS, firewalls, vnets, identity/OIDC, storage, build pipeline).
- The Flui CLI: which command to run, its flags and arguments, and the order of operations
  — grounded in the CLI reference you are given, never invented.
- Authoring and validating a `flui.yaml` manifest against the schema you are given.
- Diagnosing install/bootstrap problems and pointing to the right command or doc.

## Out of scope (refuse, then redirect)

If asked about anything unrelated to Flui — the weather, philosophy, general coding
unrelated to Flui, world facts, personal advice — do **not** answer it. Briefly state that
you are the Flui Assistant and can only help with Flui, then offer a relevant Flui starting
point. One short sentence of redirect, no lecture.

## Refusal examples

Match this behavior for out-of-scope requests (answer in the user's language):

- User: "Can we talk about philosophy?" → "I'm the Flui Assistant — I can only help with
  Flui (the platform, its CLI, flui.yaml, the catalog, install and troubleshooting). Happy to
  help with any of those, for example creating your first cluster."
- User: "What's the weather today?" → "I'm the Flui Assistant and can only help with Flui.
  Want a hand with a deploy, a flui.yaml, or your cluster setup?"
- User: "Write me a poem." → "That's outside what I do — I'm the Flui Assistant, here for Flui
  and your apps on it. Ask me about the CLI, the catalog, or an install."

## Version awareness

You are always given a version manifest describing the environment you are assisting:
the CLI version, the platform release it pins (API / dashboard / authz image tags and
bootstrap ref), and the `flui.yaml` schema version. Treat it as ground truth.

- State the versions you are bound to when it matters (e.g. "for CLI {cli} pinning platform
  {platform}…").
- Do not describe features, flags, or fields that are not present in the CLI reference,
  schema, or concepts you were given — they may not exist in this version.
- If the live platform reported at runtime differs from the version manifest you were built
  against, say so plainly and answer for the version you actually know, flagging the gap.

## No invention (anti-hallucination)

Your knowledge is exactly the corpus you are given — the CLI reference (generated from the
CLI itself), the `flui.yaml` schema, and the concept docs. Beyond that you know nothing about
Flui internals.

- Never invent commands, flags, arguments, manifest fields, defaults, or version numbers.
- If the answer is not in the corpus, say you don't have that detail and point to
  `flui <command> --help` or the docs — do not guess.
- Prefer quoting the exact command/flag/field names from the corpus over paraphrasing them.

## Safety

- Before suggesting a destructive operation (deleting an environment, cluster, node, volume,
  or data), call out that it is destructive and irreversible, and state any safer alternative.
- Do not help bypass authentication, exfiltrate credentials, or disable security controls.
- When giving a multi-step operation, prefer the order the CLI/docs prescribe.

## Credentials and secrets (hard rule)

Secrets — passwords, API keys, cloud-provider tokens, kubeconfig, SSH keys, secret
environment variables — must NEVER pass through this assistant, neither read nor write.

- **Never reveal, echo, repeat, summarize, or transcribe a secret value**, even if it is
  visible to you or a user pastes it. Secret env values appear masked (`********`) — keep
  them masked.
- **To view credentials, redirect to the secure path** — they stay in the user's terminal or
  the dashboard, never in this chat. Point to the command, e.g.
  `flui env credentials --show-secrets` or `flui config list --tokens`. You describe HOW to
  see them; you never show them.
- **Never ask the user to paste a secret into the chat.** If a user pastes one anyway, do not
  repeat it, store it, or act on it: warn them it should not be shared in chat, tell them to
  set it through the secure flow (e.g. `flui config set <provider> ...`), and suggest rotating
  it if it may have been exposed.
- **At install / onboarding**, cloud-provider credentials are configured through the CLI's
  encrypted config (`flui config set <provider> ...`) — guide the user to that command and to
  where they create the token with the right permissions; never collect or hold the token
  yourself.

## Tone

Concise and operational. Lead with the command or the answer, then the minimum context.
Use the user's language. Don't pad.

sections.title: What Flui is
sections.body:
Flui is an open source platform for hosting applications. To
start using it, all you need is an API key from one of the
[supported providers](#where-flui-runs). If you would rather not
use a provider, or you want to use Linux servers you run on
premises, you can do that too. A single command creates a
complete cloud platform: clusters, networking, TLS, DNS, identity
management, observability and a dashboard.

That is the base an installation starts from, but you can go
beyond the provider you started with. Flui is built around the
idea of a composable cloud: one surface where the capabilities
that different cloud providers offer come together in a single
platform. Flui manages a fleet of servers spread across one
provider or several, and hides that work behind a clear web
interface, a CLI and MCP.

This chapter explains the ideas behind Flui, and the gaps and
needs it was built for. If you would rather start from the
operational side, go to the [Tasks](/tasks/) section.

## The gap Flui closes

Where you run your software matters, and each kind of cloud gives
you a different experience.

### Regional, sovereign and budget clouds

Many providers compete on good machines at fair prices. What they
usually do not sell is the platform around those machines: the
virtual network, the firewall, certificate management, DNS,
scaling, application management and backups. These are the parts
that turn machines into a place to run applications. When one of
these providers does offer some of them, they tend to be its own
stack, tied to that provider.

You can assemble the missing pieces yourself, and some teams do.
Those projects usually end up as side projects that are hard to
maintain.

This is where Flui helps most. Bring a key for one of these
clouds, or a machine you already rent from one, and
`flui env create` gives you the full stack a managed PaaS would
give you. That includes something machines alone never give you:
applications that scale within the limits you set, and clusters
that buy another machine when they run out of room, with your
consent and within a spending ceiling. See
[What a cluster may buy for itself](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/).

Self-hosted panels also offer much of this stack, one server at a
time. Flui goes further. An installation is not one cluster but as
many as you need, on different providers and in different
regions, all managed together; see
[Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/). A
panel keeps the platform on the machine it was installed on. A
Flui installation can grow beyond it.

### Major hyperscalers

On the major clouds the building blocks already exist: managed
Kubernetes, managed DNS, identity and observability. They work
well, but they have a cost: vendor pricing, tight coupling to the
provider's network and identity, and an ecosystem that is hard to
leave.

Flui does not compete with what hyperscalers already do well. On a
hyperscaler, the reason to use Flui is portability: your
applications can move between clouds, and the platform on top is
not tied to one vendor's stack.

### Do-it-yourself stacks

On any provider you can build the platform yourself: an IaC tool
for provisioning, a configuration tool for the hosts, a packaging
tool for workloads, your own GitOps, ingress, certificate
management, DNS automation and observability. Each piece works on
its own. Keeping them working together is the real job.

### Managed PaaS

Hosted application platforms give you a good experience, but they
own the runtime. Your applications, your data and the format you
describe them in belong to the platform.

### Where Flui sits

Flui gives you the experience of a managed PaaS on the providers
you already use, around an open specification you can take with
you. An installation can use more than one provider, and Flui
fills in what any single provider lacks. The control plane, the
runtime, the manifest specification and every component Flui ships
are open source.

## What Flui does

From the outside, it works like this:

1. You connect a provider Flui can provision on, or point Flui at
   a Linux machine you already own. The key stays with you: the
   CLI keeps it in an encrypted vault on your machine, and the
   installation keeps what it needs in its own database, on the
   machines you run. There is no Flui-operated service that
   receives your key. See [where Flui runs](#where-flui-runs) for
   the current list.
2. You run `flui env create`. About five minutes later the
   platform is installed and ready to host applications. This
   first cluster is the **control cluster**. It runs the control
   plane: dashboard, API, identity, database and observability.
   Each component (networking, TLS, identity, observability, the
   dashboard and so on) has its own chapter.
3. From then on, Flui is where you manage the whole installation.
   You add workload clusters later, from the dashboard or through
   an agent, on the provider you started with or on another one.
   Clusters, nodes, networking, identity, certificates,
   observability and the applications themselves are all managed
   the same way, through the same CLI, dashboard and API.

## Where Flui runs

Flui can put a machine in four kinds of place, and they do not all
offer the same things.

- **Hetzner.** Flui creates the servers, the private network, the
  firewall and the storage, and manages the DNS zone. Machines
  are billed by the hour.
- **Scaleway.** The same: Flui creates the servers, the network,
  the firewall, DNS and storage. Machines are billed by the hour.
- **OVHcloud.** Flui creates the servers through OpenStack, builds
  the private network and attaches the nodes to it, all billed by
  the hour. Two things work differently. OVHcloud has no DNS zone
  Flui can manage, so a cluster there publishes its names in a
  zone hosted on Hetzner or Scaleway, or in records you write
  yourself. There is also no firewall at OVHcloud's edge that Flui
  can control, so the rules are applied on the machines
  themselves, as on a server of your own.
- **Your own server.** Any Linux machine you can reach over SSH,
  whether you rent it, keep it in an office or under a desk. Flui
  installs on top of it and buys nothing. A VPS you rent from any
  provider counts as your own server, whether or not Flui
  integrates that provider.

The difference matters most when a cluster needs to grow. A
cluster can add machines on its own only where Flui can buy them.
On your own servers it cannot, so when a cluster runs out of room
it raises an alarm that names the machine to add. Flui decides
this from what each provider declares it can do, never from the
provider's name.

The list is not closed. Each provider lives in its own isolated
module and declares the capabilities it supports, so adding one
does not affect the rest of the platform; see
[How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/).

## Bringing your own server

Flui has three ways of working with the infrastructure underneath:
Full, Partial and BYOS. All three are described in
[How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/).

BYOS means bring your own server. You point Flui at a machine and
it installs over SSH:

```bash
flui env create --host 203.0.113.10
```

No provider API is involved. `--port`, `--user` and `--ssh-key`
cover hosts where you do not log in as `root` on port 22. Flui
installs the same platform it installs on a provider (dashboard,
API, identity, observability and the rest) and applies a firewall
on the host itself, because there is no provider firewall to use.
Later, `flui node connect --host <ip>` adds another machine you
own to the same cluster.

What you give up is the work the provider would do for you. Flui
cannot create or delete your machines, so you add capacity by
hand.

## What composable means here

Composable does not mean you will run everything across five
clouds. It describes how the pieces of the platform fit together,
and you can see it in three places. The installation below is one
example.

_Diagram: One installation across three providers. The control plane runs on Ubuntu servers you own; storage, DNS, email and inference come from whichever provider offers them._

**An installation is not tied to the provider it started on.** A
workload cluster can run on another provider, in another region,
and it is still a cluster like any other: you manage it from the
same dashboard and drive it with the same commands. Flui connects
clusters that share no network with an encrypted network of its
own, the Flui network
([The network Flui builds](/concepts/10-the-network-flui-builds/)).
Inside a cluster, traffic stays on the provider's private network,
or on the Flui network where the servers have none. When a cluster
can run somewhere else, and what that costs, is covered in
[Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/).

**Some capabilities belong to the installation, not to one
cluster.** S3-compatible storage, outgoing email and model
inference attach to the installation. They can come from any
provider that offers them, wherever your servers run.

**Some pieces are supplied by Flui.** No provider offers a
complete platform, so Flui supplies some pieces itself: the Flui
network between clusters, the Flui firewall where there is no
provider firewall to control, and backups. Some exist because a
provider has none. Others exist because owning them keeps the
platform the same wherever it runs.

## How you use it

You work with Flui through four surfaces, all backed by the same
API:

- The [Flui CLI](/cli/), the main entry point and the surface this
  documentation focuses on.
- The Flui dashboard, a web interface for the same operations.
- The Flui REST API, exposed by every running control plane.
- **MCP**, a Model Context Protocol endpoint on the same API. A
  coding agent can use it to deploy and operate the platform with
  its own credential, under the same permission model as a
  person. See
  [The Flui assistant and MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/)
  and [The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/).

## What Flui is not

- **Not a fork of Kubernetes.** Flui uses upstream K3s and the
  standard Kubernetes API. `kubectl`, Helm and standard manifests
  all work.
- **Not a replacement for the open source ecosystem.** Flui builds
  on well-known tools for ingress, certificates, logs, metrics and
  identity, and integrates them instead of reinventing them.

## Status

Flui is in **alpha**. This documentation describes behaviour you
can verify in the source code or with the CLI, and leaves out
features that are not released.

- License: **AGPL-3.0**. Commercial use is allowed. If you offer
  Flui as a network service to others, the license requires you to
  share your changes to the source. The
  [`LICENSE`](https://github.com/flui-cloud/flui-core/blob/main/LICENSE)
  file is the reference.
- Roadmap and current work: see [flui.cloud](https://flui.cloud).

## Where to read next

- [Start here](/tasks/): the task pages, one job at a time, in the
  order you will need them.
- [How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/):
  how one platform works on top of many clouds.
- [Why K3s](/concepts/02-why-k3s/): the technology behind every
  Flui cluster.
- [Creating a cluster](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/): what
  `flui env create` does, step by step.
- [Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/):
  one installation, many clusters, and when a cluster can run on
  another provider.
- [The network Flui builds](/concepts/10-the-network-flui-builds/):
  the encrypted network that connects clusters with no network in
  common.
- [The Flui assistant and MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/):
  how coding agents work with the platform.
- [The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/): the
  portable specification your applications and resources use.
- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/): what Flui
  means by an app, and its lifecycle.

For a command-by-command reference, see the [CLI section](/cli/).
This section explains why Flui works the way it does.

sections.title: How Flui works across providers
sections.body:
Every later chapter about infrastructure (clusters, networks,
firewalls, DNS, credentials) builds on the abstraction described
here.

## The problem

Two cloud providers can look similar and behave very differently.

- **What sits next to a server varies widely.** One provider offers
  managed DNS, firewalls, private networks, load balancers and
  snapshots through the same API. Another gives you a server and
  almost nothing else. Building a platform on each takes very
  different work.
- **Billing models differ.** One provider bills by the hour and
  stops charging the moment you delete the resource. Another bills
  monthly under contract. Some mix both in the same catalogue.
- **The same idea has different names.** A server can live in a
  *location*, a *zone* or a *region* depending on the provider. The
  words are not interchangeable: each carries its own meaning about
  scope, redundancy and pricing.
- **SSH keys, firewalls, private networks and DNS are each modelled
  differently.** The same concept comes with a different API and a
  different shape on each provider.

Even one vendor can ship two compute products that look
interchangeable and behave very differently, and only one of them may
suit the elastic, autoscaling workloads Flui is built for.

A naive integration ends up with provider-specific branches scattered
across the CLI, the API and the dashboard. The cost grows with every
new provider, feature and edge case, until adding a third provider is
a project of its own.

## What Flui does instead

Flui's goal is to get your applications online quickly, on the cloud
provider you choose, and let you scale without rewriting your
platform as traffic, team or workloads grow. That matters most on
providers that do not ship a managed platform of their own, and also
on providers that do, when portability across clouds matters more
than one vendor's stack.

To do this across providers that vary so much, Flui puts a single
abstraction layer between the rest of the system and the cloud
provider. The layer has two properties:

1. **No lowest common denominator.** When a provider lacks a
   capability, Flui says so, and may simulate it, fall back or
   degrade gracefully, instead of pretending the capability does not
   exist.
2. **Capability awareness.** Each provider declares which of a fixed
   set of capabilities it supports, and the rest of Flui adapts its
   behaviour, without provider-specific branches in user-facing code.

The result is a two-layer architecture. Each provider has its own
**isolated module**, the only place that knows how that cloud
behaves. Above it sits Flui's **cross-cutting core** (the CLI, the
dashboard, the orchestration engine, the application model, the
operations layer), which is the same whatever provider is underneath.
The core talks to "a provider", never to a specific cloud, and the
modules below absorb provider differences so they do not propagate
upwards.

## Capabilities are the contract

Nothing on either side of the abstraction speaks in provider
products. A provider module declares what its cloud can do (buy
machines by the hour, keep a DNS zone, drive a firewall at the edge),
and everything above the layer asks for capabilities. Above the line,
a requirement is stated and the platform chooses where it can be
carried out. The provider is the execution target.

Where a capability is missing, Flui supplies what it can itself: a
firewall with no provider edge is applied on the machines, and a
cluster whose servers have no private network gets the Flui network.
Anything Flui does not supply is stated, not hidden.

The rest of this chapter describes that contract, and the chapters
after it apply it one capability at a time. Across a whole
installation, it is what lets clusters on different providers join
as one; see
[Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/) and
[The network Flui builds](/concepts/10-the-network-flui-builds/).

## Portability and lock-in

The abstraction takes an explicit position on vendor lock-in. The
portable layer covers two things:

- **The `flui.yaml` manifest** describes an application and its
  app-level resources: build, deploy, scaling profile, endpoints,
  domains. The same manifest, unchanged, describes the same app on
  any integrated provider.
- **The operating model**: clusters, environments, deployments and
  observability, driven by the CLI, dashboard and API. The surfaces
  and commands are the same whatever provider is underneath.

The runtime adds a third layer of portability. Flui runs workloads on
K3s, which is upstream Kubernetes and installs on practically any
Linux machine: any cloud, bare metal or edge box. The applications
you deploy through Flui are standard Kubernetes workloads at runtime,
so in principle they can run wherever K3s can run.

Some things stay provider-specific: the underlying machines, the
regions, the catalogue of instance types. A later section of this
chapter shows where that line falls.

Moving from one provider to another means provisioning
infrastructure again under a different credential, then redeploying
the same applications from the same manifests.

Because the operating model and the manifest are the same across
providers, an installation can also run workloads on different
providers at the same time. Where an installation allows clusters on
more than one provider, the same control plane drives them all; see
[Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/) for
when that is the case. Flui also encourages cross-provider backups:
data lives on one provider and backups land on another, so an outage
or account incident at one provider does not take everything down at
once.

## Modes of integration

Flui works with the underlying infrastructure in three modes, each
with its own automation boundary:

- **Flui Full.** Full integration with a cloud provider.
  Provisioning, firewall, DNS, private network and storage (block and
  object) are all exposed by the provider and automated end to end.
  You never have to open the provider's console for routine
  operations.
- **Flui Partial.** The provider exposes the baseline (Flui can
  provision servers, and the provider bills by the hour) but not
  every capability through its API. What it does not expose, Flui
  supplies or takes from elsewhere: the Flui firewall on the
  machines, DNS from a zone held on another provider. The platform on
  top is the same as in Full mode.
- **Flui BYOS** *(bring your own server).* No cloud provider is
  involved. You point Flui at a Linux machine you already own,
  `flui env create --host` installs over SSH, and everything Flui
  ships on top (clusters, ingress, TLS, observability and the rest)
  is the same as in Full or Partial mode. More machines join the same
  way, one at a time, with `flui node connect`. There is no
  provisioning to automate, because you already provisioned the
  machine.

The mode follows from what the provider exposes; the user does not
pick it. A provider that supports every capability Flui needs ends up
in Full mode, and one that supports only some ends up in Partial
mode.

BYOS goes through the same abstraction as any cloud. It is a provider
with its own capability declaration, with almost every capability
declared off: no API to create a server, no catalogue of machine
shapes, no region list, no price list, no managed firewall at the
edge.

The rest follows mechanically, with no special cases.
`flui env firewall apply` takes the same rules and the same command,
and because BYOS declares no managed firewall, the rules are applied
on the machine itself instead of at a provider's edge. A cluster that
needs to grow raises an alarm naming the machine to attach, instead
of buying one, because BYOS declares no way to buy one. Neither
behaviour branches on the provider's name. Both come from what the
provider says it can do.

Behind the modes, Flui tracks a finer set of capability dimensions
each provider can declare: server lifecycle, hourly billing, SSH key
registry, firewall, DNS, private network, block storage, object
storage and power management. Where the provider's API offers a
capability (managed firewalls, DNS zones, private networks, volumes),
Flui drives it directly, so the provider's strengths come through.
Where it does not, Flui supplies the piece itself or takes it from
another provider. Only where neither is possible does it become a
manual step, and that fallback is documented, so an integrator does
not have to guess what happens when their provider has no firewall.
The platform on top looks the same either way.

## The providers integrated today

Here is what the model above resolves to now. Every row is the
provider module's own capability declaration.

| | Buys machines | Billing | Private network | DNS zones | Firewall |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Hetzner** | yes | hourly | zone-scoped | yes | provider edge |
| **Scaleway** | yes | hourly | per region | yes | provider edge |
| **OVHcloud** | yes | hourly | per region | no | on the host |
| **Your own servers** | no | yours | whatever you wired | no | on the host |

<small>Hetzner, Scaleway and OVHcloud are trademarks of their respective owners. Flui is not affiliated with or endorsed by them.</small>

Four more differences matter when you choose, because each is
something you either get or arrange yourself:

- **Resizing and stopping a node.** Hetzner and Scaleway can change a
  machine's shape in place, and power one down without destroying it.
  On OVHcloud neither is exposed, so growing a node means replacing
  it.
- **Live stock.** On Hetzner, Flui reads region by region whether a
  shape can be bought right now. On Scaleway and OVHcloud it does
  not, so a sold-out shape shows up only when an order is refused.
  What Flui does with the signal where it has it is
  [described below](#live-availability).
- **Block volumes.** All three clouds create, attach and grow the
  volume that carries the cluster's shared storage. On your own
  servers that is the disk already in the machine.
- **Object storage for backups.** Backups are Flui's own, taken from
  inside the cluster, and land on any S3-compatible bucket you point
  them at, wherever it lives, including at another provider. On the
  supported clouds, setting one up takes one click: Flui creates the
  bucket and wires the credentials itself. What that click does
  differs by provider. Scaleway provisions the bucket with the
  credential Flui already holds for compute, OVHcloud mints an S3 key
  from its OpenStack one, and Hetzner asks for a second set of Object
  Storage credentials before doing the rest.

Two capabilities these clouds sell are left out of the table: server
snapshots and provider load balancers. Flui drives neither on any
provider, so listing them would describe the cloud's catalogue rather
than what Flui does with it. Ingress is Traefik running on your own
nodes, and backups work as described above.

The table also cannot show the shapes you can pick and what they
cost. These are read from the provider rather than from a list kept
inside Flui, so they follow the provider's catalogue as it changes.
On OVHcloud the regions are read live as well, scoped to your
credential, because the regions a project can use differ from one
account to the next.

Read across a row rather than ranking the columns. Hetzner and
Scaleway are Full-mode integrations: everything Flui needs is behind
the provider's API. OVHcloud is Partial: servers, the private network
and volumes go through its API, while the firewall is Flui's own,
applied on the machines, and DNS comes from a zone held on another
provider. Your own servers are BYOS: nothing to buy, and the same
platform on top.

The difference that matters most is growth. A cluster can add a node
by itself only where Flui can buy one. On your own servers it cannot,
so a cluster that runs out of room raises an alarm naming the machine
to attach. That behaviour comes from `nodeProvisioning`, never from
the provider's name.

### Live availability

A machine shape can sell out in one region and still be available in
the next. Where a provider reports its stock, Flui reads it at the
moment you choose (`flui server-types list` marks a shape that cannot
be bought in a region right now), so a purchase does not fail halfway
through.

The check matters most when a cluster buys its own machines. A
[scaling group](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/) lists the shapes it may
buy, in your order of preference. When the first is sold out where
the cluster needs it, the group buys the next one it is allowed to. A
sold-out shape moves to the back of the list but never leaves it,
because stock comes back, and when it does, the cluster buys that
shape.

If every shape on the list is sold out, the cluster raises an alarm
that says so and keeps looking. If a machine sells out between the
reading and the order, the group pauses briefly and checks
availability again. Either way, as soon as the machine can be
bought, the cluster buys it, within the spending ceiling you set and
only if the group is allowed to act on its own.

## Adding more providers

Hetzner, Scaleway and OVHcloud are where Flui starts, and it is not
limited to them. Each sits behind the same provider layer, so adding
another means writing its module and its capability declaration; the
rest of Flui adapts to what that declaration says.

Before an integration makes sense, a provider needs two things:

- **A well-documented API for its servers.** Flui has to create,
  read, delete and list servers and report their status, through an
  interface the provider documents and keeps stable. That is the
  minimum. A private network, a firewall, DNS and a catalogue of
  shapes with prices are capabilities declared on top of it, and none
  of them is required to get in.
- **Hourly billing.** A cluster that buys machines and gives them back
  on its own only makes sense where a machine costs the hours it ran.
  With monthly billing, every short-lived node would cost a full
  month.

A provider with both gets the whole platform on top, with whatever it
does not expose handled as [Modes of integration](#modes-of-integration)
describes. A provider with neither can still be used: to Flui, the
servers you rent there are [your own servers](#modes-of-integration).

## What the abstraction hides, and what it does not

The abstraction works in two directions. Most of the time you talk to
Flui in Flui terms, and anything you normally have to think about is
expressed that way.

| Flui concept | What it represents |
| --- | --- |
| `cluster` | A set of servers with a private network, a firewall, and cluster-scoped resources, all tagged as managed by Flui. |
| `node` | A machine inside a cluster. Its row records where the machine came from (provider, region, shape) and what it costs per hour. |
| `vnet` + `subnet` | A private network and one or more subnets the cluster's nodes attach to. |
| `firewall` | A set of inbound/outbound rules attached to one or more servers. |
| `dns-zone` | A managed DNS zone, when the provider exposes a DNS API. |
| `endpoint` | A FQDN with TLS, attached to a workload, backed by an A-record and a certificate. |
| `manifest` (`flui.yaml`) | Independent of any provider; see [the manifest chapter](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/). |
| `build` / `release` / `operation` | Tracked centrally by Flui. Build execution is delegated to an external system. |

A few things are not hidden. They stay provider-specific, because
hiding them would mislead you:

- **Server-type identifiers.** Each provider has its own catalogue of
  instance shapes. Flui keeps a cache with pricing and availability
  per region, but does not pretend two different providers' types are
  interchangeable.
- **Region and zone codes.** The user picks one; Flui validates it
  against the provider.
- **Prices.** Every machine carries the price of the shape it
  actually is, read from that provider's own catalogue. This lets
  Flui talk about money instead of machine counts: what a cluster
  already commits to for the month, and what one more machine would
  add. It is also why the limit on what a cluster may spend on itself
  is stated in money rather than in a number of machines, since the
  number of machines is not the bill. When Flui decides to add a
  machine, or declines to, the decision it records names the shape,
  the region and the hourly price it was weighing.

  Two readings are kept apart. A machine whose price Flui cannot see
  (your own hardware under BYOS, or a shape the provider does not
  publish a price for) is recorded as *unknown*, never as zero,
  because zero reads as free. A total built from those rows is
  therefore a floor, and the machines it could not price are counted
  next to it rather than folded in.
- **Provider-side IP ranges.** When a provider documents constraints
  on CIDRs or routes, those constraints win.
- **External-side configuration.** When something Flui needs touches
  a system outside the provider's API, for example delegating a
  domain registered elsewhere by setting NS records at the registrar,
  you configure it manually on that external side. Flui manages what
  it can reach.

## Why this design pays off

This design pays off in three ways:

1. **Adding a provider does not destabilise the rest.** A new provider
   integration is built as a self-contained piece: it implements the
   abstraction and declares which capabilities the provider supports.
   The CLI, the dashboard and the orchestration engine stay
   untouched. The work is real, but it stops at the new integration's
   boundary.
2. **Dropping a provider is also self-contained.** Every operation
   that touches a provider goes through a single point inside Flui.
   Removing a provider means removing that one integration, without
   chasing changes across the rest of the platform.
3. **Capability-driven UX without conditionals.** The dashboard and
   the CLI read the provider's capability declaration instead of
   hardcoding behaviour, so a provider that gains DNS support gets DNS
   controls in the UI as soon as its capability flag flips, with no
   client release.

## How this chapter is referenced elsewhere

- [Cluster as a concept](/concepts/03-cluster-as-a-concept/) and
  [Creating a cluster](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/) describe the
  cluster lifecycle in Flui terms; the provider work happens behind
  the abstraction described here.
- [VNet and subnets](/concepts/11-vnet-and-subnets/),
  [Firewalls](/concepts/12-firewalls/) and
  [DNS integration](/concepts/13-dns-integration/) each show the
  abstraction at work in one capability area.
- [Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/) and
  [The network Flui builds](/concepts/10-the-network-flui-builds/):
  what this layer makes possible, clusters on more than one provider
  joined as one installation.
- [The control cluster](/concepts/09-anatomy-of-the-observability-cluster/):
  the control cluster is a cluster like any other, and creating it
  goes through the same provider abstraction as any workload cluster.

sections.title: Why K3s
sections.body:
Every cluster Flui creates, control or workload, on a cloud
provider or on a machine you own, runs K3s as its Kubernetes
distribution. The rest of this documentation depends on that
choice, and this chapter explains it.

## The problem K3s solves for Flui

Flui turns a supported provider key, or a server of your own, into
a complete platform in about five minutes. For that to work, the
Kubernetes layer underneath has to:

1. **Boot fast.** Provision a VM, run cloud-init, start Kubernetes
   and reach `Ready`, all inside those five minutes.
2. **Fit on a small VM.** The largest machine an installation needs
   is the control cluster's: the API, its database, identity and the
   observability backend all share it, and the minimum there is 2
   vCPUs, 4 GB of RAM and 40 GB of disk. `flui env create` warns
   before buying anything smaller. A workload cluster carries much
   less (ingress, certificates, the agents that ship its logs and
   metrics) and starts on about 2 GB. A node that only adds capacity
   carries less again, so its size is set by the applications you
   put on it.
3. **Carry its own ingress, DNS and default storage** out of the box,
   so the first deployment does not require installing five Helm
   charts first.
4. **Stay 100% upstream-compatible**, so that everything Flui relies
   on (kubectl, Helm charts, standard manifests, cert-manager, the
   rest of the CNCF ecosystem) works.

K3s, the lightweight single-binary Kubernetes distribution
maintained by Rancher/SUSE, meets all four.

## How Flui installs K3s

The K3s installation logic lives in a separate, versioned scripts
repository, not in the Flui API. The API generates cloud-init that
downloads and runs the scripts on each node, so install behaviour
can be audited and hot-fixed independently of the Flui API release
cycle.

## Platform components on every cluster

K3s ships a set of add-ons (ingress, cluster DNS, metrics, a default
storage class), and Flui uses them as they come. On top, Flui
installs a small set of its own components: certificate lifecycle,
cluster-side authorization and additional metrics exporters.
Everything is reconciled through the same platform-components
mechanism, so what runs on a cluster is predictable and
declarative.

Components that run only on the control cluster are described in
[The control cluster](/concepts/09-anatomy-of-the-observability-cluster/).

## OS image and architecture

Every node Flui creates on a cloud provider runs Ubuntu 24.04 LTS,
with cloud-init enabled and SSH ready after first boot. Ubuntu
26.04 LTS shipped in April 2026; the default has not moved to it
yet.

The architecture a node can have depends on how it joins the
cluster.

**A node Flui provisions for you is x86_64.** You do not choose an
architecture when you create a cluster on a provider (there is no
flag for it), and where a provider sells ARM machine sizes, they
are filtered out of the list you pick from.

**A machine you bring may be ARM.** Installing onto a server you
already own (creating a cluster on it, or attaching it to an
existing cluster as a node) starts with a probe of the host: its
distribution, architecture, memory, CPUs, and whether K3s is already
there. Three findings stop the install: an architecture other than
`x86_64`, `aarch64` or `arm64`; less than about 2 GB of memory; K3s
already installed. `--best-effort` continues past them and
`--skip-precheck` skips the probe, but neither changes the machine:
an unsupported architecture is refused again by the installer itself.

Passing that check does not mean everything downstream is ready
for ARM. One place still assumes x86_64: when Flui lists
the tags available for a container image, it shows only the tags
that have a `linux/amd64` build.

**Other Linux distributions are not supported yet.** The installer
accepts Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04 and stops on anything else. Ubuntu
26.04 is the next one to support; any other distribution is
verification work that has not been done yet.

## High availability

Clusters run with a single master. The datastore is K3s's embedded
etcd, switched on from the first boot, so a cluster does not have to
change datastore to gain more masters later. Flui does not add more
masters (multi-master HA) yet.

The applications Flui runs can still be highly available;
[High availability](/concepts/31-high-availability/) explains how,
and what that covers.

## What K3s does not do

K3s does not handle:

- **VM provisioning.** That is the cloud provider's job, via the
  abstraction described in
  [How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/).
- **DNS records or external certificates.** Those flow through Flui's
  own DNS abstraction
  ([DNS integration](/concepts/13-dns-integration/)) and cert-manager
  ([TLS and certificates](/concepts/14-tls-and-certificates/)).
- **End-user authentication.** Identity flows through Zitadel
  ([Identity and OIDC](/concepts/15-identity-and-oidc/)).
- **`flui.yaml`.** Flui translates manifests into standard Kubernetes
  resources before applying them. See
  [The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/) and
  [Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/).

[Creating a cluster](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/) shows how these
choices combine in practice.

sections.title: The cluster as a concept
sections.body:
The word "cluster" appears in every Flui doc, command and screen.
This chapter explains what Flui means by it.

## What a Flui cluster is

A Flui cluster is made of:

1. **At least one K3s node.** One master and zero or more workers.
2. **A private network** that ties the nodes together below the
   public IP layer. It is the provider's own network, or the Flui
   network where the servers have none.
3. **A firewall.** It sits at the provider's edge where the provider
   has one Flui can drive, and otherwise is the
   [Flui firewall](/concepts/12-firewalls/) on the machines
   themselves. Either way the cluster gets the same rules.
4. **A baseline of platform components.** A fixed set of cluster
   workloads Flui treats as part of the cluster itself: ingress,
   cert-manager, metrics, cluster DNS, optional authorization, and,
   on the control cluster, the Flui control plane.
5. **An identity in Flui.** Every cluster has a stable UUID, a
   readable name, and a `provider` / `region` binding. Every
   provider resource that belongs to the cluster and can carry labels
   carries the Flui ownership labels (`managed-by: flui-cloud`, plus
   the cluster's identifier).

## The two cluster types

A Flui installation has two kinds of cluster, with different roles:

| Type | Role | What it carries |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Control cluster** | One per installation | The Flui control plane: API, dashboard, identity provider, database, queue, metrics and log stack, ingress, cert-manager. You can run apps here, but most installations keep it for the control plane. |
| **Workload cluster** | Zero or many | User application clusters. They run the apps you deploy plus the platform components needed to run them safely. |

Both kinds start with a single master node and can grow by adding
workers. A cluster stays one logical unit even when it runs on
several machines.

The multi-cluster picture is covered in
[Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/).

## What a cluster exposes

You work with a cluster through a small set of surfaces you can read
and act on. In the dashboard they are the tabs of the cluster's page.
The Overview summarizes most of them, each with a link to the full
surface:

_Screenshot: The Overview of a cluster named production, with two nodes._

| Surface | What lives there |
| --- | --- |
| **Overview** | Health at a glance: nodes, average CPU and memory, firewall sync state, backups. |
| **Monitoring** | Live metrics and log streams for the cluster and the apps on it. |
| **Network** | The private network and subnets the nodes attach to. |
| **Storage** | The shared storage volume and the storage classes apps can use. |
| **Nodes** | The individual master and worker nodes, their roles and their server types. |
| **Scaling** | The cluster's scaling groups, which say what the cluster may buy for itself and where it must stop: a floor, a target and a ceiling in machines; the regions and machine shapes it may choose from; how it picks between them; a spending ceiling in money; and whether it may act on its own or must ask you first. |
| **Firewall** | The ingress and egress rules attached to the cluster's servers, and, apart from them, the ports your applications may reach outside the cluster (open unless you limit them; the platform's own services are not affected). |
| **DNS** | The zones and records associated with the cluster, when the provider exposes DNS. |
| **Variables** | Cluster-scoped configuration injected into the apps that run on it. |
| **Pricing** | The provider-side monthly cost of every resource the cluster owns. |

Each surface has its own chapter later in the documentation. When
you operate a cluster, you usually work on one surface at a time.

Scaling decides whether a cluster's size ever changes. On a provider
Flui can buy from, every cluster has a scaling group from the start,
set to hold the nodes it already has, so nothing is bought or given
back until somebody changes it. Raise its floor and the cluster buys
a machine. Let it act on its own and it follows its load, within the
bounds, places, shapes and budget the group names. On your own
servers there is no group: a node joins when you attach it. See
[What a cluster may buy for itself](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/).

## Where this concept goes from here

- [Creating a cluster](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/): how you go
  from no cluster to a healthy one, step by step.
- [Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/):
  one control cluster, many workload clusters, and what follows from
  that.
- [Nodes and cluster topology](/concepts/06-nodes-and-cluster-topology/):
  the machines a cluster is built from.
- [The control cluster](/concepts/09-anatomy-of-the-observability-cluster/):
  what makes the control cluster different.
- [What a cluster may buy for itself](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/):
  the scaling group, why its ceiling is money rather than a number of
  machines, and why nothing scales until somebody allows it.

sections.title: Creating a cluster
sections.body:
You run a single command. A few minutes later you have a working
cluster with a dashboard open in your browser, an API answering on
a real URL, an identity provider managing the login, a database, a
metrics and log stack, ingress and certificates, all wired together
and reachable. There is no second step where you install the
platform on top of the cluster: the command installs the platform.

This chapter covers the choices that decide what that command
produces: where the cluster lives, how it is addressed, what kind
of certificate it presents on day one, what storage it carries and
who can reach it.

The chapter is written around the **control cluster**, the first
cluster of any Flui installation and the one that hosts the
control plane. The same applies to a workload cluster, minus the
control-plane parts.

The commands, in order, are in the task pages. This chapter
explains what you are choosing and which surface can make each
choice.

## The choices that shape a cluster

Every cluster is described by a handful of inputs. Most have
sensible defaults; the ones you change usually match a concrete
constraint (a region close to your users, a server
shape that fits your workload, a stricter firewall).

| Choice | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| **Provider** | Which cloud the cluster runs on, or your own machine (see below). |
| **Region** | Which provider region the servers sit in. Defaults to the provider's default region. |
| **Server type** | The shape (CPU / RAM / disk) of every node. Defaults to the recommended size for the chosen provider. |
| **Firewall** | Whether Flui installs and locks down a default firewall and, where the provider has a firewall of its own, which source IPs may reach the master over SSH. |
| **Certificate mode** | Whether the cluster issues a real Let's Encrypt certificate or a staging one (see below). |
| **Shared storage** | Whether the cluster includes a master-hosted shared volume (the default) or falls back to per-node local storage. |

A cluster is created master-only by default. On a provider Flui can
buy from, it already has a
[scaling group](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/) at that point, set to
hold the nodes it has: adding a worker means raising the group's
floor, and letting the cluster buy machines for itself means telling
the group it may act on its own. On your own servers a node joins
when you attach it (covered in
[Nodes and cluster topology](/concepts/06-nodes-and-cluster-topology/)).
Growing the root disk on a server type that allows it is a separate
operation you run later.

## Which surface can create one

Once the control cluster is up, the CLI and the dashboard cover
most of the same ground, but not all of it. Each gap has a
mechanical reason.

**The control cluster is created from the CLI or from the web.**
There is no dashboard to create it from: the dashboard is one of
the things the install brings, together with the API and the
identity provider. `flui env create` does it from your machine.
The same install can start from
[app.flui.cloud](https://app.flui.cloud) instead: you pick
one of the [supported providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/#the-providers-integrated-today), and either the page runs the
install with your provider token, or it hands you the
`flui env create` command to run yourself, so the token never
leaves your machine. Either way the cluster lands on your own
provider account, the page keeps no access to it, and you take
it over with `flui env adopt`.

**Workload clusters are created from the dashboard or the CLI.**
The dashboard carries a creation wizard that walks through name,
provider and region; server type; SSH keys; the private network and
its subnet; how the cluster will be addressed; the firewall; and a
review before anything is bought. It then shows you a progress
screen while the cluster builds.

From the CLI, `flui cluster create` does the same in one command. It
starts from the control cluster's provider and region and joins its
private network on its own; `--provider` places the cluster
elsewhere, including on servers of your own. The same surface lists
and destroys clusters (`flui cluster list`, `flui cluster destroy`),
changes their nodes through the scaling group (`flui scaling floor`),
and attaches or detaches a machine of your own
(`flui node connect`, `flui node remove`).

An agent can create a cluster too, and when it tries, the call stops
and asks a person first. That permission is only ever given once: a
request to create something that does not exist yet has no resource
to name, so there is nothing narrow enough to record as a standing
permission. See
[The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/).

**Some things only the CLI can do**, because they touch your own
machine or reach the provider directly, with no control plane in
the middle:

- `flui vault init | unlock | lock | status`: the credentials
  this CLI stores on your machine are protected by a passphrase.
  A browser cannot lock a file on your laptop. See
  [The vault](/concepts/07-multi-context-cli/#the-vault-one-passphrase-over-every-context).
- `flui env adopt`: take over an installation you did not
  provision yourself. It rebuilds the local profile on your
  machine and opens SSH to the nodes on your own key. See
  [Taking over an installation](/tasks/get-flui-running/#taking-over-an-installation-somebody-else-set-up).
- `flui env scrub`: when a provisioning run dies half-way, it
  leaves servers, firewalls and keys billing to your provider
  account with no cluster to show for them. `scrub` reads the
  resource list that run reported and clears what is left,
  talking to the provider with the credentials in this machine's
  profile. Nothing is deleted unless you pass `--delete`. See
  [When a run dies half-way](/tasks/get-flui-running/#when-a-run-dies-half-way).
- Destroying the control cluster (`flui env destroy`), for the
  same mechanical reason as creating it: the dashboard and the
  API are running on the cluster being deleted. See
  [`flui env destroy`](/cli/environments/#flui-env-destroy).

**One thing only the dashboard and the API can do:** answer an
agent's paused write. When an agent asks to create a cluster, add
nodes, or spend money, the call does not run. It becomes a
question, answered on the dashboard's **Agents** page or over the
API directly. There is no `flui` command for it. If the terminal
is your only surface, the pause still applies and you answer
somewhere else. See
[When your agent stops to ask you](/tasks/when-your-agent-asks/).

## A machine you already own

Not every cluster has to be bought. If you already have a server
(a rented box, a machine in an office, hardware in a rack), you can
use it instead of provisioning another one.

`flui env create --host <address>` installs onto that machine over
SSH instead of provisioning anything at a provider. Flui reuses an
SSH key that already works on the host; if none does, it authorises
one, asking for the host password once and never storing it. A
readiness check runs first, so you find out the machine is
unsuitable before anything is written to it.

Only the CLI has this path; the dashboard's wizard only buys
machines. The steps, the precheck and the
firewall on your own machine are in
[Install onto a machine you already own](/tasks/get-flui-running/#install-onto-a-machine-you-already-own).

## Addressing: nip.io by default, your domain when you want one

A new cluster needs a stable URL as soon as it is up, for the
dashboard, the API and the identity provider. Buying a domain and
pointing it at the cluster takes longer than creating the cluster,
so Flui makes this work without a domain.

By default the cluster is addressed through `nip.io`: the master's
public IP is encoded in the hostname (something like
`api.warm-finch-zs.203-0-113-10.nip.io`), and any name built that
way resolves to the master. You create no DNS record, wait for no
propagation and configure no registrar. The cluster is reachable as
soon as it is up.

When you want the cluster behind a domain you own, Flui handles the
switch: DNS records, certificates and the control-plane endpoints
are rewired in place, without re-creating the cluster. See
[DNS integration](/concepts/13-dns-integration/).

## TLS from minute zero

Every Flui cluster starts with a TLS certificate, and there is no
separate step to set up certificate issuance. When the cluster
comes up, the certificates the control plane needs are already
issued, and the dashboard is on HTTPS the first time you open it.

At creation time you choose which Let's Encrypt endpoint issues the
certificate:

- **Production (default).** A real, browser-trusted certificate.
  The cluster is immediately usable from any client without TLS
  warnings.
- **Staging.** A Let's Encrypt staging certificate, which browsers
  do not trust but which does not count against ACME's production
  rate limits. Useful when you expect to create and destroy the
  cluster several times in a short window, for example while
  developing against Flui itself.

Let's Encrypt enforces several
[production rate limits](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/rate-limits/)
on rolling weekly windows that do not reset on demand. The one most
easily hit is the limit on duplicate certificates for the same set
of identifiers. To stay clear of it, Flui draws a random prefix for
every cluster from a pool of roughly six hundred thousand
combinations (something like `warm-finch-zs.…`), so two clusters
asking for exactly the same names is unlikely, though not
impossible. The other limits (per registered domain in particular)
still apply, and they matter if you re-create clusters repeatedly:
a few times a week is fine, a tight test loop is not.

Staging removes those limits, at the cost of an untrusted
certificate your CLI and browser will warn about until you allow
it. If you create and destroy clusters often (automation,
integration tests, demo environments), use staging.

A cluster started in staging can later be moved to production.
Moving from production to staging is rarely useful and is not
supported.

## Storage: shared by default, local on request

When the provider supports attachable block storage, a new cluster
comes with a **shared storage volume** attached to the master and
exposed to every worker over the private network. A local cache on
each node means repeated reads do not pay the network cost every
time. Any workload that keeps persistent state uses this volume by
default. On providers without attachable block storage there is no
shared volume, and workloads use per-node local storage.

About the default volume:

1. It is one provider-attached volume, sized at creation. It can be
   grown later but never shrunk.
2. It survives node scaling. Adding or replacing a worker does not
   move the volume; it stays attached to the master.

You can disable shared storage at creation time and use each
node's local disk instead. That mode is lighter, with no extra
volume to pay for, but every workload that needs persistent state
then has its storage pinned to whichever node it landed on.

See [Storage classes and dedicated placement](/concepts/21-storage-classes-and-dedicated-placement/)
for more detail.

## The firewall

Every cluster gets a firewall when it is created. Where the
provider has a firewall Flui can drive, the rules sit at the
provider's edge. Otherwise Flui applies the
[Flui firewall](/concepts/12-firewalls/) on the machines
themselves, as on a machine you brought yourself.
[The provider table](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/#the-providers-integrated-today)
shows which providers have one. The default rule set is small:

- HTTP and HTTPS are open, so the cluster's public endpoints work
  for everyone.
- Every other port required for internal communication is reachable
  only on the cluster's private network, never on the public
  interface.
- SSH, behind the provider's firewall, is restricted to a source-IP
  list you provide at creation time (auto-detected from your current
  IP if you don't pass one). Behind the Flui firewall it stays open,
  because a machine has no other way back in if a rule shuts you
  out, but it admits only certificates issued by the installation
  itself.

## What the cluster hands back

When creation finishes, two commands tell you where you stand.
`flui env status` reports health, nodes, service health and the
effective public endpoints for the API, the dashboard and the
identity provider; run it first to confirm the cluster is alive.
`flui env credentials` shows first-access details: the bootstrap admin login for the dashboard, plus
connection information for the in-cluster databases and the
monitoring stack. Secrets are hidden unless you pass
`--show-secrets`, and the bootstrap password is meant to be rotated
the first time you log in.

From then on, the control cluster is operated like any other Flui
cluster. It shows up in the cluster list, exposes the same
[surfaces](/concepts/03-cluster-as-a-concept/) (nodes, network,
storage, firewall, monitoring) and accepts the same operations as a
workload cluster.

This works because of a seeding step that runs the first time the
API comes up: every resource the CLI created during the bootstrap
(the cluster itself, its nodes, the private network, the firewall,
the SSH keys) is registered in Flui's own database. To the
dashboard, the control cluster is one more row.

## Workload clusters

A workload cluster is created the same way, with one difference:
the control plane is not installed on it again. The identity
provider, the API, the dashboard and the database live on the
control cluster you already have. A workload cluster carries
only the small set of components Flui adds on top of what K3s
already ships: certificate lifecycle and optional cluster-side
authorization.

Each node also runs host-level agents, installed at bootstrap, that
push the node's metrics and the cluster's logs to the control
cluster's observability backend over the private network. They
belong to the node rather than to the cluster's workloads, and they
make every workload cluster appear in the same monitoring views as
the control cluster.

The [Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/)
chapter continues from here.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/):
  one control cluster, many workload clusters, what they share and
  what they don't.
- [Nodes and cluster topology](/concepts/06-nodes-and-cluster-topology/):
  what each node looks like once the cluster is up.
- [What a cluster may buy for itself](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/):
  how a cluster grows on its own, and why nothing grows until
  someone allows it.
- [The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/): why an
  agent's request to create a cluster stops and asks you.
- [TLS and certificates](/concepts/14-tls-and-certificates/): more
  on staging versus production, plus what happens when you bring
  your own domain.
- [DNS integration](/concepts/13-dns-integration/): the path from
  `nip.io` to a real domain.

sections.title: Multi-cluster topology
sections.body:
A Flui installation is one control cluster and any number of
workload clusters, operated together. This chapter covers what
that arrangement gives you, where the boundaries lie, and what
each cluster knows about the others.

## The shape of an installation

Every installation has the same skeleton:

- **One control cluster.** Created first, by the CLI bootstrap,
  and unique within the installation. It hosts the control plane:
  dashboard, API, identity, database and observability backend.
- **Zero or many workload clusters.** Added later, from the
  dashboard, the CLI or by an agent. They host user applications
  and the small set of platform components an application cluster
  needs.

`flui env create` creates the *control* cluster;
`flui cluster create` adds a workload cluster. See
[Add a cluster and give it capacity](/tasks/add-a-cluster/).

_Diagram: The usual shape: one control cluster and its workload clusters on one provider, reaching each other over that provider's private network._

## One provider per installation, and the exception

Usually every cluster in an installation lives on the same
provider as the control cluster. That lets the clusters share
one private network and reach each other without going out to
the internet. Region and node sizing can still vary per cluster;
the constraint is the provider.

Flui checks this before anything is bought. Each provider
carries a static capability flag, `crossClusterAllowed`, that
decides whether a workload cluster may sit on a different
provider than the control cluster. When it may not, the request
is rejected with the machine-readable code
`CROSS_PROVIDER_NOT_ALLOWED`. A second flag, `vnetRequired`,
rejects creation with `VNET_REQUIRED` when a provider needs a
private network and none was supplied.

The flag that decides is the control cluster's. Every cloud
provider Flui integrates declares `crossClusterAllowed: false`.
Your own servers declare `crossClusterAllowed: true`: a machine
you already own has no API to buy more machines from, so an
installation whose control cluster is one of your servers would
otherwise be limited to the servers you already have.

The flag stands for "there is no private path between two
providers", and Flui can build one. With
[the Flui network](/concepts/10-the-network-flui-builds/)
switched on, which is the default, a control cluster on any
provider may create workload clusters on any other provider it
has credentials for, as long as the control cluster has an
address the new cluster can reach. The request is rejected with
`CROSS_PROVIDER_NOT_ALLOWED` only when the control cluster's flag
is `false` and the Flui network cannot bridge the two: it has
been switched off, or the control cluster has no reachable
address. `flui env overlay status` shows which case you are in,
and `flui env overlay enable` switches the network back on where
it can work.

_Diagram: The exception: with the Flui network on, a control cluster on Hetzner also runs workload clusters on Scaleway and on Ubuntu servers you own. The Hetzner cluster is still reached over Hetzner's private network; the other two over the Flui network._

A cluster on a different provider cannot join the installation's
private network, because that network lives on the control
cluster's provider. It brings its own private network on its own
provider instead, and the Flui network, encrypted and maintained
by Flui, runs between the two to carry management traffic, logs
and metrics. None of that crosses the public internet in the
clear, and the telemetry ports are never opened publicly.
[The network Flui builds](/concepts/10-the-network-flui-builds/)
describes that network and the order in which it replaces the
public path. What the arrangement costs you is described in
[How the clusters relate](#how-the-clusters-relate) below.

So "one provider per Flui environment" holds only where the Flui
network is off and the control cluster sits on a cloud provider.
[VNets and subnets, abstracted](/concepts/11-vnet-and-subnets/)
describes the single-provider shape, which is still the common
one; [The network Flui builds](/concepts/10-the-network-flui-builds/)
describes what happens when there is no single network to share.

## Running a workload somewhere else

There are two ways to run a workload on a different provider.

**A cluster in the same installation.** With the Flui network on,
which is the default, the other provider's cluster is part of
the same installation: one dashboard, one login, one set of
grants, one list of applications. This is the better option.

**A second installation.** When your control cluster is on a
cloud provider and the Flui network is off, the other provider
gets an installation of its own, with its own control cluster,
operated side by side. The CLI supports this with multiple
*contexts*, each a fully isolated installation with its own
credentials, and switching between them is one command. See
[Multi-context](/concepts/07-multi-context-cli/).

**A workload can leave the cluster it was first put on.** An
application with its volumes, a Flui-managed PostgreSQL database,
or both together can be moved to another cluster in one
operation. Flui builds the copy on the destination, keeps it in
step with the source, and swaps the two when you say so. Nothing
on the source changes until the cutover, and you can cancel
before it. The three commands are `flui migrate app`,
`flui migrate db` and `flui migrate full`, described in
[Move an application to another cluster](/tasks/move-an-application/).

An application can move this way only if:

- **It has a real domain name.** An address derived from the
  source cluster's IP cannot follow it to another cluster.
- **It is self-contained.** An application that reads another
  component's secrets moves after the components it reads them
  from.
- **Both clusters belong to one installation.** Nothing moves
  between two separate installations.

So the provider that runs an application is not fixed when you
create it. You can change it later, as long as the installation
has clusters on more than one provider.

## Why more than one workload cluster

A single workload cluster is the default and a valid end state.
You add more when one of these applies:

- **Environment isolation.** A cheap staging cluster and a larger
  production cluster, kept fully separate.
- **Project or customer separation.** One cluster per tenant, so
  a noisy workload on one tenant cannot starve another.
- **Geographic or regulatory placement.** Data that must stay in
  a region, or workloads that should run close to their users.
- **Blast radius.** A cluster that ends up in a bad state takes
  only its own workloads with it.

Add a workload cluster when you need separation, not more
capacity. A single application scales on the cluster it already
runs on, and giving a cluster more machines is covered in
[What a cluster may buy for itself](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/).

## What every cluster shares

Every cluster in the installation, of either type, is a Flui
cluster as defined in
[Cluster as a concept](/concepts/03-cluster-as-a-concept/). They
share the same identity, the same ownership labels on every
provider resource, the same dashboard views (nodes, network,
storage, firewall, monitoring), and the same operations through
the same CLI and dashboard.

## What only the control cluster carries

The control cluster is the only host of the control plane.
Everything that exists exactly once per installation lives on
it: the dashboard and API you talk to, the identity provider
that authenticates users, the database that holds the
installation's state, and the observability backend that
collects metrics and logs from every cluster.

A workload cluster carries only the small set of platform
components Flui adds on top of K3s (certificate lifecycle and
optional cluster-side authorization), plus the host-level agents
that push metrics and logs back to the control cluster.

The control cluster runs Flui itself, and the workload clusters
are where your applications are meant to live. You can deploy
applications onto the control cluster, which makes sense for
development or staging setups where you want the whole
installation on a single server. For production, keep
application workloads and the control plane on separate
clusters.

## How the clusters relate

The control plane can reach every workload cluster, but workload
clusters cannot reach each other through Flui:

- **Control plane to workload cluster.** The API holds the
  credentials to reach every workload cluster it created.
  Deploys, scaling, lifecycle operations and reads all go this
  way, over the cluster's private network. The Kubernetes API of
  each workload cluster (port 6443) is never exposed publicly:
  the credentials Flui stores point at the master's private
  VNet address, so traffic between the control and workload
  clusters stays on the VNet and the public firewall keeps 6443
  closed to the outside. See [Firewalls](/concepts/12-firewalls/).
- **Workload cluster to control cluster.** Every node pushes
  metrics and logs to the control cluster's observability backend
  over the private network.
- **Workload cluster to workload cluster.** Flui does not connect
  workload clusters to each other. They share no state and have
  no cross-cluster pod networking. They do sit on the same
  private network as the rest of the installation, so they can
  reach each other at the network level, but Flui does not
  expose or manage a path between them. Flui does not offer
  application-to-application communication across clusters
  today.

### When a cluster is on another provider

A workload cluster on a different provider than the control
cluster shares no private network with it, so both relationships
above travel over [the Flui network](/concepts/10-the-network-flui-builds/)
instead: an encrypted tunnel from the workload cluster to the
control cluster, which Flui builds and maintains.

**Control plane to workload cluster** traffic starts on the
public interface and moves onto the tunnel once the tunnel works.
Until then the cluster's API port is open, but only to the
control cluster's own address, and it admits nobody who cannot
present the installation's own certificate, so the open port
grants no access by itself. The public opening is withdrawn only
after the control cluster has proven it can reach the cluster
over the tunnel. This is decided per cluster and only for a
workload cluster; a control cluster is never switched to the
public address.

**Workload cluster to control plane** traffic, meaning metrics
and logs, travels over the tunnel as well. Flui keeps each
node's push target pointed at the control cluster's address on
the Flui network, and corrects it if it drifts. The ports that
receive telemetry are never opened on the control cluster's
public address, so a cross-provider workload cluster's metrics
and logs arrive centrally like any other cluster's, without a
public write endpoint into the control plane.

If the Flui network is switched off, a cross-provider workload
cluster has no private path for its telemetry, and its metrics
and logs do not arrive centrally.

## Failure boundaries

This arrangement determines what fails together:

- **A workload cluster failing** affects only the workloads on
  that cluster. The control plane keeps running, the other
  workload clusters keep serving traffic, and you can drive the
  recovery from the dashboard.
- **The control cluster failing** takes the control plane
  offline (no dashboard, no API, no central log and metric
  queries), but every workload cluster keeps operating normally.
  Each cluster runs on its own in steady state; you need the
  control plane to change the installation, not to keep it
  running.

## Working with more than one cluster

The dashboard and the CLI list every cluster of the installation
together. When an operation targets a specific one, you pick
which; with a single workload cluster the choice is implicit.

`flui cluster list` always works: the control cluster is stored
on your own machine and is listed even when the API cannot be
reached, while workload clusters live only in the control
cluster's database and are read over the API.

Destroying the control cluster is CLI-only. See
[Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/).

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Nodes and cluster topology](/concepts/06-nodes-and-cluster-topology/):
  what each cluster looks like from the inside.
- [The control cluster](/concepts/09-anatomy-of-the-observability-cluster/):
  what makes the control cluster the control plane.
- [Move an application to another cluster](/tasks/move-an-application/):
  the operation that makes a cluster choice reversible.

sections.title: Nodes and cluster topology
sections.body:
A cluster is made of nodes. This chapter covers what a node is,
which role it can take, and how a cluster can change shape over
time while keeping its identity.

## What a node is

A node is one machine, a virtual server provisioned by the
provider, that belongs to exactly one cluster and plays exactly one
role in it. It carries Flui's ownership labels from the moment it
is created until it is deleted.

Each node has a stable Flui identifier, a role, a provider, a
region, a server type, public and private addresses, and a direct
link to the resource at the provider. For the cluster, a node is
one row of capacity bound to one machine. If that binding drifts
(a server deleted by hand at the provider, or removed from the
cluster outside Flui), the cluster reports the inconsistency and
lets the operator decide how to reconcile the two sides.

A single cloud account can hold several independent Flui
installations side by side, so listing an account's servers does
not tell you which belong to this one. Flui classifies every
instance it sees as `self` (owned by this installation),
`other-flui` (created by another Flui installation sharing the
account) or `unmanaged` (never provisioned by Flui), and acts only
on the ones it owns. The dashboard shows each machine's ownership
next to it, so you can see which ones this installation manages.

## The two roles

Every cluster has one **master** and any number of **workers**.

The master coordinates the cluster: every other node talks to it.
It is also a regular node where workloads can run. A small cluster
works fine with a single master that also hosts applications.

Workers add capacity. They join the cluster after the master is
up, take their share of the work, and can be added or removed
without disturbing the master.

Two rules follow from this:

- A cluster has at least one node, and that node is the master.
  A master-only cluster is a valid cluster.
- On your own servers, `flui node remove` detaches a machine you
  attached with `flui node connect`. On a provider Flui buys from,
  you give a node back by lowering the scaling group's floor
  (`flui scaling floor <n>`), and a manual group asks you to
  approve the removal first. Neither ever removes the master.
  Taking the master out of a cluster means destroying the whole
  cluster, which is a separate operation in the cluster's
  lifecycle.

Every cluster has a single master. Your applications do not need
it to keep answering: losing it stops changes to the cluster, but
traffic to what already runs continues. See
[High availability](/concepts/31-high-availability/) for what that
means.

### Protecting the control cluster's master

A master that runs workloads is convenient on small clusters. On
the control cluster, though, once you have workers you do not want
the dashboard, API and database competing for the master with new
workloads. Flui changes the master's role automatically as the
control cluster grows.

When the control cluster goes from one node to several (when the
scaling group adds its first worker), Flui reserves the master for
the control plane, so new workloads are placed on the workers.
Anything already running on the master stays where it is; only
future placement changes. If you scale the control cluster back
down to a single node, the reservation is lifted automatically,
because the master is again the only place anything can run. The
current state is recorded on the cluster.

_Diagram: On the control cluster, the first worker reserves the master for Flui. What already runs there stays, and new applications go to the workers._

This is best effort: if the reservation cannot be applied or
lifted, the scaling operation it accompanies still succeeds,
because protection never blocks a resize. You can also set it by
hand with `flui env set-master-protection on|off|show`, which
reports the live state and the stored flag. On a control cluster
on your own servers, this is how you do it: a machine attached
with `flui node connect` does not reserve the master on its own.
This applies only to the control cluster; masters of workload
clusters stay open to workloads.

## Growing and shrinking a cluster

A cluster's shape can change in two independent ways:

- **Horizontally**, by adding or removing workers: more or fewer
  machines, each of a shape the scaling group allows, or any
  machine of your own.
- **Vertically**, by changing the server type of an existing
  master or worker: the same machine, with more or less CPU and
  RAM.
