_Diagram: Two ways to change a cluster's size: more or fewer machines, or a bigger or smaller one._

### Horizontal: adding and removing workers

When the scaling group buys a worker, Flui provisions a new server
with the right ownership labels, joins it to the cluster's private
network, attaches it to the firewall when there is one, and waits
for it to join the cluster before marking the node healthy.
Existing workloads keep running, and the new worker starts
receiving work once it is ready.

Removing a worker follows the same steps in reverse: the cluster
stops sending new work to the node, moves the work already running
on it to the other nodes, detaches it from the network and
firewall, and then deletes the server at the provider. The cluster
keeps serving traffic the whole time.

The scaling group gives a worker back only when it can be emptied
(no application keeps its data on it and no application's
disruption rule refuses) and when its work fits on the machines
that stay. Otherwise the worker is kept, and the group says why.
A machine of your own detached with `flui node remove` gets two
minutes to empty. After that it is removed anyway, and the
operation says so.

Some workloads are easier to move than others. Applications using
the cluster's shared storage can run anywhere on the cluster and
follow the work being moved off a worker. Applications that need
fast local storage are pinned at deploy time to the worker with
the most free room (or to the master, on a workload cluster with
no worker). Their data lives on that machine, so you cannot remove
a worker holding one until you back the app up and move or delete
it. The trade-off is covered in
[Storage classes and dedicated placement](/concepts/21-storage-classes-and-dedicated-placement/),
and resizing the node that holds them is the vertical case
described below.

On your own servers nothing checks the room for you: if the
remaining nodes cannot hold what ran on the machine you detach,
that work stays unplaced until capacity returns.

Whether capacity returns on its own depends on the cluster's
**scaling group**. On a provider Flui buys from, every cluster
starts with one: a manual group holding the nodes it has, so
nothing is bought until you move its floor
(`flui scaling floor <n>`, then `flui scaling approve --yes`). On
your own servers there is no scaling group. You size the cluster by attaching machines
with `flui node connect` or by scaling the existing ones up.

A group set to `provision: automatic` changes that. The group
watches for work the cluster cannot place, and when it finds some
the cluster buys a machine without being asked. It stays inside
the limits the group sets: the shapes it may buy, the regions it
may buy them in, a ceiling on how many machines it may hold, and a
spending ceiling written in money instead of node count. A group
left on `provision: manual` decides and tells you what it would
have bought, without acting, so you keep control of the cluster's
shape.

### Vertical: resizing a node

Where the provider supports it
([see which do](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/#the-providers-integrated-today)),
a node can also be resized in place, moving from one server type
to a bigger or smaller one. The platform powers the machine off,
asks the provider to swap the server type, powers it back on,
waits for the cluster to report it healthy, and makes it available
for work again. Storage is preserved and the node keeps its
identity; only its CPU and memory change.

Vertical scaling is planned maintenance: the node is unavailable
for a few minutes during the swap, and so is any workload pinned
to it. Before doing anything, the CLI shows a plan with the cost
difference and the affected workloads (`flui env scale-node` for a
worker, `flui env scale-master` for the master).

The exact commands and trade-offs for horizontal and vertical
scaling are in [CLI: Environments](/cli/environments/).

## What stays constant when the cluster changes shape

Adding, removing or resizing nodes never changes the cluster's
identity. The cluster keeps its name, its UUID, its endpoints, its
certificates, its storage and the ownership labels on every
provider resource it owns. Where the provider offers the
capability, it also keeps its DNS names and its firewall. Apps keep
their addresses, data stays on the same volumes and users keep
their sessions.

So you can refer to a cluster, and point automation at it, while
the machines underneath it change.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/):
  how the control cluster and its workers fit into the wider
  installation.
- [VNet and subnets](/concepts/11-vnet-and-subnets/): the private
  network every node attaches to.
- [The network Flui builds](/concepts/10-the-network-flui-builds/):
  what a node attaches to when the provider supplies none.
- [Firewalls](/concepts/12-firewalls/): the rules that govern what
  can reach a node from outside.
- [What a cluster may buy for itself](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/):
  the group that decides whether any of this happens without you,
  and where it has to stop.
- [Let a cluster buy its own machines](/tasks/let-a-cluster-buy-its-own-machines/):
  writing that group, field by field.
- [CLI: Environments](/cli/environments/): the operational
  reference for adding, removing and resizing nodes.

sections.title: Multi-context: many installations from one workstation
sections.body:
[Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/)
described a single Flui installation that operates many clusters.
This chapter covers the layer above: one workstation driving several
Flui installations, each with its own control cluster, credentials
and state. The CLI calls each of these connections a **context**.

## Multi-context is not multi-cluster

The two ideas are easy to mix up:

- **Multi-cluster** means one installation governing many clusters.
  You move between clusters within an installation by saying which
  cluster the operation is for, or by letting the CLI choose when
  only one is available.
- **Multi-context** means one workstation talking to several
  installations. A consultant operating Flui for three customers,
  a developer with separate `local`, `staging` and `prod`
  installations, or a platform team running Flui for two unrelated
  business units each works with separate contexts.

Every installation has its own API, identity provider, admin
credentials, database and SSH trust root. Switching between
installations replaces the entire connection state the CLI uses, so
it is not a flag on a command.

## A context is the unit of switching

A context bundles everything the CLI needs to talk to one
installation: the URL of that installation's API, the credentials
to authenticate against it, the provider tokens it stores, the
trust anchor it uses to reach cluster nodes, and the local view of
the clusters, nodes and operations that installation knows about.

The CLI stores each context on disk. Switching between them is a
single command and takes effect at once. Nothing is copied or
fetched again; the CLI changes which context's on-disk state it
reads from. A one-off command can also use a different context for
a single invocation without changing the active one.

## What a context isolates

Contexts share nothing operational:

- **Credentials don't cross.** The provider tokens you added to
  one context are not visible to another. The same is true of the
  admin keys used to talk to the API.
- **Secrets are sealed per context.** Every context's stored
  secrets are encrypted, and each context has its own key. The next
  section explains where that key comes from.
- **Local caches are per context.** The cluster list you see, the
  recent operations and the SSH trust all belong to the active
  context. Switching to another context replaces them with that
  context's view.

A command typed in the wrong context cannot reach into another
installation, because that context does not hold the credentials
to do it.

On disk, each context is a separate directory under
`~/.flui/profiles/`, holding its own configuration, secrets, caches
and trust material:

```
~/.flui/profiles/
├── default/
└── another-context/
```

The exact layout of each directory, and the commands that create,
inspect and switch contexts, are in
[CLI: Profiles & Configuration](/cli/profiles-and-config/).

## The vault: one passphrase over every context

A context's secrets are encrypted, and the key is not stored beside
them. Anyone who could read a folder holding both the data and its
key could read both. Instead, the key comes from a passphrase you
know and the machine does not keep. That is the **vault**, and there
is one per workstation:

```bash
flui vault init      # once per machine
flui vault unlock    # once per session
flui vault status    # is it open, and for how long
flui vault lock      # close it now
```

The passphrase is never stored, never derived back from anything
and cannot be reset. Losing it means losing every credential this
machine has sealed. That is why `flui vault init` suggests a
five-word passphrase: you need one you can write down and reproduce.

**One passphrase, still one key per context.** The vault does not
put every context under the same key. Each context gets its own,
derived from the passphrase and that context's name. A command
working in one context cannot open another context's stored
secrets, even though both were sealed under the same passphrase, so
a mistake stays inside the context that made it.

**The key is held in memory, not written down.** After `unlock`, a
small background helper holds the key for the session and hands it
to commands that ask. Nothing goes to disk. On `lock` the key is
overwritten in memory and the helper exits. It also closes on its
own after thirty minutes of inactivity, and after eight hours no
matter how busy you were.

A locked vault is not an error on its own. Most commands read a
preference or an API URL, which are plain text, and never ask for
anything. Only a command that opens a stored credential stops. When
it does, it says the vault is closed and names `flui vault unlock`,
instead of reporting a decryption failure that would send you
looking for corrupt data.

## A context for an installation you did not create

A context is normally written by the machine that provisioned the
installation. That machine is not always the one that will run it.
Somebody can provision Flui on your behalf and keep nothing: no key
of their own left on the servers, and so no context for you to copy.

**Adoption** rebuilds a context on the owner's machine instead. On
the installation, someone allowed to manage its clusters issues a
token:

```bash
flui env adoption-token
```

The token is single use, valid for one hour, and tied to that one
installation. Anyone holding it can register a trust anchor there,
so treat it as a password when you hand it over.

On the owner's machine:

```bash
flui env adopt <token>
```

The CLI asks the installation to describe itself, writes a local
context pointing at it, then creates the SSH trust root **on this
machine** and registers only its public half with the installation.
The private key that opens those servers is created on the owner's
workstation, when the owner chooses, and the installation never has
one to give away or lose.

`--skip-ca` rebuilds the context and stops there, leaving SSH
unused. Use it if you only intend to use the dashboard.

Adoption rebuilds a connection, not somebody else's credentials.
The provider tokens the builder used stay on the builder's
machine. The adopted context knows where the installation is, and
you sign in to it as yourself.

## How the CLI shows which context is active

Most commands that act on an installation print a short header
before their output, naming the context and the API they are using.
If you forgot to switch, the header shows it at the top of the
output, so a command run against the wrong installation does not go
unnoticed.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/):
  the layer below, one installation with many clusters.
- [Get Flui running](/tasks/get-flui-running/): the vault, a
  first installation, and adoption, step by step.
- [CLI: Profiles & Configuration](/cli/profiles-and-config/):
  the command reference for creating, switching and inspecting
  contexts.

sections.title: Observability as first-class
sections.body:
On most platforms, observability is something you set up
later. In Flui, metrics and logs are there from the start: the
operation that brings up a cluster also brings up the place
where its metrics and logs go. They cover both the apps you
deploy and the platform's own components, and you read them
the same way on your first app and on your two hundredth.

This chapter explains the intent and the shape of that choice.
The detailed inventory of what runs inside the control cluster
is in the
[next chapter](/concepts/09-anatomy-of-the-observability-cluster/).

## Part of the platform from the start

In Flui, observability is part of the platform from the first
minute the installation is alive, and other parts of the
platform depend on it:

1. **It is part of the bootstrap.** The operation that brings
   up the control cluster also brings up the backend that
   collects metrics and logs, and the installation is not
   considered ready until that backend is. Workload clusters
   added later feed into the same backend. You do not stand up
   a second observability stack; you point the new cluster's
   agents at the one that already exists.
2. **It is modelled around the platform's own concepts.** The
   CLI and the dashboard show metrics and logs in terms of
   clusters, servers and applications, the things you already
   reason about, so you do not have to translate to
   namespaces, labels and query languages first.
3. **The platform itself relies on it.** Alerts are evaluated
   against the metrics backend, and the memory limit Flui
   proposes when an application runs out of memory is read
   from the same data. Without observability, those features
   have nothing to read.

As a result, Flui cannot run in a useful state without
observability, and monitoring is never left for later.

## What is in scope

Flui's built-in observability covers:

- **Metrics**: host-level metrics on every node, cluster-level
  metrics on every object, and the baseline per-application
  metrics (CPU, memory, restart count, replica health) that Flui
  shows for every app it manages.
- **Logs**: application logs from every cluster, indexed
  centrally and queryable per app, per cluster, per time range.
- **HTTP traffic**: request rate, status codes and latency for
  each application, measured where requests enter the cluster.
- **Dashboards**: Flui's own dashboard and CLI, which show
  what matters for a cluster and for an application, chosen
  by Flui instead of left as a blank canvas.
- **Alerts**: conditions evaluated against the metrics
  backend, recorded as episodes and readable per
  application. See
  [alerts, below](#alerts-are-recorded-as-episodes).
- **What your agents did**: once an agent holds a
  credential on this installation, the calls it makes form a
  register you can read. See
  [below](#what-your-agents-did).

Some kinds of telemetry are not part of the built-in stack:
end-to-end request tracing across services, application
performance profiling, and uptime checks from outside the
platform. Applications that need them add their own tooling.

## No database storage for logs or metrics

Flui's database holds state about the installation (clusters,
nodes, applications, operations, releases, builds) and nothing
else. Logs and metrics live in their own purpose-built
backends, with their own retention and capacity policies.

Two records that are not telemetry do live in Flui's own
database: the alert episodes described below, and the
register of what agents did. Both record events with a
beginning and an end, closer to an operation than to a log
line, and neither grows with your traffic.

When you query logs or metrics through Flui, the API acts as a
thin proxy: it resolves which application you are asking about,
scopes the query to that application's data, forwards it to
the right backend and streams the answer back. No log line and
no metric sample is ever written to Flui's own database.

This has two effects:

- **The control plane stays small.** Flui's database does not grow
  with traffic; it grows with the number of resources you manage.
- **The backends can be replaced independently.** Swapping the
  metrics or log store would not change the surfaces you use.

## Alerts are recorded as episodes

Alerts are the part of observability that comes to you, so
you do not have to be watching a metric to notice a problem.

Rules are evaluated on the control cluster against the
metrics already being collected, so there is nothing extra
to install or wire up. What Flui adds is the shape of the
record.

**One row per episode.** A condition that stays true is
re-reported every few hours for as long as it lasts. Those
repeats update the same row instead of stacking up, so
`flui app alerts my-api` reads as a history of incidents,
not a mailbox. Each row carries whether it is firing or
resolved, a severity, a one-line summary, and when it
started and ended.

**Estimated end times.** The notice that a condition cleared
is sent once. If it goes missing (the API restarting at the
wrong moment is enough), the row would stay as a permanent
false alarm. So a firing row that has been quiet for six
hours is closed, marked as closed by timeout, and given the
time it was last seen as its end. The CLI prints those with
an asterisk, and the wording everywhere is "stopped
reporting", never "recovered at". Read it as the last moment
the condition was known to be true.

**Retention.** Resolved history is kept for ninety days by
default and then deleted. A firing row is never deleted,
however old it is, because an old alert that is still firing
is the current incident.

**Alerts belong to applications.** Each one is attributed
to the application it is about, and you see the alerts of
the applications you may read. Alerts about the machines
themselves are a separate list for whoever runs the
installation, because their text carries host names and
internal identifiers a tenant should not be able to
collect.

Where to read them:

- `flui app alerts <app>`: newest first, `--firing` for
  only what is still firing, `--output json` for scripting;
- the **Alerts** section on the application in the
  dashboard;
- an agent, through the `app_alerts` tool.

**Where an alert goes.** When an alert starts or clears,
the person the application belongs to gets a notice in the
dashboard and, for a critical one, an email. An alert that
belongs to no application goes to the administrators, who
can choose to get warnings by email too
(`flui alerts warnings --on`). Any alert can also go to
another address or to a signed webhook, with
`flui alerts destination add`. Email needs mail to be set
up on the installation, and Flui does not place phone
calls.

One limit: an empty alert list does not mean everything is
fine. It means nothing was recorded.

## What your agents did

Metrics and logs answer what your applications did. Once
you connect an agent to this installation, you also need to
know what the agent did, and Flui records that too, per
credential.

Every call an agent makes through the tool surface, or
through the assistant inside Flui, is a row: when, which
action, whether it was allowed, and what it started. Calls
made straight at the API (an agent driving Flui with plain
HTTP and no tool surface in front of it) are recorded too,
on the routes that stop and ask a person first. Without
this record, they would be the least visible and least
supervised calls in the product.

**Arguments are not kept.** A value is shown as it was sent
only when it belongs to a set written in Flui's own source:
a fixed choice, a number, a flag. Every free-form string is
withheld, because the answers to a catalog install can
carry an administrator password and this table is meant to
be read. What a call actually touched is recovered from the
operation it started, which Flui wrote itself.

**Your own register needs no management access.** You
should not need to be an administrator to decide whether to
disconnect an agent you connected. Somebody who administers
access on the installation reads the whole installation's
register instead, and the page says which of the two you
are looking at. Other people's rows read as absent, not
forbidden, because a refusal would confirm that the hidden
call took place.

This is the one observability surface with no CLI. It is
the **Agents** page in the dashboard, or the API with your
own credential.

## How workload clusters feed the control cluster

The control cluster receives metrics and logs from every
workload cluster. The flow is push-based: every node runs a
log shipper and every cluster runs a metrics agent, and both
send to the central backend over the cluster's private
network.

If the control cluster is unreachable, workloads keep running
(each cluster is autonomous in steady state), and the metrics
agent buffers to local disk. When the link returns, recent
metrics back-fill.

_Diagram: Every cluster pushes its metrics and logs to the control cluster, which receives and never pulls. The CLI, the dashboard and an agent read the same data._

### Why Flui pushes

The conventional model is pull, where a central scraper reaches
into each target. Flui pushes instead, for three reasons:

- The trust boundary points outward: workload clusters start
  the connection, and the control cluster never reaches in.
- Short outages back-fill from the agent's local buffer
  instead of leaving holes in the time series.
- The control cluster does not need a registry of every
  endpoint to scrape.

## What the user sees

There are three surfaces, all backed by the same data:

| Surface | What it shows | When to use it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CLI | Single-app logs (filtered by level and full-text search), runtime status, metrics, HTTP traffic, recent crashes and alerts | Debugging a specific app, scripting, CI |
| Dashboard | Per-app live charts, traffic and log streams, plus cluster-level views | Day-to-day operation |
| Agent (MCP) | An application's logs, metrics, HTTP traffic and alerts, through its tools | Letting an agent look into a problem or report on it for you |

None of the three is authoritative over the others. They are
different views of the same data.

The register of what your agents did is the exception. It is
not in the CLI, because it is Flui's own record of who asked
for what rather than a query over telemetry.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [The control cluster](/concepts/09-anatomy-of-the-observability-cluster/):
  the detailed inventory of which components run, in which
  role, at what cost.
- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/): how the app
  surface is wired to the observability backend.
- [When your agent stops to ask you](/tasks/when-your-agent-asks/):
  answering a request, and reading the register of what
  your agents have done.
- [The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/): why an
  agent's write stops and asks a person first.

sections.title: Anatomy of the control cluster
sections.body:
The control cluster is where Flui itself runs. It also holds the
observability backend that every other cluster sends data to, and
the few platform pieces every Flui cluster needs to work. This
chapter goes through those components by role.

The components below are installed with the control cluster and
belong only to it, except for the baseline ones (certificates,
ingress, in-cluster DNS) that every cluster carries. The cluster's
Overview shows the health of each.

_Diagram: What runs on the control cluster. Only the API, the dashboard and the identity provider are reachable from outside; workload clusters send their telemetry over the private network._

## The platform itself

These components make this cluster the Flui control plane. None of
them appear on workload clusters.

### Flui API

The service every CLI command, dashboard request and third-party
integration talks to. It runs on the cluster it controls. There is
no cloud-hosted Flui API: the API that operates your installation
is the one you installed. It is reached at a public hostname
through the cluster's ingress.

Not replaceable: it is the control plane.

### Flui dashboard

The web interface of the installation: cluster lists, application
views, monitoring, deploy flows, identity, and the panel where you
answer an agent.

The dashboard and the CLI both call the Flui API, and for most work
either one will do. They differ in a few places. The control
cluster is created from the CLI or from
[app.flui.cloud](https://app.flui.cloud), never from the dashboard,
because the dashboard does not exist until that cluster is up. An
agent's request for permission is answered in the dashboard, or
against the API directly; there is no `flui` command for it.

### Identity provider (Zitadel)

The OIDC authority for the installation. It issues the credentials
the CLI uses and the tokens the dashboard uses, and federates with
external identity providers when configured. Every installation
has one.

Any OIDC-compliant identity provider could replace it in principle,
but Zitadel is the one Flui ships and tests.

### Database

The installation's state lives here: clusters, nodes,
applications, releases, builds, operations, encrypted credentials,
DNS zones, certificate metadata. Logs and metrics are kept in the
observability backend below instead.

It also holds two records about agents rather than infrastructure:
the action-cycle store and the agent activity register. Both have
their own section further down.

PostgreSQL is the engine Flui ships and tests against.

### Cache and queue backend

Every operation Flui drives (provisioning, deploys, builds,
lifecycle changes) goes through a job queue. The same component
also serves the caches the API uses to keep small pieces of state
fast. Redis is the engine Flui ships and tests against.

## What the control cluster keeps for agents

Two records in the database above are about agents. Neither is a
service you can point at. They are listed here because, besides
the state of your infrastructure, the control cluster holds the
record of what your agents asked for and what they did.

### The action-cycle store

When an agent asks for something that changes the installation,
the call does not run. It becomes a question waiting for a
person. Nothing holds a connection open while somebody decides, so
the question is written down here.

It holds two kinds of row:

- **Pending requests.** What was asked for, in one sentence,
  under which credential, and, when the action costs money, the
  price at the time of asking. A request expires after an hour,
  so nobody is offered a stale quote.
- **Standing permissions.** The "always" answers. Each one is
  tied to a specific action, a specific resource, and the single
  credential that asked. Each one can be taken back.

None of this grants anything. A standing permission only removes
a pause on something the person's own access already allowed. The
reasoning is in [The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/).

### The agent activity register

Every call an agent makes leaves a row here. The register belongs
to the credential, not to any one surface: a call through the
agent tools, a turn of the in-product assistant, and a plain HTTP
call made with `curl` all land in the same place. An agent key
presented straight to the API meets the same guards as the tool
surface and leaves the same trace.

A row records which credential acted, whether the call was
allowed, how the call ended, and the long-running operation it
started, if any. Arguments are redacted: values that come from a
fixed set of choices are stored as they were, and anything else is
withheld.

Reading it needs no special access. Anyone can read their own
rows, since you cannot decide whether to keep an agent connected
without seeing what it has been doing. Someone who administers
access reads the whole installation. Somebody else's row reads as
absent, not as forbidden, because a register that answers "you may
not see this" has already confirmed that the hidden call took
place.

## The observability backend

These components make this cluster the place where every other
cluster sends its telemetry. The stores and the alert components
run on the control cluster only. The agents that feed them run on
every cluster, the control cluster included.

### Metrics store

A time-series database that receives the metrics every cluster
pushes. It exposes a query API in a well-known dialect, which the
CLI and the dashboard read from when they show app metrics. It runs
as a single instance.

### Log store

The central destination for application logs from every cluster.
It indexes them by label and serves a query interface that both the
dashboard and the CLI use through the Flui API.

### Metrics scraper

The agent that collects metrics from cluster objects and
applications and pushes them to the metrics store. It runs on
every cluster, including the control cluster, so the control
cluster monitors itself with the same tools it uses on every
workload cluster.

### Alert evaluator

Watches the metrics store continuously and turns raw data into
signals. It fires alerts when a metric stays past a defined
threshold for long enough. It also pre-computes heavier queries
(rolling averages, per-app aggregates) so the dashboard can read
them from the store instead of recalculating each time. A baseline
set of alerts and aggregates ships predefined.

### Alert router

Receives every alert the evaluator fires and hands it to the Flui
API, which decides who hears about it: a notice in the dashboard,
an email, or a destination somebody added. See
[Alerts are episodes, not messages](/concepts/08-observability-as-first-class/#alerts-are-recorded-as-episodes).

### Object metrics exporter

Turns the state of cluster objects (deployments, pods, services)
into metrics that the scraper picks up. Like the scraper, it runs
on every cluster. It provides the per-app baseline metrics (replica
counts, restart counts, health) the dashboard shows for every
application.

## The cluster baseline

These run on every Flui cluster, control and workload. They are
listed here because the control cluster needs them too, but the
full discussion is in the cluster chapters.

### Ingress

The L7 entry point of the cluster. It terminates TLS, routes
requests by hostname and path, and exposes every public surface
the cluster offers. On the control cluster that includes the Flui
API, the dashboard and the identity provider.

### Certificate lifecycle

Issues and renews TLS certificates for every public hostname the
cluster serves, against the configured ACME endpoint (production
or staging; see
[TLS and certificates](/concepts/14-tls-and-certificates/)).
Where the zone sits on a provider whose DNS Flui can drive
([see which](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/#the-providers-integrated-today)), an extension lets the issuer solve
DNS-based challenges through it.

### In-cluster DNS

Service discovery inside the cluster. It ships with the cluster
runtime and Flui uses it unchanged.

### Short-lived metrics source

The per-node and per-pod CPU and memory readings that some
in-cluster autoscaling decisions read from. It is separate from the
observability backend above: it is the cluster runtime's own
short-window source, not where Flui's long-term metrics live.

### Default storage

A baseline storage class for cluster workloads. On a cluster with
shared storage enabled, applications can choose the shared volume
or a node-local fallback. On a cluster without shared storage,
the fallback is the only option.

## Optional cluster-side authentication gate

A small service the ingress asks before letting a request
through. It checks the Flui sign-in with the installation's API.
On the control cluster the API answers this itself. On a workload
cluster it is an optional relay, `flui-authz`. With it enabled, any
endpoint on the cluster can be put behind OIDC login without the
application handling authentication itself.

Flui uses a dedicated subdomain for this: an endpoint published
under `<app>.internal.<cluster-zone>` is treated as gated and goes
through the authentication check automatically, while the same app
on its plain `<app>.<cluster-zone>` endpoint stays public. See
[DNS integration](/concepts/13-dns-integration/) for details.

On a workload cluster it is off by default because it adds an
extra service on every request path, and that cost only pays off on
clusters that need gated endpoints. Clusters that don't need it stay
lighter. It is specific to Flui and cannot be replaced.

## What is user-facing, what is internal

The cluster exposes a small public surface and keeps everything
else internal.

- **Public, through the cluster's ingress**: the Flui API, the
  dashboard and the identity provider. These are the addresses you
  put in a browser or call from the CLI.
- **Cluster-internal**: the database, the cache/queue, the metrics
  store, the log store and their agents. They are reachable only
  from inside the cluster, with two exceptions. The metrics and log
  stores also accept connections from other clusters over the
  private network, so those clusters can send their telemetry. For
  development, the CLI can open a temporary tunnel against the
  master.

The public surface is what you build on. The internals can change
underneath without changing what you can call from outside.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Observability is not an afterthought](/concepts/08-observability-as-first-class/):
  why this anatomy looks the way it does.
- [Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/):
  when each of these components is installed.
- [Identity and OIDC](/concepts/15-identity-and-oidc/): the
  identity provider's role in detail.
- [The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/): why an
  agent's write stops and asks you first.

sections.title: The network Flui builds
sections.body:
A provider's private network stops at the edge of that provider.
Two clusters inside it reach each other without touching the
internet. A cluster at another provider cannot reach them that way.

This matters as soon as an installation uses more than one
provider. The control cluster still has to reach the workload
cluster's API to deploy anything, and the workload cluster still
has to send its logs and metrics back. Without a private network in
common, both would have to cross the public internet. Flui builds
the missing network itself.

## What it is

The Flui network is an encrypted point-to-point network that Flui
creates, addresses and maintains on top of whatever is underneath.
Every node that joins it gets an address in a private range the
installation owns. Traffic between those addresses is encrypted
before it leaves the machine and decrypted after it arrives.

It works whatever lies in between. Two machines at two providers,
in two countries, with nothing private between them, get private
addresses that reach each other. To the platform they are
neighbours.

_Diagram: Inside one provider, traffic stays on the provider's private network. Between providers it has to cross the internet, so the Flui network encrypts it before it leaves the machine._

The default range is `10.250.0.0/16`. Before an address is handed
out, the range is checked against every other network the
installation knows about, including the ranges your clusters use
internally. Flui refuses a collision instead of working around it:
a management address that silently shadows a route you already
have tends to surface weeks later as an unrelated fault.

## Who dials whom

The control cluster is the fixed point. Workload clusters dial it;
it does not dial them.

A workload cluster's address can change: providers reassign
addresses, machines are replaced, a node comes back with a
different public address after maintenance. The control cluster is
the part of the installation Flui already treats as stable, since
everything else points at it.

So the control end waits, the workload ends call in, and the
control cluster learns where each one is calling from. A workload
cluster that changes address reconnects on its own and keeps the
same private address. No configuration has to change.

As a result, workload clusters do not reach each other over this
network. Each has a path to the control cluster and none to the
others. The network carries management traffic and telemetry, and
your clusters stay isolated from each other.

## What travels on it

Only three kinds of traffic use it:

- **Cluster management.** Every deployment, status read and restart
  the control cluster performs against a workload cluster.
- **Logs.** Every line your applications write, on its way to the
  installation's log store.
- **Metrics.** Every measurement the nodes and your applications
  produce.

Your applications' own traffic does not use it. A request from the
internet reaches your application's cluster directly.

## The exchange, in the right order

What matters most is when the public path is closed.

Before this network is in place, a cross-provider workload cluster
is reachable on its public address, and the control cluster talks
to it there. Closing that path as soon as a tunnel appears would be
a mistake. A tunnel that has completed its handshake may still not
carry traffic, and a cluster reachable at neither address is a
cluster you have lost.

Flui works in this order:

1. The tunnel is established, and the workload cluster's identity
   certificate is reissued to cover its new private address.
2. The control cluster tries the new address with a real
   connection that validates the certificate, not a ping.
3. Only if that succeeds does the control cluster switch to the
   workload cluster's private address.
4. Only after the switch is the public opening withdrawn.

Each step waits for the one before it. If a step does not happen,
the public path stays open and the installation keeps working
while Flui tries again.

Your telemetry ports, the ones that receive logs and metrics, are
reachable only over this network. They are never open on your
public address, not even briefly during setup.

## When it is not used

Flui routes management traffic over this network only when it has
to.

Two clusters on the same provider already share that provider's
private network, which is faster and simpler than anything Flui
could build. There, management traffic uses the provider's network
and the tunnel carries nothing. The tunnel is still established and
maintained, so it is there if the provider's own network is not,
but traffic does not use it.

The cluster's network view shows which case applies: a cluster
reached privately through its provider and a cluster reached
through the Flui network have different labels.

_Diagram: The Scaleway cluster shares the control cluster's provider, so its management traffic stays on Scaleway's private network. The OVHcloud cluster and the Ubuntu servers you own are reached over the Flui network. The Ubuntu servers have no private network of their own, so there the Flui network also carries the traffic inside the cluster._

## Inside a cluster too

The same mechanism covers a second case.

When you install Flui on machines you already own, those machines
may have no private network between them. Two rented servers in two
datacentres have public addresses and nothing else, so traffic
between the parts of your cluster would cross the internet
unencrypted.

Flui builds a network for them with the same mechanism, and the
cluster binds to it. Your applications' internal traffic (one
component calling another, a service reaching its database) travels
encrypted between machines that have no private network of their
own.

[VNets and subnets, abstracted](/concepts/11-vnet-and-subnets/)
describes this case as a network Flui provides instead of one a
provider hands over. Between clusters, the Flui network connects
clusters that have no path to each other. Inside a cluster, it
gives the cluster the private network its provider does not offer.

## What you have to do

Nothing. There is no command to create this network, no setting to
enable it and no address to choose. Flui establishes it when a
cluster is created, repairs it when a machine is replaced and takes
it down when a cluster is destroyed.

It also survives a reboot. A machine that restarts comes back with
the same private address and rejoins on its own.

## What to look at when something is wrong

The network is rarely the cause. If a workload cluster stops
reporting, start with the usual checks: the cluster's status, its
nodes, and whether its firewall still has the rules Flui put there.

**Flui reconciles on a cycle.** A cluster created a minute ago may
not have joined yet, and a cluster whose address just changed may
take a pass or two to settle. Both correct themselves. Wait ten
minutes before treating a gap as a fault.

**A cluster can be healthy and silent at the same time.** A working
network means the two ends can reach each other. It does not mean
your logs are arriving, which also depends on the cluster's own
telemetry configuration. Check the cluster's Monitoring and Logs
views. If the connection is up but no data arrives, look at
telemetry, not the network.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [VNets and subnets, abstracted](/concepts/11-vnet-and-subnets/):
  the provider-supplied side of the same model.
- [Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/):
  when a cluster may sit on a different provider at all.
- [Firewall as a policy, not a resource](/concepts/12-firewalls/):
  how the openings above are expressed, and which of them are
  restricted to this network.

sections.title: VNets and subnets, abstracted
sections.body:
Every cloud that offers private networking models it its own way,
with different names, scoping rules and granularity. Flui gives
the cluster one consistent view, a private network with one or
more subnets, whatever the provider underneath calls it.

This is one of the clearest examples of the abstraction described
in
[How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/).
Above this layer, the rest of the platform does not deal with
provider-specific networking terms.

## The Flui-side model

In Flui terms, a cluster's private network has two parts:

- A **VNet**: a private address space (an IP range) reserved for
  the installation.
- One or more **subnets** inside the VNet, each with its own IP
  range, into which nodes are placed.

Nodes are attached to a subnet at creation time and receive a
private address inside it. Everything that talks over the private
network uses those addresses.

Where providers differ (in how the geographic scope is named, or
in whether a network can have several subnets), Flui normalises
them into this same shape, so the rest of the platform reads the
same fields on any cloud.

## One VNet per installation and provider

Flui provisions one VNet per installation and provider, shared by
the control cluster and every workload cluster on that provider.
A single private network lets the control cluster and the
workload clusters talk to each other with low latency, and lets
nodes in the same cluster talk to each other without touching the
public internet. One VNet per provider is the simplest shape that
gives both.

Clusters on the same provider share that VNet, and the same
subnet, and reach each other on their private interfaces. The
provider firewall filters only the public perimeter, not this
private traffic. A cluster on another provider reaches the
control cluster over the Flui network instead (see
[Multi-cluster topology](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/)).
The private network is enforced: on a provider that requires
one, creating a cluster without a private network is rejected
with the code `VNET_REQUIRED`. The rest of the platform can
therefore rely on the shared VNet being there.

All of that assumes a provider with a private network to give.
When the machine is your own there is none, and the shape
changes; see
[When the server is your own](#when-the-server-is-your-own).

## Default IP ranges

A fresh installation uses `10.10.0.0/16` for the VNet and
`10.10.1.0/24` for its subnet. They are large enough that you do
not have to think about them, and because they are private
addresses inside a single installation they do not collide with
anything outside it. They are not configurable.

## What a node gets when it joins a cluster

When a node is created, the provider gives it two addresses:

- A **public address** on the provider's external network, used
  by the cluster's ingress (HTTP/HTTPS for applications) and by
  the operator's SSH access from outside.
- A **private address** on the VNet's subnet, used for everything
  inside the cluster and the installation: node-to-node traffic,
  agents pushing to the central observability backend, and the
  control plane reaching into a workload cluster.

The public address carries the traffic that has to come from
outside, and the private one carries everything that stays inside
the installation.

_Diagram: Each node has a public address for traffic from outside and a private one for everything between machines. On your own servers, the private address is on the network Flui builds._

The cluster's own control API is a good example. It listens on
port 6443, but that port is never reachable from the public
internet. When Flui records how to reach a cluster, it writes the
master's private VNet address as the API endpoint, so every
control-plane operation against a workload cluster crosses the
VNet instead of the open internet. The matching firewall rule
keeps 6443 closed at the public perimeter and scoped to the
subnet; see [Firewalls](/concepts/12-firewalls/).

## When the server is your own

Everything above assumes a provider that has private networks to
create. With your own server there is nothing to create: no
network API, no address space to reserve, nothing to divide into
subnets. The machine sits on whatever network you put it on,
which may be no private network at all.

So Flui builds one: the Flui network, encrypted, created for the
installation and given to the cluster. Flui does not derive it
from the machine's own address.
[The network Flui builds](/concepts/10-the-network-flui-builds/)
describes the mechanism; this section covers what it means for
the model above.

An address on a machine tells you what that machine can reach,
not what your machines have in common. On a host that runs
containers it can even be a container bridge instead of a network
two servers share. When Flui builds the network itself, it knows
its shape.

In this case, three points from earlier in the chapter change.

**One network for the installation, one subnet per cluster.**
The subnet is the isolation boundary: the machines of a cluster
reach each other and the control cluster, and nothing else. A
cluster cannot choose its subnet, because two clusters sharing
one would silently be able to see each other.

**The range is the installation's.** It is `10.250.0.0/16`,
divided one `/24` at a time. Before an address is handed out, it
is checked against every other network the installation knows
about, and a collision is refused rather than worked around (see
[The network Flui builds](/concepts/10-the-network-flui-builds/)).

**Nothing filters at a provider edge.** There is no managed
firewall in front of the machine, so the rules are applied on
the machine itself, and everything is closed unless a rule opens
it. Web traffic on 80 and 443, and SSH for you, stay public.
Traffic between the machines is accepted only over the network
Flui built, never from a public address, so a machine that has
not joined that network yet is not reachable by the others. That
is the safe way for that state to fail. `flui env firewall status`
shows what is applied on the host, and `flui env firewall apply`
puts it back.

On a single machine with a single address, the public and private
pair described above becomes one address doing both jobs. That is
normal here and not a misconfiguration.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Firewalls](/concepts/12-firewalls/): what enforces isolation
  inside a shared VNet.
- [How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/):
  the broader abstraction this chapter is an example of.
- [Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/):
  when the VNet is set up during cluster creation.
- [The network Flui builds](/concepts/10-the-network-flui-builds/):
  what happens when the provider has no private network to give,
  or when two clusters have none in common.

sections.title: Firewall as a policy
sections.body:
In Flui the firewall is derived from what the cluster needs. It
is installed when the cluster is created, applied to every node
automatically and kept in sync as the cluster's shape changes.
Flui owns the firewall and its rules. You state which addresses
may come in for operator access, and Flui derives the rest.

## The default policy

Every Flui cluster comes up with the same baseline policy:

| Port | Source | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `22/tcp` (SSH) | a user-controlled allow-list where the provider has an edge firewall Flui drives (auto-detected operator IP, or values you pass); elsewhere open, but only certificates of the installation get in | Operator access for bootstrap and diagnostics |
| `80/tcp`, `443/tcp` (HTTP, HTTPS) | open to the world | Public ingress for the cluster's applications and platform components |
| Outbound | allow-all | Apps need to reach external services, registries, certificate authorities |

Everything else stays closed at the public perimeter. The one
addition is the Flui network's own port on the control cluster,
open only to the addresses of the clusters that belong to the
installation. The cluster runtime and the platform components
talk to each other on the private network without needing a
firewall opening (see
[VNets and subnets, abstracted](/concepts/11-vnet-and-subnets/)).

The cluster's own control port is an example. It is not in the
default rules, because the control plane reaches a workload
cluster over the private VNet using the master's private
address. If you write a rule for that port, Flui makes sure the
subnet's own range is among its sources before applying it. It
adds the private range instead of replacing what you wrote, so
your exception survives and the cluster stays reachable from
inside its own network.

With the default, the cluster is usable as soon as it comes up,
with the SSH allow-list bound to your workstation and everything
else closed. The change you will make most often is updating
that allow-list, usually when your IP changes or when more
operators need access. Use `flui env update-firewall`, which
takes `--ip` with an IP or a comma-separated list of CIDRs, or
no flag at all, in which case it detects your current public
address. `--add` and `--remove` edit the list instead of
replacing it, `--list` prints it and changes nothing, and the
command refuses a change that would leave the list empty. It
touches only the SSH rule and leaves every other rule as it is.
It updates the rules Flui keeps, so a later reconcile does not
undo it. When the Flui API does not answer, it writes to the
provider directly, so it still works when your current address
is the one locked out; run it again once the API answers.

When the default policy is not what you need, the dashboard has
a full firewall editor: you can add, change or remove rules from
the cluster's Firewall tab through **View & Manage Rules**, and
the API accepts the same operations.

## The rules you cannot remove

Because you can edit the rules, the platform holds a few of them
in place. A misconfigured firewall (a missing SSH rule, a stray
block on the certificate renewal path) is one of the most common
ways to lock an operator out of a cluster, or a cluster out of
its own certificates. So Flui enforces three invariants on every
write, at cluster creation and on every later update:

- **Ports 80 and 443 always stay open inbound.** If a submitted
  rule set leaves one out, Flui puts it back, open to the world,
  and says so in the log. You can restrict the source of those
  ports, but you cannot remove the port.
- **A workload cluster always admits the control plane on SSH.**
  Flui manages that cluster over SSH, so the control plane's own
  addresses are added to the SSH allow-list rather than
  replacing it. On a provider that filters at its own edge, a
  cluster created from the CLI admits only the control cluster
  on SSH; one created from the dashboard also admits the address
  you created it from. Use `flui ssh` and the control cluster's
  path rather than connecting directly.
- **A rule open to the whole IPv4 internet is opened to IPv6
  too.** Nodes have addresses on both, and a firewall drops what
  its rules do not match instead of refusing it. A lone IPv4
  wildcard would turn every IPv6 host into a black hole that
  looks like a slow connection instead of an error. Lists that
  name specific ranges are left alone: someone chose to narrow
  that source, and widening it would undo their choice.

## Ports that answer only over the tunnel

A third category sits between "open" and "closed", and it exists
because of the network described in
[The network Flui builds](/concepts/10-the-network-flui-builds/).

Some ports must be reachable by the installation and by nobody
else: a cluster's control-plane port, and the two that receive
logs and metrics. On a single-provider installation the private
network handles that, because the ports are scoped to it. Across
providers there is no such network to scope to, and the
addresses involved can change.

So the rule names the tunnel instead of an address: traffic
arriving over the network Flui built is accepted on those ports,
and traffic arriving any other way is not. This keeps working
when the other end's address changes, which an address-based
rule could not do.

**Your telemetry ports are never public**, not even briefly
during setup. They are opened on the tunnel and nowhere else,
and a cluster that has not joined the tunnel yet has simply not
started sending.

**The tunnel does not make your clusters neighbours.** A machine
accepts tunnel traffic addressed to itself and does not pass it
along to anyone else. Two workload clusters on the same tunnel
cannot reach each other through it.

## One policy, two ways to enforce it

The policy above is the same everywhere. What changes is the
mechanism available to enforce it.

_Diagram: One policy, two places to enforce it: the provider's firewall around the machines, or the Flui firewall inside each one._

Some providers run a firewall of their own in front of the
machine, with an API Flui drives, and Flui uses it. Where there
is no such firewall (and a Linux machine you already own has
nothing in front of it at all), Flui applies the rules on the
host itself, and the machine becomes its own perimeter.
[The provider table](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/#the-providers-integrated-today)
shows which providers have one.

Where the provider has an edge firewall, new workload clusters
also get the same rules on each node, so a node left outside the
provider firewall still exposes only SSH, HTTP, HTTPS and the
Flui network. `flui cluster host-firewall <cluster>` shows it
and turns it on or off.

Flui decides which of the two applies from the provider's
declared capabilities, never from its name, as the rest of the
platform does. So nothing above changes when you move to a
provider with no firewall API: `flui env firewall apply` is one
command with one meaning, whatever mechanism runs behind it.

## The firewall on a machine you own

This matters most when you install onto your own machine,
because there the machine can really be exposed. Where the
provider has an edge firewall, it exists before any node does,
so the host is never reachable unprotected. A machine you
already own is reachable from the moment the cluster binds a
port, unless something closes it first.

So Flui applies the host firewall before the cluster starts, as
part of the install. Everything inbound is denied by default;
SSH, HTTP and HTTPS are opened; the ports the nodes use to talk
to each other, and the port range used for service traffic
inside the cluster, are reachable only from the cluster's own
private ranges and never from the internet. The ruleset is
written to the machine and re-applied when it restarts, so a
reboot does not undo it.

The installation is not reported ready until that is in place,
because an install that leaves the machine open to the internet
has not succeeded.

One rule is not narrowed: SSH stays reachable from any address.
A cloud machine has an out-of-band console you can fall back on
when a firewall change locks you out. A machine you own usually
does not, so a wrong SSH allow-list there can lock you out for
good, and Flui will not take that risk for you. Restrict port 22
at your provider's edge, or in the machine's own SSH
configuration, where you keep a way back in.

This is also why `flui env update-firewall` behaves differently
here. There is no provider firewall to change, so it says so
instead of failing, and points you to the two commands below.

## Applying and inspecting the host firewall

Two commands, both acting on the installation's own cluster:

```bash
flui env firewall apply
flui env firewall status
```

`apply` makes sure a firewall exists and then applies it. If the
cluster has none, it seeds the default rules for that kind of
cluster first. It is idempotent: running it again is safe, and it
fixes most of what can go wrong here.

`status` reads it back: whether a firewall is configured at all,
the reconciliation state, when it was last applied, and the
inbound rules in force. If there is none, it says that nothing is
filtering inbound traffic and tells you to apply one.

It also reports drift, which means the rules Flui wants differ
from the rules it last managed to apply, for example after an
update that failed halfway or a provider call that did not land.
Drift compares Flui's own records; it is not a live scan of the
machine. `flui env firewall apply` fixes it.

One failure looks worse than it is. If the install applies the
firewall to the machine but cannot register it with the control
plane, the machine is still protected: the rules are on it and
active. What is missing is Flui's record of them, and without it
Flui cannot reconcile the firewall or report drift on it. Run
`flui env firewall apply` afterwards to close that gap.

When an agent asks for this, it stops and asks you first: the
firewall decides what can reach the cluster from outside,
including your own access to it. See
[The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/).

## How the firewall tracks the cluster

The firewall is created with the cluster and lasts as long as
the cluster. Three moments matter:

- **At cluster creation**, where the provider has an edge
  firewall, it is created before the master server or in the
  same step, so the master is never briefly reachable on the
  public internet without protection. On a machine you own, the
  same guarantee comes from applying the rules on the host
  before the cluster starts.
- **When a worker is added**, the firewall is applied to it
  before the node carries traffic, so a new node is never
  exposed.
- **When a worker is removed**, the server is deleted at the
  provider, where there is one, and the firewall's record of
  covered nodes is updated. The firewall itself stays in place
  for the remaining nodes.

You do not have to manage any of this: it is part of how nodes
join and leave a cluster, described in
[Nodes and cluster topology](/concepts/06-nodes-and-cluster-topology/).

## The provider abstraction

The firewall is one of the dimensions Flui's provider
abstraction covers. Each integrated provider implements the same
Flui-side contract (create, update, apply, remove), and the
provider integration absorbs the differences in rule shape and
direction semantics. The host firewall is one more
implementation of that contract, reached over SSH instead of an
API. Either way, the cluster sees one neutral firewall model.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/):
  where the firewall is created.
- [Get Flui running](/tasks/get-flui-running/): installing onto a
  machine you already own, step by step.
- [VNets and subnets, abstracted](/concepts/11-vnet-and-subnets/):
  the private network the firewall does not filter.
- [How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/):
  why firewall capability is one of the dimensions a provider can
  expose or lack.

sections.title: DNS integration
sections.body:
A new DNS name takes about a minute to reach the world's
resolvers. Right after a deploy, that is long enough to
wonder whether something went wrong.

A Flui cluster avoids that wait. Every application on a
cluster answers at the same addresses, and every
application name sits one label under the same subdomain.
One record can cover all of them, including the ones that
do not exist yet, and that is the record a Flui cluster
publishes.

## What an endpoint is

An endpoint is the address a browser, a service or a CLI
uses to reach an application from outside the cluster.
Endpoints are opt-in: an application that nothing outside
needs to reach can be deployed without one. When an
application does ask to be reachable, Flui handles the
rest: hostname, record, certificate and routing. You do
not allocate hostnames or edit records by hand.

A certificate that lets the endpoint serve HTTPS is
provisioned alongside it, as described in
[TLS and certificates](/concepts/14-tls-and-certificates/).

## One record for the whole cluster

When a cluster publishes under a zone, every application on
it is reachable at `<application>.<cluster>.<zone>`, and
every one of those names resolves to the same addresses: the
cluster's. So Flui publishes a single record, `*.<cluster>`,
pointing there.

_Diagram: One record, *.production, covers every application on the cluster, including the next one you deploy, and points at every node that takes traffic. A node that is not ready is left out. Gated applications sit under a wildcard of their own, *.internal._

As a result:

- **A new application answers immediately.** Its name is
  covered before it is deployed. Nothing has to propagate,
  because nothing new was published.
- **Removing an application removes nothing from DNS.**
  There is no per-application record to leave behind, so
  there are no orphans to clean up.

What you choose for an application, when you deploy it or on
its endpoint, is its name and its certificate, not this
record. An application that keeps the cluster's naming is
covered by it. One given a name of its own, such as
`shop.example.com`, sits outside `*.<cluster>` and gets its
own record.

You never configure this record; Flui derives it. Flui
builds the hostname rule itself, so it knows exactly which
names it could ever create, and the wildcard is scoped to
the cluster's own subdomain rather than the zone root. A
zone you also use for a website and a mailbox is untouched
outside `*.<cluster>`.

Two commands cover it:

- `flui dns wildcard status` says whether the record is in
  place, what it points at, and what the hostname pattern
  for this cluster is.
- `flui dns wildcard publish` writes it.

`status` reads the provider live instead of trusting a
stored value. Otherwise a record someone deleted by hand
would keep reporting as fine.

Publishing creates the record and never overwrites one. If
a wildcard is already there pointing somewhere else,
someone put it there, and taking it over would silently
redirect whatever it was serving. Flui reports it and
leaves it alone. That state is reported separately from
"not published yet", because one is work waiting to be done
and the other is a publish that would be refused.

## Every node that takes traffic

The records point at the public address of every node that
can take traffic right now: ready, running the cluster's
ingress, and reachable from the internet. An application
can run on any of them and still answer at its name.

Flui measures that set every minute. A node that stops being
ready, or leaves the cluster, is taken out of the records; a
node that joins or comes back is put in. Every record the
cluster owns moves together (the wildcard and any
per-application record), so they never disagree. While more
than one node is listed, the records carry a short time to
live of one minute, so a node that drops out stops being
handed to visitors quickly. A measurement that finds no node
at all is never published: Flui keeps the records it has,
because publishing an empty set would take every
application offline at once.

This needs a real domain. A nip.io name carries a single
address inside it, so it stays tied to the cluster's master.

## When the wildcard does not answer

A per-application record is the fallback.

Every time an endpoint is reconciled, Flui looks in the zone
for a wildcard that covers this exact name. It counts as
coverage only if both of these hold:

- **One label.** A DNS wildcard matches a single label.
  `*.production` answers for `app.production` and not for
  `a.b.production`.
- **The same addresses.** A wildcard pointing elsewhere
  gives a different answer, and skipping the
  per-application record would send visitors to the wrong
  host.

When both hold, the record would be redundant: with or
without it, the name resolves to the same place. So Flui
does not write it. When either fails (no wildcard, a
foreign one, or a provider that could not be read just
then), the application gets its own record and waits its
minute.

There is nothing to configure. Publish the wildcard and
the per-application records stop being written. Remove it
and they come back on the next reconcile.

If you look at your zone, note that an application covered
by the wildcard does not own that record. Tearing the
application down deletes what it owns, and the shared
record is not its to delete.

## Zones, and giving one to a cluster

A zone is a domain you already own, registered with Flui,
on a DNS provider Flui can talk to. You create the domain
at the provider; Flui detects it and registers it.
Registering a zone is done from the dashboard or the API.
`flui dns zone list` shows the zones an installation knows
about, with each one's provider and TTL.

Assigning a zone to a cluster moves that cluster's
applications off a nip.io name and onto the domain:

```bash
flui dns zone assign example.com --cluster production
```

You do it once per cluster, and again after a rebuild,
which is why it is available as a command and not only on
a screen. Useful flags: `--acme-email` for the address
registered with the certificate authority,
`--certificate-provider` to choose between Let's Encrypt and
its staging service, and `--no-wildcard-certificate` if you
want a certificate per application instead of one covering
them all.

A cluster can publish under more than one zone. When an
application's hostname could belong to several, the longest
match wins.

The command answers immediately. The work behind it (the
credentials the certificate flow needs, the issuers, the
wildcard record) runs in the background.

## Keeping the zone in line

Flui keeps a view of what a zone should contain. The
provider holds what it actually contains. The two can
drift: someone edits a record in the provider's console, a
delete the provider accepted gets lost, a cluster is rebuilt
at a new address.

`flui dns zone status` shows where each assignment stands
(in sync, reconciling, drifted, pending, or in error), with
the reason when there is one, and how long ago it last
settled.

`flui dns zone reconcile` re-applies what the assignment
needs. Add `--wait` when a script needs the outcome rather
than the acknowledgement; it polls, with `--timeout` in
seconds, and the work carries on whether or not you are
still watching.

## A second provider for the same zone

A DNS provider is a single point of failure you do not
control. If it stops answering, every application under that
zone becomes unreachable, however healthy the cluster is.

A replica is the same zone, carried on a second provider.
The primary is untouched; a replica only adds coverage.
Flui writes each record to the replica as well as the
primary, and a scheduled pass brings the replica back in
line if a write was missed.

- `flui dns replica add --zone <id> --provider <name>`
  registers one. It must be a different provider from the
  primary, and one this installation is configured for.
  Pass `--provider-zone-id` to adopt a zone you already
  created there instead of having Flui create one.
- `flui dns replica populate` copies every record across and
  applies the changes.
- `flui dns replica verify` runs the same comparison without
  writing anything: it reports what it would create, update
  and remove.
- `flui dns replica list` shows each replica's state:
  pending, populating, active, degraded or disabled. A write
  Flui could not make marks the replica degraded rather than
  failing your deploy.
- `flui dns replica disable` and `enable` pause and resume
  the copying without unregistering anything.
- `flui dns replica remove` removes Flui's registration
  only. Records already written at the provider stay where
  they are.

Plan for two consequences. Registering the first replica
lowers the zone's TTL from five minutes to one, because a
long TTL is what makes a failover slow; removing the last
one restores it. And Flui does not make the second provider
authoritative for you. Adding its nameservers at your
registrar is your step, and you should confirm the replica
answers correctly before you take it.

## Names without a domain: nip.io

When a cluster has no zone assigned, Flui builds the
hostname from the cluster's address, through a public
service (`nip.io`) that resolves a name back to the address
written inside it. No record exists anywhere; resolution
happens at the resolver.

This lets the first cluster of a new installation come up
without DNS as a prerequisite. You get a working URL the
moment the cluster is ready. It is also fine for development
and staging, where the hostname does not have to be
presentable.

Do not use it for production. It puts a third party in your
request path, it shares rate limits with everyone else using
it, and your cluster's address is written in every URL.

Moving to a real domain later is one operation: register the
zone and assign it to the cluster. The wildcard is published
as part of the assignment. New endpoints use the new names,
and existing ones are reconciled across without redeploying
the application.

## Public and gated endpoints

An application can be published for the public or kept
behind the installation's sign-in:

- `<application>.<cluster>.<zone>`: the public address,
  covered by the cluster's wildcard.
- `<application>.internal.<zone>`: the same application,
  behind the sign-in gate described in
  [The control cluster](/concepts/09-anatomy-of-the-observability-cluster/).
  This name sits directly under the zone, not under the
  cluster's subdomain, and is covered by its own wildcard,
  `*.internal.<zone>`.

Apart from the pattern, its wildcard and the gate in the
request path, the two work the same way.

## When the link appears

An application's URL is published only once the endpoint
serves. A hostname is decided when the endpoint is created,
minutes before anything answers on it, and if that work
then fails, the name never resolves. So the URL is withheld
until the record and the routing are in place. It is
withheld a little longer while the certificate is being
issued, because an `https://` link in that window would
show a browser security warning.

While the URL is withheld, the endpoint's state and its
reason are shown instead.

## What Flui DNS does not do

Buying a domain, and moving its authoritative DNS to a
provider Flui integrates with, are steps you take at the
registrar. Flui does not act at the registrar level: it
works on a zone you have already created at a supported
provider.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/):
  where the cluster's own addresses come from.
- [TLS and certificates](/concepts/14-tls-and-certificates/):
  the certificate lifecycle, and why the wildcard
  certificate and the wildcard record are two separate
  choices.
- [How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/):
  why DNS is one of the capabilities a provider can have or
  lack.

sections.title: TLS and certificates
sections.body:
Every Flui cluster runs on HTTPS from the first minute. There is
no separate step to set up certificate issuance: certificates
come with the same operation that creates an endpoint, and they
renew themselves.

This chapter covers which authority signs the certificates,
which shape of certificate the cluster asks for, and what it
does when it cannot get the shape it wanted.

## The three issuance modes

There are two authorities underneath: Let's Encrypt
**production** and Let's Encrypt **staging**. Three modes
combine them:

- **Production.** Certificates come from Let's Encrypt
  production: real, browser-trusted, valid for every client out
  of the box. This is the mode for anything real users reach,
  and it is the default.
- **Staging.** Certificates come from Let's Encrypt staging. The
  issuance flow is the same, but the signing authority is one
  browsers do not trust, so they show a warning. In exchange its
  limits are loose enough that you can re-issue as often as you
  like while iterating.
- **Preflight.** Start in staging, then move. A staging
  certificate is issued first, which quickly confirms that the
  whole challenge chain works end to end. Once it is valid, the
  endpoint offers you the switch to production. On a single
  endpoint you make the promotion yourself; the DNS setup wizard
  makes it for you once every staging certificate is valid. Use
  this path when you are testing a new domain setup and tripping
  a production limit would be costly.

The mode applies to the whole installation, not to one
application. Set it with
`flui config set certificateMode production|staging|preflight`;
it is written into the dashboard's configuration. A single zone
can still be pinned to one authority when it is attached to a
cluster, with
`flui dns zone assign <zone> --certificate-provider lets_encrypt_staging`.

The rate-limit background is in
[Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/).
In short: production is the default for real environments,
staging suits a tight loop of creating and destroying clusters,
and preflight sits between them. A cluster that starts in
staging can be promoted to production later. The other direction
is rarely useful and no surface offers it.

## The three certificate shapes

Within either authority, the cluster does not always ask for the
same kind of certificate. The shape depends on what the cluster
knows about DNS.

_Diagram: The three shapes a certificate can take. The wildcard is the usual one: an application deployed tomorrow is already covered._

### One wildcard for the cluster

This is the usual case. Attach a DNS zone to a cluster with
`flui dns zone assign <zone>` and you get it without asking;
`--no-wildcard-certificate` declines it.

One certificate covers every name one level under the cluster's
subdomain. Applications that do not exist yet are already
covered, so deploying one needs no new issuance. The certificate
is issued once, held in one place on the cluster, and copied to
wherever an application needs it.

The cluster proves it controls the zone by briefly writing a
record on it (a DNS-01 challenge). That needs a zone on a
provider whose DNS Flui can drive; see
[which providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/#the-providers-integrated-today).
On any other DNS provider the wildcard is not available, and the
cluster falls back to the shape below.

A wildcard is exactly one label deep. A certificate for
`*.apps.example.com` answers for `shop.apps.example.com`, but not
for `eu.shop.apps.example.com` and not for the bare
`apps.example.com`. Names a level deeper get a wildcard of their
own over their own parent, and a bare domain gets its own
certificate. So one cluster can hold more than one wildcard, and
that is normal.

### One certificate per endpoint

A cluster falls back to this shape when it has no DNS zone and
addresses applications by IP, when the zone lives on a provider
Flui cannot write to, when the wildcard was declined, or when a
single endpoint asks for the HTTP challenge by name.

Here the cluster proves it controls each name by serving a small
challenge file from that application's own address (an HTTP-01
challenge). It needs no DNS integration, so it works everywhere.

The cost is that every new endpoint is a fresh issuance. On a
cluster where applications come and go, the count adds up against
the authority's limits. That is why the wildcard is the default
rather than an option you turn on.

### One certificate listing several names

A single certificate can instead list up to twenty hostnames.
Proof of control is per name, with the same HTTP-01 challenge as
above, or DNS-01 when every name on it sits under one zone Flui
can drive.

You only get this shape by asking for it: the certificate is
created first, and endpoints are attached to it as they are
created. Flui uses it itself. When the dashboard's DNS setup
configures the platform without a wildcard, its three addresses
(the API, the dashboard and the identity provider) go into one
certificate, so the setup pays for one challenge instead of
three. It suits a small, fixed set of names known up front and
nothing else, because the list is fixed when the certificate is
created. An endpoint whose hostname is not on the list is
refused, and a different set of names means a different
certificate.

## Which shape an endpoint gets

The cluster decides per endpoint, in this order:

1. If the endpoint was attached to a multi-name certificate, that
   one is used.
2. Otherwise the wildcard, if the wildcard is not switched off,
   the endpoint asked for a certificate at all, its hostname
   falls under a zone attached to the cluster, and the cluster's
   wildcard issuance is ready.
3. Otherwise a certificate of its own.

A wildcard that cannot be used is never an error. Each failing
condition means the endpoint gets its own certificate, and the
deploy carries on. When both the production and the staging
wildcard issuance are ready on a cluster, production wins.

## The wildcard record and the wildcard certificate

A cluster serves all of its applications from one wildcard DNS
record and covers them with one wildcard certificate. These are
separate, and you can have one without the other.

`flui dns wildcard status` prints both, per zone: a `dns` line
for the record and a `certificate` line saying whether the
certificate covers everything or applications get one each. If
the record is missing, `flui dns wildcard publish` creates it.
