The difference you notice is propagation. With the record in
place, a newly deployed application answers straight away.
Without it, each new name publishes on its own and waits about a
minute for resolvers to see it.

If a wildcard record already exists on the zone and points
somewhere other than this cluster, Flui leaves it alone and
applications keep publishing their own names, rather than
overwriting someone else's record.

## Renewal

In every mode and every shape, certificates renew themselves
ahead of expiry, with no action from anyone.

Renewal follows the issuance path: a wildcard renews through the
DNS challenge against its zone, per-endpoint certificates through
the HTTP challenge served from the cluster, and a multi-name
certificate through whichever challenge it was issued with. A
renewed wildcard reaches every application it covers on its own.
Nothing is redeployed or reconciled by hand.

## Why an application's link is not there yet

An application's URL is published only once the endpoint is
settled and its certificate is no longer on its way. An address
is reachable minutes before a certificate is signed, and the link
Flui gives you is an `https://` one. Showing it early would send
a visitor to a browser warning.

The link is withheld only while a certificate is pending or being
issued, and that window closes on its own; a refresh resolves it.
A certificate that failed or expired does not hide the
application. The link appears and the browser says what is
wrong, which tells you more.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [DNS integration](/concepts/13-dns-integration/): where the
  zone, the wildcard record and the hostnames come from.
- [Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/):
  the rate-limit discussion behind production vs staging.
- [How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/):
  why the wildcard depends on the provider exposing a DNS API
  Flui can write to.

sections.title: Identity and OIDC
sections.body:
Many self-hosted platforms handle identity with a user/password
table. Flui delegates identity to an OIDC provider running on the
control cluster, with what comes with it: sessions, federation,
machine accounts, password reset and MFA. Flui keeps no user database
of its own. The identity provider decides who can sign in, and Flui
uses what it issues.

## The whole picture

The identity provider runs on the control cluster, and it is where
people sign in. The Flui API checks every request it receives: a
sign-in token by its signature, a Flui key by its fingerprint, and
then what the role and the scopes allow. The dashboard carries a
sign-in token. The CLI gets a token from the identity provider once,
and trades it with the Flui API for a key it keeps. An agent carries
a key with scopes. Your applications can use the same sign-in: an
internal app is reached only after signing in to Flui, and a catalog
app can sign its own users in with a client Flui created.

_Diagram: Who signs in where, and how the Flui API checks every request. The rest of this chapter takes each piece in turn._

## The problem identity has to cover

The control plane of an installation needs to handle:

- Sign-in for the platform: the dashboard, the CLI and the API.
- Sign-in for the applications deployed on the platform.
- Long-lived access for automation: CI pipelines, scripts,
  third-party integrations.
- Federation with corporate identity providers, when you need it.
- Account lifecycle work: password reset, MFA, an audit log of
  sign-in events.

Building any one of these is feasible. Building all of them and
maintaining them for years is a large job, so Flui delegates the
whole stack to an OIDC provider.

## How it works

The identity provider is installed on the control cluster with the
rest of the platform and is the single sign-on authority for
everything the installation runs.

What you get out of the box:

- One login for the dashboard, the CLI and the API.
- Long-lived machine-to-machine keys for automation, scoped and
  revocable independently of any human user.
- A base you can connect to a corporate identity provider.
  Federation is a configuration change on the identity provider, with
  no change to Flui's code.

The interactive login is the standard flow: the CLI or dashboard
sends you to the identity provider, you authenticate, and the result
is a session the platform trusts.

The same sign-in can protect your applications. An application
published on its gated address, `<application>.internal.<zone>`, is
reached only after signing in to the installation, with nothing to
configure in the application itself; see
[DNS integration](/concepts/13-dns-integration/).

Catalog apps can use the identity provider directly. When a
[composed catalog app](/concepts/22-composed-catalog-apps/) is
installed in OIDC auth mode, Flui creates an OIDC web client on the
identity provider at install time, with no manual client
registration. It records the client and project ids against the
install so it can remove them when the app is uninstalled. The app
gets single sign-on without the operator touching the identity
provider.

### How `flui auth login` works

The CLI needs an authenticated session for every operation that
reaches the Flui API of an installation. Read-only local commands
(managing contexts, inspecting configuration) do not.

To get that session, you run `flui auth login`. The CLI opens a
browser to the installation's identity provider, you authenticate
there, and the CLI receives the result through a local callback. The
CLI does not keep using the short-lived OIDC bearer the flow
produced. It exchanges it at once for a long-lived machine-to-machine
key that identifies the workstation, and saves that key in the active
context. From then on the CLI authenticates with that key, and the
interactive login runs only when you log in again.

The OIDC bearer is short-lived by design (minutes), and the CLI needs
a session that lasts as long as you are working. A named M2M key
gives that, and can be revoked on its own without affecting the human
user it was issued for.

## What a key is, once it is issued

A login lasts as long as somebody is at the keyboard. A key lasts
longer. It goes into a configuration file on a workstation, into a
build pipeline, or into the environment of an agent that runs
unattended for months.

Two questions follow: what happens if somebody reads the key where it
is stored, and how much can it do when it is presented?

### Flui cannot give a key back to you

Flui stores a fingerprint of each key, not the key itself. A copy of
the database therefore contains no live credential: the stored value
opens nothing, and sign-in still works because Flui fingerprints
whatever the caller presents and compares that.

You have to plan around one consequence. The key itself exists only
in the response that creates it, and nothing on the installation can
hand it back afterwards. The listing does not include it:
`flui auth api-keys` shows the name, whether the key is active,
revoked or expired, and its scopes (`--output json` adds when it was
created and when it expires), but never the key.

So save the key when you mint it. If you lose it, revoke it with
`flui auth revoke-api-key <id>` and mint another. Revoking stops that
one key immediately and affects nothing else.

You rarely handle this yourself, because `flui auth login` mints a
key for you and writes it straight into the active profile.

### A key is worth its scopes, on every path

A key is issued as its person. Everything that person may do, the key
can do, unless the key declares scopes, which can only take
permissions away.

The rule holds on every path a key can take: the agent toolbox, the
plain API with `curl`, and a live-updates connection. A read-only key
is read-only everywhere.

A key with no scopes has no ceiling and loses nothing. Keys made by
`flui auth login` work this way, and so do the platform's own internal
identities. Scopes only ever narrow; no scope on any key lets anybody
do something they were not already allowed to do.

[Who can reach what](/concepts/28-who-can-reach-what/) describes this
rule in full, together with the other half of the question: what the
key's holder may reach.

### Scopes come in groups

When people choose scopes one at a time, least privilege tends to
fail: a dozen checkboxes get granted out of fatigue, and the person
clicking cannot say afterwards what they agreed to.

So the unit you switch on is a group, defined by two choices:

- **The area** the agent is trusted with: applications,
  observability, backups, migrations, mail, access, the
  infrastructure, or the platform itself.
- **The depth** it may go to: **look**, **change** or **destroy**.

_Diagram: The sixteen groups. Each is one area at one depth; the empty cells are combinations that do not exist._

There are sixteen groups, and each carries one sentence written for
the person about to approve it. The sentence describes everything the
group carries, beyond the name of its area: "Deploy and operate
applications" also reads logs and metrics, because an agent that can
deploy but cannot read why the deploy failed is of no use.

A group is granted or refused whole. It never comes back smaller than
requested, so what somebody consented to and what the key carries
match. A group naming something the issuer does not hold is refused,
and the refusal names which group caused it, so you know what to fix.

Three rules apply whatever you pick:

- "Grant and revoke access" is a group of its own and appears inside
  no other. It never comes along with "deploy my applications".
- No agent key can be given cluster deletion, whatever groups are
  combined.
- Every scoped key also gets one thing nobody switches on: the ability
  to read the instructions for operating this installation, since an
  agent that cannot read the rules cannot follow them.

The terminal does not offer groups. `flui auth generate-api-key`
takes `--scope` (repeatable) or `--unscoped`, and refuses if you name
neither, so a key never gets its owner's full permissions by
accident. Groups exist in the API and the dashboard.

### The trap: agent scopes on a person's account

Because the identity provider is the authority, scopes can also come
from it, as roles on an account rather than on a key Flui issued.
That works, and it is a valid way to cap an agent.

There is one catch. If you put those roles on a person's account,
intending them for that person's agent, they cap every token that
account is ever issued, including the person's browser session. The
dashboard turns read-only for no visible reason.

This is correct behaviour: the credential is that account, and a
declared ceiling applies wherever it is presented. The refusal says
where the scopes came from, so the cause is on the screen.

Agent scopes belong on a machine account, not on a person. The
identity provider handles machine accounts well, and Flui mints one
for an agent on request: a machine user carrying agent scopes and
nothing else. It never gets a role from the access ladder, because a
scope narrows and a role would give the agent standing of its own.
Its secret, like a key, is returned once.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Who can reach what](/concepts/28-who-can-reach-what/): the second
  question, and the one a refusal is usually about.
- [The control cluster](/concepts/09-anatomy-of-the-observability-cluster/):
  the identity provider as a platform component on the control
  cluster.
- [CLI: Authentication](/cli/authentication/): the command-by-command
  reference for logging in and generating machine-to-machine keys.

sections.title: The app concept
sections.body:
In Flui, the app is the unit you deploy, observe, scale and retire.
Every CLI command under `flui app *` and every Apps page in the
dashboard works on an app. An app is more than a running process or
a single piece of cluster infrastructure. It bundles the name and
slug, source, runtime configuration, endpoints, certificates,
builds, releases, logs and metrics that describe one deployable
thing and everything around it during its life on the cluster.

This chapter defines the concept. The manifest that describes an
app for Flui has its own chapter
([The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/)), and so
does the difference between **Application** and **CatalogApp**
([Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/)).

## What an app carries

Wherever it comes from, an app carries the same set of things:

- **A name and a slug.** A stable slug unique within the
  installation and a readable name. The slug is what every
  other surface refers to.
- **A cluster.** Every app lives on one cluster at a time: the
  cluster whose dashboard you opened, or the one you pointed the
  CLI at. Moving it to another cluster is one operation; see
  [Moving an app to another cluster](#moving-an-app-to-another-cluster)
  below.
- **A source.** Where the workload comes from. There are three:
  a container image pulled from a registry, a source repository
  that Flui builds for you against a `flui.yaml` manifest, or an
  entry picked from the Flui catalog of ready-made building
  blocks. The source decides what happens before the workload
  runs. The rest of the app is the same whichever source it has.
- **A runtime configuration.** Replica count and scaling limits,
  healthcheck, ports and volumes: how the workload runs once it
  is up.
- **An endpoint, or none at all.** An app can declare that it
  should be reachable from outside the cluster. The deploy flow
  then gives it a hostname and a matching TLS certificate. An app
  that does not need to be reached, such as a background worker
  or a job, runs without one. Endpoints are covered in
  [DNS as part of the deploy contract](/concepts/13-dns-integration/).
  Whether the app is public on its own domain or internal behind
  the dashboard is its exposure, described below.
- **A release history.** Every deploy and every rollback is
  recorded as a new, append-only release entry. The current
  release is a pointer into that history.

The sections below cover the points that need more than a line:
resources, configuration and secrets, moving, removal, scaling and
observability.

## Resources: CPU and memory

Every app declares two numbers per instance: the **request**,
which the cluster reserves and guarantees, and the **limit**, the
ceiling the instance cannot go past. The scheduler places an
instance only if the node can honour the request, and the runtime
enforces the limit at peak.

The dashboard shows both numbers next to current usage. It flags
the app when the request is much higher than what the workload
uses (over-allocated, paying for idle capacity) or when usage runs
close to the limit (under-allocated, at risk of being killed), so
you see these signals without going looking for them.

When an app is killed for running out of memory, Flui writes a
diagnosis and proposes a higher limit, with the reason. It never
applies it on its own. Changing what an app may use restarts it
and may need room the cluster does not have, so a person decides,
from the dashboard, the CLI or an agent that was asked to.

## The capacity gate

Before an app is installed from the catalog, Flui adds up the
resource needs of the app, and of every component it brings if it
is a composed stack. If the cluster does not have room, keeping
roughly a 10% safety margin in reserve, Flui refuses the install
up front. The refusal names the shortfall: how much CPU and memory
the install needs and how much is free.

The gate treats CPU and memory differently:

- **CPU is gated on requests.** CPU is compressible:
  oversubscribing it only throttles a workload and does not kill
  it. So the gate only needs the scheduling floor (the request) to
  fit.
- **Memory is gated on limits.** Memory is incompressible: an
  instance holds the RAM it touches up to its limit, and a node
  that runs past what it can allocate starts killing workloads. So
  the gate uses the peak (the limit, falling back to the request
  when a component declares no limit).

The dashboard deploy wizard runs the same calculation, so the two
surfaces agree on what will fit.

A cluster that may grow on its own changes the answer. Where a
[scaling group](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/) on the cluster is
set to buy by itself, and one of its machines would hold the
install, the gate does not refuse. The install goes ahead and
waits for that machine to join.

## Volumes and storage

An app that needs to keep data across restarts declares one or
more **volumes**, each with a name, a mount path inside the
workload and a size. The cluster's storage configuration decides
where the data lives. On the cluster's shared storage, any node can
reach it and the app can move freely. On a node's local disk,
access is faster but the app is pinned to that node. That choice
affects placement and what happens during cluster operations such
as a node resize. See
[Storage classes and dedicated placement](/concepts/21-storage-classes-and-dedicated-placement/).

Volumes are also why removing an app needs care. See
[Removing an app takes its data](#removing-an-app-takes-its-data).

## Port protocol

Every app's main port has a **protocol**, `http` or `tcp`, with
`http` as the default. The field controls observability. An
`http` app is scraped for platform metrics such as request rates.
A `tcp` app (a database, a message broker, anything that does not
speak HTTP on its port) is not HTTP-scraped, because there is
nothing useful to scrape and probing it would only add noise.
Declaring `tcp` tells Flui the port speaks a wire protocol, not
HTTP.

Readiness probes can also carry **HTTP headers** when the plain
path-and-port check is not enough. The usual case is a `Host:`
header, so an app that only answers for a specific virtual host
still passes its health check during a rolling restart instead of
failing on a request its router does not recognise.

## How an app is reached

An app that has an endpoint is reached in one of two ways:

- **Public.** The app gets a public endpoint: a hostname, a TLS
  certificate, and routing from the internet to the app. This is
  the default and the right choice for anything meant to be
  reached from outside.
- **Internal.** The app gets only a cluster-internal address, with
  no public hostname, no certificate and no DNS record to manage.
  It is reachable only through the dashboard's authenticating
  proxy. Use it for an admin tool or a console you want behind the
  platform's own login rather than on the public internet.

Apps the catalog marks **privatizable** can choose between the
two at install time. Others keep whatever their manifest declares.

In a third case you have no choice: a **building block** installed from
the catalog (a database, a cache, a queue) is reachable only from
inside its own cluster. It has no public hostname and no proxy
route at all, because the thing that reads it is another app on
the same cluster and nothing else should reach it. To reach one
from your own machine, Flui opens a tunnel for you
([Open a database from your machine](/tasks/open-a-database/)).

### Use the URL the app gives you

Each app's API representation carries the links it should be
reached by. A public app exposes a `url` of the form
`https://<fqdn><entrypointPath>`; an internal app exposes an
`internalUrl` instead. Anything that uses these links (the
dashboard's "Open" button, the assistant) must use the value
exactly as given and must not build a URL from the slug. The slug
is not the hostname. The stored `url` / `internalUrl` accounts for
the endpoint's actual domain and path, and only that value is
guaranteed to be correct.

A URL is also published only once the endpoint serves, reconciled
and with a valid certificate. Before that the app shows no URL at
all, so you are never sent to a link that ends in a browser error.

## Configuration and secrets

Plain configuration reaches the workload as environment variables
and lives with the app. Sensitive values use the same name-value
shape but are stored encrypted and **write-only**: the surfaces
show the names so you know what is set, and never the values. You
can overwrite a sensitive value at any time, but you cannot read
it back once stored.

Three sources can set those values, and the order between them is
fixed.

_Diagram: Which value an application gets: an override at deploy beats flui.yaml, which beats a value set by hand; a linked credential is never overwritten._

**The manifest wins for the keys it declares.** Every deploy lets
the manifest take back every key it declares. A value set by hand
only survives on a key the manifest does not declare. When the
manifest overwrites a pinned value, the deploy reports it.

**Explicit overrides win over both.** A value passed at deploy
time with `--env` or `--env-file` beats the manifest and the
stored value alike.

**A linked value is never overwritten.** When a key points at a
building block's own credential, such as the password of the
database Flui installed for you, a plain manifest value does not
replace it. Swapping a live reference for a copied literal is how
a credential ends up somewhere nobody remembers to rotate.

Two further rules follow.

**"Declared but not resolved" is not "removed".** A key the
manifest declares but gets its value from somewhere else (from a
person, from another service) keeps whatever is stored for it.
Only a key the manifest stops declaring entirely is treated as a
removal.

**"Awaiting a value" is a real state.** A sensitive key that has
been declared but never supplied is listed with the others,
labelled `awaiting a value`. It is not blank, missing or an error,
and listing keys does not fail because one is outstanding.
`flui app env list` shows the three states side by side: plain
values, which sensitive keys are set, and which are still waiting.
`flui app env set <app> <KEY>` asks for the value instead of taking
it as an argument, so it never lands in your shell history.

This matters most when an agent is involved. An agent can declare
that a key is needed but cannot supply one. The pending state lets
it hand the job to you and stop, instead of inventing a
placeholder.

A changed value does not reach a running instance by itself. The
app receives it on its next deploy or restart, and the CLI tells
you so when you set one.

The whole flow, on all three surfaces, is in
[Set an application's configuration and secrets](/tasks/configuration-and-secrets/).

## How an app is classified

The dashboard groups apps along two independent axes:

- **Category.** Two values: *system* and *user*. System apps are
  the components of the platform itself (the API, the dashboard,
  the identity provider, the database, the observability stack),
  installed and reconciled by Flui as part of the control cluster.
  User apps are everything you deploy. You operate both through
  the same surfaces. The difference is that system apps are
  protected from accidental deletion: a delete command refuses
  unless forced.
- **Kind.** A broader grouping by purpose: *database*, *tool*,
  *application*, *system*. The dashboard uses it to sort apps into
  three lists: **Applications** (tools included), **Data** and
  **System**. It does not change the lifecycle.

Both are separate from the manifest's own `kind:` field
(`Application` vs `CatalogApp`), which describes where the app
comes from, not what it does. See
[Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/).

## The lifecycle

An app is in one of a few steady states:

- **Awaiting build**: for apps built from source, while the build
  is running and the platform is waiting for an image.
- **Running**: the app is up and serving its work.
- **Waiting for room**: deployed, but some copies have no node
  with room to run on. They start as soon as room appears, for
  example when a scaling group adds a machine.
- **Degraded**: the app is up but not at full health (some
  replicas down, a healthcheck failing intermittently).
- **Stopped**: scaled to zero; the configuration is still there,
  and no instances are running.
- **Failed**: a terminal failure (the last build failed, the last
  deploy failed, or an unrecoverable condition was hit).
- **Deleted**: the app has been torn down; the row remains for
  audit.

During an operation such as a deploy, a rollback or a teardown,
the app briefly passes through transient states that the dashboard
shows as progress indicators rather than steady values.

## Operations

The everyday operations on an app are:

- **Deploy / redeploy.** Apply (or apply again) the app's
  configuration. For image-based apps a redeploy can also pin a
  different image version. For source-built apps a redeploy reuses
  an existing build instead of building again. Every deploy adds a
  new release entry.
- **Rollback.** Move the current release pointer back to a
  previous entry. This adds a new release entry (marked as a
  rollback) instead of rewinding history, so the record of what
  happened stays intact. Rollback is a dashboard action. From the
  CLI, `flui app redeploy <app> <tag>` rolls out an older image
  without rebuilding.
- **Start / stop.** Bring the app's replicas back from zero, or
  scale them to zero while keeping the configuration in place.
  Stopping can be reversed without redeploying.
- **Restart.** Replace the running instances without changing
  the release. See the rolling restart section below.
- **Scale.** Set the replica count explicitly.
- **Move.** Take the app to another cluster in one operation.
- **Delete.** Remove the app from the cluster, together with the
  data it was keeping. Read the removal section below before you
  run it. System apps require an explicit force flag.

## Rolling restart

When the running instances of an app have to be replaced, to pick
up new configuration or secrets or to clear a stuck state, Flui
rolls them: new instances come up first, and the old ones go away
only once the new ones are healthy. The replica count never drops
below the declared number, so the app keeps serving throughout. The
platform also starts a rolling restart on its own whenever a change
it can apply in place needs to reach the running instances.

## Surviving the loss of a node

When an app runs two or more copies, Flui spreads them across
the cluster's nodes where there is room, so losing one node does
not take every copy with it. A dedicated app is not spread: it
stays on one node.

`flui app status` says whether the app survives losing a worker
and, when it does not, lists every reason with what to change: a
single copy, copies that all run on one node, a volume that
stays on one node, a dedicated placement, an address that names
one node, or only one node taking traffic for its names. Agents
get the same answer from the `app_availability` tool.

## Moving an app to another cluster

A move is one operation with a cutover in the middle. Flui builds
the copy on the destination cluster while the source keeps
serving. When the copy is ready, the app is rebound to the
destination and its address follows it. You can let that happen
as soon as the copy is ready, or hold it and cut over yourself
while you watch.

Two things hold throughout:

- **Before the cutover, nothing on the source has changed.**
  Aborting tears the destination down and leaves the original
  exactly as it was.
- **After the cutover, the source workload is still there,
  drained.** Destroying it is a separate, irreversible step that
  you take yourself.

Moves that cannot work are refused up front. A move of the app
alone is for an app that holds no data of its own: an app with
volumes, an app pinned to a dedicated node, or an app wired to
another app's credential is refused with a message saying which.
Data moves through its own operation, and an app together with its
database moves through a third that cuts both over at once. See
[Move an application to another cluster](/tasks/move-an-application/).

## Removing an app takes its data

Removing an app removes the storage it was using. A volume does
not outlive the app that made it, so nothing stays on the cluster
unlisted while you keep paying for it.

Because this cannot be undone, every surface shows what will be
lost before it asks. The confirmation names the volumes and how
much data they hold. For a composed install it names the whole
install, because the removal takes all of it.

When Flui cannot read the storage, for example because the cluster
is unreachable or it cannot open the credentials, it reports the
loss as **unknown**, never as none. It does not print "no data will
be lost" based on a failed read. When you see unknown, assume
there is data.

`flui cluster volumes` lists the volumes nothing mounts and no
app owns, with a way to remove them one at a time. The scan can
miss volumes: it only reports a volume when nothing mounts it and
no existing app owns it, so a volume created outside Flui and
carrying none of its labels never appears in it.

The removal flow on each surface is in
[Remove an application and its data](/tasks/remove-an-application/).

## Automatic scaling

An app carries a scaling setting. When it is on, Flui applies an
autoscaler beside the app on every deploy. It watches the app's own
resource use and moves the replica count between the app's
declared floor and ceiling, which are 1 and 5 when the app declares
neither. It watches what the app asked for: CPU utilisation, memory
utilisation, or both, given as target percentages. An app can also
set how fast it scales in each direction (how many instances at a
time, and how long the autoscaler must be sure before it acts),
which stops a spiky workload from scaling up and down constantly.

The percentages are measured against what the app reserves, not
against its limit. An app that reserves 100 MiB and scales at 80%
memory adds a copy at 80 MiB, well before it gets near a limit of
2 GiB. That is why an accurate reservation matters: it is what the
autoscaler measures against. CPU is usually the better signal for
load, because memory held after a peak rarely comes back and copies
scaled on memory tend to stay.

When a new copy has nowhere to run, it waits, and that waiting is
what a scaling group watches for. The cluster buys a machine, the
copy starts on it, and once the load has gone the machine is given
back.

Two limits apply:

- **Building blocks are not autoscaled.** A database or a queue
  installed from the catalog runs as a single stateful workload,
  and no autoscaler is attached to it. Copying a database does not
  scale it.
- **You can also set a count by hand.** `flui app scale` sets an
  explicit replica count, and stopping an app is the same
  operation at zero.

A cluster buying more machines is a separate decision, with its
own written consent and its own ceilings in money; see
[What a cluster may buy for itself](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/).
App autoscaling changes how many copies of your app run on the
machines you have. A scaling group decides whether to add a
machine.

## Logs and metrics

Every app has the same observability surfaces from the start, in
both the dashboard and the CLI:

- **Logs.** Streamed from every instance, searchable by level and
  free text.
- **Metrics.** CPU, memory, network and replica counts over time:
  the baseline Flui collects for every app it manages, with no
  setup on the app side.
- **Live status.** Replicas ready, current release, health at a
  glance.
- **Crashes.** A summary of recent crashes: exit codes,
  out-of-memory events, restart counts, and the last log lines
  before each crash.

All four read from the same central backend on the control
cluster. See
[Observability is not an afterthought](/concepts/08-observability-as-first-class/).

## Going deeper when something is wrong

When the everyday views are not enough (a first release that
won't start, a sudden burst of crashes, a configuration that
breaks the workload in a subtle way), the dashboard has two deeper
tools under an **Advanced** menu on every app:

- **Diagnoses.** An automated read of recent failures that goes
  further than the crash list. It correlates exit codes,
  out-of-memory events, healthcheck failures and the log lines
  around them, and suggests a probable cause and a fix (a missing
  environment variable to add, a memory limit to raise).
  Unresolved diagnoses also appear as a banner on the app's
  overview.
- **A per-instance deep read.** An on-demand snapshot of every
  running instance of the app, with the low-level detail you need
  when the higher-level views fall short. It refreshes on request
  rather than continuously, so the cluster does not pay for a
  constant detailed read of every app.

These tools are for when logs, metrics, status and crashes are no
longer enough. They are not part of the routine flow.

## System apps are apps

The platform's own components (the API, the dashboard, the
identity provider, the database, the observability stack) are apps
in this model too. They appear in the app list, have releases,
expose logs and metrics, and go through the same lifecycle as user
apps. The only difference is the *system* category and its
protection: their delete operation refuses unless you force it.

So you do not learn one set of commands for Flui's own components
and another for your apps. You read the dashboard's logs the same
way you read your app's logs.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Set an application's configuration and secrets](/tasks/configuration-and-secrets/):
  the precedence rules above, applied on each surface.
- [Move an application to another cluster](/tasks/move-an-application/):
  the three kinds of move and how a cutover works.
- [Remove an application and its data](/tasks/remove-an-application/):
  what the confirmation tells you, and the volumes no app owns.
- [The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/): the
  declarative file that produces an app.
- [Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/):
  the two kinds of manifest that produce apps, and how they differ.
- [Storage classes and dedicated placement](/concepts/21-storage-classes-and-dedicated-placement/):
  where an app's volumes live and how dedicated apps land on a
  worker.
- [Composed catalog apps](/concepts/22-composed-catalog-apps/):
  multi-component installs and how the capacity gate adds them up.

sections.title: The Flui manifest
sections.body:
A manifest is a written description of what you want. It sits
in your repository, next to the code it describes, and you can
read, review and revert it like any other file. Flui reads it,
but you own it.

Once people have a file that says "this is what I want, apply
it", they want one for the next thing too, which is why the
set of document kinds keeps growing.

## The spec lives outside Flui

The authoritative schema lives in its own repository,
[`flui-cloud/flui-spec`](https://github.com/flui-cloud/flui-spec),
with its own versioning, narrative docs, JSON Schemas and
example manifests. The TypeScript types and the validator
are published to npm as
[`@flui-cloud/spec`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@flui-cloud/spec),
which Flui pulls in like any other dependency. Flui uses the
schema but does not maintain it.

A manifest that named a concept internal to Flui, or that needed
a Flui-specific extension, would tie you to one tool. Because the
spec lives outside Flui and Flui depends on it, that cannot
happen: a different tool can read the same file.

## Four kinds of document

Three kinds are published in the spec:

- **Application**: an application built from a source
  repository and deployed to a cluster. This is the one you
  write yourself.
- **CatalogApp**: a pre-packaged building block (a database,
  a queue, an admin tool) installed from the catalog with the
  configuration the catalog publishes.
- **AccessPolicy**: who may reach what. `flui iam export`
  writes one as a snapshot of every grant; `flui iam apply -f`
  reads it back.

A fourth kind comes from Flui rather than from the spec:

- **ScalingGroup**: what a cluster may buy for itself and
  where it must stop. `flui scaling export` writes it, and
  `flui scaling apply -f` reads it back. It is Flui's own
  document, not part of the published spec, and it carries
  no `apiVersion`. It borrows the same shape (a `kind`, a
  name, blocks underneath) because a file that reads like the
  others is easier to review than a new format.

One rule on that file differs from the others and catches
people out: a ScalingGroup file is the whole group. A field
left out is reset to its default, not left as it was. Several
groups can live in one file, separated by `---`. What the group
is for is covered in
[Scaling groups](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/).

The rest of this chapter is about the Application shape.

## What an Application manifest says

An Application manifest has exactly six things at the top:
`kind`, `apiVersion`, `metadata`, `build`, `deploy` and
`environments`. Under `deploy` there are fourteen: `port`,
`exposure`, `healthcheck`, `smokeTest`, `resources`,
`scaling`, `domain`, `env`, `volumes`, `files`, `services`,
`browserConfig`, `startCommand` and `replaceAtStart`.

Each answers one operational question:

- **Name.** A stable identifier, under `metadata`. Every
  other surface (dashboard, CLI, observability) uses it, so
  the spec restricts it to a lowercase form that works in a
  hostname.
- **How to build the image.** A pointer to a Dockerfile in
  the repository, plus the build context and the build
  arguments. (`strategy: auto`, framework detection, is
  deprecated and kept only so older files still validate.)
  The block says what to build and where, never how the build
  runs.
- **How to run it.** The port your code listens on, the
  healthcheck to probe, replica limits, CPU and memory
  as explicit numbers (the schema also has a size preset,
  `resources.profile`, which Flui does not apply), and an
  optional start command.
- **How it is reached.** `exposure: public` means a public
  address, with a name and a certificate.
  `exposure: internal` means no public address at all: other
  applications on the cluster can reach it, and you can reach
  it through the dashboard. `exposure: none` says the
  application does not listen at all, as with a worker or a
  queue consumer. Public is the default. The `domain` block
  then says whether a hostname should be assigned
  automatically, which one to use instead, and which
  certificate flow to take.
- **Configuration and secrets.** A list of environment
  variables. An entry can carry a plain value, ask for a
  secret to be generated, point at an existing secret,
  point at a sibling application in the same project, or
  declare a value somebody must supply at install time.
- **Volumes.** Persistent volumes the application needs,
  each with a name, a mount path and a size.

The schema is closed: a key it does not name is an error, not
an extension. The list still grows with the spec, so treat what
is written here as the current vocabulary. `flui app manifest`
prints the field reference straight from the schema Flui has
installed, and `flui app manifest --example` prints an annotated
file to start from. Both run offline.

## One file, several environments

`environments` is a map. You choose the keys (`production`,
`staging`, `preview`), and each entry names the git **branch**
it belongs to. Deploy that branch and the entry is laid over
the base: environment values first, then resources, replica
limits and domain.

`build` cannot be overridden per environment. The spec leaves
it out, so what the file says about building an image is the
same everywhere, and only what surrounds the image changes.

An entry that names no branch never matches anything. A
validation that names no branch reports the base spec, because
there is no branch to pick an entry with.

## `deploy.services`: one building block, attached to one application

An `Application` can declare its own building block, most often
a database, under `deploy.services`. Each entry names the
service, the catalog block to install (`block`), and the
environment the application needs to reach it. A value can be
read off the block itself (`fromService: host`, `port` or
`url`), or taken directly from a variable the block declares
(`fromBBEnv`).

Deploying a manifest that declares one installs the block from
the catalog, waits for it to reach a running state, and wires
the resulting environment into the application before the
application's own container starts. The credential that reaches
it is never a plain value on the row; it is a reference to the
Secret the block generated. A `deploy.services` entry that names
an unknown block, or a block that is not a building block, is
refused before any application exists. (`vaultwarden`, for
example, is a full application, so installing it stays a catalog
install of its own.) Sizing the block through `resources` is
accepted by the schema but refused by the deploy, which says so
instead of installing the block at the catalog's own size.

One instance belongs to one application for its whole
lifecycle. Redeploying reuses it instead of provisioning a
second one, and a manifest that no longer declares it stops the
attachment without deleting what it already brought up. It does
not give you an instance shared by two applications: nothing in
the field says "the same one as that other unit's", so two units
of a monorepo that each declare the same block end up with two
separate installs of it. See [How
Flui reads a repository](/concepts/30-how-flui-reads-a-repository/)
for where that shows up when the map renders a monorepo.

## The composed CatalogApp surface

A `CatalogApp` can describe more than one workload. A
composed entry (`type: composed`) drops the single-image body
and carries a `components` list instead, plus a few
coordination blocks with no equivalent in the Application
shape:

- **`components`.** The workloads the entry bundles. Each
  has its own image, environment and resources, and runs as
  its own app. A component can declare `dependsOn` (other
  components that must be healthy first) and `when.option`
  (include this only when a named option is on).
- **`auth`.** Which sign-in strategies the entry supports.
  `auth.modes` lists them, and `auth.default` names the
  fallback. The modes are `oidc`, `proxy`, `native` and
  `none`; the one used is chosen at install time, not fixed
  in the file.
- **`options`.** Install-time switches, each with a `key`,
  a `label` and a `default`. Components and post-install
  steps depend on them.
- **`postInstall`.** Steps that run once the components are
  up, either an HTTP call or a command inside a component,
  each conditioned on the chosen sign-in mode or on an option.

These blocks use a few templating tokens that the consuming
tool resolves at install time rather than when the file is
written: a component's own public hostname (`{{self.fqdn}}`)
and, when OIDC is the chosen mode, the provisioned client's
`{{oidc.clientId}}`, `{{oidc.clientSecret}}` and
`{{oidc.issuerUrl}}`. The full model is covered in
[Composed catalog apps](/concepts/22-composed-catalog-apps/).

## What the manifest leaves out

- **Where it runs.** A manifest does not choose a cluster,
  a provider or a region. Whoever runs the deploy picks the
  target. The same file goes to staging on one run and to
  production on the next.
- **Credential values.** Secret values never live in the
  file. They are referenced by name, generated by the
  platform, or asked for at install time.
- **How the build runs.** The file says what to build, not
  where or how. The build runner belongs to the tool.
- **Runtime-specific resources.** The manifest describes
  the application, not the form it takes on whatever runs it.
- **Tool-specific extensions.** Internal identifiers and
  vendor tuning are not allowed. Additions go through the
  spec, so every implementation gets them on equal terms.

## Three fields that belong to the install, not the file

The same repository can be installed twice, and the two
installs cannot share a name or a hostname. So three fields
can be overridden when you deploy: `--name`, `--exposure`
and `--domain`.

These are stored on the application and applied again on every
later deploy, so a deploy from someone else's machine does not
revert an install to the manifest's domain without notice. When
an override replaces something the manifest says, the deploy
prints both values.

Take care with `--name`. It is part of what identifies an
application, together with the cluster, repository and branch.
Passing a new one installs the same repository a second time
instead of updating the first, so once you have used it, pass it
on every deploy that targets that install.

## The manifest owns the keys it declares

For environment variables, the file wins. A key the manifest
declares is taken back by the manifest on every deploy, even if
somebody had pinned a value on it in the dashboard. A key the
manifest does not declare keeps whatever was set. Values passed
explicitly at deploy time beat both.

There are two exceptions. A key linked to a real secret is never
overwritten by a plain value from the file. A key the manifest
declares but cannot resolve, because its value comes from
somewhere else, keeps its stored value. Only a key the manifest
stops declaring entirely is treated as a removal.

## Validation is two halves

Whether a file parses and whether it would work on this
installation are different questions, and getting the second
one wrong can cost you eight minutes of a failed build.

**The first half is the schema.** It needs nothing: no
cluster, no login, no network. Flui validates against the
same published schema it deploys with, so the answer cannot
drift from what the deploy accepts.

**The second half asks this installation.** It checks seven
things a schema cannot answer, and, when Flui can read the
repository, whether the file matches it:

- the **target cluster**: does one answer to that id, and
  can it take a deploy;
- the **source repository**: is it connected to this
  account;
- the **build and registry credentials**: can this account
  build the image and push it;
- **room on the cluster**: do the CPU and memory it asks
  for fit what is free right now;
- **where it lands**: a workload cluster, or the control
  cluster that also runs the API, the dashboard and
  identity;
- **what this deploy does**: create a new application, or
  update one that already answers to this identity;
- **how it is reached**: internal, public under a name of
  yours, or public with no name bound yet.

Each answer is one of four: pass, warn, fail, or unknown.
Unknown never blocks: an installation that could not be read
has refused nothing, and reporting that as a failure would send
you rewriting a manifest that was fine. Warnings describe
consequences, not problems to fix. Deploying onto the control
cluster is supported, for example, and is reported as a warning.

The check also returns the manifest as it would be applied, with
the branch entry and the stored overrides already merged in. This
is often more useful than the verdict, because it shows what the
file and this installation produce together.

A manifest can satisfy the schema completely and still fail
every one of the checks. When the second half cannot run (you
are not signed in, or no cluster is named), the output says
which half ran, so you do not assume everything was checked.

`flui deploy --validate-only` runs both halves and writes
nothing; add `--json` for a machine-readable answer.
`flui catalog validate <file>` runs the schema half only, and
takes any kind. Agents have the same check as a tool.

## Two lists of role names

The published spec package and the product use different names
for the access roles. The spec lists `viewer`, `editor` and
`manager`. The product accepts `viewer`, `operator`,
`maintainer` and `owner`.

The mismatch goes both ways. An AccessPolicy the product accepts
is rejected by `flui catalog validate`, which validates against
the published schema. A policy written with the spec's names is
refused by `flui iam apply -f`. Neither tool is broken; they read
two versions of the same idea.

Write the product's names. For an AccessPolicy, run
`flui iam roles`: it lists the roles this installation accepts,
and which ones you are allowed to hand out. The role ladder is
described in [Who can reach what](/concepts/28-who-can-reach-what/).

## From manifest to running application

At deploy time Flui reads the file, lays the branch entry over
it, merges the overrides stored on the install, and turns the
result into whatever the target needs to host the application.
The manifest is the intent, and what runs is built from it. Every
deploy builds it again from the file, so the file stays an
accurate description of what runs.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [`flui-cloud/flui-spec`](https://github.com/flui-cloud/flui-spec):
  the authoritative spec, with field-by-field schema, narrative
  docs, JSON Schemas and examples.
- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/): what
  the manifest produces.
- [Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/):
  the other kind and how it differs.
- [Composed catalog apps](/concepts/22-composed-catalog-apps/):
  the multi-component `CatalogApp` shape in depth.
- [Scaling groups](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/): what the
  fourth document kind is for.
- [Who can reach what](/concepts/28-who-can-reach-what/):
  the roles an `AccessPolicy` names.
- [The build pipeline](/concepts/20-build-pipeline-today-and-tomorrow/):
  what happens between a manifest and a running container.
- [DNS as part of the deploy contract](/concepts/13-dns-integration/)
  and [TLS and certificates](/concepts/14-tls-and-certificates/):
  what the domain block triggers.

sections.title: Catalog vs Application
sections.body:
A `flui.yaml` declares one of two kinds: `Application` or
`CatalogApp`. They share the same outer envelope and the same
identity model, and both become the same kind of app inside
the platform, with the same lifecycle, operations and
observability. The only difference is where the container
image comes from.

This chapter covers that difference and how the two kinds
combine.

## kind: Application (your code)

An `Application` manifest describes an application built from a
source repository. You own the code, and the manifest sits in
the repository root. At deploy time the platform builds an
image from that source, pushes it to a container registry, and
deploys the image to the target cluster. The manifest's `build`
block says what to build (which Dockerfile, which context); the
rest of the manifest describes how the resulting image runs.

This is the path for deploying your own service: a web
frontend, a backend API, a worker, anything you write and
iterate on.

## kind: CatalogApp (ready-to-install software)

A `CatalogApp` manifest describes a pre-packaged application
whose image already exists on a container registry. The
manifest references the image by registry, name and tag, and
adds the installation parameters that make it usable: admin
credentials to generate, volume sizes, optional features. There
is no build step. Picking a catalog entry produces the same
kind of running app as building one from source, without the
build pipeline in front of it.

`CatalogApp` is not limited to entries Flui curates. Any
container image, yours or someone else's, can become a
deployable application by wrapping it in a `CatalogApp`
manifest. Declare its registry coordinates, the port it listens
on, the healthcheck and the volumes it needs, and you can run
it through Flui the same way as the curated entries. The
curated catalog and a manifest you write follow the same path;
the only difference is who wrote the file.

## The same lifecycle on both sides

Once deployed, an application from source and an application
from the catalog behave the same inside the platform. The same
commands stop, start, restart, scale and delete them. The same
dashboard views show their logs, metrics, status and crashes.
The same release history records every deploy and rollback.
Flui has one toolchain for both, and the dashboard files apps
by what they do (Applications, Data, System) rather than by
where the image came from.

## Three flavours of catalog entry

The catalog has three kinds of entry, by what they are meant
to do:

- **Standalone.** A complete application that runs on its own
  and serves its own purpose: an admin tool, a self-hosted
  service, anything you might install just to use.
- **Building block.** An application meant to back other
  applications rather than be reached directly, most often a
  database or a message queue. Building blocks are rarely the
  end goal; your `Application` is built on top of them.
- **Composed.** An entry that bundles several coordinated
  workloads installed together as one unit: a database, a
  cache and an app tier, say, provisioned and torn down as one
  atomic install. Each bundled component is rendered as its own
  workload, the components come up in dependency order, and the
  whole stack shows up as a single bundle in its list. A data
  store it bundles is also listed under Data. See
  [Composed catalog apps](/concepts/22-composed-catalog-apps/)
  for details.

## Composing catalog entries

Catalog entries also combine with each other. A `standalone`
catalog entry can declare that it needs a building-block entry
(typically a database or a queue) to work, and at install time
you pick how the dependency is satisfied:

- **A dedicated instance** is provisioned with the consumer, in
  the same install operation. The building block is created
  first and the consumer once the building block is healthy,
  with the credentials the building block generates injected
  into the consumer's configuration.
- **An existing instance** already deployed on the cluster is
  reused. The install deploys only the consumer and wires it to
  the existing building block, whose lifecycle is not part of
  this operation.

Either way, consumer and building block each get their own
entry (the consumer under Applications, the building block
under Data), each with its own lifecycle and operations once
they are running.

## One manifest, more than one install

A manifest is a file. An install is a running thing on a
cluster. The difference matters when you want one manifest
running twice, such as production and staging from the same
repository on the same cluster.

Both installs read the same `flui.yaml`. They cannot both use
the name the file gives, and they cannot both answer on the
hostname the file names. So three fields can be overridden
when you install:

- **name**: what this install is called;
- **exposure**: `public` or `internal`;
- **domain**: the hostname it answers on.

Everything else stays with the manifest: the build, the port,
the resources and the configuration defaults. The overrides
are the few things that belong to this copy rather than to the
code.

### The name is part of the identity

On the `Application` path an app is identified by four things
together: the cluster, the repository, the branch and the
name. So changing the name does not rename anything. A deploy
carrying a name Flui has not seen installs that repository a
second time, next to the first.

This part surprises people. Exposure and domain are remembered
on the install and keep taking precedence over the manifest on
later deploys; otherwise the next deploy from anyone's machine
would quietly move an install back to the manifest's hostname.
The name is not remembered, because it is what the lookup uses
to find the install in the first place. Pass it on every
deploy that targets that install. If you leave it off once,
the next deploy targets a different application.

### The catalog side does not have that problem

Installing a catalog entry twice always produces two separate
installs, each with its own generated identifier. A second
install never lands on top of the first, whatever you call
it. Here the name is a label you read in the app list, not a
key.

Exposure works differently too: an entry offers the public or
internal choice only if it declares that it can run privately.
The others run the way their manifest says.

## Where each side lives

Where the pieces sit for each kind:

| | `kind: Application` | `kind: CatalogApp` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Manifest | In the user's repository | Curated by the catalog, or user-authored against the spec |
| Image | Built from source by the platform's build pipeline, pushed to a registry | Pulled from a registry; no build step |
| Configuration | `build` + the runtime blocks | Installation parameters published by the entry |
| Install-time overrides | Name, exposure and domain; the name is part of the app's identity | Name and address; exposure only where the entry allows it |
| Lifecycle operations | The same on both sides |
| Observability | The same on both sides |

## Writing a custom catalog entry

Anything that runs as a container can be a `CatalogApp`. The
requirements are light: the image must be reachable from the
cluster, the manifest must declare the port and the
healthcheck the runtime uses to know the app is up, and any
persistent state the app keeps has to be expressible as a
volume. You can write a `CatalogApp` for any image you want and
deploy it through the same path as the curated entries.

The curated catalog is built the same way: each entry is a
`CatalogApp` manifest, written once, reviewed, and made
available to everyone.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/): what both
  kinds produce, regardless of where the image came from.
- [The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/): the
  shared envelope both kinds sit under.
- [Composed catalog apps](/concepts/22-composed-catalog-apps/):
  the composed flavour in depth, with components, auth modes,
  options and the install-time templating.
- [Install an application from the catalog](/tasks/install-from-the-catalog/):
  finding an entry, the answers it asks for at install time,
  and the name, address and exposure you can override.
- [Deploy an application from your repository](/tasks/deploy-an-application/):
  the `Application` path end to end, including what `--name`
  does to identity.
- [Framework templates](/concepts/19-framework-templates/): how
  templates speed up the `Application` path.
- [The build pipeline](/concepts/20-build-pipeline-today-and-tomorrow/):
  what happens between an `Application` manifest and a running
  container.

sections.title: Framework templates
sections.body:
For a new self-hosted application, the hard step usually comes
before the deployment: getting from an idea in a framework to a
repository the platform can build and deploy. Templates cover
that step. One command produces a repository that already
contains everything Flui needs to build, deploy and observe the
application. From then on, the code is yours.

## What a template gives you

A Flui template is a working starting point for an application
in a specific framework. When the platform creates a repository
from a template, you get a buildable, deployable application
that you can clone, change, push and watch deploy without
writing any infrastructure file yourself.

Every template repository comes with:

- A **Dockerfile** that builds a production-ready image of the
  framework, using the framework's idiomatic base.
- A **`flui.yaml`** that declares the application: its name, the
  port it listens on, the healthcheck path, and sensible defaults
  for resources and scaling.
- A **healthcheck endpoint** wired in the framework's own way (an
  API route in JavaScript fullstack frameworks, an actuator in
  Spring Boot, a view in Django, and so on), so the healthcheck
  the manifest points at answers from day one.
- A **build pipeline** that Flui writes into the repository on
  the first deploy and drives end to end, triggered by a push.

From there the deploy works like any other `Application`:
`flui deploy` reads the manifest, the build pipeline runs, the
image lands on the cluster, and the endpoint and certificate are
wired in.

## The first deploy, and every push after it

The first push of a template becomes a running application.
What the pushes after it do is up to you.

Every push triggers a build. What a successful build does next
depends on one setting.

- **The first deploy is unaffected.** The application is not
  live yet, so the finished build rolls straight out.
- **After that, rolling out is opt-in, one application at a
  time.** It is off unless someone turns it on. While it is off,
  a successful build is recorded as an **available version** and
  waits for someone to trigger a deploy.

Two commands cover the waiting versions:

- `flui app versions <app>` lists the image versions the
  registry holds for that application, and which one is
  deployed.
- `flui app redeploy <app> <tag-or-digest>` rolls one of
  them out, without rebuilding anything.

Pushing a commit and shipping to production are two different
intentions, and a template repository is where they are easiest
to confuse: the first push is meant to go live, the fiftieth
usually is not.

The switch lives on the application: `flui app auto-deploy
<app> --on` (or `--off`), and without a flag it shows the
current setting. The dashboard shows the setting as an
**Auto-deploy on push** badge on the application's Releases tab,
but does not change it.

## The frameworks Flui covers

The supported frameworks span the languages most self-hosted
applications are written in: JavaScript and TypeScript fullstack
and backend stacks, two frontend frameworks, two static-site
generators, a JVM backend, two Python backends and a .NET
backend. A generic catch-all template covers the cases none of
these fits.

The list is kept small because each template is a real
repository that someone has to maintain. The goal is to cover
the common shapes without a long tail of variants. The exact
set, with versions and command syntax, is in the CLI reference.

## What makes a repository Flui-compatible

A template is one example of a Flui-compatible repository: a
repository the platform can find, build and deploy. The contract
is small:

- a Dockerfile that produces a runnable image,
- a `flui.yaml` at the root that describes how the resulting
  application should run,
- a working healthcheck endpoint matching what the manifest
  declares.

Any repository that meets those three requirements deploys
through the same flow as a template-generated one. If you
outgrow the official templates, you can fork one, edit it
freely, or write your own from scratch. The platform does not
care where the repository came from, as long as the contract
holds.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/): what a
  template produces, once deployed.
- [The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/): the
  shape of the `flui.yaml` every template ships.
- [The build pipeline](/concepts/20-build-pipeline-today-and-tomorrow/):
  the build flow that the template's pipeline plugs into.
- [CLI: Templates](/cli/templates/): the command-by-command
  reference, including the current list of supported frameworks
  with their versions.

sections.title: The build pipeline
sections.body:
For an application built from source, there is a step between
pushing code and a container running on the cluster: the build.
Where the build runs affects the cost model, what fails when
something breaks, and where credentials need to live.

This chapter covers the build pipeline that turns a
`kind: Application` manifest and a source repository into a
deployable image: what it does, what happens to the image once
the build succeeds, and what the pipeline does not try to do.

## Build at the source

The pipeline runs alongside your source repository, on the CI
service of the platform that hosts it. When a deploy of a
`kind: Application` is triggered, Flui writes (or refreshes) a
build workflow inside your repository, makes sure the workflow
has the credentials it needs to push the resulting image to a
container registry, and watches the run until it completes.

The pipeline uses your CI tool's runners, logs, reruns and
interface. Flui drives it but does not host it.

_Diagram: A build records a new version; whether it rolls out depends on whether the application is live yet and on deploy on push._

## Where the image is kept

The built image goes to a container registry, and the cluster
pulls it from there. An installation chooses which one when it
is created.

- **Your GitHub account's registry (GHCR).** The default. Each
  image sits next to the repository it was built from, in the
  account that owns it. Pulling a private image back needs a
  classic GitHub token, because GitHub accepts nothing else for
  its container registry, so connecting GitHub through the
  GitHub App asks for that token as a second step.
- **The installation's own registry.** Chosen with
  `flui env create --image-registry flui`. The installation runs
  a registry of its own, at the same address as its API. Every
  application gets its own place there and its own credentials:
  the build can only push that application's images and the
  cluster can only pull them. Connecting GitHub then needs
  repository access and nothing else, which makes the GitHub App
  a one-click setup. Images go away when their application does,
  each application keeps its three most recently pushed and its
  three most recently used versions, and an installation can cap
  the space one application takes.

The second option is one more component to run. It suits an
installation that several people share, where nobody should hand
over a token that sees every repository they own.

The installation's own registry keeps images on a volume of the
control cluster by default. Created with
`--image-registry-storage s3`, it keeps them in a bucket instead,
and then several copies of it serve builds and pulls side by side.
Flui can create that bucket on Scaleway with a key that reaches
nothing else, or use one of yours: see
[the registry commands](/cli/integrations/#the-installations-image-registry).
Either way, the dashboard and `flui registry storage status` show
the space the images take, and administrators get an alert before
it becomes a problem.

## When the build succeeds

Flui treats a finished build and a running application as
separate things.

When the run reports success, Flui records the image against
the application, together with the commit and the branch it was
built from. This always happens. `flui app versions <app>`
shows the images available for that application and which of
them is deployed.

Rolling that image out is a separate step. It happens
automatically only when the application has **deploy on push**
turned on. When it is off, which is the default, the new image
sits in the list as an available version, and nothing changes
on the cluster until somebody asks for it, from the
application's **Releases** tab or with:

```
flui app redeploy <app> <tag-or-digest>
```

Off is the default because, with it on, every commit to the
branch becomes a deploy whether or not its author meant it to.
That suits a hobby project but not anything someone is on call
for, so the person who owns the application decides.

An application's first deploy does not wait for this. At that
point the application is not live yet, so no running version is
being replaced, and waiting for a second instruction would only
leave a half-created application doing nothing.

When deploy on push is on, the roll-out does more than swap the
image. Flui first reads `flui.yaml` at the pushed commit, so the
push applies what the committed file says (environment
variables, port, resources) as well as the newer image.

Deploy on push is a setting on the application. Turn it on or
off with `flui app auto-deploy <app> --on|--off`. The dashboard
shows when it is on, and then disables the Releases tab's
Deploy buttons, because the next build would replace a
hand-picked version.

## Build arguments reach the image

Some values have to be present while the image is being built,
not when the container starts. The usual case is a frontend
framework that bakes a public API URL into the bundle at build
time. Setting it as a runtime environment variable is too late,
because the value was already compiled into the JavaScript.

The manifest has a place for those:

```yaml
build:
  strategy: dockerfile
  dockerfile: Dockerfile
  args:
    NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: https://api.example.com
```

Every entry under `build.args` is passed to the image build as a
build argument. Flui resolves them from the manifest and writes
them into the generated build workflow, so they stay in step
with the rest of the build description instead of being
assembled by the CI run itself.

This has two consequences:

- **They are not secrets.** The values land in a workflow file
  inside your repository and are baked into the image. Anyone
  who can read the repository or pull the image can read them.
  A credential belongs in the environment variables of the
  running application, marked as a secret, never here.
- **They do not vary per environment.** The manifest's
  per-environment overrides leave the `build` block out, so
  that one built image moves between environments instead of
  being rebuilt for each of them.

## Why an external pipeline

Building images is heavy work: compilation, dependency
downloads, layer composition, image push. Doing it on the same
cluster that serves production traffic creates a
noisy-neighbour problem at the worst moment. Running it outside
the cluster avoids that.

The CI services Flui integrates with also provide a mature
build cache that makes repeated builds fast, free build minutes
that cover a typical project, and a debugging surface you
already know: when a build fails, you open the run page and
read the logs. Flui does not have to rebuild any of that.

## The trade-offs

This choice has costs:

- **External dependency.** If the CI service is down, new
  deploys cannot land. Running applications keep running and the
  observability stack stays up, but the deploy path depends on
  a service Flui does not control.
- **Credentials in your CI.** Pushing to the registry requires
  a credential, and that credential lives where the workflow
  runs. You have to be comfortable trusting that service with
  it.
- **Latency floor.** Running the build elsewhere sets a lower
  bound on how fast the deploy loop can close. For tight
  iteration, the build time on whichever runner the CI picks is
  the floor.
- **Tied to one CI service.** The integration is specific to
  one CI service. A repository hosted elsewhere has no build
  path through Flui.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/): what the
  build pipeline produces, once the image is on the cluster.
- [The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/):
  the file the `build` block above lives in.
- [Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/):
  why the build pipeline matters only for `kind: Application`,
  and not for `kind: CatalogApp`.
- [CLI: Applications](/cli/applications/): the command-by-command
  reference for inspecting builds and managing image versions.

sections.title: Storage classes and dedicated placement
sections.body:
Most workloads need nothing special from the disk under them.
They write the occasional file, read it back later, and can move
from one node to another whenever the cluster needs them to.

Other workloads depend on the disk behaving in a precise way:
writes that land in order, locks that are honoured, and a save
that is really on disk when the kernel says it is. Databases are the usual
example, but any workload that relies on real filesystem
semantics belongs in this group. Shared storage built on a
network filesystem cannot always guarantee those semantics, and
the result ranges from surprising performance to quietly losing
the last seconds of writes.

Flui ships two storage classes, one for each group, and lets the
application pick.

_Diagram: Shared storage is reached from every node, so an application can start again anywhere; a dedicated disk pins its application to one node._

## Two storage classes

Every persistent volume on a Flui cluster ends up in one of two
classes:

- **Shared.** The default class. A single volume on the master
  is exposed to every node as a network filesystem, with a local
  cache on each node. An application on any node reads and writes
  through the same address, so if its node is lost it starts
  again elsewhere with its data. Use it for stateless apps, log
  directories and any workload that occasionally writes a file
  and reads it later.
- **Dedicated.** The node-local class, backed by a node's own
  disk. Writes go straight to that disk with no network hop, and
  the application that uses it is pinned to the node hosting the
  disk. Once placed, it does not move. Use it for databases and
  anything that depends on the disk behaving like a real disk.

The application makes the choice: a catalog manifest declares it
with `persistence.scope: dedicated`, and Flui does the rest. An
application that declares nothing gets shared placement.

A new shared volume becomes usable from every node only after
Flui has proven that every node sees the shared storage. Every
ten minutes it writes a fresh token on the master and reads it
back on each other node. While any node fails that check, new
volumes stay on the node that created them, and a volume keeps
the node it was created on. `flui app status` names any volume of
an application that is tied to one node.

## Where dedicated workloads live

When an application asks for dedicated placement, Flui decides
which node hosts its disk. By default this is a worker node, not
the master. At deploy time Flui looks at every worker's free
capacity and pins the app to the one with the most room. It
records that choice as the app's dedicated node name, so later
operations know where its disk lives. Keeping dedicated workloads
off the master keeps stateful, node-bound workloads away from the
control plane and lets their hosts grow independently.

This default needs a worker to exist. If a cluster has no worker,
the result depends on the cluster. A workload cluster places the
app on its master, since there is no Flui control plane there to
protect. The control cluster, which runs Flui itself, does not
fall back: it fails with the code `NO_WORKER_FOR_DEDICATED_APP`
and tells you to add a worker (or to use the escape hatch below).

### The master escape hatch

For small cases, such as a single-node cluster or a choice to keep
one dedicated app on the control plane, an app carries an
`allowMasterPlacement` flag (a boolean, default `false`). It
exists on the application itself and on the catalog-install
input, so you can set it when installing or later. From the CLI
it is `--allow-master`. When it is set, a dedicated app may run on
the master even though no worker is available. When it is not
set, a control cluster with no worker fails as described above.
By default, dedicated work goes to a worker unless you say
otherwise.

## A locked node

A node hosting at least one dedicated workload is locked: the
node-removal flow refuses to delete it while those workloads live
there, and lists which applications would lose their disk if it
went away.

To unlock the node, move the dedicated workloads off it (to
another worker, or to the master through `allowMasterPlacement`),
and the node-removal flow then accepts. The platform does not
move dedicated data between nodes automatically. That step is
left to the operator, who knows whether a downtime window is
acceptable and whether a backup and restore is the right way to
move the data.

## A pre-flight check before deploy

Before a dedicated workload is deployed (or redeployed after a
configuration change), Flui checks the target node: it asks the
cluster how much CPU and memory the node has free and compares
that with what the workload needs. If the node cannot fit the
workload, the deploy fails immediately with an error that shows
the gap and the ways to close it: resize the node, or move the
workload to one with room.

The check runs at every deploy, not only at install. Raising the
resource request of a dedicated workload either succeeds because
the room is there, or fails with a useful diagnosis instead of
leaving the workload stuck in a degraded state.

## Vertical scaling: giving the host more

Once a workload is pinned, the only way to give it more CPU or
memory is to give the host node more. A dedicated workload cannot
add another replica, because there is only one disk it can use,
so you grow the machine underneath it.

Resizing a node is planned maintenance. The cluster powers the
node down, asks the provider to change the server type, powers it
back up, and waits for the cluster to report it healthy before
the operation completes. The workload is unavailable for a few
minutes, which cannot be avoided on the providers Flui integrates
with, and the operation's plan shows that window before anything
happens. The command reference for resizing is in
[CLI: Environments](/cli/environments/).

## Growing the shared storage

The shared storage also fills up over time as the apps using it
accumulate data. Flui has an operation to grow it: the volume at
the provider is resized, the filesystem on it is extended, and
the new space is immediately visible to every node that mounts
it. The operation runs online, with no downtime and no
application restarts, but it cannot be reversed: the providers
Flui integrates with let volumes grow but not shrink. Plan the
target size, because the only way back to a smaller volume is a
fresh cluster.

## When an application goes away

A volume that outlives its application keeps costing money,
even though nothing is running and nothing looks broken.

So removing an application removes its volumes too. The same
applies to a catalog install with several parts: uninstalling it
removes the storage of every part, not only the one you named.

Because this cannot be undone, every surface tells you what will
be lost before it asks. `flui app delete` lists each volume with
its size, then asks you to type the application's name to
confirm. The dashboard's delete dialog shows the same list. An
agent can read the same removal preview before it proposes
anything.

All three read the same answer from the API, so they always
agree, and the removal deletes exactly what that answer named.

When Flui cannot reach the cluster to read the volumes, it
reports the loss as **unknown**, never as "none".

## Storage nobody is using

A cluster can still hold volumes no application uses, left by a
removal that could not finish or created outside Flui. Nothing
else lists them, so nobody knows they are being paid for.

`flui cluster volumes` lists them. It reports each abandoned
volume with its size, the application it belonged to when that is
still known, and a sentence explaining why it is considered
abandoned. The dashboard shows the same list on the cluster's
Storage tab.

To remove one, run `flui cluster volumes --remove <ref>` with the
reference the listing prints next to it. Removal is permanent, so
it asks you to type the volume's name first. The server then runs
the whole check again before it deletes anything, because the
list you read may be minutes old and something may have started
