using that volume since.

An agent can read this list but cannot act on it. No agent
permission deletes a volume; an agent can only tell you what it
found and give you the command.

### How the scan decides a volume is abandoned

The two possible mistakes are not equal. Missing a volume leaves
you paying for a disk. Naming the wrong one offers to delete
somebody's data. So the scan is built to miss volumes rather than
name the wrong one.

A volume is called abandoned only if all of these hold: no
running workload uses it, no application that still exists owns
it, it is not in a location the platform reserves for itself, and
it has existed for at least fifteen minutes, so it cannot be
something still being created.

It also needs a positive reason, and there are four: Flui's own
mark on it names an application that is gone; its name matches an
application Flui removed; its name could only have been made for
a workload that no longer exists; or every application that ever
lived beside it has been deleted.

A volume with none of those (no mark from Flui, a name that
matches nothing, next to applications that are still alive) is
never reported. A volume created outside Flui, with no mark from
it, can fall into that gap. So an empty list means
nothing was found by these rules, not that nothing is left. The
same goes for a cluster that cannot be read at all: the listing
says so instead of showing a false zero.

There is a second, coarser kind of leftover, at the provider
instead of inside a cluster: a block volume that survived the
destruction of its cluster. `flui env orphan-volumes` lists
those, and `--cleanup` removes them.

## What Flui does not do here

Moving a dedicated workload from one host to another does not
migrate its data automatically. Flui changes the placement, but
the disk does not follow. You have to stop the workload, copy its
data to the new host yourself (usually a backup followed by a
restore on the target), and redeploy it with the new placement.
This is the main caveat. It does not affect the common path:
install a database, later resize its host, and optionally grow
the shared volume.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/): the
  application surface that declares storage, exposure and
  placement, and the home of the install-time capacity gate.
- [Nodes and cluster topology](/concepts/06-nodes-and-cluster-topology/):
  the nodes a workload can be pinned to.
- [The database console](/concepts/25-the-database-console/): the
  first-party tooling for the databases that most often want
  dedicated, node-local storage.
- [CLI: Environments](/cli/environments/): the command-by-command
  reference for resizing nodes and growing the shared volume.
- [CLI: Applications](/cli/applications/): removing an
  application, and finding the storage of applications that no
  longer exist.

sections.title: Composed catalog apps
sections.body:
Some software is more than a single container. Nextcloud needs a
database and a cache, plus an optional document server. WordPress
needs a database next to its web tier. Immich needs several
services that only make sense together. A **composed catalog app**
is a single `CatalogApp` manifest that bundles all of those
workloads and installs them as one unit. They are provisioned
together, removed together, and shown as one entry in your app
list.

This chapter covers how a composed entry is put together, how its
pieces are wired, and the choices it offers at install time. The
broader difference between `Application` and `CatalogApp` is in
[Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/).

## What a composed app is

A composed entry sets `type: composed` (`CatalogSpecComposed` in
the schema). Instead of the single `image`, `ports` and `env` body
of a standalone entry, it carries a `components` list. Each
component becomes its own running app, with its own workload, its
own internal address and its own storage volume if it declares
one, as if it had been installed on its own. The composed manifest
coordinates them: it decides what gets created, in what order, and
how the pieces find each other.

You do not install a database, then a cache, then the app, and
then wire three sets of credentials by hand. You pick one entry,
answer a few prompts, and the whole stack comes up wired together.
If a required component fails, the install stops and is marked
failed. Running it again picks up where it stopped (see
Idempotency below).

## The component model

Each entry under `components` has a `name`, an `image`, and the
same runtime blocks a standalone app has (`ports`, `volumes`,
`env`, `resources`, `scaling`, `healthcheck`). Two extra fields
coordinate the stack:

- **`dependsOn`**: names of other components that must be healthy
  before this one starts. The installer brings components up in
  dependency order, so a web tier marked `dependsOn: [db]` waits for
  the database to pass its healthcheck first.
- **`when.option`**: includes the component only when a named
  install-time option is enabled. A component without a `when`
  is always included.

Components reference each other through templating in their `env`.
Here a web component reads its database host and credentials from
the `db` component:

```yaml
components:
  - name: db
    image:
      registry: docker.io
      repository: library/mariadb
      tag: "11"
    env:
      - name: MARIADB_USER
        value: wordpress
      - name: MARIADB_PASSWORD
        valueFrom:
          generate: secret
          length: 32
    # ...ports, volumes, resources, scaling, healthcheck

  - name: web
    dependsOn:
      - db
    image:
      registry: docker.io
      repository: library/wordpress
      tag: "6.5-apache"
    env:
      - name: WORDPRESS_DB_HOST
        value: "{{components.db.host}}:3306"
      - name: WORDPRESS_DB_PASSWORD
        value: "{{components.db.env.MARIADB_PASSWORD}}"
        secret: true
    # ...ports, volumes, resources, scaling, healthcheck
```

The `{{components.db.host}}` and `{{components.db.env.*}}` tokens
resolve at install time to the database's internal address
and the value the database generated. The generated password is
created once on the `db` side and injected into `web` as a secret
(`secret: true`), so it never appears in plaintext.

## Auth modes

A composed entry declares which authentication strategies it
supports under `spec.auth`:

- `spec.auth.modes` is the list of supported modes.
- `spec.auth.default` is the one chosen when the installer is not
  told otherwise.

At install time you pick one mode via the install's `authMode`,
which must be one of `oidc`, `proxy`, `native` or `none`. `native`
leaves the app's own login in place; `none` disables auth wiring;
`proxy` puts the app behind a header-injecting proxy; `oidc` wires
the app to Flui's identity provider.

### OIDC auto-provisioning

When you choose `oidc`, Flui sets up single sign-on for you. It
registers a web OIDC client with Flui's own Zitadel-backed identity
provider, scoped to the install's resolved hostname, and records
the resulting `oidcAppId` and `oidcProjectId` on the install
record. Flui uses those IDs to remove the client when you
uninstall, so an SSO registration never outlives its app.

The client's credentials reach the app through the channel the
manifest declares under `spec.auth.oidc`:

- **`envMapping`**: the issuer URL, client ID and client secret are
  injected as environment variables the app reads natively.
- **`configFile`**: a rendered config file is written into the
  container at a declared path.
- **A `postInstall` exec step**: the app is configured through its
  own CLI. Nextcloud, for instance, runs
  `php occ user_oidc:provider Flui` to register Flui as an OIDC
  provider after the container is up.

In every case the credentials arrive through the templating tokens
described below and are never hard-coded in the manifest.

## Install-time options

`spec.options` is a list of boolean feature toggles. Each option has
a `key`, a human `label`, an optional `description`, and a `default`:

```yaml
options:
  - key: office
    label: "Office editing (Collabora)"
    description: "Adds a document-server component."
    default: false
```

At install you pass an `options` map that sets each `key` to
`true` or `false`. Any key you omit falls back to its `default`.
Options control two things:

- **Components**, via `when.option`. Enabling `office` on Nextcloud
  adds the Collabora document-server component; leaving it off
  skips that component.
- **Post-install steps**, via the same `when.option`, so the step
  that configures the optional component runs only when the option
  is on.

This way one manifest describes both a minimal install and a full
one, without splitting into two entries.

## Multi-endpoint

A composed stack can expose more than one component to the
internet. Any component with a port marked `expose: true` gets its
own endpoint and FQDN, resolved by Flui's endpoint-mode resolver in
the same way as a standalone app's endpoint. Components with no
exposed port stay internal: a database or cache is reachable only
from the other components over the internal address, and is never
published.

## Post-install steps

`spec.postInstall` is a list of actions that run after the
components are deployed and healthy. Each step is either:

- **`http`**: an HTTP call (`method`, `path`, optional `headers`,
  `body`, `expectStatus`) against the running app.
- **`exec`**: a command run inside a component's container (the
  `occ` calls above are exec steps).

Steps can be conditioned with `when.authMode` and `when.option`, so
the OIDC provider registration runs only in `oidc` mode and the
office configuration step runs only when `office` is enabled. Use
these steps for work that needs a live, configured app, such as
trusting the public hostname, registering the SSO provider or
enabling an optional feature.

## Templating tokens resolved at install

Besides the cross-component references shown above, three groups
of tokens are resolved at install time and are specific to composed
installs:

- **`{{self.fqdn}}`**: a component's own public hostname, available
  before the component boots. The install slug is deterministic, so
  Flui knows a component's final FQDN in advance. A component that
  needs to advertise its own public URL (Collabora's `server_name`,
  for example) gets it at create time instead of being reconfigured
  later.
- **`{{oidc.clientId}}`, `{{oidc.clientSecret}}`,
  `{{oidc.issuerUrl}}`**: the credentials of the web OIDC client
  Flui provisioned for this install (see above). They appear in
  `envMapping`, in a rendered `configFile`, or in a `postInstall`
  exec command, and are filled in only when `authMode` is `oidc`.
- **`{{install.resolvedFqdn}}`, `{{components.<name>.fqdn}}`**:
  the install's public hostname and a component's, available
  to `postInstall` steps once the endpoints exist.

## How a composed install appears

In `flui app list` a composed install shows up as a single
bundle of kind `composed` (a single app is `standalone`), instead
of as several unrelated apps. The bundle represents the whole
stack, so Nextcloud appears as one entry, not as an app, a
database and a cache side by side.

To see what is inside, pass `-x`/`--expanded`:

```bash
flui app list --expanded
```

That reveals the individual components, each with its own slug,
status and exposure. Without the flag, the list stays at the bundle
level and tells you a composed app has components you can expand.

## Idempotency

You can safely run an install again. The installer looks up the
components that already exist for the install and reuses them
instead of creating duplicates. After a partial failure or a
retried job, the install continues where it left off instead of
creating a second copy of the stack. For the same reason, the
post-install steps and the OIDC wiring are safe to reach more than
once.

## A note on capacity

Before a composed install starts, Flui sums the resource requests of
every component that will be included and checks them against what
the cluster has free. If there is not enough room (keeping a
safety margin), it refuses the install. This is the same capacity
check that applies to any install. How CPU and memory are counted
is covered in [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/).

## Where to read next

- [The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/): the
  shared envelope, including the fields of a composed manifest.
- [Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/):
  the three kinds of catalog entry and where composed fits.
- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/): what each
  component becomes once it is running, and the capacity check in
  full.
- [`flui deploy`](/cli/deploy/): the command reference for
  installing and deploying.

sections.title: Inference and bring-your-own-model
sections.body:
Some Flui features need a large language model: the assistant that
drives the platform in natural language, and the AI assist in the
database console. Those features do not care where the model comes
from. Anything that wants inference asks for a single, normalized
endpoint, and a resolver works out how to produce it.

The endpoint always has the same shape: an OpenAI-compatible
`{ baseUrl, apiKey }`. Flui adds no abstraction over the model
itself; model ids, request format and streaming are plain
OpenAI-compatible. Flui only decides how the endpoint is sourced and
credentialed, and that is where the two sources below differ.

## Two ways to get an endpoint

### Native: inference as a provider capability

Some cloud providers also run an OpenAI-compatible inference service.
When they do, Flui models it as a capability the provider declares,
like firewalls or DNS: an `InferenceCapability` carrying a `baseUrl`,
an optional curated `models` list for display, a `euDataResidency`
flag and a `sharesComputeCredentials` flag.

For Scaleway, `sharesComputeCredentials` is `true`: the provider's
inference service authenticates with the same IAM secret Flui already
holds to provision your infrastructure. When you point Flui at a
Scaleway account, you get inference with no separate AI key to
create, paste or rotate. Flui reuses the compute credential as the
inference bearer token.

A provider used only for inference, never for compute, would have no
compute credential to borrow. For that case Flui supports a dedicated
credential for inference, kept under the same credential model as
everything else. Scaleway does not need one, because its single
credential covers both.

The curated `models` list on the capability is only a placeholder
shown before a key exists. Once Flui has a working credential, it
reads the live model list from `{baseUrl}/models`, so the models you
can pick are the ones the provider offers right now.

### A connection you bring yourself

The second source is a connection you configure: any
OpenAI-compatible endpoint, such as OpenAI, Mistral, a
Claude-compatible gateway, or a server you run yourself. Such a
connection declares no capabilities and provisions no infrastructure,
so Flui does not treat it as a provider. It holds only connection
config: a `base_url`, an API key (stored encrypted), an optional list
of `models`, and an `is_default` flag.

These connections have their own small API under
`inference/connections`: you can list them, create one, validate it
against its endpoint, and delete it. Validation calls the endpoint.
The dashboard validates as soon as you save, so a bad key or wrong
URL shows up then, instead of the first time the assistant tries to
answer a question. Over the API, saving does not check the key; call
validate yourself.

Native inference comes with a provider you connect. A connection you
bring is independent of any provider, and works the same whether or
not you run any Flui-managed infrastructure.

## Two levels: the installation's, and your own

A connection you bring sits on one of two levels, and the level alone
decides who can see and use it.

**The installation's connection** is visible to and usable by
everyone. It is the instance's own credential to a model provider:
one key, spent by every assistant on the installation. Whoever
manages integrations connects and disconnects it.

**Your own connection** belongs to one person. Nobody else sees it in
a list, and, more importantly, nobody else can spend it. You can
connect one and disconnect it again without any permission, because a
person who may add a key but not remove it is in the worst state a
credential model can produce.

The dashboard's settings screen manages the installation's
connections only, and hides those controls from anyone who may not
manage integrations, instead of showing a button that answers with a
refusal. You create a private connection through the API: `POST` to
`inference/connections/mine`, and `DELETE` on
`inference/connections/mine/<id>` to remove it.

### Privacy is enforced where the key is spent

Hiding a private connection from other people's lists protects
nothing on its own. Almost nothing that uses a connection reads the
list: the assistant's chat, the agent loop and each console assistant
take a connection id from a request and turn it straight into a live
key. So Flui checks whose connection it is at that point, the one
place all of those paths pass through.

As a result, a colleague who learns the id of your connection still
cannot use it. Their attempt gets the same answer, in the same words,
as an id that never existed, so guessing ids reveals nothing.

Validating a connection goes through the same check, because
validating spends it: the check calls the model provider with the
key. A colleague cannot even test your private connection, let alone
chat with it.

### Nothing is promoted quietly

A private connection stays private. Flui has no path that turns one
into the installation's connection: not when it is created, not
later, and not when the person who brought it stops using Flui. It
goes with that person, and nobody inherits it. If the installation
should have a shared model, somebody connects one at the
installation's level.

### Defaults do not cross levels

Marking your own connection as the default makes it the default for
you. It does not replace the installation's default for anyone else,
and it is never handed to a colleague who asked for no connection in
particular. That would leak the connection without anyone needing its
id.

### One person can see everything, and still cannot spend it

Someone who may manage users (the `owner` rung) sees every connection
in the list, private ones included, because somebody has to be able
to answer "what is plugged into this instance?". They can also remove
one. They cannot use it: seeing a colleague's row does not let them
charge that colleague's model account, and the resolver answers them
as if the connection did not exist, as it does for anyone else.

### An empty list is not proof

Because private connections are listed to nobody else, an empty list
does not mean nothing is connected. It means nothing is connected
that you can see. This matters most for an agent reporting on the
installation, and Flui tells the agent so explicitly, so it does not
draw the wrong conclusion.

## How the default endpoint is chosen

Most of the time the assistant does not name a specific source; it
asks for the inference endpoint. The resolver answers in a fixed
order of preference:

1. **A configured native provider**, EU-first by the order providers
   are declared. If an inference-capable provider has a usable
   credential, it wins.
2. Otherwise, **a connection flagged as default that you can use**:
   your own first, then the installation's.
3. Otherwise, **the most recent connection you can use**. When
   nothing is flagged, a usable connection is better than failing for
   lack of a flag.

If none of these produce an endpoint, resolution fails with "no
inference endpoint configured" instead of guessing. Native providers
come first because, when one is present, inference is usually
already paid for and credentialed through the account you provision
with, which is the simplest path.

## What an agent may do with a model connection

An agent connected to Flui speaks through the model, so giving it
authority over the model connection needs care. Two rules apply.

**An agent cannot unplug the installation's model.** Deleting that
connection requires the permission to manage integrations, and no
agent scope carries it. An agent that could remove the endpoint every
assistant on the installation runs on would be one bad turn away from
a silent outage.

**An agent can ask a person to connect one.** The tool
`inference_connection_request` does this. It has no argument that
could carry an API key, and it never sees one. It reports the
connections it can see, states that private connections are not
counted, and returns the settings screen where a person picks a
provider and pastes the key.

## EU data residency is first-class

`euDataResidency` is a property of the capability, shown alongside
each native provider. For a self-hosted platform that may run under
European data rules, where the prompt goes is part of the decision,
so Flui shows it when you choose a provider. Scaleway's inference,
for example, declares EU residency. A connection you bring points
wherever you configure it, so residency there is up to you.

## Recommended models

Picking a model id from a raw `/models` list is not obvious. Names
are version-pinned and not portable across providers, and some
models are a poor fit for tool use or cost more than you want for a
first run. Flui ships a recommendation policy that you can override.

The policy is a config file at
`assistant/config/recommended-models.json`. It names a
`recommendedProvider` to start with, Scaleway, with the model
`deepseek-v4-flash-0731`: it runs in the EU on the credential you
already use for your servers, and it gave the most accurate answers
in Flui's own test questions. Then, per provider, it lists
version-pinned model ids with short descriptions. For Scaleway that
is `deepseek-v4-flash-0731` as the default and `gpt-oss-120b` as a
cheaper alternative. An entry can carry a caveat `note` so a
trade-off is visible before you switch. A connection you bring
yourself is not in the list, and its models stay selectable in the
picker under the other models. An environment override can replace
the whole file, so an operator can change the recommendations
without a code change.

The recommendations are read at startup, validated, and exposed
through the assistant API, so the dashboard can preselect a sensible
default instead of showing an unfiltered model list.

## Who consumes inference

Every AI feature uses the resolved endpoint:

- **The Flui Assistant**, the natural-language layer over the
  platform, runs against whatever the resolver returns. See
  [The Flui assistant and MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/).
- **The database console's AI assist**, which turns a question into a
  query, uses the same resolved endpoint in every console family that
  has one. See [The database console](/concepts/25-the-database-console/).

Each asks for the endpoint as the person on the other end of the
conversation, which keeps a private connection private in a chat as
well as in a list.

Because they all go through one resolver, configuring inference once
enables every AI feature at the same time, with the same data
residency and credentials.

## Where to read next

- [How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/):
  why inference is modelled as a provider capability, like firewalls
  or DNS, rather than a special case.
- [The Flui assistant and MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/):
  the primary consumer of the resolved endpoint.
- [The database console](/concepts/25-the-database-console/): the
  other consumer, where AI assist turns questions into queries.
- [Who can reach what](/concepts/28-who-can-reach-what/): the role
  ladder the `owner` rung above belongs to.

sections.title: The Flui assistant and MCP
sections.body:
Flui's assistant is a full surface of the product. It answers
from a compiled knowledge base, it can act through a shared tool
registry, and every action it can take follows the same rules
whether a person drives it in the dashboard or an external agent
calls it over MCP.

This chapter covers how that is built and the safety model
underneath it. For an assistant that can deploy and uninstall your
apps, the part that matters most is what stops it from doing the
wrong thing.

## Two surfaces, one tool registry

There are two ways into the same capabilities:

- **The in-product assistant**: the chat inside Flui's dashboard.
  You ask a question or make a request in plain language. It
  answers from the docs, and when you ask it to act it runs a
  tool-use loop on your behalf.
- **The MCP server**: a
  [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/)
  endpoint that offers the same tools to external agents: your own
  scripts, an agent in your editor, another LLM application.

A tool is written once. One registry backs both the assistant loop
and the MCP server, so there is no second surface to keep in sync
and no second place where the safety checks could drift apart.

The registry holds over a hundred and sixty tools in about twenty
families: applications, the catalog, observability, manifest
validation, infrastructure and the operations that change it,
scaling, DNS, the gateway, backups, migrations, scheduled jobs,
mail, repositories, access, how this installation is run, and a
family that asks a person for a credential. Nobody sees all of them
at once, for reasons covered in the safety model below.

Both surfaces get their model from Flui's inference layer instead
of a hard-coded provider. See
[Inference and bring-your-own-LLM](/concepts/23-inference-and-byo-llm/)
for how that endpoint is resolved.

### A tool has no private door into the product

The rest of the safety model rests on one rule: a tool reaches Flui
only by calling Flui's own API, as the caller's own principal. It
does not hold the services underneath and does not create a token
for itself. It sends a request over the same route your browser
would use, carrying the credential the agent presented.

Every guard Flui has sits on the request path: who may reach this
application, which sections you hold, what a guest is kept out of.
A tool that called the code directly would bypass all of them, so
it makes a real request instead.

As a result, a tool call meets exactly the checks a person clicking
would meet. An agent cannot be given a shortcut that a person does
not have.

## The assistant answers from a knowledge base

The assistant does not use a general-purpose model's training data
to answer questions about Flui. Flui's documentation is compiled
into a knowledge base: a single versioned artifact (`kb.json`)
built by a script from the concept docs, the CLI prose, a generated
CLI reference, the `flui.yaml` schema and a hand-written guardrails
file. The assistant answers only from this corpus.

The guardrails ask the assistant not to invent commands, flags,
manifest fields or version numbers. If the answer is not in the
corpus, it says so and points you to `flui <command> --help` or the
docs. The knowledge base is also
stamped with the CLI, platform and schema versions it was built
against, so the assistant can tell you which version it is
describing.

This is why these docs have to be accurate. The page you are
reading is one of the sources compiled into the knowledge base, so
an inaccurate page becomes a wrong answer the assistant gives with
confidence.

### A scope gate that also routes

Sending the whole corpus to the model on every message would be
slow and expensive. Flui avoids that with one cheap model call, a
guard step, that does two jobs:

1. **Scope gate.** It decides whether your message is about Flui at
   all. A clearly off-topic question (the weather, philosophy,
   general trivia) gets a short, friendly reply in your own
   language saying the assistant only helps with Flui, and the
   question itself is not answered. The gate leans strongly toward
   answering: greetings, follow-ups and anything that plausibly
   concerns running apps on Flui count as on-topic.
2. **Router.** For an on-topic message, the same call returns the
   ids of the one to four most relevant knowledge sections. Only
   those go into the answering prompt, which keeps it small.

### The tool-use loop

When you ask the assistant to do something, it runs a loop: the
model can call tools, see their results and call more tools, up to
a bounded number of rounds, before it writes a final answer. In the
dashboard this is streamed, so you see the text and each tool step
as they happen.

The loop has safeguards so it stays reliable on medium and small
models. Some of them:

- **A URL guard.** Application endpoint URLs are passed through
  only when they came from a tool result; anything else is stripped
  before it reaches you. Every link you get was produced by the
  platform, not assembled in the answer.
- **Doc-link surfacing.** The sections the router used for the
  answer are turned, deterministically, into links to the published
  docs.
- **Parameter recovery and rate-limit handling.** If a tool call
  comes back malformed, or a provider's per-minute limit is hit,
  the loop recovers and retries instead of failing the whole turn.

Because the router narrows the corpus, the answers are grounded in
it, and these guards are code rather than model behaviour, the
assistant does not need a large frontier model. A medium or small
model is enough, and that is what Flui's inference layer recommends
by default.

## The safety model

### Scopes, ordered into tiers

Every tool declares a scope, and scopes are ordered into four tiers
by blast radius:

```
read  →  plan  →  write  →  destructive
```

- **read**: list and inspect applications, the catalog, logs and
  metrics, backups, migrations, mail, who can reach what.
- **plan**: analysis that changes nothing, such as validating a
  `flui.yaml`.
- **write**: operations that change state: install, deploy, scale,
  restart, stop, connect a repository.
- **destructive**: delete and uninstall.

A grant at a tier implies every lower tier, so granting write also
grants read and plan.

Three areas are in no tier at all: the machine room (reading it as
well as operating it), granting or revoking someone's access, and
updating the platform itself. A tier is what a credential falls
back to when it names no scopes of its own, so anything inside a
tier can be obtained without being asked for. Stopping somebody's
cluster or handing out access has to be an explicit choice, so
those scopes are only ever held by naming them. See
[Choose what your agent may do](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/).

### Default-deny, with three exceptions

The system is default-deny. A tool runs only if its scope is in the
calling principal's set, and an explicit grant on the credential
always wins: a scoped key stays least privilege even when the
person who created it is an administrator.

What a principal gets when its credential names no scopes depends
on who it is:

- **An ordinary authenticated principal** gets the safe default:
  read and plan only.
- **A platform administrator** driving the assistant from their own
  dashboard session gets the full tier. Writes still stop for a
  person, and destructive ones stop for a person every time.
- **A guest in the demonstration sandbox** gets one group instead,
  "deploy and operate applications", because the platform default
  spans backups, migrations and mail, areas where a guest would
  only be refused.

So "no explicit grant means read and plan" is the ordinary case,
not a universal rule.

### Everyone is handed a different toolbox

`tools/list` is filtered to the calling key's scopes. A tool this
credential could never run is not advertised at all, on either
surface. Two agents connected to the same installation with
different keys see different toolboxes, and neither sees the whole
registry.

An offered tool costs the agent context, invites a plan built
around it, and ends in a refusal. Hiding it is cheaper and leads to
better behaviour. Execution is still checked separately: the filter
only trims what is offered and never decides what is allowed.

The two kinds of refusal are worded differently. "Missing required
scope" means the tool was never given to you. That is a grant
problem, fixed by reissuing the credential, and no other resource
will make the call work. "Refused by Flui access control" means you
hold the tool but not access to this resource. That is a permission
problem, fixed by changing who can reach what. An agent that cannot
tell them apart tells you the wrong thing.

### Arguments are strict

An unknown argument name is rejected, and the error says both what
was sent and what is accepted.

A permissive schema silently drops an unknown key, which is the
worst failure for a model-driven caller. The plausible but wrong
argument disappears, the real parameter is left empty, the tool
runs unfiltered, and the agent gets a confident, successful answer
to a question it never asked. Rejecting costs one turn, while
accepting silently corrupts every step that follows.

### Long work hands back an operation id

Installing, deploying, uninstalling, migrating and scaling do not
finish when the call returns. They return an operation id and a
status, and the tool result says so.

Nothing polls the operation for the agent. On the MCP surface, the
agent is told that it must follow the operation itself with
`operation_status` until it is done, and never claim it finished
before then. In the in-product assistant, the dashboard shows a
live progress panel, so the assistant is told the opposite: do not
wait or re-check, just say it started.

### One route waits instead of handing back a receipt

`repo_map` and `repo_map_apply` are how an agent reaches
[the repository-mapping engine](/concepts/30-how-flui-reads-a-repository/).
The first reads a connected repository (units, services, blockers,
a verdict, one rendered `flui.yaml` per unit), and the second acts
on it. They sit at the same [tiers](#scopes-ordered-into-tiers) as
everything else: `repo_map` needs `mcp:app:read` and
`repo_map_apply` needs `mcp:app:write`. Because `repo_map_apply`
writes to a real repository and starts real builds, it goes through
[the action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/) like any other
write. A third tool, `app_deploy_image`, goes straight from a
container image to a running application with no repository at
all, at the same tier and through the same cycle. All three tools
say in their own descriptions that they are one way among equals:
reading a repository, writing a manifest by hand and shipping an
image you already built are equally supported, and none is
presented as the preferred path.

`repo_map_apply` is also the only route in the registry that does
not return an operation id. Within the one call, it waits for every
service the applied units declare to reach a running state before
it answers, which takes minutes when the manifest attaches a new
database. An MCP tool call, meanwhile, is capped at 120 seconds by
default on this installation's own API. An apply that installs a
database can outlast that limit while the work keeps running on the
server. When that happens, the agent is told that a mutation that
timed out may still have been applied: it must read the current
state before repeating it, and never repeat it twice. The CLI's
equivalent, `flui repo map apply`, sets no client-side timeout of
its own and does not hit this limit.

### Secrets never pass through an agent

An agent that needs a credential (an API key, the token that pulls
container images, a mail provider, a backup destination, provider
credentials, a model connection, an invitation for a new user) does
not ask you to paste it into the chat. Seven tools exist only to ask
a person instead, and they share three properties:

- **None of them has an argument that could carry a value.** Not
  even an optional one for automation: an argument is context, and
  context ends up in the transcript.
- **Each one answers whether a thing is configured, never what it
  is.**
- **None performs the privileged write.** They return either a
  command for you to run in your own terminal or the screen you
  should open, so you make the write yourself.

An invitation link is itself treated as a credential and is never
returned to an agent.

### The destructive gate

A destructive tool (delete or uninstall) is offered only to a
credential that carries a destructive scope. A credential without it
does not see the tool at all: if an agent cannot find a delete tool,
that is the reason.

Every destructive call stops for a person, every time. There is no
"always" for removing something, nor for widening what a key may do.

When an agent needs a scope its key does not carry, it asks for it
with `credential_scope_request`. You approve the request at a link,
the key gains the scope, and the agent reconnects to see the new
tools.

Whoever runs the instance can switch destructive tools off
altogether with `MCP_ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE=false`. The refusal is then
deterministic and recorded.

### A person in the loop

The checkpoint for each action is a person.

Flui declares more than sixty write routes as inside the action
cycle. When the caller is an agent, the call does not run: it comes
back as a request addressed to a person, with one plain sentence
describing what was asked for and a link to the page where they
answer once, always or no. The agent learns the answer by making
the identical call again.

**The in-product assistant is inside the same cycle**, on the same
person's own session. That may look redundant with the person right
there, but what decides the pause is who wrote the arguments, not
whose credential it is. A dashboard form and a `flui` command carry
what a person typed. A tool call carries what a model chose, so
confirming it means checking something the person did not write.

**A pause is not an error.** It is returned in the shape the
protocol has for waiting, so a client that understands it shows you
a decision to make, and one that does not still shows a sentence
saying what is being asked. An agent that mistakes it for a failure
either gives up or starts changing its arguments to get around it,
and changing them only raises a second question instead of
answering the first.

[The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/) covers the
details, including how narrow "always" is and why a standing
permission can never widen what anyone may do.

### Why this shape

The design starts from blast radius. The most useful thing an
assistant can do is also the most dangerous, so instead of relying
on every proposal being correct, the design makes a wrong one cheap
to recover from. Reads and plans run freely. Writes run with the
caller's own permissions and stop for a person. Irreversible
operations need a destructive scope and a person's yes, every time. No
single mistaken token and no single bad turn should be able to
destroy your data.

## Getting an agent connected

Three task pages cover the whole path:

- [Connect an agent](/tasks/connect-an-agent/): creating the
  credential and pointing an agent at `POST /mcp`. The first tool
  an agent should call is `get_started`, which returns the
  instructions for operating this installation and records that the
  credential has connected.
- [Choose what your agent may do](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/):
  the permission groups a person picks from, and what each one
  carries.
- [When your agent stops to ask you](/tasks/when-your-agent-asks/):
  answering a request, and taking a standing permission back.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/): why an agent's
  write stops and asks, and what "always" means.
- [How Flui reads a repository](/concepts/30-how-flui-reads-a-repository/):
  what `repo_map` and `repo_map_apply` do, and the citation and
  confidence behind every fact they report.
- [Who can reach what](/concepts/28-who-can-reach-what/): the access
  model every one of those tool calls lands on.
- [Inference and bring-your-own-LLM](/concepts/23-inference-and-byo-llm/):
  how the assistant and MCP get their model endpoint.
- [Identity and OIDC](/concepts/15-identity-and-oidc/): where the
  authenticated principals, and the machine keys the MCP surface
  accepts, come from.
- [Observability is not an afterthought](/concepts/08-observability-as-first-class/):
  the logs and metrics the read tools surface when you ask the
  assistant to debug an app.

sections.title: The database console
sections.body:
A database you run on Flui has no address on the internet.
That is the right default, but the first time a row looks
wrong you need a way to look inside it. The usual options
all cost something. Opening the database to the internet
undoes the default. Hosting a second web tool in front of
it means you run, patch and secure that tool as well. A
native client means setting up a tunnel every time.

The console is a data browser built into the dashboard and
served through Flui's own backend. Nothing is exposed, and
there is nothing extra to install.

This chapter covers what it opens, who may open it, how it
connects, and the limits it sets.

## The kinds of console

There are about ten kinds of console. The list follows the
building blocks Flui's catalog installs, and each console
has the same shape: a panel of connection details, a way to
browse what is stored, and a way to run something by hand.

- **Relational**: Postgres and MariaDB. A query editor, a
  schema browser that reads tables, columns, primary keys
  and foreign keys, and the connection details.
- **Key-value**: Redis and Valkey. A keyspace summary
  (counts, not contents), a key scan, a value reader and a
  command runner.
- **Cache**: Memcached. Read a key, set one, delete one,
  flush.
- **Document**: FerretDB, driven with the shell statements
  a MongoDB user already knows, plus a browser for
  databases, collections and fields.
- **Full-text**: Meilisearch. The indexes, a search box,
  and a raw call for anything the box does not cover.
- **Kafka**: the cluster, its topics and its consumer
  groups, plus a command shell.
- **Messaging**: NATS and RabbitMQ. Streams, publish, and a
  peek at what is waiting.
- **Object store**: Garage, which speaks S3. Buckets and
  objects, upload and download, and signed share links that
  expire and can be revoked. Even a share link streams
  through Flui's backend, so the store itself is never
  reachable from outside. Images, PDFs, plain text, audio
  and video open in the browser; anything else, web pages
  included, is downloaded.
- **Search**: OpenSearch. Indexes, mappings, queries and
  counts.
- **Secrets**: OpenBao. Browse a path, read a version,
  write one, undelete one.

You do not choose which console you get. Flui reads the
engine the catalog manifest declared when the service was
installed. Where an install declares no engine, Flui falls
back to what it can recognise from the image name, and then
from the settings the install carries.

### Backup, disk and going back in time

Three more panels sit alongside the consoles, on the
database side:

- **Backup**: a logical dump produced by the engine's own
  tool and streamed to you, and a restore that runs that
  dump back into the live database. The restore overwrites
  what is there, and it says so before it asks you to
  confirm.
- **Disk**: how full the storage under the database is,
  with a near-full warning. The number is for the filesystem
  hosting the volume, because that is where the database
  actually stops.
- **Point in time**: where continuous backup is on, the
  window you can recover to, and a restore as of a moment.
  That restore never touches the source: it builds a fresh
  install and recovers into it, and you connect to the copy.

The same three have CLI equivalents: `flui db dump`,
`flui db restore`, `flui db disk`, `flui db backup-status`
and `flui db pitr-restore`.

## Who may open one

Opening a console goes through the same access engine as
every other route in the product. Four things follow from
that:

- **Ownership alone is not enough.** A grant can select
  applications by owner, but owning one does not give you
  access to it. If nothing grants you access to that
  application, its console does not open, even though the
  record is yours.
- **Revoked or narrowed grants apply here too.** The
  console checks on every open, so a revoked grant closes
  it like every other door in the product.
- **A key's ceiling is checked before the record is
  loaded.** An agent credential carries a ceiling: a limit
  on what it may do, whoever holds it. Flui checks that
  ceiling first, before it even looks the application up,
  so a narrowly scoped key held by an application's own
  owner cannot open a query prompt its scopes never
  mention. Checking first also keeps that refusal safe: it
  can be specific about the key's own limits without
  revealing whether the id you named exists.
- **Applications the platform installed answer to the
  installation.** Flui's own workloads belong to nobody in
  particular. Their consoles open only to a principal
  holding authority over the whole installation, held
  globally and not narrowed to one cluster or one set of
  applications.

The check asks for the level that lets you change an
application, not only see it, because one console gives
you arbitrary queries, decrypted connection details and a
restore. A viewer grant does not open a console; an
operator grant does. The roles are the ones in
[Who can reach what](/concepts/28-who-can-reach-what/).

### Refusals that say nothing

Only one refusal tells you what happened: the application
exists, and it is not yours to reach.

Every other refusal reads as an absence, in the same words.
A console that is fenced off, an id that does not exist and
an application with no recorded owner all read identically,
and none of them repeats the id back to you. A refusal that
names its reason tells a stranger that the id runs
something here, and refusals that differ from each other
can be told apart. Somebody guessing ids learns nothing
from them.

## Read-only by default

Every console defaults to read-only. A write has to be
asked for explicitly.

On the relational console this is enforced at the database
session, not by watching for the word `DELETE`. Each query
opens a transaction, sets it read-only, applies the limits,
and then rolls back instead of committing. A statement that
tries to write fails at the engine, and nothing it did
survives, because the transaction is discarded either way.

Every query also has two more limits:

- **A statement timeout of about 30 seconds.** A missing
  `WHERE` or an accidental cross join is cut off by the
  database instead of holding a connection open.
- **A row cap of about 1000 rows.** The grid shows the first
  slice and tells you it was truncated. The console is for
  inspection, not for bulk export.

The other consoles follow the same rule in their own terms.
Browsing only reads. A command runner passes through a
read-only gate: commands are allowed while they are reads,
and a write or destructive command (a flush, a delete, a
topic removal) is refused unless the write path was asked
for.

The reason is blast radius. The console is the everyday
tool for checking something, and it should not be able to
break what it inspects.

## How it connects: the owner's own credentials

To run anything, the console has to authenticate to the
service. It uses the service's own owner credentials: the
same user, password and database the catalog generated when
it installed the building block.

You never type them and they are never stored a second
time. Flui reads them at the moment of the query from the
secret the install already owns. Relational engines carry a
user and a database. Caches authenticate with a password
alone, and are often installed with no authentication at
all, in which case the console connects anonymously.

This means everyone who can open a console connects as the
owner of that service. Flui accepts that because the
default is read-only, opening a console requires a grant,
and every query is recorded on the server, allowed and
refused alike. It is still a limitation.

### One narrow seam

One narrow piece, a connection resolver, turns "this
application" into a live connection. It resolves the owner
credentials and reports the role as `owner`. The query
layer, the transport and the helper above it never handle
credentials themselves.

## How the browser reaches a private database

Flui databases are not reachable from outside the cluster
network, so a console in your browser goes through Flui's
backend. The browser talks only to the Flui API. The
backend opens a private link to the running database, runs
the query over it and returns the result. The link stays
open for about a minute so a burst of queries reuses it,
then it closes. The browser never holds a connection to the
database and never learns its address.

For the same reason, the connection-details panel is safe.
It returns what you need to reason about a connection
(engine, database name, user, port) and never the password,
which does not travel over the API at all.

For a native client, `flui db tunnel` does the same on your
own machine: a local port, bound to loopback, forwarded
through the control plane, with nothing opened to the
internet. See
[Open a database from your machine](/tasks/open-a-database/).

## Two things it does not open

Two databases under the product are always closed to the
web console. One is Flui's own database, which holds every
user, key, encrypted provider token and application record.
The other is the identity provider's tables, which live in
the same place, so access there would open every session
and credential on the installation.

That exclusion is declared in one place, with its reason
next to it, and it does not depend on anything that could
go missing: no label, no declared engine, no recorded
owner. Taking a database out of it means deleting that
line.

They are still reachable from the CLI, by someone holding
authority over the whole installation. Because the stakes
are higher, that has its own task page:
[Reach the platform's own database](/tasks/reach-the-platform-database/).

## The helper is data-blind

Most consoles offer a helper: describe what you want in
plain words, and it writes the query or the command, with
an explanation, for you to read and run yourself. It never
runs anything for you, and it never sees your data.

What is sent to the model is structure and your question.
On the relational console that means table and column
names, types, primary keys and foreign keys, your prompt,
and Flui's own built-in notes on that engine's dialect and
its pitfalls. On the key-value console it is narrower: a
key count and a breakdown by type, never key names or
values. On the document and search consoles it is names,
field paths and inferred types, never the contents of a
record. On Kafka it is topic and group names, never a
message.

Row data is never sent. The helper reads the shape of the
data and does not read, sample or forward what is stored.
That is what makes it safe to point a hosted model at a
production database.

Whatever the helper writes then runs under the same rules
as a hand-typed query: read-only by default, the timeout,
the row cap. A suggestion that would change data is flagged
so the dashboard can ask for confirmation, but the flag is
only a hint. The read-only session underneath is the real
boundary.

The helper has no model of its own. It uses the same
inference layer as Flui's other assistant features, so it
uses whatever you configured there: Flui's native inference
or your own provider. See
[Inference and bring-your-own LLM](/concepts/23-inference-and-byo-llm/).

## What it is for

- It is a fast, safe way to look inside the data services
  you already run on Flui (query, browse, scan, read a
  value, get a draft) without exposing anything and without
  a second tool to host.
- It is not an administration suite, a migration runner or
  a bulk-export tool. The row cap and the read-only default
  make it the right thing to reach for first.

## Where to read next

- [Open a database from your machine](/tasks/open-a-database/):
  `flui db tunnel` and a native client.
- [Reach the platform's own database](/tasks/reach-the-platform-database/):
  the two reserved names, and the rules around them.
- [Who can reach what](/concepts/28-who-can-reach-what/):
  the roles and grants a console asks about.
- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/):
  databases are applications in Flui's model, with the same
  lifecycle, logs and metrics as anything else.
- [Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/):
  where the building blocks these consoles operate on come
  from.
- [Inference and bring-your-own LLM](/concepts/23-inference-and-byo-llm/):
  the inference layer the data-blind helper draws on.

sections.title: The action cycle
sections.body:
An agent connected to Flui acts as the person who connected
it. It holds their credential, so it can do what they can do.
That makes it useful, and it is also a risk: the same key that
deploys an application can add machines you pay for, move a
database between clusters, or remove an application along with
its storage.

Flui keeps the agent fully capable and puts a person between the
model and the action. More than sixty write routes are declared
inside the action cycle: when the caller is an agent, the call
does not run. It becomes a question addressed to a person.

This chapter explains that pause. It is written for the person
connecting an agent and for the agent itself, since both end up
reading it.

_Diagram: An agent's write becomes a request; a person answers; the agent repeats the same call._

## What the agent gets instead of an effect

The call is refused, but the refusal is not an error. It
carries:

- a request id;
- one plain sentence describing what was asked for, naming the
  resource ("change how this cluster scales itself", not just
  "infrastructure");
- a link to the page where a person answers;
- when the action has a price, the fact that a price exists;
- when the route provides it, what happens if the person allows
  it.

The person answers in one of three ways:

- **Once**: let this exact call through and remember nothing.
- **Always**: let it through and record a standing permission.
- **No**: refuse it.

The message the agent receives says that this is a wait and not
a failure, that nothing was changed, and that changing the
arguments to get around it only raises a second question instead
of answering the first.

## The agent learns the answer by retrying

Nothing holds a connection open while someone decides. The agent
finds out by making the identical call again: if the person
allowed it, it goes through.

This has two benefits. A request can wait an hour for an answer
without a socket held open anywhere. It also works for an agent
with no special client support: an agent driving Flui with plain
HTTP calls meets the same pause and learns the answer the same
way.

## Who counts as an agent

Two things make a caller an agent, and the caller cannot set
either of them itself:

- its credential carries agent scopes;
- the call arrives through an agentic surface, which is the
  assistant inside Flui.

A person filling in a dashboard form or typing a `flui` command
is not paused. They are the approver, not the applicant, and
asking them to confirm what they just typed would add nothing.

The assistant inside Flui is paused too, even though the same
person is at both ends of it. What decides the pause is who wrote
the arguments, not whose credential it is. A form carries what a
person typed. A tool call carries what a model chose, so
confirming it is a real check: the person confirms something they
did not write.

## An agent cannot answer its own request

An agent key is issued as its person, so every permission check
on the page where requests are answered would pass, and the
applicant could approve its own request.

That page therefore refuses a caller for what it is, whatever it
may do. An agent credential is turned away from the decision
routes even though its permissions are sufficient by
construction. The same rule keeps the assistant inside Flui on
the applicant's side: the chat cannot approve its own request,
while the person reading it in the dashboard can.

A request also belongs to someone. Only the person it was
addressed to can answer it. Running the whole installation does
not let you answer a question asked of someone else, and another
person's request looks as if it does not exist, rather than
forbidden.

## A request lasts one hour

A request expires after one hour, because of the price. A request
carries an estimate of what the action will cost, and that
estimate goes stale. Once the hour is up, the request can no
longer be answered. The agent's next attempt refreshes it with a
new hour and a new price, and keeps the same id, so the number the
agent already reported still points at what the person is looking
at.

## "Always" is one action, one resource, one credential

A standing permission is recorded against a specific action and
the specific resource that action names: "change how this cluster
scales itself", not "change scaling". Pointed at another cluster,
it does not match, and the agent has to ask again.

It is also tied to that one credential. A different key, even one
the same person created a minute later, starts by asking again.
The permission belongs to one agent, not to everything the person
may run later.

A request that cannot name its own resource is only ever offered
once. With no resource to record, there is no narrow permission
to grant, so "always" is not offered.

## A standing permission grants nothing

Allowing an agent to stop asking can never let it do something it
could not already do.

The pause is the last check. By the time a call reaches the action
cycle, every check that decides whether the call is allowed has
already run and passed. The cycle can only remove the pause in
front of it. "Always" removes a question about something the
person's own access already allowed; it grants nothing new.

## Taking it back

A person can see what their agents may do without asking, revoke
any of it, and, before deciding, see what is still running under
that permission.

Revoking takes effect immediately for anything that has not
started. The standing permission is read on every request, so once
it is revoked nothing new starts under it.

It does not abort work already running. A separate option also
asks running work to stop, and even that takes effect at the next
safe step, never mid-step. A ten-step provisioning run cut in half
would leave resources you pay for orphaned somewhere, which is
worse than what the person was trying to stop.

That is why the revoke dialog shows the running list first. After a
revoke, provisioning runs already in progress continue, and the
dialog makes that visible before you confirm.

## Small rules that follow from the same thinking

**Repeated attempts collapse.** An agent retrying the same call
with the same arguments finds the request it already raised.
However many attempts it makes, there is one question.

**The arguments are never stored.** They are read once, to
recognise a repeat, and discarded. Some of them are secrets (the
answers to a catalog install can include an administrator
password), and a table meant to be read by a person deciding
whether to say yes should not hold them. Only the sentence is
kept.

**A dry run does not ask.** A route that can be told to check and
change nothing, such as validating a manifest, skips the pause.
Asking a person about a deploy that is not happening would
describe the wrong action, and that sentence is what gets stored.

**The price is withheld from the agent.** Where a request has a
cost, the agent is told that a price exists, that it cannot see
it, and that the person deciding can. It is instructed to say
exactly that, and not to describe the action as free or invent a
figure.

**A settled "no" reads as settled.** Retrying something that was
already refused gets a distinct answer: the person answered, so
stop, tell them what was refused and offer another course of
action. It is not phrased as an access-control failure, because an
agent that reads it as one goes off asking for permissions the
person just declined.

## Where a person answers

In the dashboard, on the **Agents** page, where requests raised by
your agents wait for you. For the assistant inside Flui, your yes
in the chat answers the request once. The link in the refusal
points straight to the individual request. The API serves the same
thing directly.

There is no CLI command for this. You cannot list requests, approve
one or revoke a standing permission from the terminal. If the CLI
is your only surface, the pause still applies and you answer it
elsewhere.

## The trade-off

A pause the agent does not understand is a bad experience. The
agent stops, reports something confusing, and the person wonders
why nothing happened.

That is why the refusal says it is a wait, what was asked for, and
who can allow it and where. There is a known gap: the onboarding
document Flui gives an agent when it connects does not mention the
action cycle. The tool that serves it says the document teaches the
pattern, but version 1.3.0 of the document does not contain it. An
agent following it meets its first pause with no idea what it is.

The fix is manual and cheap: tell the agent about the cycle, or
point it at this page. An agent that knows the rule reports "I
asked, and someone needs to allow it" instead of "it failed".

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [The Flui Assistant and MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/):
  the surfaces an agent reaches Flui through, and the scope model
  underneath them.
- [Identity and OIDC](/concepts/15-identity-and-oidc/): where the
  credential an agent carries comes from, and whose it is.

sections.title: What a cluster may buy for itself
sections.body:
On most platforms autoscaling is a switch. Once you turn it on,
something you cannot see spends your money with nobody watching,
and when the bill arrives the only record of why is a graph.

Flui has no such switch. Nothing on an installation buys a machine
on its own until somebody writes down what a specific cluster may
buy, where it must stop, and that it may act. That record is a
**scaling group**, and this chapter explains how it is shaped.

## The group is the consent

A scaling group is a resource on a cluster. A cluster can have
more than one, for example one for general work and one for heavy
jobs, because those two fleets differ in every field below.

A group says:

- **Three bounds.** A floor (`min`), held now and always; a
  target (`desired`), where the fleet would like to sit; and a
  ceiling (`max`), as far as the urgent side may go right now.
  Being under the target buys nothing on its own. The fleet
  reaches it when the market allows, and returns to it after a
  burst.
- **Where** it may buy: one or more regions. Several regions are
  what make "cheapest, anywhere" possible.
- **What** it may buy: machine shapes, in order of preference.
- **A placement strategy**: `cheapest`, `closest`, `roomiest` or
  `uniform`.
- **A ceiling in money**, a monthly figure. Optional on a
  manual group; an automatic group needs one above zero.
- **A settle window**: how long work must have been stuck before
  the group buys anything. Thirty seconds by default.
- **Whether it may act.** `provision: manual` means the group
  decides and tells you. `provision: automatic` means it may
  go and buy, never past its money ceiling. This field is the
  consent.

Every cluster on a provider Flui buys from gets one manual group,
named `default`, holding the nodes it has. Nothing autoscales until
a person sets a group to `automatic`. There is no installation-wide
grant above it. A second ceiling outside the group would guard only
some of the ways money can be spent, and the group already carries
its own ceilings, in money and in nodes, where you can see them.
The consent needed is for acting without a person, and it is one
word on the group.

Removing a group takes no machine away. Where Flui buys a cluster's
machines, the cluster's last group cannot be removed, because its
nodes change through it. Set it to `manual` to stop it buying.

_Diagram: A group holds the fleet between a floor and a ceiling, under a ceiling in money. Urgency buys within those limits, and opportunity stands down while it acts._

## What the settle window is for

The thirty-second window makes sure the work is stuck rather
than caught mid-placement: another workload shutting down, a node
finishing a drain, the scheduler partway through. It has nothing to
do with price. Once the window passes, the urgent side buys without
holding out for a cheaper machine.

Three things do hold it back, and none of them is price:

- While one machine is on its way, nothing else is bought.
- A purchase the provider refuses as sold out pauses the group for
  ten minutes, then the next reading decides.
- Any other failed purchase holds the group until a person runs
  `flui scaling retry`, so a broken purchase is not repeated every
  minute.

## Two forces on one fleet

Two different pressures act on a fleet, and Flui keeps them apart.

**Urgency.** Work cannot be placed. Its clock is seconds and it
never waits. It walks a ladder of fallbacks and takes the first
rung that would work:

1. the preferred shape, in the cluster's own region;
2. the preferred shape, in any region this group may buy in;
3. anything that holds the work, in the cluster's own region;
4. anything that holds it, anywhere the group may buy.

"Anywhere" has one limit that no setting changes: a machine Flui
buys has to join the cluster's private network, so it can only
land in a region that network reaches. Where the provider publishes
live stock, Flui checks whether a shape is on sale with a fresh
reading every few minutes instead of a cached result.

When no rung can be taken, the alarm names every machine on the
list with its own reason (sold out and where, too small, over the
ceiling), because the first choice alone is rarely the one a person
can act on.

**Opportunity.** Patient growth toward the target when the market
allows. Its clock is hours, and it works by waiting. Nobody is held
up if it never fires. It also gives a machine back when the fleet
has gone past its target, and replaces a stand-in that urgency
bought in a hurry with the shape the group wanted.

Giving back has two conditions. Nothing is given back within ten
minutes of a machine joining, because the load that called for it
rarely leaves that fast, and a machine given back only to be bought
again is paid for twice. And a machine is only given back if
everything running on it fits on the machines that stay, so the
work it holds always has somewhere to run.

The patient side also carries standing orders: a machine somebody
asked for by hand, bought when the market allows. An `expand` order
is a purchase that closes itself once the fleet reaches the target
it was written for. A `replace` order is a purchase plus the
draining of a named machine, with both nodes running for a while.

## The one rule where they meet

**Urgency always wins, and opportunity stands down entirely
while anything is waiting.**

That includes when Flui cannot ask the cluster whether anything is
waiting. A cluster that does not answer may still have waiting
work, so the patient side stays down and nothing is decided.

One thing still holds while the cluster is silent: the floor. The
floor comes from the fleet's own records, not from a reading of the
cluster. Otherwise an installation could drop below its floor
exactly when its cluster is in trouble, which is when the floor
matters most.

## Why the ceiling is money

A limit of "at most six nodes" tells you little. Six of one shape
and six of another are different bills.

So the ceiling a group carries is an amount of money per month,
weighed against what the fleet already commits. A shape that would
push the total past it loses, and the row says so with both figures
in it.

Two details follow from that:

- Flui refuses only on certainty. A machine with no published price
  adds nothing to the committed figure, so clearing the ceiling
  does not prove the fleet is under it. Where the fleet is only
  partly priced, the decision states that the figure is a lower
  bound and not the bill, and counts the machines it could not
  price.
- On an automatic group, a machine with no published price is not
  bought automatically, because a ceiling cannot be enforced
  against an unknown amount. The machine is named in an alarm for
  a person instead.

A group can also refuse shapes billed only by the month. They make
autoscaling cost-neutral at best, because you cannot give the
machine back at the end of the hour.

## How placement chooses among shapes that fit

The four strategies choose among the shapes that already fit.

A shape that cannot hold the waiting work is not a candidate. If
fitting were only a preference, `cheapest` could pick a shape that
helps nobody: the money is spent, the machine arrives, and the work
is still waiting. So fitting is a filter that runs first, and the
strategy only breaks the tie among the shapes left:

- **cheapest**: lowest price first;
- **closest**: the cluster's own region first;
- **roomiest**: the largest machine first;
- **uniform**: keep the fleet one shape. This is the default when
  nobody chooses.

Before asking whether the waiting work fits, Flui subtracts what
the system itself needs on every machine. A machine that holds the
request only with nothing left over does not count as holding it.

## Every decision is a row, including the ones that did nothing

The question people ask an autoscaler is almost always why it did
not scale.

So a decline is written down in the same shape as a purchase: what
it saw, what it did, why, and what it still needs from a person,
along with every rung it skipped and the reason that rung lost.
`flui scaling why` prints them, for the whole cluster by default,
naming the group each decision came from. Declines are not filtered
out, because they are the answer the command exists to give.

The rows are updated in place rather than appended like a log.
The same answer is rewritten when it changes, and once an hour
otherwise, so you can see the
loop is alive without the one useful row being buried under a
thousand copies of "still nothing to do".

`flui scaling preview` asks the same engine what it would do if a
machine were needed right now, without spending anything. It shows
the whole ladder, the room left on each machine (counted on what
apps reserve), and the largest app that still fits. Anything bigger
than that app makes the group buy.

### Why `refused-by-limit` has its own name

One reason a shape can lose is named separately from the others:
`refused-by-limit` means the shape was available and affordable,
and this group's own rules excluded it.

From the outside that looks the same as the provider having nothing
to sell. Someone sees an empty result and goes looking for an
outage, when the cause is a rule they wrote themselves: a ceiling
already reached, a region their cluster's network does not reach,
a shape marked deprecated, or an hourly-billing-only rule against a
provider that bills by the month. The separate name tells you that
changing one of your own settings would allow the purchase.

For the same reason, the reasons are ordered by how close the rung
came to buying, and the decision reports the nearest miss, since
that is the one a person can act on.

## How Flui learns what a provider can do

Flui never infers a provider's capabilities from its name. It takes
them from what that provider has declared, on three separate
questions:

- **Can Flui create a server here?**
- **Is there a catalogue**, a list of shapes with prices attached?
- **How is it billed**: by the hour, by the month, or not visibly
  at all?

These are three separate flags rather than levels on one scale,
because a provider that publishes a price list but has no create
API needs a different outcome, addressed to a person. There,
deciding is all that happens: the group raises an alarm that names
the shape, the region and the price, and asks somebody to buy one
and join it with `flui node connect`. Where no catalogue exists at
all, the alarm says what a machine has to hold instead.

A provider Flui knows nothing about gets the most restrictive
answer: it buys nothing, publishes nothing, and is billed for
nothing anyone can see.

This is also why `flui scaling list` shows clusters that seem to
need no attention. A cluster with no scaling group at all, and a
cluster whose provider can only raise an alarm, are both listed.
Hiding them would report that all is well in the two cases where
somebody is needed.

## Bounds count the whole fleet

Every bound counts the master too, so all three sit between 1 and
20. A group never describes an empty fleet. To stop a group acting,
set `provision: manual`.

## The group is a file

A scaling group can be written as a `kind: ScalingGroup`
document. `flui scaling export` writes one and
`flui scaling apply -f` reads it back. `--dry-run` shows what
would be written without writing it. Several groups can live
in one file, separated by `---`.

The file describes the whole group: a field left out is reset to
its default, not left as it was. A reviewer reads the file that
way, so the command does too, and applying the same file twice
leaves the same group.

Only what a person wrote is exported. What the provider can do,
and what the market is doing today, are read fresh every time,
since they would be out of date as soon as the file was committed.

## When an agent asks for this

Writing or changing a scaling group is one of the actions that
stops and asks a person when an agent is the caller. The person
agrees to a standing figure rather than a single machine: how large
this cluster may become and how much money it may spend with nobody
watching. The question shows that figure, not just the word
"scaling".

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Nodes and cluster topology](/concepts/06-nodes-and-cluster-topology/):
  the machines a group decides about, and attaching or resizing
  one by hand.
- [The cluster as a concept](/concepts/03-cluster-as-a-concept/):
  what a cluster owns, and where its scaling groups sit.
- [How Flui works across providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/):
  why buying, cataloguing and billing are three capabilities a
  provider can have or lack.

sections.title: Who can reach what
sections.body:
[Identity](/concepts/15-identity-and-oidc/) answers who someone
is. Once more than one person uses the installation, you also
need to know what each of them may touch. This chapter covers
that second question.

## Nothing is implied

Access is **deny by default**. An account that signs in
successfully but holds no grant reaches nothing. It can open
the home screen and its own settings, but no applications,
clusters or sections. Signing in establishes identity only.

The alternative, a baseline that every signed-in person gets
for free, is convenient until someone asks what a new colleague
can see and nobody can answer. With deny by default, the answer
is always whatever someone granted them, and nothing else.

The one exception is the installation's administrators, who
pass every check. The `owner` role below is the version of that
which can be written down, handed out and taken back.

## The ladder: viewer, operator, maintainer, owner

There are four roles on a ladder, and one beside it. Each role
carries everything the role below it carries, plus more.

**Viewer.** Reads the applications in scope, and can open the
Clusters section so the machines those applications run on are
visible.

**Operator.** The whole life of the applications in scope:
create, deploy, operate, scale, migrate and remove them. No
access management and no infrastructure.

Removal belongs to the operator role, not a higher one. What
protects an application from a careless removal is the scope of
the grant: you can only remove what your grant already reaches,
and the removal tells you how much data goes with it before it
asks you to confirm.

**Maintainer.** An operator, plus the installation itself: the
clusters, who may reach what, the shared integrations, the
showcase and the demonstration.

**Owner.** Everything, everywhere, including who else runs this
installation.

**Platform operator.** Beside the ladder, not on it. It runs
clusters, nodes, updates and backups, and reads the applications
without reaching their data. Give it with `--expires`, so it
ends on its own.

`flui iam roles` prints the five roles and exactly what each one
carries. `flui iam whoami` prints what the identity you are
using holds right now, which is the quickest way to find out why
you cannot see something.

### Who can make an owner

Giving someone the `owner` role, or removing it from someone
else, needs user-management authority over the whole
installation, not narrowed to one cluster or one set of
applications.

Without this rule there would be a gap. A maintainer can
already hand out roles; that is most of the job. A maintainer
could then give themselves the top role through the access
screen, and the ladder would have no top. The same rule covers
removal, because removing an installation's owners one row at a
time is the same climb in reverse.

## A grant is a principal, a role, and a reach

Access is stored as grants, not on people. A grant says three
things:

- **who**: a person, a group or a service account;
- **which role**: one of the five above;
- **how far it reaches**: the scope.

The scope can be:

- **the whole installation**: everything, everywhere;
- **one cluster**: everything that lives on it;
- **one portal section**: the Clusters section, the Mail
  section and so on;
- **a selector**: a standing description of applications.

A selector is a rule about applications rather than a list of
them. It can constrain the application kind, the project, the
provider, the cluster (by id or by name), whether the
application is a platform one or a user one, a list of slugs, a
set of tags, and the owner.

Every constraint you write must hold at once. Slugs are a
membership test: the application must be one of them. Tags are
an all-of test: the application must carry every tag you name,
not just one. An attribute the application does not have never
matches a selector that constrains it.

Because a selector is a rule, an application deployed tomorrow
that matches it is covered tomorrow, with nothing to grant again
and nothing to remember. It also means a selector is wider than
it looks when you write it, so the sentence a person is asked to
confirm states it explicitly: *over every application a standing
rule matches, including ones deployed later*.

From the terminal:

```bash
flui iam grant add \
  --principal alice@example.com \
  --role operator \
  --scope selector \
  --project shop --tag production
```

`--dry-run` shows what the grant would open and what the same
change closes, without creating anything.
