Groups let you write a grant once instead of once per person:
`flui iam group create`, `add-member`, `remove-member`, `list`,
`delete`. Members are named by email address, and a grant
addressed to the group reaches all of them.

### Taking a grant back says what it costs

`flui iam grant remove <id>` lists what the holder will no
longer be able to reach before it asks you to confirm.
`--dry-run` prints that and removes nothing.

## Sections have three states

Holding the governing permission over the whole installation
opens a portal section in full. Without it, by default, you do
not see the section at all. That leaves no way to express what
two kinds of reader need. A guest on a public demonstration
should be able to look around the product without changing it.
A read-only operator should be able to open the Backup section
and read what is there without being able to start anything.

So there is a third state: **read-only**. The section is
visible, its screens open, and its controls are shown disabled.
Behind it, only safe reads get through and every write is
refused, so the disabled buttons show the rule while the server
enforces it.

There is one limitation. The only role that opens sections at
this level is the one the platform writes for a guest of the
public demonstration; none of the assignable roles carries it.
The reason, as the product states it, is that two of these
sections, Mail and Access, return other people's personal data
once the screen loads, and those screens do not filter per
person. Opening them read-only to a colleague would expose more
than it seems to.

## A refusal that tells you nothing

There are two kinds of refusal, and confusing them leaks
information about the installation.

"You may not do this" is useful: it tells a person what to ask
for. But on some surfaces the existence of the thing is itself
the secret, and a refusal that differs from "there is nothing
here" gives a stranger a map: they can guess ids, read the
wording and learn which ones run something worth reaching.

So on those surfaces (the data consoles, a shell on a machine,
someone's own model connection), every refusal other than "this
belongs to someone else" reads as if nothing were there. It uses
one wording and does not repeat the id back to you.

On the console the sentence is the same whether the application
does not exist, exists but records no owner, belongs to the
platform instead of a person, or is one of the two
[platform databases](/concepts/25-the-database-console/) that no
console may ever open. Four situations get one answer, so
probing ids teaches you nothing.

"It belongs to someone else" stays a separate answer, because
you can act on it: ask the owner.

Routes that take an id straight from the URL follow the same
idea. A permission check made without a resource is satisfied
by any grant that carries that permission, so a permission
alone would let an operator scoped to their own applications
reach someone else's row by guessing a uuid. Those routes load
the row and check that row: a row that records an owner cannot
be reached by id by anyone else.

## A key's scopes are a ceiling

When a call arrives, two separate questions are asked:

1. what may this person do: access control, the grants above;
2. what may this key in their hand do: its scopes.

Scopes can only take away. A key issued to look at applications
can do only that, even when the person who created it is an
administrator. This holds everywhere, not only in the agent
toolbox: plain HTTP calls and live-updates connections are held
to the same scopes. A key is issued as its person, so without
this rule a narrow key would quietly carry its owner's full
rights anywhere nothing checked.

A credential that declares no scopes at all (an interactive
login, the CLI's own key, the platform's own service
identities) has no ceiling and loses nothing. Scopes only
narrow: no scope on any key lets anyone do something their
grants do not already allow.

A key can also be limited to named applications, named
projects, or both. The two lists are alternatives: an
application is reachable as soon as either list covers it.

### Why the two refusals are worded differently

A **scope** refusal says the credential's scopes do not carry
the permission this call needs. That is a grant problem, and you
fix it by issuing the credential again with the right permission
groups. No change to IAM will help.

An **access-control** refusal says the caller is not allowed on
this resource. That is a permission problem, and you fix it
with a grant.

Given the wrong one, a person goes to the wrong screen and an
agent retries forever, so the two never share a wording.

The application-list refusal is a third case and says so: you
fix it by widening the same key's application list. Nothing
needs to be issued again, and whatever holds the key keeps
working with the new list.

The refusal also points out one trap. If agent scopes are
attached to a person's account in the identity provider instead
of to a machine account, they also limit that person's browser
session, which is correct, because the key is that account. The
refusal says where the scopes came from, so you can see the
cause. Put agent scopes on a machine account, not on a person.

_Diagram: A call may do only what the person's grants allow and the key's scopes allow, both at once._

## Access as a file

Grants can be read and written as a document:

```bash
flui iam export > access-policy.yaml
flui iam apply -f access-policy.yaml
```

`export` writes a `kind: AccessPolicy` document with every grant
on the installation. `apply` reads one back and is idempotent:
it creates what is missing and leaves the rest alone. `--prune`
makes it a full sync that deletes grants the file does not
name.

**A naming caution.** The published `@flui-cloud/spec` package
types the roles as `viewer`, `editor` and `manager`, but the
product's names are viewer, operator, maintainer and owner. Use
the product's names. If a tool built on the spec package rejects
`operator`, the package is out of step with the product and your
file is correct.

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Identity and OIDC](/concepts/15-identity-and-oidc/): who
  somebody is, the question this chapter starts from.
- [The database console](/concepts/25-the-database-console/):
  the most sensitive surface the rules above govern.

sections.title: How Flui protects data
sections.body:
This page explains which of your data Flui keeps and which it does not.

Flui protects three kinds of thing with three different mechanisms, and none of
them replaces another: Flui itself, databases and volumes. Protecting a cluster
uses the same three: it gives every application on the cluster the mechanism
that fits it, including applications installed later.

## What protects what

| Subject | Mechanism | Runs | Restores as |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Flui itself** | encrypted dump of the control-plane database, sealed to a key only you hold | nightly | a new installation, by an operator, from a runbook |
| **A database** | continuous backup where the image allows it; scheduled dumps otherwise | continuously, plus a nightly base or dump | a new database, to a moment you pick (continuous) or to a dump |
| **An application's volumes** | encrypted, deduplicated snapshots, one repository per application | nightly, before a deploy if you ask, or when you say | a new volume beside the app, or single files put back |

Everything above is stored in object storage outside the cluster, in a
[destination](/cli/backups/#flui-backup-destination) you register. Ideally the
destination is on a different provider from the cluster it protects.

### Flui itself

The control-plane database holds every user, API key, provider token, cluster
and application record Flui has. It is dumped, encrypted and sealed to an
**age** key you generate on your own machine and keep in your vault. The private
half never touches the server, because a key stored on the machine you are
trying to recover is lost with it.

When the installation is gone, every other restore starts from this backup: the
records say which applications existed, where, and with what configuration.
There is no button for it. Rebuilding an installation from it is an operator
procedure with a runbook; see
[Rebuild the control plane](/tasks/rebuild-the-control-plane/).

**What it does not cover:** your applications' data. This backup holds only the
platform's own records.

### A database

A database Flui recognises (PostgreSQL or MariaDB, from the catalog) is backed
up by its own engine instead of by copying its files, because a file copy of a
database that is being written to does not reliably open again.

- **Continuous backup**, where the image supports it: every change is shipped
  off the cluster as it happens, on top of regular base copies it is replayed
  onto. You can restore the database to any moment you name inside the retained
  window, not only to last night.
- **Scheduled dumps**, where the image cannot ship its changes, for instance a
  database inside another application's bundle. Each dump restores to the
  moment it was taken, and dumps are kept for the retention you set, in days.

Recovery never touches the database you are looking at. It builds a new
database beside it, with its own credentials, and you decide what to do next.

**What it does not cover:** a database Flui does not recognise. Flui does not
quietly copy its files; it lists it as [needing a decision](#needs-a-decision).

### An application's volumes

Uploads, media, generated files: everything an application keeps on its
volumes that is not a recognised database.

Each application gets its own encrypted repository in the destination, with a
key derived from the destination's passphrase and never stored. Each snapshot
stores only what changed since the previous one, so a nightly snapshot of a
large volume that barely changes costs very little.

What is kept:

- **Nightly snapshots**: the last 7 daily and 4 weekly, and always the most
  recent one. You can add 3 monthly snapshots, for about 30% more space and two
  more months of history.
- **Snapshots you take yourself** stay until you delete them. They do not push
  a nightly one out.
- **Snapshots taken before a deploy** have their own history, separate from the
  nightly one.

You can restore in two ways:

- **Whole**, into a new volume beside the application (or into another
  application). The running app is left alone until you switch to the restored
  volume.
- **File by file**: browse a snapshot, pick files or folders, and write them
  back into the live volume or into a folder beside the current files.

When a database is writing to a volume, Flui copies the volume only if it knows
how to pause that database for a consistent copy (Redis, Valkey, SQLite).
Anything else is refused and listed as needing a decision instead of being
copied half-written.

**What it does not cover:** data outside the application's volumes, and
container images.

## Protect a cluster

You can set these up one application at a time, which is how you protect a
single thing. Protecting a cluster does it for all of them:

- a recognised database gets continuous backup, or dumps when its image cannot
  do continuous backup, and a first base copy right away;
- every other application with volumes gets nightly snapshots;
- Flui's own components are skipped (the platform backup covers them), and so
  are applications that keep no data;
- an application that already has a policy keeps it unchanged;
- an application a person decided is not backed up
  (`flui app backup skip`) gets no policy;
- applications installed later get a policy too, within minutes of their first
  successful deploy.

The policies it creates are ordinary policies: you can see, pause or delete each
one. Stopping the protection of a cluster only stops new applications from
getting one; the policies already created keep running.

## Needs a decision

Two things end up here instead of being copied badly:

- a database Flui does not recognise (an engine it has no consistent backup
  for, or an application marked as a database that does not say which engine it
  runs);
- a volume the last nightly snapshot had to refuse because a database was
  writing to it.

Each one is a question for a person, shown per cluster in `flui backup status`
and on the Backup overview, with two answers:

- **stop the application during each copy**, so the volume is copied at rest
  (a short, scheduled outage every night);
- **leave the volume out**, and protect that data another way.

Until someone answers, the volume is not backed up, and Flui says so instead of
producing something that looks like a backup.

## Backup before each deploy

This is set per application and is off by default. When it is on, each deploy
first takes:

- a **restore point** for a database with continuous backup. The deploy waits
  the few seconds this takes, and restoring to that point returns the database
  to just before the deploy;
- a **dump** for a database kept by dumps, and a **snapshot** of the other
  volumes. Both are started but not waited for.

With **required**, a deploy stops when the backup before it cannot be taken.
Otherwise the deploy goes ahead and the failure is logged.

## Copies on the cluster

Separately from all of the above, an application's volume can be copied inside
the cluster. These copies are faster and cheaper to make, and faster to
restore. A copy lives on the same disk as the application and is deleted with
it, so it protects against a bad upgrade but not against losing the application
or the cluster.

## When a whole cluster is lost

Applications come back from Flui's records and their data from the backups:
databases from their continuous backup or their last dump, volumes from their
most recent snapshot, whichever was taken last (nightly, by hand or before a
deploy). See [Rebuild a lost cluster](/tasks/rebuild-a-lost-cluster/).

When the lost cluster was the one running Flui, Flui itself comes back first,
from the platform backup, followed by the applications that ran beside it. See
[Rebuild the control plane](/tasks/rebuild-the-control-plane/).

## Which one do I want?

- *"I want to be able to go back to before that migration."* Use continuous
  backup for a database, with a backup before each deploy. For anything else,
  take a snapshot first.
- *"Someone deleted a folder of uploads."* Restore a volume snapshot file by
  file.
- *"I want to survive losing the whole cluster."* Protect the cluster, and
  answer what needs a decision. A copy on the cluster does not survive this.
- *"I want to survive losing Flui itself."* Use the platform backup, and keep
  the key somewhere else.

## Summary

If you protect a cluster and answer everything it lists as needing a decision,
every application on it, including those installed later, has its data off the
cluster, except the ones a person decided not to back up. Databases can be
restored to a moment, and volumes whole or file by file. Flui's own records are
covered by the platform backup, which is a separate decision because you keep
its key.

sections.title: How Flui reads a repository
sections.body:
There are three ways to get from a repository to a running
application on Flui, and none of them ranks above the
others. You can write `flui.yaml` yourself. You can bring an
image you already built. Or you can ask Flui to read the
repository and tell you what it found. That result is called
a map, and it is the subject of this chapter.

A tool that reads your code and writes a deploy
configuration for you can easily become a black box: it says
"deployable" and you either trust it or you don't. Flui
avoids this by never letting the map say more than it can
back up. Every fact it reports carries where it was read and
how sure the engine is of it. Where it could not tell, it
says so and asks instead of picking a default.

## What gets read

Flui reads a repository as one in-memory archive of a single
commit: no clone, and nothing left on disk once the read
ends. Symlinks are refused, never followed. The read runs
under ceilings: how much of the archive it will decompress,
how large a single file it will look inside, how many paths
it will list, and how long the whole read may take. Every
ceiling is reported back in the response, together with
whether the read hit one. A fact missing because the read
stopped at a ceiling is different from a fact that was
looked for and not found, and the response says which one
happened.

## What comes back

Producing a map is read-only: the route is
`POST /repositories/:id/map`, and calling it touches nothing
on the repository or on a cluster. A map holds:

- **Units**: the directories Flui would deploy, each with
  the reason it counts as one (its own Dockerfile, a compose
  service, the repository root).
- **Services**: the databases, caches and queues the
  repository seems to want, each matched against a catalog
  block where one exists.
- **Inputs**: the values you would have to supply, secret or
  not, before a unit can start.
- **Externals**: dependencies on things outside Flui's
  catalog, such as a third-party API or a managed service
  the repository was written to expect.
- **Blockers**: things Flui cannot provide, such as a Docker
  socket mounted in, a build that wants a private-registry
  secret at build time, or a GPU reservation.
- **Caveats**: cases where the unit runs, degraded. For
  example, an embedded SQLite on what Flui would put on
  shared storage, or two composition files that might
  declare the same database twice.
- **Open questions**: where the evidence does not settle
  something on its own.
- **Decisions**: a choice made on your behalf where more
  than one reading was possible, with the reason and the
  alternative.

For every unit the render could produce a manifest for, the
map also holds one rendered `flui.yaml`: the same kind of
file you would write by hand, generated from what was read.

## A citation and a confidence, on every fact

Every entry (a port, a service, a blocker) carries an
`evidence` list: the file, the line where there is one, and
the exact token that was read. You can open the file at that
line and check it yourself.

Every entry also carries a confidence: `declared` (the
repository states it outright, such as an `EXPOSE` in a
Dockerfile or a `DATABASE_URL` read straight out of
`docker-compose.yml`), `derived` (inferred from something
else that is itself declared), or `circumstantial` (a weaker
signal, such as an import or a naming convention).
Corroboration never promotes a reading: three circumstantial
signals pointing the same way are still circumstantial.

## A verdict, always, from a closed list

Every map ends in a verdict, one of six: `deployable`,
`deployable_pending_inputs`, `partial`, `blocked`,
`insufficient_capacity`, `not_assessed`. There is no seventh
answer.

The verdict depends on the repository and the cluster
together, not on the repository alone. Ask for a map with no
`clusterId` and you get only the repository half (each
unit's own readiness, and whatever blockers or caveats
apply) with `verdict.capacity.assessed: false` and the
reason. A `deployable` that was never weighed against a real
cluster must never read as one that was. Name a cluster and
the map also adds up the CPU and memory every unit and every
matched service would request (a catalog block's own
declared resources, or the platform default for a unit that
declares none) and compares the total with what that cluster
has free, using the same safety margin as the rest of the
platform's capacity gate. Anything that would run but could
not be weighed (a service with no catalog block behind it,
say) is named in `uncounted` rather than silently counted as
free.

`coverage` on a map always reads `best_effort`. The engine
reserves `supported` for accuracy earned by measurement,
never for structure alone, so no map claims it, whatever
else it reports.

## Where it stops instead of guessing

Open questions are expected. Where the evidence does not
settle something (which of two declared databases is the
real one, or whether a route the repository exposes is a
health check), the map says so, names the readings the
evidence supports, and leaves the choice to you.

A blocker is something Flui has no way to provide: a Docker
socket mounted into the container, a build that needs a
secret at build time, a kernel capability the platform does
not expose. A blocked unit always carries a remedy.

One blocker applies to the repository as a whole rather than
to a unit: more than five deployable applications. Past that
number, the reader stops instead of reading each one on its
own files, and the verdict says so by name. It lists the
roots it found, says why each was promoted, and asks you to
name at most five and map them separately, or to split the
repository. It does not rank them for you: on a workspace
that large, any ranking it could apply would recommend a
test harness or a build helper with the same confidence as
an application.

## Acting on the map

Reading a map changes nothing. Acting on one is a separate
call, `POST /repositories/:id/map/apply`, and its scope is
narrow.

Flui cuts its own branch, `flui/deploy-<sha7>`, at the exact
commit the map was read from, not at the tip of your branch,
which may have moved since. Flui reads from your branch and
cuts from it, but never writes to it. One commit lands on
the new branch, carrying every applied unit's rendered
`flui.yaml` and a build workflow beside it, and that single
commit starts every build. That is why the apply lands as
one commit and not one per unit: several commits would mean
several builds racing each other over the same webhook.

If a unit's rendered manifest declares `deploy.services` (a
database, say), that service is installed from the catalog
and Flui waits for it to reach `RUNNING` before anything is
written to GitHub. The application row and its database both
exist before the commit lands; the commit starts the build
on top of them. An apply refuses on a verdict of `blocked`,
`insufficient_capacity` or `not_assessed`, since spending
your repository's Actions minutes to reach a conclusion the
map already reached for free would be pointless. You can
also apply only some of the units (`--unit`, repeated, on the
CLI; `unitIds` on the API and MCP) instead of the whole map.

Because an apply provisions real things (databases,
applications) before it touches GitHub, a failure partway
through can leave something behind. If one unit of several
cannot be prepared, Flui deletes the branch it cut, so your
repository stays untouched, but the units prepared before
the failure already exist, with whatever they attached
already running. Flui names them in the error instead of
deleting them, and the next apply of the same repository
reuses them instead of creating a second copy.

This is also the one place where the time an apply needs and
the time a caller is given can disagree. Waiting for a newly
installed database to reach `RUNNING` takes minutes, which is
longer than an MCP tool call lasts. See [The Flui assistant
and MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/) for what
happens when the two collide, and why the CLI does not have
this problem.

## Three paths, at parity

The map is one of three ways to reach a running
application, and Flui's own tools state this: reading the
repository is "ONE way to reach a deploy and not the
required one," and bringing an image you already built
"carries the same standing as the two routes that go through
it." None of the three is a fallback for the others:

- **The map**: Flui reads the repository and renders the
  manifest for you.
- **Your own manifest**: you write `flui.yaml` by hand;
  `flui deploy` or `app_deploy_from_yaml` takes it from
  there.
- **An image already built**: the dashboard's **Deploy New →
  From a Docker image**, or `app_deploy_image` over MCP,
  skips the repository and the build entirely.

See [Deploy an application](/tasks/deploy-an-application/)
for the map and the hand-written manifest side by side.

## A limit: two units, two databases

`deploy.services` attaches a building block to one
application. Ownership is recorded per application: an
install belongs to the row that asked for it, and nothing
else can claim it.

That works for a single application, but it leaves a gap for
a monorepo. Two units that each declare the same database (a
shared Postgres that two services in one repository both
want to use) are two separate applications once deployed, so
each gets its own database. No field in the manifest says
"this is the same instance as that other unit's": the spec
does not carry one, and the render does not emit one. If
your repository's units are meant to share a database, wire
that by hand after the apply.

## Getting to it

- **CLI**: `flui repo map show` and `flui repo map apply`, in
  [Integrations and repositories](/cli/integrations/).
- **Dashboard**: **Repositories**, then **Readiness map** on
  the repository you want to read.
- **API / MCP**: `repo_map` and `repo_map_apply`, alongside
  `app_deploy_image`, in [The Flui assistant and
  MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/).

## Where this chapter goes from here

- [Deploy an application](/tasks/deploy-an-application/):
  the map and the hand-written manifest, walked end to end.
- [The Flui manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/): what
  a rendered `flui.yaml` can say, and what `deploy.services`
  wires up once it lands.
- [The Flui assistant and MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/):
  `repo_map`, `repo_map_apply`, and the safety model every
  write on this engine goes through.
- [The action cycle](/concepts/26-the-action-cycle/): why
  `repo_map_apply` stops and asks a person before it commits
  anything.
- [The build pipeline](/concepts/20-build-pipeline-today-and-tomorrow/):
  what the workflow an apply commits does.

sections.title: High availability
sections.body:
High availability has a separate answer for each thing that can
fail, and in Flui those answers differ. This page takes them one at
a time: what happens, what Flui does about it and where the current
limits are.

## What can fail, and what happens

| What fails | Applications on that cluster | Your data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A worker | Those with two or more copies keep answering from the other nodes | Unaffected, unless a database or a volume tied to that node lived on it |
| The cluster's master | Keep answering from the other nodes; nothing new can be deployed until it returns | Shared storage waits for the master; nothing is lost |
| The node a database lives on | The database is down until it is restored | At most the last few minutes of changes |
| The control cluster | Keep answering | Unaffected; the dashboard, the API and central logs are gone until it returns |

## A worker

A cluster with at least two nodes keeps serving when a worker goes
away. Flui spreads an application's copies across nodes wherever
there is room, and the application's address points at every
ready node that takes traffic. An application with two or more
copies keeps answering from the ones that are left.

For about the first minute, until the cluster marks the worker as
gone, some requests still go to the copy that was on it and fail.
After that, the remaining copies answer every request. The copies
that were on the lost worker start again elsewhere once the cluster
stops waiting for it.

Once Flui has checked that every node of the cluster sees the
shared storage, new volumes are not tied to the node that created
them, so an application that keeps its files there starts again
elsewhere with its data. Until every node sees it, new volumes stay
on their node, and an application with one of them waits for that
node to come back.

`flui app status` tells you, for each application, whether it
survives losing a worker. That needs:

- at least two copies, running on at least two nodes
- no dedicated placement, which keeps it on one node
- no volume tied to one node
- a real domain
- more than one node taking traffic

When an application falls short, the command lists each reason
with what to change. Agents get the same answer from the
`app_availability` tool.

_Diagram: A worker is lost: within about a minute the other copy answers every request, its name stops pointing at it within a minute or two, and the lost copy starts again on another node._

## The cluster's master

Every cluster has one master. It does not sit between your users
and your applications: an application's domain points at every
ready node of its cluster that takes traffic. Flui measures that set every minute
and moves the name when it changes, with a one-minute lifetime
on a name that points at several nodes. Clients that looked the
address up before a node dropped out can take a minute or two to
move on.

What still depends on the master is the cluster's ability to change.
While it is down, nothing new is deployed, lost copies are not
started again, and [shared storage](/concepts/21-storage-classes-and-dedicated-placement/),
which is served through the master, waits for it. The data on it is
kept: where the provider sells volumes, it lives on one, separate
from the machine's own disk.

The automatic address an application gets when it has no domain of
its own encodes the master's IP, so it cannot point at more than one
node. An application that needs to stay up needs a real domain.

Flui runs one master per cluster. [Why K3s](/concepts/02-why-k3s/#high-availability)
explains how more could be added without changing how a cluster
stores its state.

## The node a database lives on

Databases from the catalog run as a single instance on the disk of
the node they are placed on, because a local disk is the fastest
thing a database can write to. This also makes that node a single
point of failure for the database. If the node is lost, the database
is down until it is restored on another one.

PostgreSQL and MariaDB ship every change off the cluster as it
happens, so a restore loses at most the last few minutes of changes.
[How Flui protects data](/concepts/29-how-flui-protects-data/)
explains how this works and how to check it is on before you need
it.

### In progress: databases that survive the loss of a node

The design is settled and being built, PostgreSQL first.

A database marked for high availability runs as two copies on two
different nodes, each on its own local disk, so it keeps the fast
storage. The copies are kept in step synchronously:
a change is confirmed only once both have it, so the copy that takes
over has everything.

A vote decides which copy takes over. Each of the two nodes has
one vote, and the control cluster has the third. A copy becomes the
primary only with two votes out of three, so a node cut off from
the others can never become a second primary. Losing any one of the
three, the control cluster included, still leaves a majority to
decide. The smallest setup that covers this is a control cluster
plus a workload cluster of two machines.

MariaDB and Redis follow, on the same pattern.

## The control cluster

The control cluster runs Flui itself. Losing it takes away the
dashboard, the API, sign-in and the central logs and metrics. Every
workload cluster keeps serving its applications, because a cluster
needs the control plane only to make changes. See
[Failure boundaries](/concepts/05-multi-cluster-topology/#failure-boundaries)
and, for the worst case, [Rebuild the control plane](/tasks/rebuild-the-control-plane/).

The API can run as more than one copy, which is what keeps it
answering when many people use the dashboard at once:

```bash
flui app scale flui-api --replicas 2
```

Requests are shared between the copies, and one of them runs the
scheduled work. If that copy stops, another takes over within
seconds. The count, and any CPU or memory you set on `flui-api`,
stays in place after a platform update. The API refuses to drop
below one copy, or to go above six unless `FLUI_API_MAX_REPLICAS`
allows more.

## A cluster across several locations

Where a provider network spans several locations, a cluster's
nodes can sit in more than one of them, as long as its
[scaling group](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/) is allowed to buy
there. Every node accepts traffic and copies are spread across
nodes, so losing a location takes only what ran there.

## Making an application highly available

- **Run at least two copies.** Set `deploy.scaling.min: 2` in the
  application's [`flui.yaml`](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/).
- **Give the cluster at least two nodes,** so the copies have
  somewhere else to be.
- **Give it a real domain,** in a zone whose DNS Flui can
  drive ([see which providers](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/#the-providers-integrated-today)), so its address can point
  at every node.
- **Protect the cluster,** so its databases are backed up
  continuously and any loss is counted in minutes.
- **Keep the control cluster separate** from the clusters your
  applications run on, so a problem with one does not reach the
  other.

## What is not here yet

- Databases that survive the loss of their node (in progress, see above).
- Shared storage that does not depend on the master.

sections.title: Add a cluster and give it capacity
sections.body:
A cluster is a stable name for a changing set of machines.
You can add machines to it, make one bigger, or take one
away, and the cluster keeps its name, addresses, storage and
certificates throughout. The applications on it keep running.

Each of these changes still costs money: a machine is billed
from the moment it boots, whether or not anything runs on it.
So every change on this page follows the same order: check
what you have, check what the change costs, then make the
change.

## Create a workload cluster

The first cluster of an installation is the **control
cluster**. It runs the dashboard, the API, the login and the
database. A **workload cluster** is a second cluster that
runs only applications.

You add one when you want work kept apart: a different
region, a different provider, or a customer who should not
share machines with anyone else. The control plane is not
installed again; the new cluster reports back to the one
you already have.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui cluster create edge
flui cluster create edge --worker-count 2
flui cluster create edge --provider hetzner --region hel1
flui cluster create edge --no-wait
```

The new cluster starts on the control cluster's provider and
region and joins its private network on its own.
`--provider` places it somewhere else. That works only when
the control cluster can reach that far, and the command checks
before anything is bought. `--worker-count` builds workers
beside the master; the default, 0, is master-only.

The command waits up to half an hour for the cluster to be
ready. `--no-wait` returns the operation instead.
`flui env create` does something else: it creates the control
cluster.

To see all your clusters:

```bash
flui cluster list
flui cluster list --output json
```

The list shows the control cluster first, then the workload
clusters, each with its type, provider, region, node count and
status. The control cluster is stored on your own machine, so
it is listed even when the API cannot be reached. Workload
clusters live only in the control cluster's database, so they
are read over the API. If that read fails, the command says so
instead of showing an incomplete list as if it were complete.

Note that `flui node connect`, `flui node list` and
`flui node remove` work on the clusters stored on your
machine, which means the control cluster. The `flui scaling`
commands reach any cluster in the list above.

**Dashboard:**

Open **Clusters** and choose **Create Cluster**. The wizard
asks seven things, in this order:

1. **Infrastructure**: a name and a provider.

   _Screenshot: The Infrastructure step: a cluster name and a choice of provider._

2. **Resources**: the region and the server type every node
   gets, whether the cluster carries shared storage, and how
   many nodes it starts with. Prices and availability are
   shown per region. How far it may grow later is set on its
   **Scaling** tab once it exists.

   _Screenshot: The Resources step: regions with prices, node sizes, shared storage and the number of nodes._

3. **SSH Keys**: optional.

4. **Network**: on the control cluster's provider the
   cluster joins that network and there is nothing to choose.
   Elsewhere, you pick an existing network or one Flui builds.

5. **Endpoint**: where the cluster's hostnames come from,
   either test addresses or a DNS zone you registered.

   _Screenshot: The Endpoint step: test addresses or custom domains._

6. **Firewall**: optional rules.

7. **Review & Create**: everything you chose, with the
   monthly estimate.

   _Screenshot: The Review and Create step: the summary and the monthly cost estimate._

After you create it, a progress page follows the
provisioning to the end. When it finishes, the cluster has
its own page with tabs for Overview, Monitoring, Network,
Storage, Nodes, Scaling, Firewall, DNS, Variables and
Pricing.

**Agent (MCP):**

`cluster_create` takes a name, a provider, a region, a node
size, and how many workers to build beside the master (0
means master-only). Region and node size are provider codes,
and the tool tells the agent to get them from you rather
than invent them.

The call does not run straight away. It stops, and a person
answers it. It is also the one action on this page you can
only approve once: there is no "always" for
creating a cluster, because a cluster that does not exist yet
cannot define the scope a standing permission would cover. A
standing permission to create clusters would be a standing
permission to spend.

When it runs, it returns an operation handle, not a finished
cluster. Provisioning takes 8 to 15 minutes, and nothing polls
it on the agent's behalf.

## Read the capacity before you buy

Adding a machine is easy, and it starts costing money
immediately, often without anyone noticing until the bill
arrives. Every surface here can show you the cost first.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui env capacity
flui env capacity --top 5
flui env capacity --direction upgrade
```

This reports the control cluster's master: its server type,
how much CPU and memory it has, how much is used and free,
what it costs per month, and the shared volume behind it. It
then lists the server types you could move to, sorted, each
with the difference in monthly cost.

Read it before you run `flui env scale-master` or
`flui env scale-node`.

**Dashboard:**

The cluster's **Pricing** tab shows what has been spent this
month, the projected cost for a full month at the current
size, and a line per node and per volume. The **Nodes** tab
shows what is there right now, and how many nodes the cluster
expects.

_Screenshot: The Pricing tab: spent so far, expected by month end, the monthly cost of this setup, and a line per machine and volume._

_Screenshot: The Nodes tab: each node with its size, location and address._

**Agent (MCP):**

`cluster_capacity_plan` returns the same capacity and the
same resize candidates with their monthly deltas.
`cluster_node_list` returns the nodes with their ids.

Both are reads, so neither stops to ask anybody. The tool
instructs the agent to read the plan and tell you the monthly
difference before asking you to approve adding or removing a
node.

## Add workers

A cluster's master can host applications by itself, and a
small cluster runs fine that way. You add workers when the
work no longer fits.

On the control cluster, adding a worker has a second effect:
as soon as its first worker joins, Flui reserves the master
for the control plane, so new work lands on the workers.
Scale back to a single node and the reservation is lifted
automatically.

On a provider Flui buys from, a cluster's nodes change
through its [scaling group](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/).
Every such cluster has one from the start, set to hold the
nodes it has. You add a worker by raising its floor (the
fewest nodes it may run, master included) and then approving
the machine it proposes. A group allowed to act on its own
buys without asking, within its ceiling; see
[Let a cluster buy its own machines](/tasks/let-a-cluster-buy-its-own-machines/).

**CLI:**

```bash
flui scaling floor 3
flui scaling approve
flui scaling approve --yes
```

`floor` moves the minimum. `approve` shows what the group
proposes (the server type, the region, the price per hour)
and buys nothing; `--yes` buys it. Pass `--cluster` to reach
a workload cluster.

If your control cluster runs on servers you already own, you
join a worker instead of buying one:

```bash
flui node connect --host 203.0.113.10
```

It reaches the host over SSH, checks it is a clean Linux
machine with enough memory, and joins it. The host has to be
able to reach the master over the private network the nodes
share. Pass `--master-ip` when the address the cluster knows
is not the one the new machine can use. On a cluster
whose machines came from a cloud provider the command joins
nothing and points you to `flui scaling floor`.

**Dashboard:**

On the cluster's **Scaling** tab, **+** next to the node
count raises the floor. Confirm it, and a manual group then
asks whether to buy the machine it picked (server type,
region and price), with **Buy** or **Later**. The **Nodes**
tab points you there.

_Screenshot: The Nodes tile after pressing +: the new floor, with Confirm or Cancel._

On a cluster built from servers you already own, the
**Nodes** tab has **Connect node** instead, because there is
nothing to buy.

**Agent (MCP):**

`scaling_group_floor` moves the floor and
`scaling_approve_purchase` buys what a manual group
proposes. Both stop and ask you. Every tool that adds a node
does it through the group's floor; none buys a machine
outside it.

## Resize a node

Sometimes you need a bigger machine rather than more of
them. Applications that need fast local disk are placed on a
specific node and cannot be moved off it, so growing the
machine under them is the only way to give them more room.

Treat this as planned maintenance. The machine is powered
off, the provider changes its server type, and it comes back
and rejoins. This takes roughly three to five minutes, during
which everything on that node is down. Storage survives and
the node keeps its identity; only CPU and memory change.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui env scale-node <cluster>-worker-1 --type cx32
flui env scale-master --type cx32
```

Both target the control cluster. The node is named as
`flui node list` shows it. `--type` is a provider
server-type code; leave it out and the CLI picks the next
size up with the smallest increase in monthly cost.

Before anything happens it prints the plan: the type it is
moving from and to, the monthly cost and the difference,
the expected downtime, and any application pinned to that
node. Then it asks you to type the node's name back.
`--confirm` skips that prompt.

On Hetzner, `--upgradeDisk` also grows the machine's own
disk. This cannot be reversed: afterwards you can never move
the node back down to a smaller type.

**Dashboard:**

The dashboard does not resize a node. The cluster's
Scaling tab changes how many machines there are; changing
the size of one is done from the CLI or through an agent.

**Agent (MCP):**

`cluster_node_resize` takes a node id and the server type to
move to. Read `cluster_node_scale_preview` first: it names
the current type, the downtime and the applications pinned
to that node that go down with it.

The call stops and asks you, and the question you answer
states that the node goes down while the resize runs. Growing
the machine's own disk is not offered to an agent at all,
because it cannot be undone.

## Remove a worker

Removing a machine is the only way to lower the bill. The
machine is deleted and you stop paying for it.

In order, the cluster stops sending new work to the node,
moves the work already there onto the other nodes, and only
then deletes the server. Anything that was
sitting on that machine's own disk rather than on the
cluster's shared storage goes with it.

Moving the work off has a limit of 120 seconds. If something
does not move in time, the node is removed anyway and the
operation returns a warning. Read that warning: it means
something was cut off rather than relocated.

The master is never removed this way. Taking the master out
means destroying the whole cluster, which is a different
operation.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui scaling floor 2
flui scaling approve
flui scaling approve --yes
```

Lowering the floor makes a manual group name the node it
would give back. `approve` shows which one; `--yes` moves
its work off and deletes it.

A machine you attached yourself goes the other way:

```bash
flui node list
flui node remove <node-id>
flui node remove <node-id> --no-wait
```

The id comes from `flui node list`. The CLI checks it
against the cluster's real nodes before queuing anything, so
a wrong id fails immediately instead of halfway through. If
you point it at the master, it refuses and names the command
you need: `flui cluster destroy` for a workload cluster,
`flui env destroy` for the control cluster. It waits up to
five minutes. If the move takes longer, you get control back
with a note that the work is still running.

**Dashboard:**

On the **Scaling** tab, **−** lowers the floor. A manual
group then names the node it would drain and delete, with
**Remove** or **Later**.

_Screenshot: The Nodes tile after pressing −: the lower floor, with Confirm or Cancel._

On a cluster built from servers you already own, every
worker row on the **Nodes** tab has a **Remove** button; the
master has none. You are told the removal cannot be undone
and asked to type the node's name back before it starts. The
dialog then shows each step as it happens.

**Agent (MCP):**

`scaling_approve_removal` gives back the node a manual
group names; `cluster_node_remove` detaches a machine you
attached yourself. Both need the *destroy* depth of the
infrastructure permission group, and both sit behind a
second, independent gate: the installation must have
destructive operations switched on. If either gate is
missing, the tool is not offered to the agent, and the agent
should not try to work around that.

When both gates pass, the tools still stop and ask you.

## Getting onto a machine yourself

You should rarely need this. Use the higher-level commands
for metrics, logs, restarts and deploys. When you do need a
shell on a node:

```bash
flui ssh master
flui ssh workload-cluster-1/master
flui ssh workload-cluster-1/worker-1
```

A bare node name means the control cluster.
`<cluster>/<node>` reaches any cluster the CLI can see,
workload clusters included. The node part is `master`,
`worker-N`, or the server's own name.

There is no key to set up. The CLI signs a short-lived
certificate for you from the SSH authority your profile
manages.

## What an agent may never do here

No agent credential can destroy a cluster, not even with
your approval. No agent permission group carries that
permission, and the source enforces this in two places so it
cannot be granted by accident, however the credential is
assembled. An agent can create a cluster, grow it, resize it
and remove its workers. Destroying the whole cluster is left
to a person.

Every other write on this page (create, add, resize, remove)
stops and waits for a person. The agent is not notified when
you answer. It finds out by making the identical call again,
and that retry is what runs the work, so the action is
attributed to the agent rather than to your click. A pending
request expires after an hour.

The refusal the agent gets does not include the price, even
when there is one; you see the price on the page where you
decide. The agent is told that a cost exists and that it
cannot see it, so it can tell you so instead of calling the
action free.

How you answer those requests is
[When your agent stops to ask you](/tasks/when-your-agent-asks/).

## Where this goes next

- [Nodes and cluster topology](/concepts/06-nodes-and-cluster-topology/):
  what a node is, and why the master is a special case.
- [Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/):
  the choices that shape a cluster, and what it hands back.
- [Storage classes and dedicated placement](/concepts/21-storage-classes-and-dedicated-placement/):
  which applications can move between machines and which
  cannot.
- [CLI: Clusters, nodes, and SSH](/cli/clusters-and-nodes/):
  the flag-by-flag reference for the commands above.

sections.title: Choose what your agent may do
sections.body:
A long list of checkboxes tends to get approved in full.
Nobody reads twelve of them carefully, and the twelfth
is usually the one that mattered.

So Flui does not ask you to tick scopes. You switch on
permission groups: sixteen of them, each described by
one sentence written for a person, and each granted or
refused as a whole. The sentence you agree to is exactly
what the key carries.

This page assumes you already have an agent connected,
or are about to. If not, start at
[Connect an agent](/tasks/connect-an-agent/).

## Two axes

A group is a pair of an area and a depth. The area is
what the agent is trusted with. The depth is how far
into it: look, change or destroy. Within one area a
deeper group contains every shallower one, so switching
on "Delete applications" also switches on the other two.

Not every pair exists. There is no group for deleting a
backup and none for sending mail, because the scopes
those would be built from are not in the catalogue.

| Area | Look | Change | Destroy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Applications | See applications | Deploy and operate applications | Delete applications |
| Logs and health | Read logs and health | none | none |
| Backups | See backups | Run backups | none |
| Migrations | See migrations | Run migrations | Abort and tear down migrations |
| Mail | See mail delivery | none | none |
| Who has access | See who has access | Grant and revoke access | none |
| Infrastructure | See the infrastructure | Operate the infrastructure | Remove infrastructure |
| Platform | none | Update the platform | none |

The sections below give the sixteen sentences in the
product's words.

## Applications

**See applications.** Read the applications on this
instance, their non-secret configuration and their
history, together with the catalogue, templates,
repositories and clusters behind them, and change
nothing.

**Deploy and operate applications.** Deploy, install,
scale, restart, stop and roll back applications, change
how much CPU and memory they may use, set their
non-secret configuration, set up the routes, schedules,
wildcard DNS and repository links they need, choose
whether a backup is taken before each deploy, read a
connected repository and commit the manifests Flui
renders for it onto a branch of Flui's own (never
yours), starting builds that spend that repository's own
GitHub Actions minutes, read the logs, metrics, traffic
and alerts of what it is running, and ask you in person
for a sensitive value it must never hold itself, on top
of everything *See applications* reads, but never delete
one.

**Delete applications.** Everything *Deploy and operate
applications* can do, plus deleting an application, a
schedule or a gateway route for good.

The middle group is wider than its name, and its
sentence says so: deploying includes reading logs and
metrics. An agent that can deploy but cannot read why a
deploy failed is of little use, and the design avoids
needing a second switch to make the first one work.

One side effect: groups are worked out from the scopes
a key holds, so a key carrying only this group also
reads back as *Read logs and health*. That is accurate,
since the key can read logs.

## Logs and health

**Read logs and health.** Read the applications on this
instance together with their logs, resource metrics,
edge traffic and alert history, and change nothing.

## Backups

**See backups.** Read the backup posture: which policies
exist, where they write, how the recent jobs went, and
which volumes on a cluster are still being paid for by
applications that no longer exist.

**Run backups.** Read the backup posture and act on it
(run a backup now, pause or resume a policy) without
deleting a policy or a stored backup.

## Migrations

**See migrations.** Read the migrations on this instance
and how far each one has got.

**Run migrations.** Start and cut over migrations
between clusters, and read the applications and clusters
they move between.

**Abort and tear down migrations.** Everything *Run
migrations* can do, plus aborting a migration and
destroying the source it moved away from.

## Mail

**See mail delivery.** Read whether mail is set up here,
what the provider did with recently sent messages, and
which addresses have been suppressed.

Recipient addresses are personal data, which is why this
is its own area rather than part of logs. An agent with
access to logs does not get everyone's email with it.

## Who has access

**See who has access.** Read who on this instance can
reach what, and what removing or changing one of those
grants would take away from them, and change none of
it.

**Grant and revoke access.** Everything *See who has
access* reads, plus giving somebody a role over this
instance or taking one away; an agent holding this
decides what other people can reach, and it can never
hand out more than you hold yourself.

This is the only switch that lets an agent decide what
someone else may reach, so it is a group of its own. It
is not included in any other group on the instance, so
it can never arrive hidden inside "deploy my
applications". An agent holds it only if you switched it
on by name after reading the sentence. Even then, it
cannot hand out more than you hold yourself.

## Infrastructure

**See the infrastructure.** Read how this instance is
built and what changing it would cost (the capacity
plan of a cluster, its nodes and what resizing one would
take down, its shared storage, its platform components,
its certificate issuers, whether it hosts its own DNS,
and the scaling groups that say how large each cluster
may grow together with what they decided and declined to
decide), and change none of it.

**Operate the infrastructure.** Everything *See the
infrastructure* reads, plus acting on it: creating a
cluster, adding, resizing and uncordoning its nodes,
expanding its shared storage, stopping and starting it,
changing its autoscaling, enabling its firewall,
redeploying a platform component, configuring its
certificate issuers, issuing a SAN certificate,
publishing the records a sending domain needs and
setting the scaling group that says how large a cluster
may grow and how much it may spend unattended; and every
one of those stops to ask you before it happens, with
what it costs attached.

**Remove infrastructure.** Everything *Operate the
infrastructure* can do, plus draining a worker node and
deleting the machine at the provider. It cannot delete a
cluster, which no agent credential can be given.

The middle group states the pause in the sentence you
read before saying yes. Holding the group does not count
as approval: every route behind it goes through Flui's
action cycle, so the agent gets a request with the
estimate attached, and nothing happens until a person
answers. See
[When your agent stops to ask you](/tasks/when-your-agent-asks/).

Deleting a cluster is not on the list and cannot be
added. No scope on this instance carries it, and a test
checks this so nobody adds it while tidying up.

This area is separate from applications because
stopping a cluster stops everything on it, and expanding
a volume is a one-way cost. Neither is what "deploy my
applications" promises.

## Platform

**Update the platform.** Plan a new Flui release phase
by phase (backup, system manifests, platform images, K3s
and the checks) and apply that plan, which stops to ask
you first, naming the release, because it replaces the
control plane and runs database migrations only the
backup can undo.

It is kept apart from operating the infrastructure for
that last reason: a rollback does not undo a migration.

## Granted whole, or refused whole

A group never comes back smaller than you asked for.

If a group names something your own permissions do not
cover, the whole request fails, and the refusal names
the group that caused it, not only the underlying scope.
A message naming only a scope would leave you guessing
which switch to turn off.

The same rule applies when you are already holding a
limited key yourself. A key is never worth more than
whoever asked for it, so the scopes a group names must
already be among the scopes of the credential making the
request.

A request that names no group is also refused. The
widest credential the instance can issue has to be asked
for explicitly.

## A key only narrows access

Switching on a group can only take away. It narrows what
a credential may reach and never adds to what the person
behind it may do: every call still meets the same access
checks it would have met anyway. An agent given "Grant
and revoke access" by someone who cannot assign roles
can assign nothing.

The ceiling applies everywhere the key is presented, not
only to the agent toolbox. The same key used against
plain HTTP, or on a live-updates connection, is held to
the same scopes.

Two ceilings can apply at once, and each is fixed
differently:

- **The scope ceiling**: the key was never granted this
  capability. Fix it by issuing a new key.
- **The application ceiling**: the key is limited to
  particular applications or projects. Fix it by
  widening the same key, which keeps working; nothing
  has to reconnect.

The two refusals are worded differently so that an
agent relays the right instruction instead of retrying
forever.

## One capability nobody switches on

Every scoped key carries one thing you did not pick: the
ability to read the "how to operate this instance"
document.

It is added to every key when the key is minted, so an
agent can learn how work is done here before it is
trusted with any of it. The document is the same for
every credential on an installation, it is read-only,
and it permits nothing on its own, so there is no
checkbox for it.

## The caution about attaching scopes to a person

Agent scopes can also arrive from the identity provider,
as roles on an account. If someone attaches them to a
person's account, meaning "this is for their agent",
they cap that person too. Every session that account
opens is capped, including their browser session.

That enforcement is correct: a credential that declares
a ceiling is held to that ceiling wherever it is
presented. When the dashboard goes read-only for this
reason, the refusal says where the scopes came from and
what to do: agent scopes belong on a machine account,
not on a person.

## Choosing them

**CLI:**

There is no `--groups` flag. Groups are an API and
dashboard concept, and the CLI does not know their
names. From a terminal you mint by raw scope:

```bash
flui auth generate-api-key \
  --name agent \
  --scope mcp:app:read \
  --scope mcp:obs:read
```

Repeat `--scope` for each one. A scope you do not hold
yourself is refused, not trimmed, which is the same rule
the groups follow, one scope at a time.

You must name something. Naming neither `--scope` nor
`--unscoped` is refused before the command touches the
network:

```bash
flui auth generate-api-key --name ci --unscoped
```

`--unscoped` issues a key with no ceiling at all,
carrying your full weight. Use it only when you mean to.

To list and revoke keys:

```bash
flui auth api-keys
flui auth revoke-api-key <id>
```

`flui auth api-keys` prints names, state and the raw
scope list. It does not translate scopes into group
names; that view lives on the dashboard and in the API.
An unscoped key shows as "the full weight of the
issuer".

The terminal also differs in two ways. The key is saved
straight into the active profile instead of being
printed; the server keeps only a digest of it, so
nothing on the installation can hand it back later. And
the command needs a session token from the identity
provider, passed with `--token` or `FLUI_SESSION_TOKEN`,
not the API key you already have.

**Dashboard:**

**Settings → Agent keys** is where the groups appear:
one row per area, with a level to pick (**None**,
**See**, **Change** or **Delete**, only the ones that
area has). A deeper level includes every shallower one,
so each area holds one pick. **Details** on a row shows
each level's sentence and the scopes it carries, in
full.

_Screenshot: Minting an agent key: one row per area with a level to pick, None, See, Change or Delete._

_Screenshot: Details open on the Applications row: each level's sentence and the scopes it carries._

Above the rows, the screen tells you how many of the
groups on this instance are yours to hand on. A level
that is not yours is shown disabled, not hidden: it has
a lock, and under **Details** it is marked "Not yours to
grant", with a line naming the capability your own
permissions do not cover. It is the same refusal you
would meet when minting the key.

You also give the key a name and an expiry. The name
helps you later, when you revoke a key and need to tell
this agent from the next. The expiry defaults to 30
days, so the consent ends on its own.

At least one area must be set. A key with nothing
picked would carry your full weight, and you should not
end up with that by leaving a form empty.

Two optional narrowings sit under the areas,
independent of the groups:

- **Which applications**: limit the key to particular
  applications. The default is every application you can
  already reach.
- **Which projects**: grant whole projects instead. An
  application added to a granted project later is
  reached too, with nothing to reissue.

They combine: an application is reachable if either
list covers it. Both can be changed on an existing key
without reissuing it, with the **Applications** and
**Projects** buttons on each row in the list below.

The list of keys you have issued shows each one as the
groups it carries. Two labels can appear there:

- **Wider than its name**: the key holds scopes that the
  groups on its row do not account for, because it was
  assembled by hand rather than from the levels. Read
  the scopes under **Details**, not the badges.
- **You are signed in with this**: the key you are using
  right now.

## No agent chooses its own

There is no agent tab above, because nothing in the
agent toolbox mints a key.

An agent can ask for one. `api_key_request` takes what
the key is for, in one line, and the scopes the agent
thinks it needs. It returns a command for you to run in
your own terminal, plus the keys that already exist on
the account, by name and scope, never by value. None of
its arguments can carry a key in either direction.

It never puts `--unscoped` in that command, so the
widest credential on the instance is never the easiest
thing for an agent to ask for.

## Where this goes next

- [Connect an agent](/tasks/connect-an-agent/): minting
  the credential and pointing an agent at it.
- [When your agent stops to ask you](/tasks/when-your-agent-asks/):
  what happens when a write behind one of these groups
  pauses for a person.
- [The Flui assistant and MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/):
  what the toolbox is and how a scope decides which
  tools an agent is offered.
- [CLI: Authentication](/cli/authentication/): the flag
  surface for keys and sessions.

sections.title: Set an application's configuration and secrets
sections.body:
Every application needs values it does not carry in its own
code: a database URL, a log level, an API key. Two places hold
those values. The `flui.yaml` in your repository says what the
application needs. The platform stores what it was given, deploy
after deploy. This page explains which of the two wins.

## The manifest owns the keys it declares

Values pinned by hand are how configuration drifts: the file
says one thing, the running application does another, and
nothing reports the difference. So the manifest reclaims what it
declares. On every deploy, for every key `flui.yaml` names, the
value in the file is the value that lands.

From lowest to highest priority:

1. **A stored value on a key the manifest does not
   declare.** Kept. This is the only place a hand-set value
   survives.
2. **`flui.yaml`.** Authoritative for every key it declares, on
   every deploy, including a key someone had pinned by hand.
3. **`--env` / `--env-file` at deploy time.** Passed by a person
   on this deploy, and wins over both.

So a value you set by hand outlives the next deploy only if the
manifest says nothing about that key. To use a different value on
a key the manifest declares, pass it at deploy time.

There is one exception, which prevents a credential from leaking.
A key **linked** to another building block's secret, such as a
database password Flui wired in for you, is never overwritten by
a plain value from the manifest. The link stays a link.

## Declared keys without a value

A manifest can name a key without carrying its value. It might
declare a value someone supplies later, or point at a sibling
application that cannot be found right now.

A key like that keeps whatever is already stored. Declaring it
tells the platform that the variable exists and its value comes
from elsewhere. It does not tell the platform to blank it.

Only a key the manifest stops declaring altogether is removed.
That rule is what lets an application keep its API key across a
redeploy.

## A deploy-time value is plain text unless you say so

`--env DATABASE_URL=…` stores exactly what you typed, in plain
text, and it stays that way. That is fine for a log level and bad
for a password.

Name the key with `--secret` to change that:

```bash
flui deploy --env-file .env \
  --secret DATABASE_URL --secret API_KEY
```

`--secret` is repeatable, and each name must be a key you are
passing on this deploy. Naming one you are not passing fails the
command, so you never believe a credential was protected when it
was not. A key marked this way is stored encrypted, delivered to
the application as a secret, and never printed back by
`flui app env list` or by `flui app status -o json`.

Use `--env-file` for anything sensitive. Values in a file never
appear on the command line, so they are not written to your shell
history and are not visible to other processes while the deploy
runs.

Flui also warns you. If a key looks like a credential (its name
contains `SECRET`, `PASSWORD`, `TOKEN`, `PRIVATE` or `_KEY`) and
you did not mark it, the deploy prints a warning that it is about
to be stored and shown in plain text. The deploy still goes
ahead, since you may have a reason.

## Keys awaiting a value

A sensitive variable can exist without a value. The manifest
declares a key as a secret and carries no value for it, or an
agent asks a person to supply one. Either way the key is
recorded, by name, as **awaiting a value**.

Every surface lists that state beside the others. It is a
distinct state, not a blank, a missing key or an error. Asking
for the variables of an application that is still waiting for
one is a successful request.

A key still awaiting a value is not delivered to the running
application at all until a person supplies it.

## Setting and reading them

**CLI:**

`flui app env list` shows everything for one application: plain
variables with their values, which sensitive keys are
configured, and which are still waiting.

```bash
flui app env list my-api
```

Sensitive values are not shown, because none is available to
show. A configured secret reads as set, and a waiting one reads
as `awaiting a value`.

To deliver a sensitive value:

```bash
flui app env set my-api STRIPE_SECRET_KEY
```

There is no `--value` flag; the command prompts you instead. An
argument would land in your shell history and be visible to
every other process on the machine while it ran. When an agent
composes the command, it would also pass through the model. For
a script, pipe it in:

```bash
printf '%s' "$KEY" | flui app env set my-api STRIPE_SECRET_KEY --stdin
```

The value is not read back afterwards. The command tells you
the key is configured, and nothing on this path can tell you
more.

Both commands accept `-c, --cluster <name|id>`; it is detected
for you when the profile has only one cluster.

**Dashboard:**

Open the application and go to its **Configuration** tab.

There are two lists. One holds plain variables: names and
values, both visible and editable. The other holds sensitive
ones and is write-only: you see which keys exist, never what
they hold. You can replace a masked value at any time, but you
can never read it back.

_Screenshot: The Configuration tab: plain variables with their values, and sensitive ones that are write-only._

A key still awaiting a value appears in the second list with
`awaiting a value` where the mask would be. Type a value into it
and save, and the key becomes configured.

Keep in mind:

- A value you type in this tab is a pin. If the manifest
  declares that key, the next deploy reclaims it. For a value
  that should survive, change the manifest or pass it at deploy
  time.
- Saving stores the value. It does not restart the
  application; see below.

**Agent (MCP):**

There are three tools. An agent may read the shape of the
configuration and write the non-secret part, but never holds a
secret.

- **`app_variables`** reads. It returns plain variables with
  their values, the sensitive keys that are configured, and the
  keys still awaiting one. A sensitive value is never returned,
  to anyone. Asking again does not help, and an agent must never
  invent a value to fill the gap.
- **`app_variable_set`** writes non-secret configuration: a
  hostname, a log level, a feature flag. Keys it does not name
  are left alone. It refuses a key the application already holds
  as sensitive, and it refuses a value shaped like a credential.
  When it refuses, it writes nothing at all, not even the
  acceptable keys in the same call, so an agent is never left
  guessing which part landed.
- **`app_variable_request`** asks a person for a sensitive
  value. It has no `value` argument. The tool records the key as
  awaiting a value and returns the command for a person to run
  in their own terminal, so the value goes from that terminal
  straight to encrypted storage without passing through the
  agent.

That last call comes back as *input required*. This is a state,
not a failure: the agent should relay the command and stop, not
retry the call unchanged.

Reading needs a credential that may look at applications; both
writes need one that may change them.

## When the new value reaches the application

Writing a variable updates what Flui stores immediately. The
running application picks up the new value the next time it
starts: on its next deploy, or on a restart.

```bash
flui app restart my-api
```

This is why delivering a secret is usually followed by a
redeploy or restart, and why reading the variables back right
after setting one shows it as configured while the application
still runs with the old value.

## Where this goes next

- [The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/): the
  `deploy.env` block these rules are about, and what else a
  manifest can and cannot say.
- [The app concept](/concepts/16-the-app-concept/): what an
  application is, and where its configuration sits among
  everything else it carries.
- [`flui deploy`](/cli/deploy/): the full flag surface,
  including the install-time overrides that work the same way
  for a name and a domain.
- [The Flui Assistant and MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/):
  the surface the three tools above belong to.

sections.title: Connect an agent
sections.body:
You already have a credential that works, but do not hand it to
an agent. Your key carries all of your permissions, it is the
key your own terminal uses, and once it is in a model's context
you cannot take it back out.

Give the agent a key of its own instead. That key decides how
far the agent reaches, and it is the only thing you have to
revoke when you change your mind.

## One address, and nothing held open

Flui speaks [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) at a single
address: your installation's API base with `/mcp` on the end.
Every call is a `POST` to that address with the key in an
`Authorization: Bearer` header.

There is no session to open, keep alive or re-establish after a
network drop. Each request is answered on its own, and the
server built to answer it is then thrown away.

This follows protocol revision 2026-07-28, which removes
sessions and the opening handshake from MCP. Clients built
against the 2025 revisions are served too, with the same tools,
so an older agent does not need upgrading before it can connect.

The endpoint answers `POST` only. A `GET` for an event stream is
refused, because there is no stream: nothing is ever published
outside the reply to a call.

## The key is shown once

Flui stores a hash of the key, never the key itself. After
minting, the value does not exist anywhere on the installation,
so nobody can show it to you again, including whoever runs the
installation.

If you lose it, revoke it and mint another. There is no recovery
step.

## What the key may touch: two lists

Two separate questions decide what an agent can do.

**What kind of work** is set by the key's scopes: deploying,
reading logs, touching access and so on. Scopes have their own
page: [Choose what your agent may
do](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/).

**Which applications** is what this page covers. A key can name
specific applications, specific projects, or both.

The two lists are alternatives. An application is reachable as
soon as either list covers it. Naming an app individually and
naming its project are two ways to reach the same app, and a
key holding both reaches the union of the two.

This has three consequences:

- **A project grant keeps working as the project grows.** An app
  added to a granted project later is covered on its next
  request. The project is checked against the application as it
  stands, every time, so there is nothing to refresh or reissue.
- **An app named individually stays reachable even if it leaves
  a granted project.** That follows from the lists being a union
  rather than an intersection.
- **Naming neither list means every application you can already
  reach.** That is the default.

You can change both lists on a live key. The agent holding it
keeps working against the new lists, with nothing reissued and
nothing to reconnect.

The refusal tells the agent this too. When an agent asks about
an application outside the key's reach, it is told that the
credential is intentionally limited, where a person can extend
it, and that a new key is not needed because the same key can be
widened. The agent then asks you to widen the key instead of
demanding a fresh credential or giving up.

These lists only narrow; they never grant. An application id on
the list that you cannot access yourself opens nothing.

## The first call is `get_started`

Once the agent is connected, `get_started` comes before every
other tool.

It returns the instructions for operating this installation:
how deployment works here, how secrets are handled, and what
happens when an action needs a person's approval. It also
records which version of those instructions this credential is
working from.

That second part matters to you as well as to the agent. Until a
key calls it, the agent keys screen says the key has never
reported which instructions it is working from. Once it has, you
know the agent actually connected.

Every key can call `get_started` from the moment it exists,
whatever you switched on when you minted it.

## A properly-scoped agent can deploy

A key that carries write access can take an application from a
repository to running on its own, through any of the three ways
Flui supports. It can write and deploy a `flui.yaml` manifest,
read a connected repository and deploy the map Flui renders from
it, or ship an application straight from a container image with
no repository at all. The agent's own tools state that none of
the three is the preferred path.

The deploy still does not happen silently. A deploy an agent
asks for stops and becomes a question addressed to you (see
[When your agent stops to ask you](/tasks/when-your-agent-asks/)).
Which of these an agent may attempt at all depends on the
permission group you switch on, in [Choose what your agent may
do](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/).

## Minting the key

**CLI:**

Minting a key needs a different credential from logging in: a
session token from the installation's identity provider, passed
with `--token` or in `FLUI_SESSION_TOKEN`. The command works
only where Flui is running in OIDC mode.

```bash
flui auth generate-api-key \
  --name "claude-code-on-my-laptop" \
  --scope mcp:app:read \
  --scope mcp:obs:read \
  --expires 30 \
  --token "$FLUI_SESSION_TOKEN"
```

You must say what the key is for. If you pass neither `--scope`
nor `--unscoped`, the command fails before it touches the
network, and the error explains why: a key with no scope is the
widest credential the installation can issue, so you have to ask
for it by name.

`--scope` is repeatable. `--unscoped` is its opposite, a key with
no ceiling that carries all of your permissions, and the two
cannot be combined. `--expires` is a number of days; leave it
out for a key that never expires.

A scope you do not hold yourself is refused. You cannot mint a
key stronger than you are, and the command does not silently
give you a weaker one instead.

Watch out for one thing: the command saves the key into a
profile (the active one, unless you name another with
`--profile`), replacing the key that profile was using. Your own
terminal then runs as the agent, with the agent's narrower
reach.

Point `--profile` at another profile you already have if you
want to keep working in this one. If you forget, `flui auth login`
mints you a fresh key and puts it back.

The key lives in your own encrypted profile, and the CLI uses it
from there. The platform cannot show it to you again.

To see what exists:

```bash
flui auth api-keys
```

Each row shows a name, a state (active, expired or revoked), the
scopes the key carries, and its id. An unscoped key says so
instead of showing an empty list.

To take one back:

```bash
flui auth revoke-api-key <id>
```

The key stops working immediately.

Two things are not available on the CLI. There is no `--groups`
flag: from the terminal you mint by raw scope or with
`--unscoped`. There is also no flag for the application or
project lists. Keys that use either are minted where the person
giving consent can read what they are agreeing to: the
dashboard, and the API underneath it.

**Dashboard:**

Open **Settings**, then **Agent keys**. Here you give an agent a
key, see what each key can do, and take it back.

Minting asks for four things:

1. **A name**, so you can tell this agent from the next one when
   you come to revoke it. Something like *Claude Code on my
   laptop* is the right level of detail.
2. **An expiry.** A consent that ends on its own is one less
   thing to remember.
3. **What it may do.** One row per area, with a level: **None**,
   **See**, **Change** or **Delete**. **Details** on a row shows
   what each level allows, in one sentence written for a person.
   At least one area must be set, because a key with nothing
