   picked would carry all of your permissions. Which level to
   pick has [its own page](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/).
4. **How far it reaches.** By default, every application you can
   already reach. Two optional settings narrow that: *limit to
   specific applications*, and *also grant whole projects*.
   Either one alone is enough. They are alternatives, so an app
   is reached if either covers it.

Then choose **Create key**.

_Screenshot: Minting an agent key: a name, an expiry, and one row per area with a level to pick._

The key appears once, in full, with a **Copy** button, under a
line saying this is the only time the value is shown. Copy it
before you leave the screen.

Below it is a block of text to **paste into the agent's chat**.
It covers Claude Code, Codex CLI and OpenCode, and the agent
reads whichever section matches it. The text tells the agent to
have a person put the key in a terminal, not in the chat, and
then run the one command that registers this endpoint. Its last
step tells the agent to call `get_started`.

The key itself is never in that text. Anything typed into a chat
stays in the model's context from then on, so the value goes
from your clipboard to a terminal and nowhere else.

Back on the list, every key shows what it may do, which
applications and projects it reaches, when it was made, when it
expires, and whether it has ever connected to this instance. A
key that has never connected says so. You can edit the
application and project lists there, on a key that is already in
use.

_Screenshot: Keys you have issued: what each may do, what it reaches, and when it was made, used and expires._

For an agent that cannot make MCP tool calls at all, the same
instructions are available as a plain document under *Not using
MCP?*: read it on the screen or copy it. It is the same content
`get_started` returns, it carries no credential, and it is safe
to commit to a repository.

**Agent (MCP):**

This tab is for the agent on the other end of the key.

**Call `get_started` first.** It explains how work is done on
this installation, and it tells the person who issued the key
that you have arrived. Everything below is easier to follow
after it.

**Your tool list depends on your key.** The tools you are offered
are filtered to what this credential can execute. A missing tool
is the answer to a question about your key, not a fault or a
version problem. Do not work around it; say what you were unable
to do.

**Arguments are strict.** An argument name that is not in a
tool's schema is rejected, not ignored. A permissive tool would
drop the unknown key, leave the real parameter empty, run
unfiltered, and give you a confident answer to a question you
never asked. The error names both what you sent and what the
tool accepts.

**A refusal about an application can be fixed.** If the key is
limited to specific applications or projects, a request outside
that reach is refused with an explanation: the same key can be
widened in **Settings → Agent keys** without issuing a new one.
Relay that to the person. Do not ask for a fresh credential when
the fix is one field on the key you already hold.

**You never hold a secret.** Eight tools exist only to ask a
person for a credential: an API key, an application's secret
variable, the token that pulls container images, a mail
provider, a backup destination, provider credentials, a model
connection, a user invite. None of them has an argument that
could carry a value, because an argument becomes context, and
context ends up in the transcript.

Each one tells you whether a thing is configured, never what it
is, and hands back either a command for the person to run in
their own terminal or the screen they should open. An invite
link counts as a credential too and is never returned to an
agent.

When one of these reports that the thing is still not
configured, treat it as a state, not a failure. Stop, relay it,
and carry on with everything that does not depend on it.

## Where this goes next

- [Choose what your agent may
  do](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/): the permission
  groups, area by area, and what each one carries.
- [When your agent stops to ask
  you](/tasks/when-your-agent-asks/): what happens the first
  time your agent tries to change something, and where you
  answer.
- [The Flui Assistant and
  MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/): why there is
  one tool registry behind both the in-product assistant and
  this endpoint.
- [How Flui reads a repository](/concepts/30-how-flui-reads-a-repository/):
  what `repo_map` and `repo_map_apply` actually do when an agent
  reaches for the second of the three deploy paths.
- [Authentication](/cli/authentication/): `flui auth login`, and
  how the CLI's own key differs from the one you just made.

sections.title: Connect an application to a managed PostgreSQL
sections.body:
Every connection to PostgreSQL costs the database memory and a
process. An application with a few replicas, each holding a pool
of its own, can use up the database's connections long before it
uses up its CPU.

A PostgreSQL you install from the catalog comes with a
**connection pooler** in front of it. Your applications connect to
the pooler, and the pooler shares a small number of real database
connections among all of them. The pooler is PgBouncer. You will
see that name in the Sessions view, and nowhere else.

The pooler also changes what happens when the database moves to
another cluster: writes wait in the pooler instead of failing. See
[Move an application to another cluster](/tasks/move-an-application/#when-the-database-has-a-pooler).

## Two addresses

A managed PostgreSQL publishes two connection strings among its
variables:

| Variable | Goes to | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FLUI_CONNECTION_URL` | The pooler | Your application's normal traffic |
| `FLUI_DIRECT_URL` | The database itself | Schema migrations, `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY`, session advisory locks, admin tools |

A database without a pooler has both variables too, and both point
at the database. So an application can always name the one it
means, and keeps working if the pooler is not there.

An application that takes its database from a manifest with
`fromService: url` gets `FLUI_CONNECTION_URL`, the pooled one.

Run schema migrations on `FLUI_DIRECT_URL`. Tools such as Prisma
migrate, Flyway and Liquibase hold a lock for the whole session
while they work, and the pooler in transaction mode cannot keep
that lock for them.

`flui db tunnel` and the browser console always reach the database
directly. They never go through the pooler.

## Choose it at install

The pooler is on by default. You decide two things when you
install: whether there is a pooler, and which mode it runs in.

**CLI:**

`flui catalog install` takes `--option key=true|false`, once per
option:

```bash
# pooler on, transaction mode (the default)
flui catalog install postgresql

# pooler on, session mode
flui catalog install postgresql --option poolerSessionMode=true

# no pooler
flui catalog install postgresql --option pooler=false
```

| Option | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pooler` | `true` | Put a connection pooler in front of the database. |
| `poolerSessionMode` | `false` | Run the pooler in session mode instead of transaction mode. Only with the pooler. |

**Dashboard:**

The install wizard has a **Features** step with two boxes:

- **Connection pooler**, ticked by default.
- **Session pooling**, unticked by default. It cannot be ticked
  while the pooler is off.

**Agent (MCP):**

`catalog_get_app` lists the two options with their defaults.
`app_install` takes them in `options`, for example
`{ "pooler": true, "poolerSessionMode": false }`. A key left out
takes its default.

Three things to know about the choice:

- **Existing databases are unchanged.** A PostgreSQL installed
  before the pooler existed keeps connecting directly.
- **A database the catalog creates for another entry has no
  pooler.** When a catalog app needs a database and you let the
  install provision one, that database is wired to its app directly.
- **It is fixed at install for now.** You cannot add, remove or
  switch the mode of a pooler on an existing database yet. To get a
  different setting, install a new database with it and copy the
  data across with `flui db dump` and `flui db restore`.

## Transaction mode or session mode

**Transaction mode** is the default. A client keeps a real
database connection only for the length of one transaction. The
next transaction may run on a different connection. That is what
lets a few database connections serve many clients, and most web
applications never notice.

**Session mode** gives each client one database connection for as
long as the client stays connected. Everything PostgreSQL offers
works, but you save far fewer connections. Pick it when your
application relies on the session features in the table below and
you cannot move them to `FLUI_DIRECT_URL`.

## What works through the pooler

| What your application does | Transaction mode | Session mode |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single statements and short transactions | Works | Works |
| Prepared statements sent by the driver (protocol level); the pooler tracks up to 200 | Works | Works |
| `SET LOCAL` inside a transaction | Works | Works |
| Transaction advisory locks (`pg_advisory_xact_lock`) | Works | Works |
| Temporary tables used inside one transaction | Works | Works |
| `SET` without `LOCAL` (a session setting) | Breaks | Works |
| SQL `PREPARE` and `EXECUTE` | Breaks | Works |
| Cursors declared `WITH HOLD` | Breaks | Works |
| `LISTEN` / `NOTIFY` | Breaks | Works |
| Session advisory locks (`pg_advisory_lock`) | Breaks | Works |
| Temporary tables kept across transactions | Breaks | Works |
| Migration tools that hold a session lock (Prisma migrate, Flyway, Liquibase) | Breaks: use `FLUI_DIRECT_URL` | Use `FLUI_DIRECT_URL` |

"Breaks" does not mean the pooler refuses the statement. It runs,
but your next transaction may run on another database connection,
where the setting, the lock or the table is not. If your
application does one of these things, give that part of it
`FLUI_DIRECT_URL`, or choose session mode at install.

### PostgREST

PostgREST works behind the pooler in transaction mode with two
settings:

| Setting | Value | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PGRST_DB_PREPARED_STATEMENTS` | `false` | Otherwise a request for a table that does not exist makes the pooler drop PostgREST's connection, and other requests get a 503 for an instant. |
| `PGRST_DB_CHANNEL_ENABLED` | `false` | PostgREST reloads its schema cache by listening with `LISTEN`, which does not work in transaction mode. |

With the channel off, PostgREST does not pick up schema changes by
itself. Restart it after you change the schema.

## Check the pooler

**CLI:**

```bash
flui db pooler my-postgres
flui db pooler my-postgres --json
```

It prints the mode, how many instances of the pooler are ready, the
image it runs, and the two addresses with the variable that carries
each. When `FLUI_CONNECTION_URL` does not go through the pooler yet,
for example while the pooler is still starting, it says so and
why. A database with no pooler shows its one direct address.

The full flag list is in [the databases CLI](/cli/databases/#flui-db-pooler-app).

**Dashboard:**

Open the database and go to the **Sessions** tab. Its **Pooler**
section shows the mode, each pool with its clients, the clients
waiting for a connection, and the database connections in use. See
[See who is connected](/tasks/open-a-database/#see-who-is-connected).

**Agent (MCP):**

`db_pooler_get` takes the database application's id and returns the
same facts as the CLI: whether there is a pooler, its mode, whether
`FLUI_CONNECTION_URL` goes through it and why not, and the two
addresses. It only reads.

## What it costs

The pooler runs next to the database, on the same cluster. Measured
in use, it takes about 1m of CPU and 8 MiB of memory. Against the
cluster's capacity check it counts for 25m of CPU and 128 MiB of
memory, so an install with the pooler needs that much room on top
of the database.

The pooler runs as one instance. It accepts up to 1000 client
connections and opens at most 50 to the database.

## Where to go next

- [Open a database from your machine](/tasks/open-a-database/):
  the tunnel, the console, and the Sessions view.
- [Move an application to another cluster](/tasks/move-an-application/):
  what the pooler does to writes during a move.
- [Install an application from the catalog](/tasks/install-from-the-catalog/):
  the rest of the install.
- [The databases CLI](/cli/databases/): `flui db pooler` and
  `flui db sessions`.

sections.title: Deploy an application from your repository
sections.body:
The details of an application (the port it listens on, the
memory it needs, the variables it reads) belong next to its
code. So instead of asking you to type them into a form, Flui
reads a file from your repository, `flui.yaml`, and deploys
from what it says.

This page takes you from a repository Flui has never seen to an
application running on a cluster. What the manifest can express
is covered in [The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/),
and where the build runs in
[The build pipeline](/concepts/20-build-pipeline-today-and-tomorrow/).

## Three ways in

Writing `flui.yaml` by hand, as the rest of this page does, is
one way to deploy from a repository. There are three, and
Flui's own tools treat them as equals:

- **Write the manifest yourself.** This page walks through it.
- **Let Flui read the repository for you.** Flui maps it
  (units, services, blockers, a verdict) and renders a
  `flui.yaml` per unit, which you can inspect before anything
  is deployed. See step 2 below.
- **Bring an image you already built.** No repository and no
  build. In the dashboard: **Deploy New → From a Docker image**.
  Over MCP: `app_deploy_image`.

The model behind the second path (what gets read, what never
leaves the read as a guess, and the citation and confidence
attached to every fact) is in
[How Flui reads a repository](/concepts/30-how-flui-reads-a-repository/).

## 1. Connect the repository

Flui builds your code, so it needs to read the repository and
push the resulting image. You make that connection once, and
every later deploy reuses it.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui integration connect github
flui repo connect acme/my-app
flui repo list
```

`flui integration connect github` follows the way the
installation connects GitHub. With a personal access token, the
recommended setup, it asks for your classic token (or reads it
from `--stdin` in a script) and connects it. With a GitHub App
it opens a browser so you can install the App on your account
or organisation; add `--headless` to print the URL instead,
which is what you want over SSH.

`flui repo connect` takes `owner/repo`. Leave the argument off
to get a picker over the repositories that connection can see.
`flui repo list` shows what is connected; `flui repo disconnect`
removes one.

Before any of this works, whoever runs the installation has to
set up the GitHub integration once, with
`flui integration setup github`. A personal access token is the
recommended choice. That step and both of its modes are in
[Integrations and repositories](/cli/integrations/).

**Dashboard:**

Open **Repositories**, in the sidebar under Deploy. **GitHub
Setup**, under Management, is the one-time step for the whole
installation and is shown only to administrators. Repositories
is where you connect your own account and import individual
repositories.

_Screenshot: Repositories: the GitHub connection and each imported repository with Deploy and Readiness map._

The **Deploy New** wizard leads here too. With nothing
connected, its repository step shows a *Connect Repository*
button instead of a list, and there is an *Import them here*
link under the picker when the repository you want is missing.

**Agent (MCP):**

Four tools, in the order an agent needs them:

- `integration_status`: whether GitHub is connected at all.
- `github_connect`: starts connecting your account. With a
  personal access token it returns the command or screen where
  you paste the token; with a GitHub App, a URL for you to
  open. The agent does not sign in for you and never sees a
  token.
- `repo_list`: the repositories already connected.
- `repo_connect`: connects one, by `owner/repo` or by its full
  URL.

## 2. Write or check `flui.yaml`

The manifest is a small file. It names the application, says
how to build the image and how to run it.

```yaml
kind: Application
apiVersion: flui.cloud/v1beta1
metadata:
  name: my-api
build:
  strategy: dockerfile
  dockerfile: ./Dockerfile
deploy:
  port: 3000
  healthcheck:
    path: /healthz
  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: "250m"
      memory: "256Mi"
    limits:
      cpu: "500m"
      memory: "512Mi"
  env:
    LOG_LEVEL: info
```

Two commands help you write it:

- `flui app init nextjs` copies a `flui.yaml` and a
  production-ready Dockerfile from an official framework
  template into the current directory. `flui app init --list`
  shows the available frameworks and versions.
- `flui app manifest` prints the full authoring reference, with
  every field annotated. It is generated from the published
  spec, so it always matches what a deploy validates, and it
  runs offline.

Get two fields right the first time. `port` must be the port
your code binds. `healthcheck.path` must be a real route that
answers with a 2xx; a path that does not exist makes every
probe fail without an obvious error.

### Build arguments

`build.args` are passed to the image build. They are baked into
the image, so they are the same in every environment. Use them
for build-time configuration that does not vary:

```yaml
build:
  args:
    NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: https://api.example.com
```

Anything that differs between environments, or must not be
compiled into the artifact, belongs in `deploy.env` instead.

### Or: let Flui read the repository for you

Instead of writing the file by hand, you can ask Flui to read
the connected repository and render it for you: units, the
services they want, blockers, a verdict, and one `flui.yaml`
per deployable unit. Each fact records where it was read and
how confident the engine is. Reading a map deploys nothing; a
separate step acts on it.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui repo map show acme/shop
flui repo map show acme/shop --unit api
flui repo map apply acme/shop
```

`show` reads and prints the map. `apply` is the separate write
step: it creates Flui's own branch at the commit the map was
read from, commits the rendered manifests and their build
workflows to it, and starts the builds. Your own branch is only
read, never written to. Both commands are in
[Integrations and repositories](/cli/integrations/).

**Dashboard:**

Open **Repositories**, then **Readiness map** on the repository
you want to read. The page shows the same verdict as the CLI
(*Ready to deploy*, *Ready once you fill in the values below*,
*Partly ready*, *Not deployable yet*, *Too big for this
cluster*) and a **Deploy from this map** button that stays
disabled until the verdict allows it.

_Screenshot: A readiness map: the verdict, what you need to provide, what would run, and Deploy from this map._

**Agent (MCP):**

`repo_map` reads and `repo_map_apply` acts. Like every other
write, `repo_map_apply` stops and asks a person first. The two
are equal alternatives to `app_manifest_validate` +
`app_deploy_from_yaml`: picking one pair over the other is a
choice about where the facts come from. Unlike most writes,
`repo_map_apply` does not return an operation id. It waits, in
the same call, for any database the manifest declares to come
up, which can take longer than the surface's own timeout. See
[The Flui assistant and MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/)
for what that means for an agent calling it.

## 3. Check it before you deploy

A manifest can be well formed and still be wrong for the place
you are sending it. So the check answers two questions:

- **Does this parse?** The schema. This half needs no cluster,
  no sign-in and no network.
- **Would this land here?** Only this installation can answer
  this half.

The second half starts with seven checks about this
installation:

| Check | What it answers |
| --- | --- |
| Target cluster | A cluster answers to that id, and it can take a deploy. |
| Source repository | The repository is connected to your account. |
| Build and registry | GitHub is connected and there is a credential to push the image with. |
| Room on the cluster | The CPU and memory the manifest asks for fit what is free right now. |
| Where it lands | A workload cluster, or the control cluster (supported, and stated in the result). |
| What this deploy does | Whether this creates an application or updates one that already exists. |
| How it is reached | Public or internal, and whether a DNS zone is bound to the cluster. |

When the repository can be read, more checks compare the
manifest with the code: the Dockerfile it names, the build
context, the port, the health path and the environment the
code reads. A last check says whether the manifest uses an
out-of-date form.

Read each check by its status. `fail` blocks a deploy. `warn`
is a consequence to be aware of, not a problem to fix.
`unknown` means this installation could not answer: a cluster
that could not be read has refused nothing, so an unknown never
blocks and is never a reason to rewrite a manifest.

The check also returns the manifest as it would be applied,
after merging the branch's environment profile and the
overrides you send with the check. Overrides already stored on
an install are not part of this preview; the deploy itself
applies them.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui deploy --validate-only
flui deploy --validate-only --cluster my-cluster
flui deploy --validate-only --json
```

The schema half always runs. The installation half runs when
you are signed in and a cluster can be resolved; name one with
`--cluster` when the profile has more than one. When the
installation half does not run, the output says which half ran
and why the other did not, so a missing check is never mistaken
for a pass.

The CLI prints the checks and the verdict. The effective
manifest is returned by the API and the agent tool, not by the
CLI.

**Dashboard:**

The **Deploy New** wizard checks the manifest for you, and the
whole flow depends on what it finds on the branch you picked:

- **Found**: it shows the manifest and tells you that port,
  healthcheck and resources come from it and that the
  repository is built as it is.
- **A monorepo**: one `flui.yaml` per application. You pick the
  one to deploy; the others are separate runs of the wizard.
- **Invalid**: it names the files it found and stops. Fix the
  manifest, push it and retry.
- **Missing**: it stops and offers a way forward instead of
  guessing a configuration for you.
- **Could not read**: the repository could not be read just
  now. Retry; nothing is wrong with the manifest.

_Screenshot: The Analysis step when the manifest is found: app name, port and healthcheck read from flui.yaml._

Once you pick a cluster, the **Review** step shows the
installation checks above.

_Screenshot: The Review step: what will be built, and the installation checks with their verdicts._

**Agent (MCP):**

Use `app_manifest_validate`. It takes the manifest verbatim,
plus an optional `clusterId`, `repoFullName` and `branch`, and
returns the schema result, the `checks`, `wouldDeploy` and
`effectiveYaml` (the manifest as it would be applied).

If you omit `repoFullName`, the repository check comes back
unanswered, not failed.

`spec_validate` does something else. It validates the catalog
contract, and a `kind: Application` manifest comes back from it
as the wrong kind. Use it only for `kind: CatalogApp`.

## 4. Deploy

**CLI:**

```bash
flui deploy
flui deploy ./apps/api/flui.yaml
flui deploy --repo acme/my-app --branch main
flui deploy --detach
```

With no arguments it reads `./flui.yaml`, takes the repository
from `git remote origin` and the branch you are on, and targets
the only cluster in the active profile. Pass `--cluster` when
there is more than one.

By default the command waits for the build and the deploy.
`--detach` returns as soon as the work is queued; follow it
with `flui app status <name>`.

Two shortcuts for when the image is already right and only the
configuration changed:

```bash
flui deploy --no-build
flui deploy --image ghcr.io/owner/repo:abc123
```

**Dashboard:**

Click **Deploy New** in the sidebar, then *From an existing
repository*, and pick the repository and its branch. The
wizard reads the manifest, shows what it found, and lets you
set the install overrides below on its Cluster step.

_Screenshot: Deploy New: the four ways to start._

_Screenshot: The Cluster step: the chosen cluster, its free room, the exposure, and the install overrides._

The deploy runs in the background and shows its progress on
screen.

**Agent (MCP):**

`app_deploy_from_yaml` creates or updates an application from a
manifest. `app_deploy` deploys an application that already
exists, from an image, a commit or a build.

An agent needs to know two things:

**The work is not finished when the call returns.** A deploy
returns the application and, once there is work to follow, an
operation id. A deploy that has to build first comes back
waiting for its build. Nothing polls it for the agent: read
`operation_status` and the application's status to learn the
outcome, and do that before telling anyone the deploy worked.

**A deploy requested by an agent can stop and ask you.** Both
deploy routes are part of the action cycle: when the caller is
an agent, the call does not run. It is refused with a request
id, a plain sentence describing what was asked for, and a link
where you answer. Nothing holds the call open while you decide.
The agent is told to retry the identical call once you have
answered, and that is how it learns your answer. A
validate-only call never asks, since checking a manifest should
not put a question in front of you about a deploy that is not
happening.

## 5. Name, exposure and domain at install time

Three things belong to the installation, not the code: what
this install is called, whether it is reachable from the
internet, and on which hostname. The same repository deployed
twice needs two different answers, and neither can live in a
file both installs share. So you can override all three at
deploy time.

| Override | CLI | Agent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Name | `--name` | `overrides.name` |
| Public or internal | `--exposure public\|internal` | `overrides.exposure` |
| Hostname | `--domain app.example.com` | `overrides.domain.fqdn` |

In the dashboard the same three are in the wizard's **Install
overrides** panel and its public/internal choice.

An application is identified by cluster, repository, branch and
name together. Give a deploy a name it has not seen and you
install that repository a second time, next to the first,
instead of updating it.

This also works the other way, which surprises people: the name
is never read back from storage. Exposure and domain are
remembered on the install and keep overriding the manifest on
later deploys, but the name is not. **Pass `--name` on every
deploy that targets that install.** Leave it off once and the
next deploy targets a different application.

The validation check called *What this deploy does* exists for
this case. Before anything runs, it tells you whether you are
about to create an application or update one.

## 6. After the first deploy, a push does not redeploy

The first deploy of an application always goes through. What
happens on later pushes is a separate setting, and by default
nothing happens.

Auto-deploy on push is opt-in per application, and the setting
is called `deployOnPush`. While it is off (the default), a
successful build of a new commit is recorded as an available
image and waits. The running version does not change until
someone asks for it.

To deploy a recorded image:

```bash
flui app versions my-api
flui app redeploy my-api a1cac27
```

`deployOnPush` is a setting on the application itself, not a
field in `flui.yaml`. From the terminal, run
`flui app auto-deploy my-api --on` (`--off` turns it off
again). There is no agent tool for it.

## Where to go next

- [The flui.yaml manifest](/concepts/17-the-flui-manifest/):
  everything the file can say, and what it leaves out.
- [How Flui reads a repository](/concepts/30-how-flui-reads-a-repository/):
  the map in depth, including what gets read, what a verdict
  means, and the limit on sharing one database across a
  monorepo's units.
- [Deploy and catalog validate](/cli/deploy/): every flag on
  `flui deploy`.
- [Integrations and repositories](/cli/integrations/): the
  one-time GitHub setup, both modes, the registry credential,
  and `flui repo map show` / `apply`.

sections.title: Get Flui running
sections.body:
Everything else in these docs assumes you have done what this
page describes.

This page has no dashboard tab, because the dashboard is one of
the things this command installs. Until it has run, there is no
dashboard to run it from. So the first hour belongs to the CLI,
or to [app.flui.cloud](https://app.flui.cloud), which runs the
same install from the web on [the providers Flui
integrates](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/#the-providers-integrated-today)
and hands it over to you with `flui env adopt`.

What you end up with is the **control cluster**: the cluster that
carries Flui itself, with the dashboard, the API, the identity
provider, the database, and the metrics and logs. One command
brings all of it up together.

## First, the vault

Flui keeps provider tokens and SSH keys on your machine. A key
kept in the same folder as what it seals protects nothing from
anyone who can read the folder. So set up the vault before you
store a single credential.

```bash
flui vault init      # choose a passphrase, once per machine
flui vault unlock    # open it for this session
flui vault status    # is it open, and for how long
flui vault lock      # close it now
```

`flui vault init` asks for a passphrase and suggests a five-word
one you can remember. Write it down before you continue. It is
not stored anywhere and cannot be reset. If you lose it, you lose
every credential this machine has sealed.

`flui vault unlock` asks once. A small background process then
holds the key in memory for the session and overwrites it when
you lock. You are asked once per session, not once per command.

A locked vault is not an error by itself. Commands that only read
a preference or an endpoint never ask for anything. Only a
command that opens a stored credential stops, and it tells you to
run `flui vault unlock`.

If this machine already holds credentials sealed outside the
vault, the first `unlock` moves them in and removes the plaintext
copies.

## Two ways to get a machine

Flui can buy the server for you, or install onto a Linux machine
you already have.

- **A provider Flui provisions on.** `flui env create` creates
  the control cluster on [a provider Flui
  integrates](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/#the-providers-integrated-today).
  Flui buys the server, sets up the private network and the
  firewall, then installs on top. Where the provider has no
  firewall Flui can drive, the Flui firewall is applied on the
  machine itself; everything else is the same.
- **A machine you already own.** A rented server, a server in an
  office, a spare machine under a desk. Pass `--host` and Flui
  installs over SSH. It buys nothing and creates nothing at any
  provider. The machine has to run Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04.

Both paths give you the same result, and nothing later in these
docs depends on which one you took.

## Store the credentials it needs

If you skip this, `flui env create` asks for the same things when
it needs them and saves your answers. Storing them up front lets
the run go unattended.

```bash
flui config set email you@example.com
flui config set hetzner --stdin      # then paste the token
flui config set scaleway             # a pair of values, interactive
flui config set ovh                  # a pair of values, interactive
```

For OVHcloud, the pair is the OpenStack username and password
of a Public Cloud user, not an OVH API application key. Create
the user in the OVH Manager under **Public Cloud → Users &
Roles**; the password is shown once, when the user is created.
The credential must reach exactly one OpenStack project.

Prefer `--stdin` over passing the value as an argument. Every
process on the machine can see an argument through the process
list, which is not acceptable for a credential on a shared or
managed host.

## Create it on a provider

```bash
flui env create
```

That is the whole command for the common case. It picks the
provider you have credentials for, the provider's recommended
server size and its default region, and streams the installation
log as it runs.

The main flags:

| Flag | What it decides |
| --- | --- |
| `-p, --provider` | `hetzner`, `scaleway` or `ovh`. Omit it when only one is configured. |
| `-r, --region` | Where the server sits. Defaults to the provider's default. |
| `--node-size` | The shape of the server. Defaults to the provider's recommended size. |
| `--node-count` | Worker nodes. Default `0` (master only). |
| `--acme-staging` | Issue a staging certificate instead of a real one. |
| `--auth-mode` | Only `oidc`. |
| `--ssh-mode` | Whether this machine keeps a way in afterwards. |
| `--non-interactive` | Never ask a question; fail instead. |

### Region and size are provider words

A size code that exists on one provider means nothing on another.
To see what a provider offers:

```bash
flui server-types list --provider hetzner
flui server-types list --provider scaleway --region fr-par
flui server-types list --provider ovh --region EU-SOUTH-MIL
```

Flui accepts a fixed set of regions per provider. If you ask for
one outside it, the command stops before anything is bought and
names the regions it accepts: `nbg1`, `fsn1`, `hel1`, `ash`,
`hil` and `sin` on Hetzner; `fr-par`, `nl-ams`, `pl-waw` on
Scaleway; `GRA`, `SBG`, `RBX-A`, `EU-WEST-PAR`, `EU-SOUTH-MIL`,
`DE`, `UK`, `WAW`, `BHS`, `SGP` and `SYD` on OVHcloud.

On OVHcloud the list is only part of the picture. Which regions
your account can reach is decided per project, so Flui reads them
from OVHcloud itself rather than from a table. Once your
credentials are stored, `flui server-types list --provider ovh
--region <code>` shows what a region offers. Milan and Paris
carry only the current-generation `c3`/`b3`/`r3` shapes, so the
cheap `d2` family is not available there.

### `--acme-staging`, and why you might want it

By default the cluster comes up with a real, browser-trusted
certificate. That is what you want for an installation you intend
to keep.

`--acme-staging` asks for a Let's Encrypt staging certificate
instead. Browsers do not trust it, and your CLI complains until
you allow it, but it does not count against the production rate
limits. If you expect to build and tear down the same
installation several times in a week, use it. The production
limits run on rolling windows and cannot be reset on request.

### `--auth-mode`

Only `oidc` is supported. Naming anything else stops the command
instead of falling back silently. The identity provider is
installed as part of the cluster, and you log in against it
afterwards.

### `--ssh-mode`, or: who can open a shell later

This flag decides who holds the keys.

- **`ca`** (the default) enrols this machine's SSH certificate
  authority on every node and leaves it there. Your machine can
  open a shell on those servers from now on. Use it when you are
  building your own installation.
- **`ephemeral-key`** creates no certificate authority at all.
  The run uses a throwaway key, revokes it on the nodes and
  deletes it at the provider before it finishes. When the run
  ends, nothing can open a shell on those servers, neither you
  nor Flui, until the owner runs `flui env adopt`. Use it when
  you are provisioning on someone else's behalf.

`--ssh-mode ephemeral-key` requires `--wait` or
`-d`/`--detached`. The default mode follows the installation log
over SSH, and this mode enrols no certificate to authenticate
with. Without one of those flags the command would not fail; it
would hang for ten minutes while you pay for the servers.

### `--non-interactive`

In a script or a managed runner, a prompt does not fail. It waits
forever while you pay for the servers. `--non-interactive` turns
every missing answer into an error instead of a question.

It adds one rule. If the firewall is being configured, you must
also pass `--firewall-ip`. Auto-detection resolves the address of
whichever machine runs the command. That is right on your laptop
but wrong in CI, where it would open the cluster to the runner
and lock you out. Pass `--no-configure-firewall` to skip firewall
setup entirely instead.

## Install onto a machine you already own

With `--host`, nothing above about providers applies. There is no
region, size or worker count to choose; you install on the
machine you have.

```bash
flui env create --host 203.0.113.10
flui env create --host box.example.com --user ubuntu --port 2222
```

| Flag | What it decides |
| --- | --- |
| `--host` | The address to install onto. Passing it turns this mode on. |
| `--port` | SSH port. Default `22`. |
| `--user` | SSH user. Default `root`. |
| `--ssh-key` | A private key to use. Optional; see below. |
| `--ssh-password` | The host password, for unattended runs. |
| `--master-public-ip` | The address the world should use, when it differs from `--host`. |
| `--skip-precheck` | Do not ask the machine about itself first. |
| `--best-effort` | Ask, warn, and carry on anyway. |

If you leave out `--ssh-key`, Flui reuses a key that already
works on that host. If none does, it authorises one: it asks for
the host password once, uses it only in memory, and never stores
it. A key with a passphrase works only when it is already loaded
in your ssh-agent, so run `ssh-add` first.

For an unattended install, `--ssh-password` accepts the password,
but prefer the `FLUI_SSH_PASSWORD` environment variable so it
stays out of your shell history.

### The precheck, and ARM

Before installing anything, Flui asks the machine to describe
itself: operating system, architecture, memory, cores, and
whether a cluster is already installed on it. It stops on an
architecture it does not support, on less than about 2 GB of
memory, and on a machine that already carries an install.
`--best-effort` turns those into warnings; `--skip-precheck`
skips the question.

A 64-bit ARM machine works. The check accepts 64-bit Intel/AMD
and 64-bit ARM alike, so a small, cheap, quiet ARM machine is a
supported target.

### The firewall on your own machine

There is no provider firewall to create here, so Flui applies
one on the host itself: everything denied by default, with SSH,
HTTP and HTTPS open. The installation is not reported ready until
that firewall is in place, because an install that leaves the
cluster reachable from anywhere has not succeeded.

You can inspect and re-apply it later:

```bash
flui env firewall status
flui env firewall apply
```

## What the run hands back

```bash
flui env status         # state and nodes
flui env credentials    # the endpoints, and the first login
```

`flui env credentials` prints the public addresses of the
dashboard, the API and the identity provider, together with the
bootstrap admin email and its one-time password. Change that
password the first time you log in. Other secrets are hidden
unless you ask for them with `--show-secrets`.

If a run failed, `flui env logs` reads the log the CLI wrote
while driving the operation, and `flui env inspect` opens the
machine's own system log over SSH.

## When a run dies half-way

Provisioning creates real, billable resources before it finishes:
a server, a firewall, an SSH key. If the run dies while holding
your provider token, it cannot clean up after itself. You are
left with a few resources in your account that nothing points at.

`flui env scrub` removes them. It works from the JSON resource
list the failed run reported:

```bash
flui env scrub --ledger ./flui-run.json
cat flui-run.json | flui env scrub --stdin
flui env scrub --ledger ./flui-run.json --delete
```

Without `--delete` it changes nothing. It asks the provider what
exists, matches that against the list, and prints what it would
remove.

Two rules limit what it deletes. The list decides what to look
for and the provider decides what is really there; anything that
is not in both is left alone. And if part of the account could
not be listed, it refuses to delete anything, because a part it
cannot see is not necessarily empty.

A different leftover, from a `flui env destroy` that failed
rather than a create, is handled by `flui env orphan-volumes`.

## Reinstalling in place

Sometimes the server is fine and the installation on top of it
is not. `flui env reinstall` wipes Flui and everything inside the
cluster off the existing server and runs the installation again
from the start.

```bash
flui env reinstall
flui env reinstall --dry-run    # print the teardown, run nothing
flui env reinstall --force      # skip the typed confirmation
```

The server itself, its firewall, its network attachment and its
attached shared storage volume all stay. Everything in the
cluster (your applications, the database, the dashboard's state)
is lost. It is the same data loss as `flui env destroy`, without
losing the machine.

It asks you to type the cluster's name back before it starts. Two
limits apply: it works only on clusters Flui provisioned on a
provider, and only on single-node ones. On your own machine, the
equivalent is `flui env destroy --purge-host` followed by
`flui env create --host` again.

## Taking over an installation somebody else set up

Someone can provision an installation for you and keep no access
to it. With `--ssh-mode ephemeral-key`, the key that built the
machine is destroyed at the end of the run, and no certificate
authority was ever created. The servers are running and sealed.

**Adoption** is how the owner opens them, on their own terms.

On the installation, ask for a token:

```bash
flui env adoption-token
flui env adoption-token --format json
```

The token is single use, valid for one hour, and tied to that one
installation. Anyone holding it can register a certificate
authority there, so treat it like a password and hand it over
the way you would hand over a password.

On the owner's machine:

```bash
flui env adopt flui_adopt_eyJlbmRwb2ludCI...
flui env adopt <token> --endpoint https://your-install.example.com
flui env adopt <token> --skip-ca
```

Adopting does four things: it asks the installation to describe
itself, writes a local profile pointing at it, creates the SSH
certificate authority on this machine, and has the installation
enrol the public half on every node.

Because of the third step, the key that opens those servers is
created on the owner's machine, at a moment the owner chose.
Nobody who built the installation ever holds it.

`--endpoint` is only needed when the token does not carry one.
`--skip-ca` rebuilds the local profile and leaves SSH dormant,
which is the right choice if you only use the dashboard.

## Where to go next

- [Creating a cluster from zero](/concepts/04-creating-a-cluster/):
  the reasoning behind the choices above (addressing,
  certificates, storage, firewall).
- [Environments](/cli/environments/): the full `env` command
  surface, including power state, scaling and the diagnostic
  commands.
- [Getting started](/cli/getting-started/): installing the CLI,
  logging in, and connecting GitHub.

sections.title: Give a teammate access
sections.body:
In Flui, a new account starts with no access. Somebody who
signs in for the first time sees the home page and their
own settings, and nothing else. There is no default role
and no rule that signed-in users can read.

As a result, every bit of access somebody has is a grant
you can find in a list. Nobody can reach an application
because of a rule nobody remembers writing. This page
shows how to create those grants.

## What a grant is

A grant has three parts:

- **Who**: a person, a group, or a service account.
- **Which role**: how much they may do.
- **How far it reaches**: the scope.

Removing the grant removes the access.

## First, they need somewhere to sign in

A grant is written against an email address, so you can
make it before the account exists. The person still has
to be able to sign in, though.

You create the account in the dashboard, under
**Access → People** with **Invite user**. Fill in the
email and a first and last name, and Flui creates the
account and gives you either an invite link to send them
or a temporary password.

There is no CLI command for this, and an agent cannot do
it either. An agent has `user_invite_request`, which
creates nothing: it says whether an account with that
address already exists and points you to the screen where
you invite them. An invite link is itself a credential
(whoever opens it becomes that account), so it never
passes through an agent.

If your installation signs people in through your own
identity provider, a role can also be assigned there. It
counts when they sign in, but Flui does not hold it, so it
does not appear in any list on this page and you cannot
take it back from here.

## The roles

Four of the roles form a ladder. Each one carries
everything the one below it carries, and adds to it.

- **Viewer**: reads the applications in scope and the
  clusters they run on. Changes nothing.
- **Operator**: manages the whole life of the applications
  in scope. It can create, deploy, configure, scale,
  migrate and remove them. No access management, no
  infrastructure.
- **Maintainer**: everything an operator has, plus the
  installation itself: clusters, who may reach what, the
  shared integrations, the showcase and the demonstration.
- **Owner**: everything, everywhere, including who else
  may run this installation.

The fifth role sits outside the ladder:

- **Platform operator**: runs the installation (clusters,
  nodes, updates, backups) without reaching the data of
  any application.

Only an owner can make another owner. Granting `owner`
requires user-management authority over everything, and
no role but `owner` carries that. A maintainer can hand
out every other role and no more.

The same rule applies to removal. Removing a grant that
carries a role you could not have granted is refused too.
Otherwise a maintainer could remove an installation's
owners one grant at a time.

`flui iam roles` prints the ladder, what each role
carries, and whether you may hand out each one.

## How far it reaches

A grant reaches in one of four ways.

**Everything.** The whole installation. This is the
default, and it is what you want for the few people who
run the installation.

**One cluster.** The role applies to what is on that
cluster and nothing else.

**One portal section.** The grant names a section of the
interface, such as Clusters, Backup or Mail.

**A rule over applications.** Instead of naming
applications one at a time, you describe them: their
kind, their project, the provider underneath, their tags,
their slugs. Everything you name has to match at once,
and an application must carry all of the tags you list.
The rule keeps applying: an application deployed tomorrow
that fits the description is covered as soon as it
exists, with nothing to add.

A grant that reaches only some applications opens the
workload screens and nothing more. The management
sections (Clusters, Infrastructure, Providers, Firewall,
Backup, Mail, Projects, Access) open only for a role
granted over everything. Scoping a maintainer to one
cluster does not give them the Infrastructure section for
that cluster. It gives them no management sections at all.

## Give the grant

**CLI:**

```bash
# somebody who helps run the place
flui iam grant add -p alice@example.com -r maintainer

# a group, read-only, on one cluster
flui iam grant add -t group -p platform -r viewer \
  -s cluster --cluster <cluster-id>

# every database application, whatever it is called
flui iam grant add -p bob@example.com -r operator \
  -s selector --kind DATABASE

# a build identity, over two named applications
flui iam grant add -p ci-deployer -t service_account \
  -r operator -s selector --app acme-api --app acme-web

flui iam grant list
```

`-t` is the principal type: `user` (the default),
`group` or `service_account`. For a user it takes an
email, for a group the group name, for a service account
the identity's id.

`-s` is the scope: `global` (the default), `cluster`
with `--cluster`, `section` with `--section`, or
`selector`.

With `-s selector` you describe the applications with
`--kind`, `--project`, `--provider`, `--cluster-id`,
`--cluster-name`, `--app-type`, `--app` (a slug,
repeatable) and `--tag` (repeatable, and all of them
must match). At least one is required. `--selector`
takes the same thing as raw JSON if you prefer to write
it that way.

`--dry-run` says what the grant would open (and what the
same change closes) and creates nothing.

`--expires` makes the grant temporary: a duration from
now (`8h`, `7d`, `2w`) or a date. Without it the grant
stays until somebody removes it.

**Dashboard:**

**Management → Access** in the sidebar, then the
**Grants** tab. The builder at the top has four fields,
in the order you think about them: **Who**, **Role**,
**What** and **Ends**. **Ends** is never, unless you pick
a time or a date.

**What** offers everything, one cluster, one project,
one specific app, apps of a kind, a collection by tag,
or a portal section. Underneath, a **Preview** counts
the applications the grant would reach and names them,
so you see the blast radius before you save it.

_Screenshot: The Grants tab: the builder with Who, Role, What and Ends, and the preview of the applications it reaches._

The **Who** list holds the people and the groups on the
installation. Service accounts are not in it; their
grants are made from the CLI or the API.

The **People** tab offers a second way in: create
somebody's account and give them their first grant in
one step. The form previews which sections the new
person will see.

_Screenshot: Invite user on the People tab: the account, its first grant, and the sections the person will see._

Below the builder, every grant Flui holds is listed with
who, which role, what it applies to, how many
applications that comes to, and when it ends. Grants
that end on their own also have their own tab,
**Temporary access**.

**Agent (MCP):**

- `access_grant_list`: every grant on the instance, with
  who holds it, which role and how far it reaches. Start
  here; the other access tools take a grant id.
- `access_grant_add`: makes one, in the same shape as the
  CLI: a principal, a role, a scope, a selector when the
  scope is a selector, and an end when it should be
  temporary.

Two limits apply:

- **No more than the person.** An agent can never grant
  more than the person whose credential it holds. The
  call is made as that person and checked by the same
  code a browser meets. A role above them is refused, and
  the refusal names it.
- **It stops and asks you.** Granting a role is part of
  the action cycle: the call does not run, a request
  appears for a person to answer, and the agent finds out
  the answer by trying again. Every grant asks. There is
  no "always" for granting access, because the grant does
  not exist yet, so a standing yes would cover every
  grant that followed.

Making a grant needs the **Grant and revoke access**
permission group on the credential, and no other group
includes it. It is never bundled into something like
"deploy my applications": somebody has to turn it on by
name. See
[Choose what your agent may do](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/).

## Look before you take it away

Removing a grant is the riskier half, because the damage
is invisible: nothing breaks in front of you, and
somebody finds out on Monday that half their work is out
of reach.

So Flui tells you first. Before a grant is removed, you
get a sentence saying what its holder will no longer be
able to reach: which applications, which portal sections,
which permissions. It is computed by the same engine that
enforces access, so it matches what actually happens.

Before you trust an empty list, check what kind of grant
it is:

- When the grant named applications by slug, the listed
  applications are complete.
- When the grant is a standing rule, they are what
  matches today. The grant also covers whatever comes to
  match later.
- **not known** means the application list could not be
  read. It never means nothing.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui iam grant list
flui iam grant remove <grant-id> --dry-run
flui iam grant remove <grant-id>
```

The preview is printed before you are asked to confirm,
so you read it before you have said yes. `--dry-run`
prints it and removes nothing. `--yes` skips the
confirmation.

After the removal the CLI prints what actually happened.
It can differ from the prediction if somebody else
changed the same person's access in between.

If the preview cannot be read, the command says so and
carries on. It does not report an empty loss.

**Dashboard:**

In the **Grants** tab, remove a row with the bin icon at
its end. The confirmation dialog shows the same sentence
and the same detail lines. If the preview cannot be read,
it says so instead of showing nothing.

Rows carrying a role you may not administer have no
remove button.

**Agent (MCP):**

- `access_revocation_preview`: what the holder of a
  grant would stop reaching. Changes nothing.
- `access_grant_remove`: removes it.

The preview tool lets an agent show you the loss in plain
words before anything happens. The remove tool is told to
call it first and to repeat the summary afterwards.
Removing also stops and asks a person, like granting.

## Groups

A group is a name with a list of email addresses. Grant a
role to the group and everybody in it holds the grant.
Add somebody to the group later and they hold it from
then on.

Group membership lives in Flui, not in your identity
provider. Deleting a group does not delete the grants
that point at it; they stop matching anybody.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui iam group create platform --description "Platform team"
flui iam group add-member platform alice@example.com
flui iam group list
flui iam group remove-member platform alice@example.com
flui iam group delete platform
```

A group name is lowercase letters, digits and hyphens,
and starts with a letter.

**Dashboard:**

**Access → Groups**. Create a group, expand it to see
its members, and add or remove people from the picker
under the list.

No agent tool creates or edits a group. An agent with
access permissions can grant a role to a group that
already exists, and nothing more.

## Sections have a third state

A portal section has three levels: hidden, full and
read-only. A read-only section appears and its screens
open, but its controls are disabled.

The server also refuses every request behind a read-only
section that would change something, so a script using
the same credential gets the same answer as the buttons.

No role you can hand out carries this level. It is what a
guest of the public demonstration gets. Two of the
sections it opens, Mail and Access, show other people's
personal details, which is why it stays limited to that
use.

## Access as a file

Grants can be exported to a file and applied back, so you
can review access in a pull request instead of in a
screenshot.

```bash
flui iam export > access-policy.yaml
flui iam apply -f access-policy.yaml
flui iam apply -f access-policy.yaml --prune
```

The document is `kind: AccessPolicy`, and every line in
it is a principal, a role and a scope. Applying is
idempotent: grants already there are left alone, and you
are told how many were created and how many already
matched the file.

Without `--prune`, applying makes sure the listed grants
exist. With it, the installation is made to match the
file, and grants the file does not name are deleted. It is
off unless you ask for it.

Every line is checked before anything is written, so a
file naming a role you may not grant is refused whole
instead of applied halfway.

Groups are not in the document, and neither are
temporary grants: export leaves them out and `--prune`
never removes them. Manage those with the commands
above.

## What am I allowed to do?

This helps when a refusal does not make sense, and
before you promise somebody something.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui iam whoami
flui iam roles
```

`whoami` prints the permissions the identity you are
signed in as actually carries. `roles` prints the roles,
what each one holds, and which of them you may hand out.

**Dashboard:**

**Access → Roles** describes the roles and what each
one carries.

_Screenshot: The Roles tab: each built-in role and the permissions it carries._

If you can see the Access section but cannot change
anything in it, a line above the list says so.

**Agent (MCP):**

`my_permissions` answers all of it at once: who the
agent is acting as, what that person may do, which
portal sections are open and at which level, and which
tool scopes its own credential carries.

It separates three refusals that look alike but mean
different things: a tool the credential was never given,
a resource the person is not allowed on, and something
this installation does not include. An agent should read
it before telling you a capability is missing.

## Where this goes from here

- [Identity and OIDC](/concepts/15-identity-and-oidc/):
  where accounts and sign-in actually live, and why Flui
  does not keep a password table.
- [Connect an agent](/tasks/connect-an-agent/): the
  same question for something that is not a person.
- [Choose what your agent may do](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/):
  the permission groups, and why granting access is a
  switch of its own.

sections.title: Write down how this installation is run
sections.body:
Every installation has rules that are not in the code. The first
cluster is not resized. Deploys happen after five. One application
is somebody's demo and must not be touched. Nobody writes these
rules down, because everybody already knows them.

Then someone new arrives, or an agent does. An agent has read
everything about the product and nothing about your installation.
It cannot guess a local rule, and it does not know there was one
to guess, so it does the reasonable thing with confidence.

Flui gives these rules a place to live. The people who run an
installation write them down, and everyone who acts on it reads
them before acting, agents included.

## A note has a level and a kind

The level is where the note applies:

- **Everything**: the whole installation.
- **One cluster.**
- **A rule that picks out applications**: by name, project, kind,
  tag, provider, or the cluster they run on.

The kind is what the note says:

- **A practice**: how it is done here.
- **A rationale**: why it was decided that way.

## Who reads a practice and who reads a rationale

A practice descends. Everyone who acts inside the level reads it,
whether or not they own anything there. A practice written on a
cluster reaches a tenant with a single application on that
cluster. A practice written on the whole installation reaches
every tenant on it, and the guests of the demonstration too. Tenants
know least about your local rules, so they need them most.

A rationale does not descend. Only someone whose access covers
the whole level reads it. The incident behind the rule, the
customer's name and the commercial reason stay with the people
who own the level.

Before you save a note, every surface shows one sentence saying
who will read it. For a practice on the whole installation it
reads:

> Everyone who works on this installation reads this:
> every tenant, and the guests of the demonstration. It
> does not stop at the people who run the platform.

Read that line before you press save. It is computed in one place
and shown by the CLI, the dashboard and the approval screen, so
all three tell you the same thing about the same note.

## Every note says whether it is still true

A rule that has been written down goes out of date. The reason it
was true stops being true, nobody notices, and the note keeps
advising people and agents to do the wrong thing.

So each note carries a verdict on its own premise, and when you
write the note you choose what that verdict rests on:

- **Nothing.** The note is prose. Nothing checks it, and the note
  says so.
- **A signature, with a shelf life.** You put your name to it and
  say how many days that is worth, from 1 to 365. When the window
  runs out, the note goes quiet instead of staying confident.
- **A live fact.** The note is pinned to something the platform
  can read, and is compared with it every time somebody reads the
  note.

That gives four verdicts:

| Verdict | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **checked** | A live fact agreed just now, or a person confirmed it inside their window |
| **stale** | A confirmation ran out. Not known to be wrong, only unconfirmed |
| **broken** | The platform's own state contradicts the note |
| **unverified** | Prose, or a live fact that could not be read |

Two of them need care:

- **Do not follow a broken note.** Only a note pinned to a live
  fact can go broken, and when it does, the platform has
  contradicted it. Treat it as something to fix. Agents receive
  the same instruction.
- **A fact that could not be read gives `unverified`, never
  `checked`.** A comparison that did not happen is not evidence.

Only a note backed by a signature can be confirmed, so you cannot
sign away a note the platform has already contradicted.

### What a note can be pinned to

Three live facts ship with the platform, and other parts of Flui
can publish more:

| Fact | What it answers |
| --- | --- |
| `app.field` | One readable field of an application, named by slug |
| `cluster.field` | One readable field of a cluster, by id or by name |
| `cluster.appCount` | How many applications currently sit on a cluster |

The comparison is one of `equals`, `notEquals`, `atLeast`,
`atMost` or `exists`. The two ordering comparisons, `atLeast` and
`atMost`, only work on a fact that answers a number.

Only shape and placement can be read this way: how many nodes a
cluster is allowed, an application's status, which cluster it
runs on. Nothing that holds content or credentials is readable,
and that is a fixed list rather than a convention.

A note about the whole installation cannot be pinned to a live
fact, because there is nothing at that level to compare it with.
If the note states an intention, write it as prose or sign it.
Otherwise it belongs on a narrower level.

## When two notes disagree

Two notes about the same subject, written at different levels,
will eventually contradict each other.

Flui shows the disagreement and does not resolve it. The narrower
note does not win: a rule about one application must never
overrule a rule of the platform, and usually one of the two notes
is simply older.

Anyone reading gets both notes and is told they conflict. An agent
is instructed to show you both and ask which one applies, never to
pick one.

A disagreement is also the best sign that one of the notes is out
of date, a signal no check on a single note can give.

## Notes do not change permissions

A note never widens or narrows what anybody may do. Permissions
decide that, separately, and they have already decided by the time
a note is fetched.

A note saying you may restart the database does not make the
restart succeed. A note saying never restart it does not stop it.
Both are things to repeat and ask about. Neither is ever the
reason something was done.

This safety comes from how notes are delivered. They are text a
person wrote and a model reads, so they are handed over as data,
with a preamble saying exactly that.

## Read what has been written down

**CLI:**

```bash
flui operating-context list
```

This lists every note that reaches you, each with its verdict,
most suspicious first: broken notes, then unconfirmed ones, then
prose, then the notes that still hold.

Each note prints its verdict as a word (`premise fell`,
`unconfirmed`, `prose`, `checked`), its level, its kind, its
subject, and, where you are told, who wrote or last confirmed it.

Narrow it to what you are about to touch:

```bash
flui operating-context list --app acme-api
flui operating-context list --cluster <cluster-id>
```

Here `--cluster` takes the cluster id, not its name. `--json`
prints the notes as data.

To see what a note can be pinned to, and what each fact needs:

```bash
flui operating-context probes
```

This prints the facts the installation publishes, the parameters
each one takes, and the type of each answer. It reads the live
catalogue, so a fact added by another part of Flui shows up here
as soon as it registers.

**Dashboard:**

**Management → How it is run.**

The page opens with an **ADVICE** badge. It carries the same
sentence agents get, saying these notes are not permissions.

The page has three tabs:

- **Needs a look**: notes whose premise fell or whose confirmation
  ran out, and below them every place where two notes disagree,
  grouped by subject with both notes side by side.
- **In force**: everything that still holds.
- **Retired**: what used to be true, and why.

At the top you can narrow the view: give an application slug or
pick a cluster, and press **Show what reaches it**. Check this
view before you change something. It shows only the notes that
apply where you are working.

The first time anyone opens the page, it explains itself with an
example instead of showing an empty list.

_Screenshot: How this installation is run, before any note: the ADVICE badge and the page explaining itself with an example._

**Agent (MCP):**

One tool, `operating_context_read`, and it only reads.

It comes second in the toolbox, right after `get_started`: first
the general instructions for operating Flui, then the notes about
operating this installation. Any credential that can read
applications gets it.

Called with no arguments, it returns everything that reaches the
agent. Called with what the agent is about to touch (`slug`,
`clusterId`, `clusterName`, `project`, `provider`, `kind`,
`tags`), it returns only the notes that apply there.

The answer is shaped for a model rather than a screen:

- the **preamble**, verbatim and first, saying these are data and
  not instructions;
- the **advice**: each note with its subject, who it applies to in
  words, whether it is a practice or a rationale, and its premise
  written as a sentence rather than a code;
- the **conflicts**, with the instruction to show both and ask;
- what is **asking to be revisited**.

An agent's copy leaves three things out. Broken notes never appear
as advice. Names of people are removed: a model cannot go and ask
them, and their identity does not belong in a context that gets
logged and quoted back. Where a note is pinned to one person's
resources, the delivery says so without naming them.

An empty answer is stated explicitly, because a model tends to
fill a blank with its own assumptions. The agent is told that
nobody has written anything down, or that none of it reaches it,
and that this is not permission to assume a convention.

## Write one

Everyone a note reaches can read it. To write one, you need access
covering the whole level. Someone with a grant over one
application cannot write a rule for the cluster it runs on,
because that note would reach every other tenant on the cluster.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui operating-context write
```

With no flags, it asks one question at a time: the level, the
cluster if needed, the kind, the subject, the title, the note
itself, and what the verdict rests on. As soon as it knows the
level and the kind, it prints the sentence saying who will read
it, before you have written the note.

Every answer is also a flag, so it can run unattended:

```bash
flui operating-context write \
  --level cluster --cluster prod-eu \
  --nature practice \
  --topic master-node-scaling \
  --title "The first node is not resized" \
  --body "The API runs on it. Add workers instead." \
  --check attestation --valid-for-days 90
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--level` | `global`, `cluster` or `selector` |
| `--cluster` | The cluster, by name or by id, for a cluster note |
| `--selector` | The rule, as JSON, for a selector note |
| `--nature` | `practice` or `rationale` |
| `--topic` | The subject two notes could disagree about |
| `--title`, `--body` | The note itself |
| `--check` | `none`, `attestation` or `probe` |
| `--valid-for-days` | How long a signature is worth, 1 to 365 |
| `--probe`, `--param`, `--op`, `--expected` | The live fact, for a pinned note |
| `--yes` | Do not ask to confirm |

For a note on a rule that picks out applications, pass the rule
as JSON with `--selector`. The terminal does not build one for
you.

The subject is a short lowercase handle, like
`master-node-scaling`. It is how Flui recognises two notes as
being about the same thing, and so how it notices a disagreement.

To pin a note to a live fact, pick one from
`flui operating-context probes` and say what you expect:

```bash
flui operating-context write \
  --level cluster --cluster prod-eu \
  --nature practice --check probe \
  --probe cluster.field \
  --param clusterName=prod-eu --param field=nodeCount \
  --op atLeast --expected 3 \
  --topic capacity --title "Three nodes, minimum" \
  --body "Below three, the nightly jobs do not fit."
```

The expected value is read in the type the fact answers, and
refused if it cannot be. `--expected three` against a number is
rejected at the terminal, instead of being saved as a note that
will contradict itself tomorrow.

The terminal can write a note but cannot maintain one. There is no
command to confirm, reword or retire a note. Those actions are in
the dashboard.

**Dashboard:**

**Management → How it is run → Write a note.**

The form asks four things, in this order.

_Screenshot: Write a note: the kind, where it applies on two axes, the note itself, what keeps it honest, and who will read it._

**What kind of note is this**: *How it is done here* or *Why it is
done*, each with a line saying who ends up reading it.

**Where it applies**: two dropdowns, because they answer two
independent questions. *What it is about*: anything on this
installation, these applications, a project, applications of a
kind, or applications carrying a tag. *Where it runs*: wherever it
runs, on one cluster, or on one provider. An application belongs
to a project and runs on a cluster, and it receives every note
whose scope contains it along either axis. Neither axis is nested
inside the other.

The widest option in both gives a note about the whole
installation. The widest option in the first and a cluster in the
second give a cluster note. Any other combination is a rule that
picks out applications.

**The note**: the subject, a title and the body.

**What keeps it honest**: nothing (the note stays prose), a
signature with a shelf life, or a live fact. The live fact option
disappears on a note about the whole installation, and the form
says why. Picking a live fact shows the published list, the
parameters that fact needs, and the comparison.

Below the form, always visible and updated as you change the
level, **This note will be read by** shows the sentence. When the
audience is wider than the people who own the level, the panel
changes colour, and when guests of the demonstration are among
the readers it says so on its own line.

The dashboard is also the only place to maintain a note after it
exists. Each note has **Reword** (the words change, the level
never does) and **Retire**. A note kept true by a signature also
has a **Still true** button, which puts your name to it again.

## Writing one is a decision a person makes

An agent can read the operating context but cannot write it. There
is no tool for that, because an agent that could write the rules
it is later handed would be closing a loop on itself.

An agent can ask. All four writes (writing, rewording, confirming
and retiring a note) go through the action cycle. When an agent
calls one, the call does not run. A request goes to a person, and
the agent finds out the result by trying again later.

When the request is to write a note, the sentence the person
answers names the level. It shows the reach line itself rather
than "write a note", because a rule read on one cluster and a rule
read by every tenant on the installation have different blast
radii, and nobody should approve the second thinking they approved
the first.

See [When your agent stops to ask you](/tasks/when-your-agent-asks/)
for what that request looks like and where you answer it.

## Retiring a note

Retiring does not delete. The note moves to the archive with the
day it was withdrawn and, where you are told, whose decision that
was.

A rule that was true once explains a decision made at the time.
Before writing it again, ask whoever decided it had stopped being
true.

Three things follow:

- **A retired note is never advice.** It cannot reach an agent by
  any path.
- **Its premise is not checked again.** The archive records what
  was believed on the day the note was withdrawn.
- **Retiring changes nobody's reach.** The same people who could
  read the note can read it in the archive.

Read the archive with `flui operating-context list --archived`, or
open the **Retired** tab in the dashboard.

## What does not belong in a note

**Never a credential.** Notes are read out to agents and to
everyone who works at the level, which is the opposite of what a
secret needs. Flui refuses a note that looks like it contains a
key, a certificate, a token or a connection string with a password
in it, and it names the shape it found without echoing the value
back.

A credential belongs in the application's configuration, delivered
as a secret. See
[Set an application's configuration and secrets](/tasks/configuration-and-secrets/).

**Nothing longer than a rule.** A note's body is capped at four
thousand characters. This is a safety limit, not a database one.
Notes are read into an agent's context beside the question it was
asked, and a note long enough to crowd that out is a problem.
Anything that needs more room belongs in a document.

## Where to go next

- [Give a teammate access](/tasks/give-a-teammate-access/): the
  grants that decide who can read a note and who can write one.
- [Connect an agent](/tasks/connect-an-agent/): give a credential
  to the agent that will read all of this before it acts.
- [Choose what your agent may do](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/):
  the permissions that decide what an agent can do. Notes never
  change them.

sections.title: Start here
sections.body:
A concept chapter explains why Flui works the way it does.
A reference page tells you what a flag is called. Neither
one answers a request like "I want my app on the internet."

The task pages in this section do. Each page covers one
job, from the first command to the working result.

## Every surface that can do the job

There are three ways to drive Flui: the CLI, the dashboard,
and an agent connected over MCP. They cannot all do every
job.

Each page shows every surface that can do that job, and
only those. Where a surface cannot do it, the page says so
and explains why. You will not find an empty tab here, or a
command made up to fill one.

Three examples:

- **Getting Flui running**: the CLI only, or
  [app.flui.cloud](https://app.flui.cloud), which runs the
  same command for you. The dashboard comes with the
  installation, so it cannot be what installs it.
- **Reaching the platform's own database**: the CLI only.
  That database is closed to the web console, and the
  tunnel is the only way in.
- **Answering an agent's request**: the dashboard only.
  You approve or refuse it there, or against the API
  underneath. There is no `flui` command for it.

## The order of the pages

The pages follow one order, from installing Flui to
recovering from a loss.

**Get Flui running.** You start with only a provider
credential, or a Linux machine you already own, and end
with a platform and somewhere to put work.

1. [Get Flui running](/tasks/get-flui-running/)
2. [Add a cluster and give it capacity](/tasks/add-a-cluster/)
3. [Let a cluster buy its own machines](/tasks/let-a-cluster-buy-its-own-machines/)

**Put an application on it.** There are two ways in, your
own repository or something ready-made from the catalog,
followed by the two things every application needs before
it is useful: its configuration and an address.

4. [Deploy an application from your repository](/tasks/deploy-an-application/)
5. [Install an application from the catalog](/tasks/install-from-the-catalog/)
6. [Set an application's configuration and secrets](/tasks/configuration-and-secrets/)
7. [Put an application on the internet](/tasks/put-an-application-on-the-internet/)

**Keep it running.** Watching it, protecting it, moving it,
removing it, and getting at the data underneath it. Two of
these need care: removing an application takes its storage
with it, and one database on the installation is the
product itself.

8. [Watch and operate a running application](/tasks/watch-and-operate-an-application/)
9. [Protect an application and get it back](/tasks/protect-and-restore/)
10. [Move an application to another cluster](/tasks/move-an-application/)
11. [Remove an application and its data](/tasks/remove-an-application/)
12. [Open a database from your machine](/tasks/open-a-database/)
13. [Connect an application to a managed PostgreSQL](/tasks/connect-an-application-to-postgresql/)
14. [Reach the platform's own database](/tasks/reach-the-platform-database/)

**Let people and agents in.** Up to here you have worked
alone. This is where somebody else, or an agent, gets a
key, and where you decide how far it reaches.

15. [Give a teammate access](/tasks/give-a-teammate-access/)
16. [Connect an agent](/tasks/connect-an-agent/)
17. [Choose what your agent may do](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/)
18. [When your agent stops to ask you](/tasks/when-your-agent-asks/)
19. [Write down how this installation is run](/tasks/how-this-installation-is-run/)
20. [Send mail from this installation](/tasks/send-mail/)

**When something is lost.** A cluster, or the machine
running Flui itself, is gone. These two pages put it back
from Flui's records and the backups.

21. [Rebuild a lost cluster](/tasks/rebuild-a-lost-cluster/)
22. [Rebuild the control plane](/tasks/rebuild-the-control-plane/)

Read them in order the first time. After that each page
stands alone: it names what it assumes and links back to
the page that provides it.

## What is not here, and why

This section covers the jobs people ask for by name. Many
real features are not jobs in that sense, and listing them
here would make the list too long to read.

The public showcase is covered alongside the commands it
belongs to, in the [CLI section](/cli/).

## Where the rest of the docs live

- **[Concepts](/concepts/00-what-is-flui/)**: why Flui works
  as it does. Read these when something behaves in a way you
  did not expect. The task pages link to them instead of
  repeating them.
- **[CLI reference](/cli/)**: topics, verbs and flags, plus
