  the conventions that recur everywhere. Every command also
  has `--help`, which is generated from the CLI itself and is
  never out of date.

If you have never run Flui at all, start with
[Get Flui running](/tasks/get-flui-running/).

sections.title: Install an application from the catalog
sections.body:
Not everything you run is something you wrote. Most installations
end up with a photo library, a status page, a wiki or a database:
software that already exists and that you want running somewhere
you control.

The catalog holds that software, already described. Someone has
written the manifest: which image to pull, what it listens on, how
much memory it wants, and what it has to ask before it can start.
You pick an entry, answer its questions, and Flui installs it on
one of your clusters.

The result is an ordinary application. It sits in the same list as
the apps you build from your own repositories, and the same
commands and screens restart it, read its logs and remove it. The
catalog is only where the image comes from.

For what an entry is, read
[Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/).
For entries that bundle several workloads, read
[Composed catalog apps](/concepts/22-composed-catalog-apps/).

## Before you start

You need a cluster to install onto and the right to create
applications on it. The image is already built, so there is no
repository to connect and no build to wait for.

## Install one

**CLI:**

**Find something.**

```bash
flui catalog list
flui catalog list --search umami
flui catalog list --category productivity
```

Each row shows a slug, a name, a category and a version. You
install with the slug.

`--building-blocks` lists the databases, caches and queues that
other entries are built on, and `--json` prints the same rows for a
script.

**Install it.**

```bash
flui catalog install umami --wait
```

Without `--cluster`, the cluster is picked automatically when your
profile has only one. `--wait` polls until the install has
finished, up to `--timeout` seconds (900 by default). Without
`--wait`, the command prints the install id and returns. The
install carries on either way.

**Answer what the entry asks for.**

```bash
flui catalog install pocketbase \
  --input PB_ADMIN_EMAIL=me@example.com \
  --input PB_ADMIN_PASSWORD='choose-one' --wait
```

`--input KEY=value` is repeatable, one per answer. The related flag
`--env KEY=value` changes a setting the entry has marked as yours to
change, instead of answering a question it asks.

`--option key=true|false` turns on or off a feature the entry
declares, also once per option. PostgreSQL, for example, comes with
a connection pooler unless you pass `--option pooler=false`; see
[Connect an application to a managed PostgreSQL](/tasks/connect-an-application-to-postgresql/).

There is no file form of `--input`, so an answer given this way
lands in your shell history like any other argument. For a value
you want to keep out of it, leave the flag out: in a terminal, the
command asks for every required answer you did not pass, and a
sensitive one is typed without being shown.

**Follow it, then operate it.**

```bash
flui catalog status <install-id>
flui app list
flui app status <name-or-slug>
```

**Check a manifest you wrote yourself.**

```bash
flui catalog validate ./flui.yaml
```

This runs entirely on your machine against the spec, with no
cluster and no login. It takes several files at once and handles
both `kind: CatalogApp` and `kind: Application`.

**Dashboard:**

Open **App Catalog** in the sidebar. Entries are shown as
cards; opening one gives you four tabs:

_Screenshot: The App Catalog: search, categories, and entries as cards._

- **Description**: what the software is, and its tags.
- **Configuration**: what you will be asked for, and which
  settings you can change.
- **Install**: the install button.
- **Manifest**: the entry's file exactly as published.

_Screenshot: A catalog entry on its Configuration tab: what the install will ask for, with secrets marked._

**Deploy to cluster** takes you to the deploy wizard with the entry
already chosen. The steps depend on the entry, and steps that do not
apply are not shown:

1. **Source**: the catalog, already chosen.
2. **App**: the name this install will have.
3. **Configuration**: the questions the entry asks.
4. **Settings**: the values it lets you change.
5. **Features**: optional parts you can switch on or off, such as
   a PostgreSQL's connection pooler.
6. **Cluster**: where it goes.
7. **Dependencies**: for an entry that needs a database or a queue,
   provision a new one or point at one already running.
8. **Link**: for a client of a database or a queue, the running one
   to connect it to after install. Optional; you can connect it
   later from the app's page.
9. **Domain**: the address it answers on.
10. **Review**: what it needs against what the cluster has free.
11. **Install**: the install runs in the background and the screen
    follows it step by step.

_Screenshot: The App step: the entry chosen, the display name, and what kind of app it is._

_Screenshot: The Configuration step: the questions the entry asks, with secrets hidden as you type._

_Screenshot: The Domain step: an address assigned by the cluster, your own hostname, or none for now._

_Screenshot: The Review step: what the install needs against what the cluster has free, and where it goes._

Only the dashboard has the dependency picker, and only the
dashboard lets you install despite a capacity warning. The review
step shows what the entry needs against what is free, lets you
lower what it asks for, and has an **Install anyway** box you have
to tick yourself.

**Agent (MCP):**

Use three tools, in this order:

1. **`catalog_search`**: free text, by name, category or tags.
   With no exact hit it falls back to the closest names, so search
   for the name the person used rather than guessing a slug.
2. **`catalog_get_app`**: the full entry, with which inputs are
   required, what it depends on, how it is reached, and
   `installable` against the target cluster. When `installable` is
   false, say what is missing instead of trying anyway.
3. **`app_install`**: takes `slug` and `displayName`, and
   optionally `clusterId`, `domain`, `exposure`, `authMode`,
   `options`, `userInputs` and `envOverrides`. Arguments are
   strict: an unknown argument name is refused, not ignored.

`app_install` returns an `installId` and an `operationId`
immediately. On an external client nothing follows that operation
for you: call `operation_status` with the id until `done` is true,
and only then say whether it worked.

Which of these tools an agent can see depends on its permission
groups. **See applications** carries the two catalog reads;
**Deploy and operate applications** adds `app_install`. A tool
outside the key's groups is not listed at all, so an agent that
cannot install does not see the tool and cannot try.

## The answers an entry asks for

An entry can declare that it cannot start until someone gives it a
value, such as an admin email, a site title or a password. Those
questions are part of the manifest, keyed by the variable the value
goes into, which is why you write an answer as
`PB_ADMIN_EMAIL=me@example.com` and not by position.

- **An answer you leave out falls back to the entry's own
  default.** A question with no default has to be answered, and for
  a single-workload entry an install missing one is refused before
  anything is created.
- **Answers marked sensitive are stored as secrets.** They are
  never printed back to you: `flui app env list` tells you a
  sensitive key is set, never its value.
- **Values the entry generates for itself**, such as a database
  password it creates at install time, are secrets too, and you
  never have to invent them.

Some entries ship with a built-in account instead of asking you for
one. The dashboard shows that login on the configuration step, with
the entry's own note about changing it.

The terminal has no command that only prints an entry's questions;
`flui catalog install` asks them as it goes. To read them first,
open the entry's page in the dashboard, or have an agent call
`catalog_get_app`.

## One entry, several applications

A composed entry is one manifest carrying several workloads (a web
tier, a database, a cache) that only make sense together.
Installing it creates all of them in dependency order, wired to
each other. If the install fails partway, what was already created
stays where it is and the install is marked failed. Remove it to
clean up.

It still counts as one install:

- `flui catalog status <install-id>` counts the applications the
  install owns.
- `flui app list` shows the bundle as a single row with its
  component count; `flui app list --expanded` opens it.
- Removing it removes the whole install, every application in it,
  and the data they all hold.

[Composed catalog apps](/concepts/22-composed-catalog-apps/)
covers the component model in detail.

## Name, address and exposure

Three things the entry declares can be overridden at install time,
because they belong to this install rather than to the software:

| | CLI | Dashboard | Agent |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Name | `--name` | the App step | `displayName` |
| Address | `--domain` | the Domain step | `domain` |
| Exposure | none | offered when the entry allows it | `exposure` |

**Name** is the display name. Installing the same entry twice gives
you two separate installs, each with its own generated slug, so a
second install never overwrites the first.

**Address** is a fully qualified domain name. If you leave it out,
a cluster with a DNS zone assigns one, and a cluster without one
gives the app an address built from the cluster's own IP.
`--skip-endpoint` installs it with no public address at all. On a
cluster with no worker, `--allow-master-placement` lets a component
that keeps its data on one machine's disk run on the control-plane
node; see [storage classes](/concepts/21-storage-classes-and-dedicated-placement/).

**Exposure** is `public` or `internal`. Public means a public HTTPS
address. Internal means the app is reachable only through the Flui
dashboard, behind Flui sign-in, and it only works on a cluster set
up to host internal addresses. An entry accepts this override only
if it says it can be private, and `flui catalog install` has no
flag for it, so an internal install has to come from the dashboard
or an agent.

## When an install is refused

These checks run before anything is created:

- **The cluster does not have room.** Flui adds up what the install
  needs against what is free, keeps a small safety margin, and says
  how much of each is short. Free something up, add capacity, lower
  what the install asks for, or use the dashboard's
  **Install anyway**.
- **The cluster cannot host it.** An entry that is internal by
  default needs a cluster with the DNS and certificate setup behind
  internal addresses. The entry's page says this before you try.
- **A required answer is missing**, as above.
- **A dependency has not been chosen.** An entry that needs a
  database offers you a new one or an existing one, and that choice
  can only be made in the dashboard. Neither the CLI nor the agent
  tool can pass it.

## Where to go next

- [Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/):
  the two kinds of manifest, and how to wrap any image you like in
  one.
- [Composed catalog apps](/concepts/22-composed-catalog-apps/):
  components, options, and what install time resolves.
- [Deploy an application from your repository](/tasks/deploy-an-application/):
  the other half of the same job, for code you wrote.
- [Set an application's configuration and secrets](/tasks/configuration-and-secrets/):
  changing a value after the install.
- [Watch and operate a running application](/tasks/watch-and-operate-an-application/):
  logs, metrics and the levers, once it is up.

sections.title: Let a cluster buy its own machines
sections.body:
On many platforms autoscaling is a single switch. Once it is
on, the platform buys machines for you, and the bill is where
you find out how many.

Flui has no such switch. A cluster grows on its own only when
someone has written down, in one place a person can read, what
it may buy, where it must stop and whether it may act at all.
That record is a **scaling group**. On a provider Flui can buy
from, every cluster starts with one, set to keep the machines it
has and to buy nothing on its own until someone changes it. On
other clusters there is no group until you write one, and until
then nothing scales: no machine is bought, and no alarm is
raised when one should have been.

This page covers writing a group and reading what it decided.
The reasoning behind the design is in
[Scaling groups](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/).

## What a group says

A scaling group belongs to a cluster, and a cluster can have
more than one, for example a general group and a second one for
heavy jobs. Each group holds the same few settings.

**Three bounds.** Each plays a different role, and they only
make sense together:

- `min` is the floor. It is held now, and always.
- `desired` is the target. The group moves toward it only when
  the market allows. Being below it buys nothing by itself.
- `max` is the ceiling: as far as the cluster may grow right
  now when work cannot be placed.

`min` must not exceed `desired`, and `desired` must not exceed
`max`, or the write is refused. Every bound counts the whole
fleet, master included, and must be between 1 and 20.

**Where it may buy, and what.** `regions` is a list of regions.
`shapes` is a list of machine shapes in order of preference, so
the first entry is the one the group prefers. Where the provider
publishes no catalogue of machine sizes, those two fields are
refused and you set `requirement` instead: the CPU and memory a
machine has to hold. Where a catalogue exists, it is the other
way round.

Where Flui buys the machine itself, the machine must land in a
region the cluster's private network reaches. If that network
spans several regions, a group may buy in any of them, and the
new machine joins the same private network as the rest of the
fleet. A region the network does not reach is refused, and the
decision says so. Listing such a region is still useful on a
provider Flui cannot buy from, because there the outcome is an
alarm, and an alarm that names a shape and a region tells you
more than one that cannot.

Where the provider reports it ([see which
do](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/#the-providers-integrated-today)),
Flui reads from the provider whether a shape can be bought right
now, and reads it again every few minutes. A shape the provider
reports as sold out can come back at any moment, and the next
decision will see it.

**A placement strategy**, one of four:

| `strategy` | Picks |
| --- | --- |
| `cheapest` | the lowest hourly price, in any region this group may buy in |
| `closest` | the cluster's own region first, then the others in the order listed |
| `roomiest` | the largest that stays within the limits, so the next piece of work fits too |
| `uniform` | the same shape as the machines already running (the default) |

All four choose only among the shapes that already fit the
waiting work. Otherwise `cheapest` could buy a machine that
helps nobody, and the work would still be waiting after the
money was spent.

**A spending ceiling in money.** `limits.maxMonthlyCost` is an
amount of money per month. The number of machines does not tell
you the bill, so the ceiling is set in money. Leaving it out
means no ceiling at all, which is different from a ceiling of
zero, and only a group that does not buy on its own may leave it
out. `limits.hourlyBillingOnly` refuses shapes billed by the
month, which make growing and shrinking cost-neutral at best.

**A settle window.** `settleSeconds` (default 30, at most 3600)
is how long work must have been stuck before this group buys
anything. It makes sure the work is really stuck and not halfway
through being placed. The group never uses it to wait for a
cheaper machine.

**Consent.** `provision` is `manual` or `automatic`. This one
field decides whether the group may act:

- `manual` (the default): the group decides, records what it
  decided, and tells you. Nothing reaches a provider.
- `automatic`: the group may act.

`automatic` is refused on a provider Flui has no way to create
servers on, on a cluster with no private network for a new
machine to join, and without a monthly ceiling above zero. There
is no installation-wide spending grant. Each group carries its
own ceilings, in money and in machines, where you can read them.

## Write the group

**CLI:**

You write a group as a file. Start from this one:

```yaml
# scaling.yaml
kind: ScalingGroup
name: general
cluster: prod-eu
bounds:
  min: 1
  desired: 2
  max: 4
regions:
  - fsn1
  - nbg1
  - hel1
shapes:
  - cx33
  - cpx32
strategy: cheapest
settleSeconds: 30
limits:
  hourlyBillingOnly: true
  maxMonthlyCost: 40
provision: manual
standingOrders: []
requirement: null
```

Then apply it:

```bash
flui scaling apply -f scaling.yaml
flui scaling apply -f scaling.yaml --dry-run
```

`--dry-run` reads the file, checks it, says whether it would
create or update, and writes nothing.

A group is matched by name on the cluster: the same name updates
the existing group, a new name creates one. If the file names no
`cluster`, pass `--cluster`. If the file and `--cluster` name
different clusters, the command is refused.

Then read it back:

```bash
flui scaling get                      # the cluster's only group
flui scaling get general --cluster prod-eu
```

`flui scaling set` changes single fields and keeps the rest, and
`flui scaling floor` moves the minimum.

```bash
flui scaling set default --max 4 --desired 2
flui scaling set default --provision automatic --max-monthly 40
flui scaling set default --shapes cx33,cx23 --regions fsn1,nbg1 --dry-run
flui scaling set default --max-monthly none      # a manual group only
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--min`, `--desired`, `--max` | Floor, target and ceiling in nodes, master included (1 to 20). |
| `--max-monthly <euros>` | The spending ceiling. `none` removes it, on a manual group only. |
| `--provision automatic\|manual` | Whether Flui buys on its own or proposes and waits for a person. |
| `--shapes <list>` | The machines it may buy, comma separated, in order of preference. |
| `--regions <list>` | The regions it may buy in, comma separated. |
| `--strategy <name>` | `cheapest`, `closest`, `roomiest` or `uniform`. |
| `--settle <seconds>` | How long an app waits for room before the group acts. |
| `--[no-]hourly-only` | Buy only machines billed by the hour. |
| `--dry-run` | Show each setting before and after, with what the limits would cost, and write nothing. |
| `--yes` | Save a lower floor or target that gives a machine back, after reading which one. |
| `-c, --cluster` | The cluster, when it is not the only one. |

A lower `--min` or `--desired` that gives a machine back first
says which machine goes, what runs on it and where it starts
again, Flui's own parts first, or why the removal would wait.
Nothing is saved until you run the command again with `--yes`.
`flui scaling floor` behaves the same way.

`flui scaling delete` removes a group. It cannot remove the only
group of a cluster Flui can buy for, because that cluster's
machines change through it.

**Dashboard:**

Open **Scaling** in the sidebar, choose **Manage** on the
cluster's row, and go to the **Group** tab. Every field of the
group is there: the three bounds, the regions, the machines in
order of preference, the strategy, the settle window, the
monthly ceiling, and the mode (**manual** or **automatic**).

_Screenshot: The Group tab: provisioning, the three bounds, settle window, regions, machines in order of preference, strategy and spending ceiling._

Next to **Save**, the page states in one sentence what the group
will do once saved: how far it may grow and how much it may
spend without asking you. Saving gives your consent to that
sentence, so read it first. A group set to buy on its own
without a monthly ceiling is refused until you set one.

_Screenshot: An edited group, not yet saved: the sentence beside Save says how far Flui may grow the cluster and the spending ceiling._

When the new bounds give a machine back, the first **Save**
does not save. It shows which machine goes and what runs on it,
with Flui's own parts marked, or why the removal would wait. The
button then reads **Save and give back** followed by the machine,
and the second click saves. The **−** on a cluster's **Scaling**
tab shows the same before you confirm.

The machine list only offers shapes the provider sells, and
marks the shapes already on the list.

**Agent (MCP):**

`scaling_group_set` writes a group or changes one. Pass
`groupId` to change an existing group, or `clusterId` plus
`name` and `bounds` to write a new one.

The call stops and asks a person. The route is inside Flui's
action cycle, so the agent's call does not run. It comes back as
a request that states what the agent's bounds and limits allow,
for example "up to 5 nodes, never past a spending ceiling of €40
a month, without asking you", and a person answers it. The agent
learns the answer by retrying the identical call; nothing tells
it directly.

Two things catch agents out:

- `bounds` is replaced whole, and so is `limits`. Sending
  `limits` without `maxMonthlyCost` removes the monthly ceiling.
  Restate the cap every time.
- `provision: "automatic"` is refused wherever the provider has
  no way to create servers, and without `limits.maxMonthlyCost`
  above zero. Read `scaling_group_get` first; retrying will not
  help.

When the new bounds give a machine back, `scaling_group_set`
and `scaling_group_floor` read the same preview first and carry
it in their answer, and in the request a person approves: which
machine goes and what runs on it, or why the removal would wait.
The agent has to pass that on.

No agent tool removes a scaling group.

## Read what it decided, including the decisions to do nothing

A group decides in a loop and records every decision. The
decisions to do nothing are the ones people most often come
looking for, so they are recorded in the same form as a
purchase, and nothing filters them out.

A decision ends in one of five outcomes: a machine was added,
one was bought and another drained, one was drained and removed,
the group chose to do nothing, or nothing could be bought and a
person is asked instead.

Under each decision is the ladder: every candidate the group
looked at, with the reason for each.

| Reason | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| `would-buy` | this is the one it would buy |
| `unavailable` | nothing to buy there right now |
| `does-not-fit` | too small for the work that is waiting |
| `over-budget` | the monthly ceiling would be passed |
| `refused-by-limit` | available and affordable, and this group's own rules exclude it |
| `alert` | nothing can be bought here, so a person is asked instead |

`refused-by-limit` is the reason to learn. The provider was not
out of stock and the ceiling was not reached: the machine was
available and affordable, and this group's own rules excluded
it. It was in a region you did not list, it was a shape you did
not name, or it was billed by the month when you refused monthly
billing. Without its own reason, this case would look exactly
like an outage.

A second set of reasons covers a group that decided to buy and
still did not: the group is set to decide and not act, a machine
is already on its way to this cluster, the cluster is not in a
state to attach one, the winning shape has no published price
and you set a ceiling, the winning shape is in a region the
cluster's network does not reach, the group buys on its own
with no spending ceiling, a machine has just joined, or the last
purchase failed. Each needs a different fix, and the decision
names the one that applied.

A failed purchase waits for you, unless the provider simply had
none of that machine left. In that case nothing was created, and
the group checks availability again on its own ten minutes
later. Any other failure stops the group from buying until a
person has read why and says to try again: from the page, with
`flui scaling retry`, or with the `scaling_group_retry_purchase`
tool. Buying again without that check would usually fail the
same way, or pay twice.

When nothing at all can be bought, the alarm lists every machine
with its own reason (sold out and where, too small for the
waiting work, or over the monthly ceiling) and what a person can
do about it: widen the shapes or regions, raise the ceiling, or
attach a machine by hand.

## How a fleet grows and shrinks back

Growing is fast. Once work has waited longer than the settle
window, the group buys the machine the ladder chose and the work
waits for it to join. While that machine is on its way, nothing
else is bought for the same work.

Shrinking is slow. A fleet above its target gives a machine back
only when both of these are true:

- No machine has joined the cluster in the last ten minutes. The
  load that called for it rarely leaves that fast, and giving a
  machine back only to buy it again means paying twice.
- Everything running on it fits on the machines that stay. If it
  does not, the machine is kept, and the decision says what would
  have had nowhere to run.

A machine that runs the Flui API is never emptied. The API is what
carries out the removal, so emptying its machine would stop the
removal halfway. The removal waits instead, the decision says why,
and nothing on the machine is touched in the meantime.

Both checks are made again just before the removal starts, because
the cluster may have changed since the decision. If either fails,
the removal stops before the machine is touched, and the operation
says "Nothing was changed" and why.

When the last worker of a control cluster leaves, its master is
opened to apps before anything is moved, so what the worker ran has
somewhere to start again. The operation lists the apps it started
again on another machine, Flui's own first.

The machine is emptied first, and only then removed from the
provider.

## Standing orders

A group can also carry **standing orders**: machines you want,
bought when the market allows instead of when work is waiting.

- `expand`: buy this shape in this region, this many times. The
  order closes itself once the fleet reaches the target it was
  written for.
- `replace`: buy this shape, then empty and remove a named
  machine. This moves the fleet to a better shape without a gap.

An order never runs while any work is waiting; waiting work
always comes first. On the dashboard, **Now** lists the open
orders and what holds each one back, and **Add a machine**
writes an `expand` order.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui scaling list                     # one line per cluster
flui scaling list --cluster prod-eu   # that cluster's groups
flui scaling why                      # the latest decision on the cluster
flui scaling why --limit 10
flui scaling why --outcome added,removed,alerted
flui scaling why --since 2026-09-25T08:00 --until 2026-09-26T08:00
flui scaling preview                  # what it would do right now
flui scaling retry                    # buy again after a failed purchase
```

`flui scaling list` shows every cluster, including those with no
group and those that can only raise an alarm. Those are the two
cases that need a person, so the list never filters them out.

`flui scaling why` asks about the whole cluster and names the
group each decision came from. On a cluster with two groups,
asking one group why nothing happened can give you an answer
about the wrong fleet.

`flui scaling preview` asks the same engine what it would do if
a machine were needed right now, and spends nothing. It shows
every rung of the ladder with its reason, and the room left on
each machine: memory and CPU reserved against what the machine
can give, and the largest app that still fits. Anything bigger
than that makes the group buy.

Room is counted from what apps reserve rather than what they use
at the moment, because reservations decide where work can be
placed.

`list`, `why` and `preview` take `--output json`; `get` also
takes `--output yaml`.

**Dashboard:**

The **Scaling** section in the sidebar lists every cluster in
the installation, whether or not it can scale itself.

_Screenshot: The Scaling overview: every cluster, who can add a node, nodes as floor, target and ceiling, and spend._

A group has four tabs:

- **Now** shows what the group would do at this moment: the
  nodes, the spend against the ceiling, the work with nowhere to
  run, any open alarm, the room left on each machine and the
  largest app that still fits, the ladder it would walk, and the
  standing orders.
- **Group** holds the configuration, which you can edit and save
  here.
- **Market** shows which machines can be bought, and where.
  Where the provider reports availability, the tab reads it from
  the provider, the same reading the group buys from, and says
  which provider it read. The tab appears only where the
  provider publishes a catalogue.
- **History** shows the fleet over time, one band per machine
  shape, with what the fleet cost on the same samples and the
  decision log underneath.

_Screenshot: The Now tab: nodes against the bounds, spend against the ceiling, work with nowhere to run, standing orders._

_Screenshot: Room on the Now tab: the largest app that still fits, and memory and CPU on each node._

_Screenshot: The Market tab: each machine's state, the regions where it can and cannot be bought, and its place in the group._

_Screenshot: The History tab: the fleet over thirty days, one band per machine type, with the decisions on the same axis._

History shows one band per shape because a total only says
"three machines", and you need to know which three to tell
whether the next piece of work fits.

A cluster's own page also has a **Scaling** tab. There you add
and remove machines (one more or one fewer moves the group's
floor), see how full the cluster is and how many apps are
waiting, and read the latest decisions. The tab also states in
one sentence how the cluster grows. You cannot edit that
sentence: it is derived from the groups, so it changes as soon
as one of them is set to `automatic`.

_Screenshot: How this cluster grows, on the cluster's Scaling tab: one sentence derived from its groups._

**Agent (MCP):**

Five read tools, all under the "See the infrastructure"
permission group:

- `scaling_overview`: one row per cluster, including the
  clusters with no group and the clusters that can only raise an
  alarm. `needsPerson` says which.
- `scaling_group_get`: one group, or every group on a cluster:
  the bounds, what it may buy, what it may spend, and what the
  provider actually allows.
- `scaling_why`: what was decided and what was declined, newest
  first. Ask it about the cluster.
- `scaling_preview`: what the group would do if a machine were
  needed right now, with the ladder and the room left on each
  machine. It spends nothing.
- `scaling_cost`: what node limits would cost before anything is
  written, from always at the minimum to the maximum all month,
  and where a ceiling would stop the fleet.

`scaling_group_retry_purchase` lets a group buy again after a
failed purchase, `scaling_group_floor` moves the floor, and
`scaling_approve_purchase` carries out what a manual group
proposes. They change what the group does, so they need
"Operate the infrastructure". Giving a machine back with
`scaling_approve_removal` needs "Remove infrastructure".

Two values need care. `pendingPods: null` does not mean zero. It
means the cluster could not be asked what was waiting; read as
zero, a cluster in the middle of an outage would look like the
quietest row on the list. `monthlyEur: null` means Flui has no
bill to show, not that the fleet is free. Where `unpricedNodes`
is above zero, the figure is only a lower bound on the bill.

An empty decision list means the group has not decided anything
yet, rather than that it looked and found nothing to do.

## A group is a file

You can export a group to a file, keep it in a repository next
to everything else, and apply it again:

```bash
flui scaling export > scaling.yaml
flui scaling export --all --cluster prod-eu > scaling.yaml
flui scaling apply -f scaling.yaml
```

- **The file is the whole group.** A field left out is reset to
  its default, not left alone. A reviewer reads the file the
  same way, and it is why applying the same file twice leaves the
  same group.
- **Several groups can share one file**, separated by `---`.
- **Only what a person wrote is exported.** What the provider
  can do and what the market is doing are read fresh every time,
  because they would be out of date the day after the file was
  committed.

## What the provider can do

Flui cannot buy machines from every provider. It works out what
it can do from what the provider declares, never from its name,
and the result is one of three cases:

- **Flui can add machines here.** The group can be set to
  `automatic`.
- **Flui cannot add machines, but there is a catalogue.**
  Scaling ends in an alarm for a person, naming the shape it
  would have bought and what it costs.
- **Flui cannot add machines and there is no catalogue**, as on
  your own servers. Scaling ends in an alarm that describes what
  a machine has to hold, since there is no shape name to give.

Write a group in all three cases. In the second and third, the
group's decision is the alarm, and it is the only thing that
tells you the cluster has run out of room.

## Where this goes from here

- [Scaling groups](/concepts/27-scaling-groups/): the two forces
  on a fleet, why the ceiling is money and not a machine count,
  and why `refused-by-limit` is a reason of its own.
- [Add a cluster and give it capacity](/tasks/add-a-cluster/):
  creating a cluster and changing its machines.
- [Nodes and cluster topology](/concepts/06-nodes-and-cluster-topology/):
  what a machine is to a cluster.
- [CLI: Clusters, nodes, and SSH](/cli/clusters-and-nodes/): the
  command reference for the fleet itself.

sections.title: Move an application to another cluster
sections.body:
If you redeploy somewhere else, copy the data by hand and
change the address, every step can lose writes or traffic,
and none of it can be undone once you are halfway.

In Flui, a move is one operation. Flui builds the new copy
beside the old one, keeps it in step, and swaps the two
only when you say so, or as soon as the copy is ready if
you asked for that. Until the swap, nothing on the source
has changed and you can cancel the whole move.

## Three kinds of move

There are three commands because each kind of move carries
different risks.

| You want to move | Command | What crosses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| An application | `flui migrate app` | The running copy, its volumes, and its address |
| A Flui-managed PostgreSQL database | `flui migrate db` | The data |
| An application *and* the database it reads | `flui migrate full` | Both, in one cutover |

**`migrate app` moves the application and the files it
keeps.** The application keeps its name and address, and
its volumes are copied to the new cluster. At cutover its
address is repointed there, and the old cluster keeps
forwarding to the new one for a while, so nobody lands on
an empty cluster (see
[What your users see during the cutover](#what-your-users-see-during-the-cutover)).
A database it reads is not included: use `migrate db` for
that, or `migrate full` for both.

**`migrate db` moves only the data.** When both clusters
are on [the Flui network](/concepts/10-the-network-flui-builds/),
a live move copies the database privately over that
network. The copy is exact and kept in step continuously,
and nothing is opened to the internet. The new database
keeps the same database name, user and password as the
source; only its address changes.

In the other cases (the Flui network is off, or you
rebuild from backups) the destination comes up with its
own new address, name, user and password.

At cutover the source stops taking writes. After a
private copy it stops accepting connections altogether;
otherwise it is left read-only. Either way it stays like
that and is not removed. `migrate db` does not change what
your application connects to. `migrate full` does that for
you.

## The shape of every move

Every move has four steps, and only the last two are
permanent.

1. **Create.** The destination is built and kept in step
   with the source. The source keeps serving.
2. **Cut over.** Traffic, writes, or both move to the
   destination. `--cutover auto` does this as soon as the
   destination is ready. `--cutover manual` pauses and
   waits for you.
3. **Abort.** Available until the cutover passes its point
   of no return. The destination is removed and the source
   is left as it was.
4. **Destroy the source.** Optional, and only after the
   cutover. It gives the old cluster its capacity back, and
   cannot be undone.

Steps 2 and 4 are separate so you can check the result
first. After the cutover the old copy stays in place until
you destroy it. It still uses capacity, and while the old
cluster is forwarding to the new one it is still doing a
job.

A restart of Flui in the middle of an application move, a
full move or a private database move does not lose it. The
move picks up where it was.

## What can move, and what cannot

Flui refuses a move it cannot finish when you ask for it,
not halfway through. The refusal says which rule you hit.
A full move checks the application's rules too, before it
copies the database.

An application can move when:

- it runs somewhere other than the target cluster;
- it does not read values out of another application's
  secrets (move the applications it depends on first);
- it answers at a real domain. An application still on
  the fallback address built from its cluster's IP cannot
  move, because that address belongs to the old cluster.
  Assign a DNS zone first: see
  [Put an application on the internet](/tasks/put-an-application-on-the-internet/);
- the target cluster has that DNS zone assigned too, so
  the name can follow the application;
- no other application that is staying behind answers at
  the same address. Give one of them its own name first;
- if it has volumes, there is a backup destination for
  them to travel through: the one protecting the
  application, your only one, or the one you name with
  `--backup-destination`. See
  [Protect and restore](/tasks/protect-and-restore/).

Only one migration can run at a time for each application.

`migrate full` has one more rule. Flui has to see, in the
application's own configuration, that it points at the
database you named: either the standard `PGHOST` setting
matching the source database, or a `postgres://` URL that
matches it. An application that reads its connection from
a linked secret cannot be rewired, so the move is refused
instead of guessed at. The exception is a database with a
connection pooler: an application that reads
`FLUI_CONNECTION_URL` or `FLUI_DIRECT_URL` from the database
itself is accepted, here and under the rule about other
applications' secrets above, and Flui rewires it. In that case the
application must also be the only one using the database.
Move or repoint the others first; the refusal names them.

A private database move also needs the target cluster to
be live on the Flui network. Flui checks this before it
starts and refuses otherwise, telling you which node is
missing. The network reconciles every 10 minutes, so you
can wait for it and start the move again.

## Start the move

**CLI:**

```bash
# an application, with its volumes
flui migrate app create my-api --to production-eu

# a managed database
flui migrate db create orders-db --to production-eu

# both together
flui migrate full create my-api --db orders-db --to production-eu
```

`--to` (`-t`) is required and takes a cluster name or id.
You can give the application and the database by name or
by id. `--from` (`-f`) is optional: Flui looks for the name
on every cluster, workload clusters included, and asks you
for `--from` only when the same name is on more than one.

`--cutover auto` is the default on all three. Pass
`--cutover manual` to pause the move and start the cutover
yourself.

`flui migrate app` and `flui migrate full` take
`--backup-destination` to choose where volumes travel
through. `flui migrate app` also takes `--no-bridge`, which
moves only the DNS record at cutover and leaves the old
cluster out of it.

`flui migrate db` has four more flags:

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--mode live\|restore` | `live` copies from the running database, then cuts over. `restore` rebuilds from its backups instead, for when the source is already gone. Default `live`. |
| `--at <ISO-8601>` | Restore mode only: the point in time to recover to. |
| `--name` | A display name for the new database. Defaults to the old one's slug with `-migrated` on the end. |
| `--no-verify` | Skips the per-table row-count comparison Flui makes at cutover. The check is on by default, and a mismatch stops the cutover. A private copy is exact, so it has no row count to compare. |

`flui migrate full` has `--staging`, which decides how the
new copy of the application waits:

- **`scaled-down`** (the default): the copy is built but
  not started until cutover. This is safe, and the write
  pause at cutover is a little longer.
- **`live-fenced`**: the copy is started at full size
  against the destination database while that database is
  still read-only, so it is already warm at the swap. This
  shortens the pause, but your application has to meet two
  conditions. It must start and pass its health check
  without writing anything, and it must not run background
  work with effects outside the database (queue consumers,
  scheduled jobs, outgoing mail or webhooks) until cutover.
  Flui holds back only its database writes.

When the database has a connection pooler, `flui migrate full`
also takes `--pause-deadline <seconds>`. See
[When the database has a pooler](#when-the-database-has-a-pooler).

**Dashboard:**

Go to **Management → Migrations**. **New migration** opens
one form for all three kinds.

Pick the type first (**App**, **Database** or **Full
app**), then the source and target clusters. The
application and database pickers fill from the source
cluster once it is chosen, so pick the source first. The
form refuses a target that is the same as the source.

_Screenshot: The New migration form for a full app: source and target clusters, the app and database to move, cutover and staging._

The rest of the form depends on the type. Cutover
(automatic or manual) is always there. An application move
asks which backup destination its volumes move through
when you have more than one. A database move adds the
mode, and once the mode is **Restore**, the new database's
name and the recovery time. A full move adds the staging
choice, with the warning about what `live-fenced` requires
of your application next to it.

The row-count check stays on, and an application move
always uses the bridge. To change either, use the CLI or
an agent.

**Agent (MCP):**

There is one tool per kind:

- `migrate_app`: takes `srcAppId`, `targetClusterId`, and
  optional `cutover`, `backupDestinationId` and `bridge`
  (`false` moves DNS only).
- `migrate_db`: takes `srcAppId`, `targetClusterId`, and
  optional `cutover`, `mode`, `displayName`,
  `recoveryTargetTime` and `verifyRowCounts`.
- `migrate_full`: takes `appId`, `dbAppId`,
  `targetClusterId`, and optional `cutover`, `staging` and
  `pauseDeadlineSeconds`.

Application ids come from `app_list` (a managed database
is an application of kind `DATABASE`), and cluster ids from
`cluster_list`.

All three are in the **Run migrations** permission group.

The work is not finished when the call returns. Each call
returns a migration id and an operation id. Nothing polls
for the agent, and an agent should not report a move as
done based on the create call.

Starting a database move or a full move stops and asks
you. Both are part of the action cycle: when the caller is
an agent, the call does not run. It returns a request id
and a sentence you answer in the dashboard. The sentence
names the database or application, the cluster, and
whether the move will also finish by itself. An automatic
cutover is stated explicitly, because approving it
approves the whole move.

Starting an application-only move is the exception. It is
not part of the action cycle and runs when the agent asks.
Every later step (cutting over, aborting, destroying the
source) does stop and ask.

## Watch it

A move takes time. These are the states it goes through:

- `pending`, then `provisioning`: the destination is
  being built. A full move shows `db_replicating` and
  then `app_staging` instead.
- `replicating`: a database move is copying and keeping
  in step. A database restored from backups goes through
  `restoring` instead, straight to `completed`.
- `ready` (an application or a full move) or `synced` (a
  database): the paused state. Under `auto` the move
  passes straight through it. Under `manual` it waits here
  for you.
- `cutover`.
- `bridging` (an application or a full move): the
  application is served from the destination and the old
  cluster still forwards to it. For traffic the move is
  done. It stays here until you destroy the source.
- `completed`, `failed`, or `aborted`.

A full move has one more state, `failed_forward`: it
failed after the database was promoted, which is the one
point that is never rolled back. You can recover by
running the cutover again.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui migrate app list
flui migrate db show <migration-id>
flui migrate full list --json
```

Each of the three kinds has its own `list` and `show`.
`list` prints the id, the state, the target cluster and
the cutover mode. `show` adds what is moving and where,
and the error, if there was one. Both take `--json`.

`show` for an application or a full move also prints the
bridge: whether it is planned, open or closed, the names
it forwards and their certificates, when the DNS record
moved, and from when it can be closed. When the move goes
by DNS only, it says why.

`show` for a database or a full move also prints:

- `Kind`: `physical` for a private copy over the Flui
  network, `logical` otherwise;
- `Link`: the state of the private link between the two
  clusters, and whether the two ends have reached each
  other;
- `Copy`: how far the copy has got, and how much is still
  to catch up once it runs;
- `Fence`: when the source stopped taking writes and when
  the destination was asked to take over;
- `Write pause`: how long writes were paused, and what
  ended the pause;
- `Pooler` and `Cut`, when the database has a connection
  pooler: the pooler's pause and the clients cut at its
  deadline (see
  [When the database has a pooler](#when-the-database-has-a-pooler));
- `Next`: what is left for you once the move has
  completed. Flui does not protect the new database with a
  backup policy for you, so that comes first. A database
  move also reminds you to point your applications at the
  new database, and a full move to destroy the source.

When an interrupted cutover can be resumed, `show` prints
the command to do it.

**Dashboard:**

The **Migrations** table shows the type, state, source and
target, cutover mode and time of each move, plus the
actions still available on each row. Those actions are the
quickest way to tell where a move is.

A database or full row also shows the kind of copy and
the measured write pause, and an application or full row
how long the application was stopped while its volumes
moved. While a bridge is open,
the row says so and from when it can be closed. A
completed move has a **Next steps** list.

**Agent (MCP):**

`migration_list` takes an optional `type` (`app`, `db` or
`full`). Without it, all three kinds come back grouped.
`migration_get` takes `type` and `id` and returns one
migration's state, cutover mode, error, bridge, kind of
copy, measures and next steps.

Both are in the **See migrations** permission group, which
changes nothing.

## Cut over

With `--cutover auto` there is nothing to do here. The
move cuts over as soon as the destination is ready.

With `manual`, the move waits at `ready` (or `synced` for
a database) until you start the cutover, so you choose
when it happens.

What the cutover does depends on the kind:

- **An application** is repointed at the destination
  cluster and its address follows it. It keeps its name
  and identity throughout. With the bridge, the
  certificate for its address is prepared on the
  destination before the cutover; the old cluster then
  starts forwarding to the new one, its own copy stops,
  and the DNS record moves. If the application has
  volumes, it stops while the last changes to its files
  are copied, then starts on the destination. The move
  tells you this when you start it, and records how long
  the pause lasted. If the copy fails, the application
  starts again on its original cluster.
- **A database** stops taking writes. After a private
  copy, Flui waits until the destination has caught up
  with the last write and promotes it. Otherwise it checks
  the row counts table by table against the copy, unless
  you turned that off, and promotes the copy. From then on
  the source does not take writes and stays that way.
- **A full move** does both together, and rewrites the
  application's connection settings to the new database
  in the same step.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui migrate app cutover <migration-id>
flui migrate db cutover <migration-id>
flui migrate full cutover <migration-id>
```

Use the command that matches the kind of move. You cannot
drive the parts of a full move on their own. Flui refuses
and tells you to drive the full move instead.

The same command resumes a cutover that was interrupted,
an application cutover that failed after the bridge
opened, and a full move in `failed_forward`.

**Dashboard:**

A **Cutover** button appears on the row once the move is
paused, and only then. It runs as soon as you press it.
When a cutover can be resumed (it was interrupted, an
application cutover failed after the bridge opened, or a
full move is in `failed_forward`), the button reads
**Resume cutover**.

**Agent (MCP):**

Use `migration_cutover`, with `type` and `id`. It also
resumes the cutovers listed for the CLI. It is in the
**Run migrations** group, and it stops and asks you first.

Driving one part of a full move directly is refused, and
the agent is told to drive the full move.

## What your users see during the cutover

**Moving an application.** The old cluster keeps answering
at the application's address and forwards everything to
the new cluster while the DNS record moves. This is the
bridge. A client that still has the old address in its DNS
cache reaches the application anyway, so nobody is sent to
an empty cluster.

The bridge has limits:

- it runs on the old cluster, so it helps only while that
  cluster is up;
- while it is open, requests that come through it reach
  the application from the old cluster's address, not from
  the client's own;
- it is skipped, and the move goes by DNS only, when an
  address is a wildcard name, has DNS that Flui does not
  manage, has an IP allow-list, uses a shared certificate,
  or when the target cluster has no public IPv4 address to
  forward to. It is also skipped when no valid certificate
  is ready on the destination at cutover. The move tells
  you why.

**Moving a database on its own.** At cutover the source
stops taking writes. After a private copy it refuses every
connection, so an application still pointing at it loses
its database until you point it at the new one.

**Moving both with `migrate full`.** Writes pause from the
moment the source stops taking them until the application
on the destination can write again. The move records how
long that was.

With a private copy, `--staging live-fenced`, the bridge,
and no volumes, the pause is as short as it gets. The new
copy of the application is already running on the
destination against the read-only copy of the database.
At cutover the old cluster starts forwarding to it before
writes stop, so reads keep working the whole time. Writes
pause only from that moment until the destination database
is promoted: a few seconds in our tests. When the database
has a pooler and the application connects through it, those
writes wait instead of failing; see
[When the database has a pooler](#when-the-database-has-a-pooler).
With any other
combination the application on the old cluster cannot
write during the cutover, and after a private copy it
cannot reach its database at all, until traffic reaches
the destination.

## When the database has a pooler

A managed PostgreSQL installed from the catalog usually has
a connection pooler in front of it (see
[Connect an application to a managed PostgreSQL](/tasks/connect-an-application-to-postgresql/)).
When you move it together with its application, writes
are not refused at the switch. They wait in the pooler.

At cutover:

1. The pooler is paused. New transactions wait in it.
2. Transactions already running get a deadline to finish:
   5 seconds by default.
3. A transaction still open at the deadline is cut. Its
   client gets an error and must retry.
4. The new copy of the database is promoted, and the
   pooler resumes against it. The waiting transactions go
   through.

Measured on a move with a private copy, `--staging
live-fenced` and the bridge, writes waited 7.8 seconds with
nothing in flight, and 14.3 seconds when a transaction held
on until the deadline. A probe writing and reading
throughout saw no failed write and no wrong read.

If Flui itself restarts during the pause, writes keep
waiting until it is back (59.4 seconds in our test) and
none is lost. A client with a short HTTP timeout may give
up before then.

Set the deadline with `--pause-deadline <seconds>`, from 1
to 60, on `flui migrate full create`, or on
`flui migrate full cutover` to replace it for a manual
cutover. An agent passes `pauseDeadlineSeconds` to
`migrate_full` or `migration_cutover`. The dashboard has no
field for it and uses the default.

`flui migrate full show` prints what happened: the `Write
pause` line, for example
`7.8s (writes waited in the poolers, none failed)`, a
`Pooler` line with when it paused, when it resumed and the
deadline, and a `Cut` list with each client cut at the
deadline. The dashboard row shows the clients that were
cut.

What this covers, and what it does not:

- **Only clients on `FLUI_CONNECTION_URL` wait.** A client
  on `FLUI_DIRECT_URL` talks to the database directly and
  sees the switch as before.
- **Zero refused writes holds in transaction mode.** In
  session mode every client still holds its connection at
  the deadline, so every client is cut and must reconnect.
- **A database without a pooler moves as before.** Writes
  are refused for a few seconds at the switch.
- **`flui migrate app` refuses a database with a pooler.**
  Moving it as an application would leave the pooler
  behind. Use `flui migrate db` or `flui migrate full`.

## Abort a move

An abort removes what was built on the destination and
leaves the source as it was. Nothing has moved yet, so
there is nothing to move back.

You can abort from `pending` up to the paused state, and
also from `failed`, so a broken move can be cleaned up. A
private database move can also be aborted during its
cutover, until the destination has been asked to take
over. After that it only goes forward.

Abort is no longer available once traffic has moved. An
application move whose bridge is open refuses an abort and
tells you to resume the cutover. For a full move the limit
comes earlier: once its database has started its cutover,
abort is refused. After that point there is no consistent
old state to return to, so you finish the cutover instead.
The refusal tells you so.

When you abort a database move, Flui closes the link
between the two copies but leaves the half-built
destination database in place for you to inspect. You have
to remove it yourself.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui migrate app abort <migration-id>
flui migrate db abort <migration-id>
flui migrate full abort <migration-id>
```

Each asks you to confirm. `--yes` (`-y`) skips the
question.

**Dashboard:**

An **Abort** button appears on rows that can still be
aborted, failed ones included. It is not offered while an
application move's bridge is open.

**Agent (MCP):**

Use `migration_abort`, with `type` and `id`. See
[What an agent may do with this](#what-an-agent-may-do-with-this)
for the permission it needs.

## Destroy the source

After the cutover the old copy is still there. With the
bridge it forwards to the new cluster; without it, it is
drained. Either way it still uses the old cluster's
capacity.

`destroy-source` frees that capacity. It works on a move
in `bridging` or `completed`, it touches only the copy on
the source cluster, and it cannot be undone. When the
bridge is open, it closes the bridge first and the move
becomes `completed`.

While the bridge is open, `destroy-source` is refused
until twice the DNS record's TTL has passed since the
switch, because clients may still hold the old address
until then. The refusal gives you the time. You can close
the bridge earlier on purpose; clients that still resolve
the old cluster then lose the application.

A database move has no destroy step. The source database
is left as the cutover left it, not removed. To remove it,
remove it as an application, which also deletes its
storage. See
[Remove an application and its data](/tasks/remove-an-application/).

**CLI:**

```bash
flui migrate app destroy-source <migration-id>
flui migrate full destroy-source <migration-id>
```

Both ask you to confirm. `--yes` (`-y`) skips the
question; use it only in scripts. `--close-bridge` closes
an open bridge now instead of waiting.

**Dashboard:**

A **Destroy source** button appears on application and
full migrations in `bridging` or `completed`, and it asks
for confirmation before it runs. If the bridge is still
needed, the confirmation says so and the button reads
**Close bridge and destroy**.

**Agent (MCP):**

Use `migration_destroy_source`, with `type` and `id`, and
`closeBridge: true` to close an open bridge before its
time. Asking for `db` is refused with an explanation, so
the call never silently does nothing.

This tool and `migration_abort` are in **Abort and tear
down migrations**, the highest of the three migration
permission groups. A key with only **Run migrations** can
start and finish a move, but cannot cancel it or destroy
the source.

Both tools can also be missing from the agent's tool list.
Removing things needs two independent conditions: the key
must carry that permission depth, and the installation
must have destructive operations switched on. If the tool
is missing, that is the reason; nothing is broken.

Both stop and ask you before they run.

## What an agent may do with this

There are three permission groups, from lowest to highest:

| Group | What it reaches |
| --- | --- |
| **See migrations** | `migration_list`, `migration_get`. Changes nothing. |
| **Run migrations** | The above, plus `migrate_app`, `migrate_db`, `migrate_full` and `migration_cutover`, and reading the applications and clusters involved. |
| **Abort and tear down migrations** | The above, plus `migration_abort` and `migration_destroy_source`. |

A group is granted or refused as a whole, so what you
agreed to is exactly what the key carries.
[Choose what your agent may do](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/)
explains how to choose one.

Every step that changes something on the destination or
removes something on the source stops and asks a person.
You approve it in the dashboard, and the agent finds out
by trying again.
[When your agent stops to ask you](/tasks/when-your-agent-asks/)
explains why it works that way.

## Where to go next

- [Add a cluster and give it capacity](/tasks/add-a-cluster/):
  the cluster you are moving to has to exist first.
- [The network Flui builds](/concepts/10-the-network-flui-builds/):
  the network a private database move travels over.
- [Put an application on the internet](/tasks/put-an-application-on-the-internet/):
  the DNS zone an application needs before it can move.
- [Remove an application and its data](/tasks/remove-an-application/):
  what removing the source database deletes.

sections.title: Open a database from your machine
sections.body:
A database you run on Flui is not on the internet. It has no
public address, no port anyone can scan and nothing to point a
client at. That is the safe default, since a database exposed to
the world is an expensive mistake, but it means you need a way in
the first time you want to look at a row.

There are two ways in:

- **A tunnel.** `flui db tunnel` puts the database on your own
  machine, at `127.0.0.1`, for as long as the command runs. Your
  usual tools connect to it: `psql`, DBeaver, `mongosh`, your
  application's ORM.
- **The console in the browser.** Nothing to install or run, and
  read-only by default. Good for a quick check.

Neither one opens the database to anybody else. The tunnel is bound
to your loopback address and closes with the command. The console
runs every request through Flui's own API, so the browser never
talks to the database.

## The tunnel, and the console

**CLI:**

The application's name is the only argument:

```bash
flui db tunnel my-database
```

It stays in the foreground, so an open tunnel is always visible in
a terminal. Press **CTRL-C** to close it.

While it is open, it prints everything a client needs:

```
✅ Tunnel up. Connect a client to:

   Host:     127.0.0.1
   Port:     55432
   Database: appdb
   User:     appuser
   Password: ...

📝 Connection string:
   postgresql://appuser:...@127.0.0.1:55432/appdb

🧪 PostgreSQL client:
   PGPASSWORD='...' psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 55432 -U appuser -d appdb
```

Copy the connection string into your ORM, or paste the client line
into a second terminal. Both match the engine you are running.

If the connection drops, the command reconnects on its own and
prints the coordinates again. Pass `--no-retry` to turn that off
when you would rather see the failure.

### Which port it binds

The local port is chosen per engine and differs from the engine's
usual port: `55432` instead of `5432`, so a tunnel does not clash
with a Postgres already running on your machine. Tunnels to
different kinds of database do not collide either, except Redis and
Valkey, which share one port.

| Engine | Local port |
| --- | --- |
| PostgreSQL | `55432` |
| MariaDB | `53306` |
| Redis / Valkey | `56379` |
| FerretDB | `57017` |

Pass `--local-port <n>` to pick another port, for example to run
tunnels to two Postgres databases at the same time.

The tunnel covers only these five engines. For anything else it
answers that the database is not supported. For Kafka, an object
store or a search engine, use the browser console.

### The other flags, and the other commands

`-c, --cluster <name|id>` picks the cluster. You can
leave it out when your profile has only one.

The rest of the `db` commands work on the same databases:

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `flui db credentials <app>` | The in-cluster address and credentials, which another app running on Flui uses. The password is hidden unless you pass `--show`. |
| `flui db dump <app-id>` | A logical SQL dump of a Postgres or MariaDB database, produced by the engine's own tool. `-o <file>` to name it, or `--s3-destination <id>` to send it to a backup destination instead of downloading. |
| `flui db restore <app-id> <file>` | Runs a dump back into the live database. It overwrites existing data and asks before it does; `--yes` skips the prompt. |
| `flui db disk <app-id>` | How full the storage under the database is. When it is full, the database can no longer write. |
| `flui db backup-status <app-id>` | For Postgres: whether continuous backup is on, how far back you can recover, and the last base backup. `--json` for machine-readable output. |
| `flui db pitr-restore <app-id> --name <new>` | Rebuilds a Postgres database as of a point in time into a new install. The source is never touched. `--at <ISO-8601>` sets the moment; without it, the latest. |

`tunnel` and `credentials` take a name, a slug or an id;
the others take the application's id, from
`flui app list`.

### What the tunnel needs from you

If you can run the CLI, you already have both things the tunnel
needs.

The first is access to the application, the same access opening
its console needs. See
[Who is allowed to open one](#who-is-allowed-to-open-one) below.

The second is a way onto the cluster. There is no key to set up:
the CLI signs a short-lived certificate for you from the SSH
authority your profile manages, uses it and discards it.

That connection is also why the tunnel can show the password. The
API returns only the coordinates (engine, database, user), and the
CLI reads the password from the cluster itself, over the connection
it already opened. No password crosses the HTTP API on this path,
which is the same rule the console follows.

**Dashboard:**

Open the application. Every database, cache or store gets an
**Access** tab, including ones bundled inside a larger install,
like the Postgres that came with a catalog app. It shows the
in-cluster address and a button that opens the console.

_Screenshot: A database's Access tab: the in-cluster address and the button that opens the console._

The **Overview** tab has a console button too (**Open SQL
Console** for a SQL database), with two panels you can open below
it:

- **External client**: the exact `flui db tunnel` command for this
  application, ready to copy, with the host, port, database and
  user you need once it is up. The password is not shown. The
  command prints it in your terminal, and the dashboard never
  displays it.
- **Use from another app**: the in-cluster address for wiring this
  database into another application's configuration, with the
  `flui db credentials` command that prints the password. No tunnel
  is involved; applications on the same cluster reach it directly.

### Ten kinds of console

Flui picks the console from the engine the application declares:

| Kind | Engines | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Relational | PostgreSQL, MariaDB | A query editor and a schema browser |
| Key-value | Redis, Valkey | Keyspace overview, key scan, value reader, command runner |
| Cache | Memcached | Hit ratio, items, memory, evictions; look up, set or delete by key |
| Document | FerretDB | Databases, collections, documents, and a shell |
| Full-text | Meilisearch | Indices, search with filters, raw requests |
| Kafka | Apache Kafka | Topics, consumer-group lag, and a command shell |
| Messaging | NATS, RabbitMQ | Server stats, streams and queues, peek and publish |
| Object store | Garage | Buckets and files: browse, upload, download, share |
| Search | OpenSearch | Indices, full-text and query-DSL searches |
| Secrets | OpenBao | The secret path tree, versioned values, history |

### Read-only by default

Every console starts read-only. On the SQL side, the query runs
inside a transaction the database itself holds read-only, and the
transaction is discarded afterwards. A statement that tries to
write fails at the engine, and nothing it did is kept. On MariaDB,
statements that would commit on their own are also refused before
they are sent.

Every query also has two limits: it is stopped after about 30
seconds, and the grid shows 1000 rows (up to 10,000 if you raise
the limit) and tells you when it truncated. The console is for
looking at data, not exporting it.

The other consoles work the same way. Browsing is read-only by
nature. A command runner passes through a gate that allows reads
and refuses writes unless the write path is explicitly turned on
for that request. Some consoles (the object store, the secrets
browser and the messaging console) exist partly to write, and
offer writes openly.

The natural-language helper, on the consoles that have one, never
sees your data. It gets the shape (the schema or a keyspace
summary), your question, and Flui's own notes on that engine. It
writes a query for you to read and run, and does not run anything
itself. See [the database console](/concepts/25-the-database-console/)
for the full reasoning.

## Who is allowed to open one

Opening a database is decided by the same access engine as every
other route in the product:

- **Owning the application is not enough by itself.** You need a
  grant that reaches it (the same grant that lets you operate it
  anywhere else) and the right to reach an application's data,
  which every role carries except Platform operator.
- **Revoked access applies here too.** A grant revoked, or narrowed
  to a different set of applications, closes the console and the
  tunnel along with everything else.
- **An agent credential is checked first**, before the application
  is even looked up. A key scoped to reading logs cannot reach an
  arbitrary query prompt, even when the person who created it owns
  the database.
- **Applications the platform installed for itself** open only to
  someone with authority over the whole installation.
- **A refusal does not say "it belongs to somebody else".** It
  reads as an absence, with the same words every time. Trying ids
  until one answers differently tells you nothing.

The whole `db` family shares that gate: the tunnel, the
credentials, the dumps, the disk report and the point-in-time
restore all run the same check before they answer.

Every query the console runs is recorded on the server, whether it
succeeded or not.

## See who is connected

A database that slows down, runs out of connections or stops on a
lock usually has one session behind it. For a managed PostgreSQL,
the **Sessions** view shows every session connected to the
database and what each one is doing, and lets you stop one.

For each session you see:

- **Who** it is. Flui names the application when it recognises it
  from its address. Otherwise you get the name the client gave
  itself, or else its address. A session that comes through the
  connection pooler is marked as such.
- Its **state** (running, idle, idle in transaction, waiting for a
  lock), how long it has been in it, and what it is waiting on.
- **Who blocks whom.** A session waiting for a lock is drawn under
  the session that holds it.
- **The query**, with every value in it hidden. You see the shape
  of the statement, never the data in it.

When the database has a connection pooler, a **Pooler** section
follows: each pool with its clients and database connections, and
the clients waiting in the pooler for a connection. See
[Connect an application to a managed PostgreSQL](/tasks/connect-an-application-to-postgresql/)
for what the pooler is.

There are three ways to stop something, from the gentlest:

| Action | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| **Cancel the query** | The running statement stops with an error in the application that sent it. The connection stays open. |
| **Close the session** | The connection is closed and its open transaction, if any, is rolled back. The application has to reconnect. |
| **Close a pooled client** | The pooler drops that client's connection, with the database connection it holds. Its open transaction is rolled back and the application has to reconnect. |

Each one asks you to confirm first, is recorded in the activity
log, and needs the right to change the application, not only to
read it. If the session has already ended when you confirm,
nothing is stopped and you are told so.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui db sessions my-postgres
flui db sessions my-postgres --all
flui db sessions my-postgres --watch 2
```

The first line sums it up: how many sessions are connected out of
the database's maximum, how many are running, idle in a
transaction or blocked, and how many clients wait in the pooler.
Idle sessions are left out unless you pass `--all`. `--watch <n>`
redraws every *n* seconds until you press **CTRL-C**, and `--json`
prints the same data for a script.

To stop one, take the session's number (its pid) or the pooled
client's id from that list:

```bash
flui db sessions cancel my-postgres 4242
flui db sessions terminate my-postgres 4242
flui db sessions close-client my-postgres 17
```

Each asks you to confirm. `--yes` (`-y`) skips the question, for
scripts. The flags are in
[the databases CLI](/cli/databases/#flui-db-sessions-db).

**Dashboard:**

Open the database and go to the **Sessions** tab. It appears only
for a managed PostgreSQL, and only for people whose access
includes the database's data.

**Show idle** adds the idle sessions, **Every 5 s** keeps the list
fresh, and **Refresh** reads it once. Open a row for the details:
user and database, the name the client gave, its address, what it
waits on, and how long its transaction and statement have run.

The buttons on each row are **Cancel query** and **Close session**.
A button you cannot use says why when you point at it. The
**Pooler** section lists the pooled clients, each with a button to
close it.

The note under the list reads "Values in queries are hidden",
with the time the list was read.

**Agent (MCP):**

- `db_sessions` takes the database application's id and an
  optional `all`. It returns the sessions, with the values in
  their queries hidden, and says for each one which actions are
  allowed.
- `db_session_cancel` and `db_session_terminate` take the
  session's `pid` and `backendStart` exactly as `db_sessions`
  returned them.
- `db_pooler_client_close` takes the pooled client's id and the
  other fields that identify it, exactly as the pooler part of
  `db_sessions` returned them.

Listing sessions changes nothing. The three actions do, and each
one stops and asks a person before it runs. See
[When your agent stops to ask you](/tasks/when-your-agent-asks/).

## No agent opens a console or a tunnel

No tool on the agent surface opens a console or a tunnel, by
design. A tunnel is a live connection to your data and a console
is an arbitrary query prompt; a person opens, watches and closes
both. An agent that needs a fact about your data should be asked
for a query you run yourself.

The Sessions view is different: it shows who is connected, not
your data, so an agent can read it as described above.

## The platform's own two databases

Two names do not belong to any application, and `flui db tunnel`
handles them itself: `platform-postgres` and `identity-provider`.
They are Flui's own database and the identity provider's. The
browser console never opens them. The tunnel is the only way in,
and it needs authority over the whole installation.

They have their own page:
[Reach the platform's own database](/tasks/reach-the-platform-database/).

## Where this goes next

- [The database console](/concepts/25-the-database-console/): how
  the console connects, why the helper never sees your data, and
  what it will not do.
- [The databases CLI](/cli/databases/): the full flag surface for
  `flui db tunnel`, `flui db credentials` and `flui db sessions`.
- [Connect an application to a managed PostgreSQL](/tasks/connect-an-application-to-postgresql/):
  the pooled and direct addresses, and the pooler shown in the
  Sessions view.
- [Give a teammate access](/tasks/give-a-teammate-access/): the
  grants that decide whether any of the above opens for someone
  else.
- [Catalog vs application](/concepts/18-catalog-vs-application/):
  where the database building blocks come from.

sections.title: Put an application on the internet
sections.body:
Running an application and letting people reach it are
separate jobs. The deploy does the first. The second needs a
name that resolves, a working certificate and a decision about
who is allowed in.

This page covers both: first make the application reachable,
then decide who may reach it.

## Where the address comes from

A cluster publishes its applications under a domain you own.
You register the domain with Flui once as a zone and assign
that zone to a cluster. From then on every application on the
cluster answers at `<app>.<cluster>.<zone>`.

A cluster with no zone assigned falls back to `nip.io`
hostnames built from its own IP address. They need no setup,
which is why a first cluster is reachable as soon as it comes
up, but the address contains the cluster's IP and is not one to
give real users. The trade-off is explained in
[DNS as part of the deploy contract](/concepts/13-dns-integration/).

You register the zone in the dashboard, under
**Domains → Registered Zones**. The rest of this page assumes
the zone is already registered.

**CLI:**

```bash
# what is registered
flui dns zone list

# publish this cluster's applications under it
flui dns zone assign example.com --cluster production

# follow the work
flui dns zone status --cluster production
```

`assign` takes a zone name or a zone id. It also takes
`--acme-email`, `--certificate-provider` (`lets_encrypt` or
`lets_encrypt_staging`) and `--wildcard-certificate`, which is
on by default. Pass `--no-wildcard-certificate` to issue one
certificate per application instead of one for all of them.

The work on the cluster runs in the background, so `assign`
returns before it is finished. `flui dns zone status` shows how
far it got. If it drifts, or after a cluster is rebuilt,
`flui dns zone reconcile` applies it again; add `--wait` to
stay until it settles.

**Dashboard:**

Open the cluster and go to its **DNS** tab. Pick a registered
zone, choose one wildcard certificate or one per application,
and assign it.

The same tab then shows the reconciliation state, so you can
watch it complete.

_Screenshot: A cluster's DNS tab: the assigned zone, its certificate and DNS state, and the wildcard certificate issuers._

**Agent (MCP):**

No tool assigns a zone to a cluster. Binding a domain to a
cluster is a one-time decision for a person. An agent can only
read the result and publish the record described below.

## One record for every application

A new hostname takes about a minute to reach resolvers around
the world, and you notice that minute right after a deploy,
when you open the link to the new application.

Every application on a cluster is published at
`<app>.<cluster>.<zone>`, and all of them resolve to the same
address. So a single wildcard record covers all of them,
including applications that do not exist yet. Publish it once
and a newly deployed application answers straight away,
instead of waiting for its own name to propagate.

Publishing never overwrites anything. If a wildcard already
exists and points somewhere else, Flui leaves it as it is and
reports it as `foreign`. Applications on that zone keep getting
their own per-application records, which still work but take
longer to appear.

A cluster can carry more than one zone, and each gets its own
record. The CLI publishes all of them in one run; an agent
publishes one zone per call.

**CLI:**

```bash
flui dns wildcard status --cluster production
flui dns wildcard publish --cluster production
```

`status` reports, per zone, one of these: the wildcard covers
the cluster; there is none and each application waits to
propagate; one exists but points somewhere else; the DNS
provider could not be read just now; or the cluster has no
address yet. It also says whether the certificate is one
wildcard or one per application.

**Dashboard:**
