confirm them before they run.

A person filling in a form, or typing a `flui` command,
is not paused. There, you are the approver as well as
the one asking, and confirming what you just asked for
would add nothing.

An agent can never answer its own request. An agent key
is issued as you, so every permission check on the
answer route would pass. The refusal is therefore based
on what the caller is, not on permissions. An agent that
tries to approve itself is told to stop and ask you.

## An hour, and a price it cannot see

A request stays answerable for one hour.

A request carries an estimate of what the action will
cost, and a price agreed on Tuesday against a quote
taken on Monday may no longer be true. When the hour is
up the request can no longer be decided, and the agent's
next attempt reopens the same request with a fresh
hour, priced again when you open it.

The agent never sees the figure. It is told that a price
exists and is not being shown to it, along with an
instruction: tell the user, do not describe the action
as free, and do not invent a number. An agent that
reports "I asked to add a node, and it costs something I
could not read" is describing its position accurately
while it waits.

You see the figure, because the page you answer on reads
it with your own session.

## "Always" is narrower than it sounds

"Allow always" sounds broader than it is. What gets
recorded is:

- **one specific action**: the route shape, not a
  category;
- **on one specific resource**: "add nodes to this
  cluster". Against another cluster it does not match
  and the agent asks again;
- **for that one credential**. A different key, even one
  you minted yourself for the same agent an hour later,
  starts from requests again.

In some cases "always" is not offered at all. If a
request cannot name the resource it acts on, or has no
credential of its own behind it, it can only be allowed
once. A standing permission with an unclear boundary
would be a wider grant than anyone agreed to, so the
page does not offer one, and says why.

## A standing permission grants nothing

Allowing something always does not give your agent a
permission. It removes a pause on something your own
access already allowed. By the time the question reached
you, Flui had already decided the action was one this
installation permits and one you may perform. All that
was left to decide was whether a person had to be asked.

So a standing permission can never widen what anyone
may do, and revoking one never takes anything away from
you. The dashboard says this at the top of the page: "an
agent can never do more than you can."

## Where you answer

In the dashboard, under **Agents**. The path is
`/agents`, and `/agents/requests` is the same page. A
link in a refusal points at
`/agents/requests/<request-id>`, which opens the page on
that request.

_Screenshot: Agents: what is waiting on you, what stands granted, and what each agent has done._

When the request comes from the assistant inside the
dashboard, it also appears in the chat, as a card with
the same sentence. Saying yes there allows it once,
never always.

The page has three sections, in the order you need
them.

### Waiting on you

Each request is a card with the plain sentence as its
headline. Under it, when the route declares one, is a
line beginning **"If you allow it:"**, which says what
the action will do. That can differ from what was asked
for.

Then the facts: which of your credentials is asking, the
action, the route, and each resource the request names.
Where a price or an impact estimate exists, its numbers
appear beside them, with money highlighted; **See full
estimate** opens the whole estimate.

The buttons are **Allow once**, **Allow always** and
**Deny**. **Allow always** appears only when the request
could state its own boundary. When it does, a line above
the buttons quotes the exact sentence it would grant,
and says: no other action, no other resource.

If you followed a link to a request someone already
answered, the page tells you so.

The count beside the heading also tells you how many
requests expired without an answer. Keep an eye on it:
an expired request was not refused, nobody answered it
in time.

### Granted permanently

Everything your agents may now do without asking, one
row each: what it can do, on what, when it was granted,
and when it was last used, or **Never used**.

Every row has **Revoke**.

### What it has done

The activity register, described further down this
page.

## Taking a permission back

**Revoke** opens a dialog before anything happens,
because revoking does less than people often assume.
The dialog tells you two things.

First, what you are taking back, quoted in the words you
originally agreed to rather than re-derived from a
route.

Second, what is still running under it. Revoking takes
effect immediately for anything that has not started:
the permission is checked on every call, so from the
moment you confirm, nothing new starts under it. It does
not stop work already in flight. If three provisionings
started under this permission, they carry on.

So the dialog lists them and offers a checkbox: **also
ask them to stop**. That stop is a request, honoured at
the next safe point in the work and never in the middle
of a step. A ten-step provisioning cut in half leaves
paid-for resources behind, which is worse than the
outcome you wanted to avoid.

If nothing is running, the dialog says so too, and the
revoke is clean.

## Three behaviours that save you trouble

**Repeated attempts collapse into one request.** An
agent that retries the same call with the same arguments
finds the existing request and gets the same id back, so
your page does not fill up with copies of one question.

**A dry run does not ask.** Some routes have a mode that
checks without changing anything, such as validating a
manifest. Those do not stop, because the question would
describe a deploy that is not happening.

**A settled "no" stays settled.** When an agent retries
something you refused, it does not get a generic access
error. It gets a distinct answer saying that the person
it acts for decided this and the answer stands: do not
retry it, do not reword the arguments to get around it,
tell the user what was refused and offer a different
course of action. An ordinary permission error would
send a coding agent off asking you to grant it
something, which is exactly what you just declined.

## What your agent did

Alongside the requests sits the register: every call
made through an agent credential, newest first, recorded
by the call itself rather than by anything reporting on
it.

_Screenshot: The register: each call an agent made, newest first, with what let it through._

Each row shows when, which tool or action, what it
touched (where the platform recorded that itself), and,
on the right, what let it through:

- **standing grant**, with the sentence you agreed to;
- **allowed once**: you answered that one and the answer
  was used on it;
- **stopped to ask you**: the agent was paused there;
- **refused**, with the refusal message available to
  read.

You can read your own register without any management
access, because deciding whether to disconnect an agent
should not require being an administrator. Someone who
administers access on the installation sees every agent
on it instead, and the page says which of the two views
you are looking at.

Other people's rows are absent, not forbidden. A
register that answered "you may not see that" would
confirm the call it was hiding, so another person's
request or row reads as not found.

The register also covers calls a credential made
straight at the API (an agent using `curl`, with no tool
surface in front of it) on the routes that stop and ask.
The least supervised case is recorded like every other.

## There is no command, and no tool

This is the one job in this section that only the
dashboard does.

No `flui` command lists, answers or revokes any of this:
there is no `flui agent proposals`, and nothing under
another name. No agent tool can answer a request either,
on any surface, for the reason above: the agent that
asks cannot also be the one that approves.

You answer in the dashboard, or through the API
underneath it with your own credential.

## Where this goes next

- [Connect an agent](/tasks/connect-an-agent/): minting
  the credential that raises these requests, and what it
  may touch.
- [Choose what your agent may
  do](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/): the
  permission groups, and why "operate the
  infrastructure" states that everything behind it stops
  to ask.
- [Give a teammate access](/tasks/give-a-teammate-access/):
  the access an agent's key is a ceiling on, and never a
  grant of.
- [The Flui Assistant and
  MCP](/concepts/24-the-flui-assistant-and-mcp/): the
  surface these calls arrive on.

sections.title: What Flui does and does not do
sections.body:
Flui is in alpha. This page answers the questions where a wrong "yes"
does the most damage. When something here is "not yet", say so plainly
and point to the page that explains it.



## Where Flui can run

- **Cloud providers Flui buys machines on:** Hetzner, Scaleway and
  OVHcloud, all billed by the hour.
  
  
- **Your own server:** any Linux machine you reach over SSH, installed
  with `flui env create --host <address>`. A VPS rented from a provider
  Flui does not integrate counts as your own server.
  
- **No other cloud is integrated today.** AWS, Google Cloud, Azure and
  DigitalOcean are not providers Flui can buy machines on; a VM rented
  there can still be used as your own server.
  
- **Differences between providers matter.** OVHcloud has no DNS zone
  Flui can manage and no edge firewall Flui controls, so names go in a
  zone on Hetzner or Scaleway (or records you write) and the firewall
  runs on the machines. On your own servers Flui buys nothing, has no
  DNS zone and applies the firewall on the host.
  
- **Resizing or stopping a node in place** works on Hetzner and
  Scaleway, not on OVHcloud, where growing a node means replacing it.
  
- **Server snapshots and provider load balancers** are not driven by
  Flui on any provider. Incoming traffic goes through Flui's own proxy
  on your nodes.
  

## Operating system and CPU architecture

- **Operating system:** Ubuntu 22.04 or 24.04. The installer stops on
  any other distribution or Ubuntu version. Machines Flui creates on a
  provider run Ubuntu 24.04 LTS.
  
  
- **ARM:** a 64-bit ARM machine you bring is accepted (x86_64, aarch64
  and arm64 pass the installer check). Machines Flui buys on a provider
  are x86_64; ARM sizes are filtered out of the list.
  
  
- **On an ARM server, catalog apps run normally, but apps deployed from
  a repository are built for x86 and will not run on it.** Flui warns
  about this when an ARM server is chosen.
  
- **Memory:** the install precheck on your own server warns below about
  2 GB of RAM and stops unless you pass `--best-effort`.
  

## How long things take

- **Installing the platform:** about five minutes, depending on the
  machine and its network.
  
- No other timing is promised on this page. For a specific operation,
  say it runs in the background and can be followed (operation status,
  dashboard progress), rather than quoting a duration.

## Clusters

- **One installation, one control cluster, any number of workload
  clusters.** Workload clusters can be on the same provider as the
  control cluster or on another one, joined over the encrypted Flui
  network (on by default).
  
- **One master per cluster.** Flui does not add more masters
  (multi-master) yet. While a cluster's master is down, its apps keep
  answering but nothing new can be deployed on that cluster.
  
- **A cluster adds machines by itself only where Flui can buy them.**
  On your own servers it raises an alarm naming the machine to add; you
  add capacity by hand (`flui node connect --host <ip>`).
  

## Applications across clusters

- **An application lives on one cluster at a time.** It is not spread
  over several clusters.
  
  
- **Flui does not connect applications across clusters.** Workload
  clusters share no state and Flui offers no app-to-app path between
  them. A catalog app that reuses an existing database requires it on
  the same cluster.
  
  
- **Databases, caches and queues from the catalog are reachable only
  inside their own cluster.** To reach one from your machine, Flui opens
  a tunnel for you.
  

## Failover and moving between providers

- **Flui does not fail over automatically between clusters or
  providers.** What it offers is a move you start and finish yourself:
  an application with its volumes, a Flui-managed PostgreSQL, or both
  together can be moved to another cluster, including one on another
  provider, with `flui migrate app`, `flui migrate db` or
  `flui migrate full`. The copy is built on the destination and the
  switch happens when you say so; you can abort before it.
  
  
- **A move needs** a real domain name (an address derived from the
  source cluster's IP cannot follow), an application that is
  self-contained, and both clusters in the same installation.
  

## High availability inside a cluster

- **Apps with two or more copies on a cluster with two or more nodes
  keep answering when a worker is lost** (after about a minute).
  `flui app status` says whether an app survives losing a worker; it
  also needs a real domain and no volume tied to one node.
  
- **Catalog databases run as a single instance on one node.** If that
  node is lost the database is down until restored. PostgreSQL and
  MariaDB ship changes off the cluster continuously, so a restore loses
  at most the last few minutes.
  
- **Databases that survive the loss of their node are in progress, not
  available yet** (PostgreSQL first).
  

## Deploying applications

- **Three sources:** a container image, a source repository that Flui
  builds against a `flui.yaml` manifest, or an entry from the Flui
  catalog.
  
- **Repositories come from GitHub.** It is the only integration the CLI
  connects today.
  

## Around the platform

- **Backups** are Flui's own and go to any S3-compatible bucket,
  including one at another provider.
  
- **Email** goes through Scaleway Transactional Email, Brevo, ZeptoMail
  or an SMTP relay you configure.
  
- **The assistant's model** comes from Scaleway's inference service
  (reusing the Scaleway credential) or from any OpenAI-compatible
  endpoint you connect, such as OpenAI or Mistral.
  

## The public demo

- **A visitor can look at everything the demo shows, ask the assistant
  and connect an agent that only reads.** Deploying, installing from the
  catalog, connecting GitHub or keeping a space needs signing in.
  

## License

- Flui is open source under **AGPL-3.0**. Commercial use is allowed; if
  you offer Flui as a network service to others, you must share your
  changes to the source.

sections.title: Dashboard map
sections.body:
Each block below is one page of the dashboard. "Menu" is the path in the
sidebar. "CLI" and "Agent tool" are the equivalent command and MCP tool;
none listed means the page has no direct equivalent.

## Home

- Menu: Home
- Address: `/dashboard`
- Shows: The installation at a glance: a status line (API online, providers, clusters, running apps, operations in progress), cluster metric tiles, the Clusters table, Needs you, Agent, Backups, Certificates & DNS, Recent cluster activity and Workloads cards. On a fresh installation it leads with the DNS not configured first step; a demo guest sees a dedicated guest home instead.
- You can: Pick the metrics window; Refresh; Deploy a workload; Create a cluster; Open a cluster; Set up DNS & certificates; Open backups or protect an app
- CLI: `flui cluster list`
- Agent tool: `cluster_list`

## Topology

- Menu: Topology
- Address: `/topology`
- Shows: A live map of clusters, servers and apps, viewed as Services or Infrastructure and shown as a map or a list, with an inspector panel for the selected item. From an item you can drill into a cluster's capacity or an app's request path.
- You can: Filter by project; Toggle system apps; Switch view (Services or Infrastructure); Switch between map and list; Export the map as an image

## Clusters

- Menu: Cluster › Clusters
- Address: `/cluster`
- Shows: Cards for every cluster with status, provider, region, node count, auto-scaling badge, version and creation date. Search and filter by provider, status and region.
- You can: Create a cluster; Search and filter clusters; View a cluster; Delete a cluster (optionally force delete); Refresh
- CLI: `flui cluster list`, `flui cluster create`, `flui cluster destroy`
- Agent tool: `cluster_list`, `cluster_create`

## Scaling

- Menu: Cluster › Scaling
- Address: `/scaling`
- Shows: Every cluster in the installation, whether or not it can scale itself: situation cards (need a person, open alarms, billed to Flui) and a table with who can add a node, nodes and spend per cluster.
- You can: Open a cluster's scaling group; Set up scaling for a cluster
- CLI: `flui scaling list`, `flui scaling set`, `flui scaling apply`
- Agent tool: `scaling_overview`, `scaling_group_set`

## Projects

- Menu: Workloads › Projects
- Address: `/apps/projects`
- Shows: Every workload grouped by project, across kinds and clusters, with an Unassigned section for workloads outside any project. Each project section shows its slug and a summary, can be collapsed, and lists its workloads.
- You can: Create a project; Edit a project; Delete an empty project; Search workloads and filter by kind; Include system workloads or hide empty projects; Open or delete a workload
- CLI: `flui project list`, `flui project create`, `flui project rename`, `flui project delete`
- Agent tool: `project_list`

## Applications

- Menu: Workloads › Applications
- Address: `/apps/applications`
- Shows: A table of your applications with cluster, ready count, source, CPU and memory, backup state and last release, with apps that need attention listed first. A summary line counts applications and clusters, and applications shared as a showcase appear in a separate "In the showcase" section.
- You can: Add an application: deploy from a repository or install from the catalog; Filter by type, view (All, Running, Needs attention, No backup), cluster and project; Search by name, domain or image; Refresh the list; Open an application
- CLI: `flui app list`, `flui deploy`, `flui catalog install`
- Agent tool: `app_list`

## Data

- Menu: Workloads › Data
- Address: `/apps/data`
- Shows: The same list as Applications, restricted to data stores: databases, caches, queues and object stores. Data stores bundled inside a multi-component app are also listed here on their own, and the name column is headed "Data store".
- You can: Add a data store: deploy from a repository or install from the catalog; Filter by type, view, cluster and project; Search by name, domain or image; Open a data store
- CLI: `flui app list`
- Agent tool: `app_list`

## System

- Menu: Workloads › System
- Address: `/apps/system`
- Shows: The same list restricted to Flui's own system applications, with no Add button.
- You can: Filter by type, view, cluster and project; Search by name, domain or image; Open a system application
- CLI: `flui app list`
- Agent tool: `app_list`

## App Catalog

- Menu: Deploy › App Catalog
- Address: `/apps/catalog`
- Shows: A searchable marketplace of ready-made open-source apps, grouped into Data, Applications, Tools and System, with category chips and tag filters. Each card opens the app's detail page.
- You can: search apps by name or purpose; filter by category and tags; show or hide system apps; open an app to deploy it
- CLI: `flui catalog list`, `flui catalog install`
- Agent tool: `catalog_search`, `catalog_get_app`, `app_install`

## Git Repositories

- Menu: Deploy › Repositories
- Address: `/apps/repositories`
- Shows: The GitHub connection state and the repositories imported into Flui, with counts of total, connected and auto-deploy enabled repositories. Each repository card shows its branch, language, detected framework and badges such as Webhook Active or Auto-deploy.
- You can: connect GitHub or set up the GitHub integration; import repositories from GitHub; deploy from a repository; open a repository's readiness map; remove a repository from Flui
- CLI: `flui repo list`, `flui repo connect`, `flui repo disconnect`, `flui integration status`, `flui integration connect`, `flui integration setup`
- Agent tool: `repo_list`, `repo_connect`, `integration_status`, `github_connect`, `github_setup`

## Flui Templates

- Menu: Deploy › Templates
- Address: `/apps/templates`
- Shows: Framework templates with a production-ready Dockerfile, each card showing its port, health check path and build tool. Filter by Frontend, Backend or Generic.
- You can: search frameworks; filter by category; use a template (opens Deploy New); view the template on GitHub
- CLI: `flui template use`, `flui app init`
- Agent tool: `template_list`, `template_get`

## Deploy New Application

- Menu: Deploy › Deploy New
- Address: `/apps/deploy/new`
- Shows: A step-by-step wizard that starts by choosing a source: a Flui template, a Docker image, an existing repository, or the Marketplace. Later steps cover the image or repository, environment variables and resources, the cluster, exposure and domain, and a final review.
- You can: create a new repository from a template and deploy it; deploy a Docker image; deploy an existing repository from its flui.yaml; install a catalog app
- CLI: `flui deploy`, `flui template use`, `flui catalog install`
- Agent tool: `app_deploy_image`, `app_deploy_from_yaml`, `app_install`

## Compute Instances

- Menu: Infrastructure › Compute
- Address: `/infrastructure/compute`
- Shows: The virtual machines Flui manages across providers, with status, region and IP address. Instances appear automatically when a cluster scales up.
- You can: search instances; filter by provider, status and region; copy an instance IP; open instance details

## Costs

- Menu: Infrastructure › Costs
- Address: `/infrastructure/costs`
- Shows: What the machines and volumes of your clusters cost month by month, deleted clusters included: spent this month, expected by month end and last month, a per-provider table, and a per-cluster breakdown for each provider. Amounts exclude VAT.
- You can: choose how many months to show; refresh
- CLI: `flui costs`
- Agent tool: `cost_overview`

## Virtual Networks

- Menu: Infrastructure › Virtual Networks
- Address: `/infrastructure/vnet`
- Shows: The Flui network card (which connects clusters on another provider to the control cluster) above a list of private networks with their provider, IP range, subnets and attached servers, plus totals.
- You can: create a VNet; switch the Flui network on or off; search and filter VNets by provider and status; open a VNet's details
- CLI: `flui network list`, `flui network create`
- Agent tool: `management_network_status`, `management_network_set`

## SSH Keys

- Menu: Infrastructure › SSH Keys
- Address: `/infrastructure/keys`
- Shows: The SSH keys used for server access, with name, fingerprint, the providers each key is synced to, and totals for total, active, recent and auto-generated keys.
- You can: add an SSH key (generated by the server); sync a key to a provider or remove it from one; copy or download a key; delete one or several keys

## DNS Zones

- Menu: Infrastructure › Domains
- Address: `/infrastructure/domains`
- Shows: Three tabs. Registered Zones lists your DNS zones with provider, redundancy and the clusters using each one. Certificate Issuers shows, per cluster, the standard (HTTP-01) and wildcard certificate issuers. Internal Hosting shows, per cluster, whether internal apps reachable only through the dashboard are available and which requirements are met.
- You can: register a zone; manage provider redundancy for a zone; delete a zone; configure, reconfigure or delete certificate issuers for a cluster; check internal hosting requirements for a cluster
- CLI: `flui dns zone list`, `flui dns replica list`, `flui dns replica add`, `flui dns replica remove`, `flui dns replica enable`, `flui dns replica disable`, `flui dns replica populate`, `flui dns replica verify`
- Agent tool: `dns_issuer_list`, `dns_issuer_configure`, `dns_internal_hosting`

## Platform Components

- Menu: Infrastructure › Platform
- Address: `/infrastructure/platform-components`
- Shows: Live status of core system components across all clusters, grouped by cluster, with counts of healthy, degraded and missing components. Expanding a component shows its resources, replicas and errors.
- You can: search and filter by status or cluster; expand a component; view its logs; redeploy a component
- Agent tool: `platform_component_list`, `platform_component_redeploy`

## Cluster Firewalls

- Menu: Infrastructure › Firewall › Cluster Firewalls
- Address: `/infrastructure/firewall/clusters`
- Shows: Firewall rules for your clusters: one card per cluster with sync status, coverage, drift, node readiness, rule count and last reconciliation, plus totals for in sync, in progress, out of sync and coverage gaps.
- You can: search by cluster or firewall ID; filter by status and coverage; reconcile a firewall that drifted or failed; open a firewall's details; debug on provider
- CLI: `flui env firewall status`, `flui env firewall apply`
- Agent tool: `cluster_firewall_enable`

## Now

- Menu: Management › Now
- Address: `/management/now`
- Shows: A live screen of what runs out first under a crowd: firing alerts, requests at each cluster (requests per second, surges, rate-limited and server errors over 10 minutes), each node's CPU, memory, link and month-at-this-pace, platform components with restarts in the last hour, and image registry traffic for the last hour. On a demo installation it also shows demo spaces in use, ready, waiting and turned away.
- You can: Pause or resume the live refresh
- CLI: `flui now`
- Agent tool: `installation_now`

## Cloud providers

- Menu: Management › Providers
- Address: `/management/providers`
- Shows: The cloud accounts Flui creates your machines on, with summary tiles and a searchable list filterable by status (connected, not connected, needs attention, disabled) and sign-in type. Choosing a provider opens a configuration wizard to connect it.
- You can: Search and filter providers; Connect a provider through the configuration wizard; Refresh the list
- CLI: `flui config list`, `flui config set`, `flui config test`, `flui config remove`
- Agent tool: `provider_credentials_request`

## Backup & Restore

- Menu: Management › Backup
- Address: `/management/backup`
- Shows: What you can protect (a cluster, a database, Flui itself), backups that need attention, a protection card per cluster, overview counts (destinations, policies, total storage, restore jobs), the platform backup card for Flui itself, and links to destinations, policies, jobs and restores.
- You can: Enable backups on a cluster (Flui can create the bucket on another cloud in the same step); Review backups that need attention; Set up the platform backup of Flui itself; Open destinations, policies, jobs or restores
- CLI: `flui backup status`, `flui backup quick-setup`, `flui backup enable cluster`, `flui backup enable platform`, `flui backup platform status`
- Agent tool: `backup_status`, `backup_coverage`, `backup_cluster_protection`

## Image registry

- Menu: Management › Image registry
- Address: `/management/registry`
- Shows: Where the images Flui builds for your applications are kept: the storage location, space in use with a space alert, traffic (pulls, pushes, data out and in) over selectable windows, and the largest applications. When builds still push to GitHub Container Registry, it offers to switch to the Flui registry on a volume or a bucket.
- You can: Measure space now; Use the Flui registry (volume or bucket); Create a bucket on Scaleway or connect a bucket of your own; Replace or remove a bucket; Send new builds back to GitHub Container Registry
- CLI: `flui registry status`, `flui registry traffic`, `flui registry enable`, `flui registry disable`, `flui registry storage connect`, `flui registry storage list`, `flui registry storage remove`, `flui registry storage status`
- Agent tool: `registry_storage_request`, `registry_traffic`

## Migrations

- Menu: Management › Migrations
- Address: `/management/migrations`

# Flui CLI reference (generated)

> Generated from `oclif manifest` for flui CLI `0.14.0-rc.4`. Do not edit by hand —
> regenerate with `pnpm kb:cli-ref`. This is the assistant's ground truth for commands.

CLI version: **0.14.0-rc.4** · commands: **341**

## (root)

### `flui account`

Show your own account: name, email, password, authenticator app, passkeys and linked sign-ins.
Change your name with `flui account profile`. How your account signs in is changed on the
dashboard's Account page, signed in as yourself.

Flags:
  - `--json` — Format output as json.
  - `--profile` — Profile to read the credential from (default: active profile)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
```

### `flui costs`

What your clusters cost: spent and forecast, month by month and provider by provider, deleted clusters included

Flags:
  - `--months` (default: 6) — Calendar months to show, ending with the current one (1-24)
  - `--provider` — Only this provider, e.g. hetzner
  - `--json` — Print the answer as JSON

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --months 12
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider hetzner
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --json
```

### `flui deploy`

Deploy an application from a flui.yaml manifest to a cluster. Supports both kind:CatalogApp (pre-built image) and kind:Application (source build via GitHub Actions). Author a manifest with `flui app init <framework>`; see every field with `flui app manifest`.

Arguments:
  - `file` — Path to flui.yaml manifest (default: ./flui.yaml)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Target cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-p, --project` — Project a new application goes to (slug, name or id, see flui project list). Default: your personal project. An existing application stays where it is.
  - `-r, --repo` — GitHub repository full name owner/repo (default: auto-detect from git remote origin). Required for kind:Application.
  - `-b, --branch` — Git branch to deploy (default: auto-detect current branch). Used for kind:Application.
  - `-d, --domain` — Custom FQDN for the app (default: auto-assign from cluster DNS zone)
  - `--name` — Release name override (default: metadata.name from the manifest). Part of the app identity, so passing a new one installs the same repo and branch a second time instead of updating the first install. Pass it on every deploy that targets that install.
  - `--exposure` [public | internal] — Override deploy.exposure for this install: public (Ingress + TLS) or internal (private URL behind Flui authentication).
  - `-e, --env` — Environment variable override in KEY=VALUE format. Repeatable.
  - `--env-file` — Path to a KEY=VALUE file of env overrides (one per line, # comments and blank lines ignored). Values never appear in the process arguments, so this is the safe way to pass secrets. --env entries take precedence. Name a key with --secret to also mark it as one.
  - `--secret` — Mark a key from --env/--env-file as a secret (repeatable): stored encrypted and delivered as a Kubernetes Secret rather than a plain ConfigMap entry, and never printed by `app status -o json` or `app env list`. Without this, every --env/--env-file value is stored as plain text — including one that looks like a credential.
  - `--detach` — Return immediately after triggering the build/deploy without waiting for completion. Use `flui app status <name>` to track progress.
  - `--no-build` — Skip the GitHub Actions build and re-deploy the current image. Useful for fast iterations on flui.yaml config (env, ports, healthcheck, endpoint) without rebuilding. If the app was deleted, falls back to the GHCR latest tag for {owner}/{repoName}.
  - `--image` — Deploy a specific image reference (e.g. ghcr.io/owner/repo:sha). Skips the build pipeline. Useful for rollback to a known tag, or to deploy from GHCR when the app was deleted from Flui.
  - `--skip-endpoint` — Skip DNS and TLS provisioning for this install
  - `--no-tls` — Provision the endpoint with DNS only, without a per-app TLS certificate. Overrides the manifest domain.tls. Avoids Let's Encrypt rate limits; the app is served over HTTP.
  - `--cert-challenge` [http-01 | dns-01] — ACME challenge for the app endpoint. http-01 works without a DNS zone and forces a per-host cert; dns-01 needs a cluster DNS zone with a wildcard issuer. Default: derived from cluster config.
  - `--cert-provider` [lets-encrypt | lets-encrypt-staging] — Certificate issuer for the app endpoint. Default: cluster default.
  - `--hostname` [ip | domain] — How the app is exposed: ip (nip.io) or domain (cluster DNS zone). Default: derived from manifest/cluster.
  - `--no-wait` — Alias for --detach (kind:CatalogApp compat)
  - `--validate-only` — Validate the manifest locally against the flui.cloud/v1beta1 schema without deploying (no cluster or login needed). Combine with --json for machine-readable output.
  - `--json` — With --validate-only, emit the result as JSON: { valid, kind, errors[], warnings[] }.
  - `--skip-checks` — Bypass the framework post-checks (e.g. Next.js standalone output). Only use when you are certain the Dockerfile will succeed despite the warnings.
  - `--allow-master` — Allow dedicated (node-local) storage to be placed on the control-plane node when the cluster has no worker. Escape hatch for single-node clusters (kind:CatalogApp).
  - `--api-url` — Override the API base URL (e.g. http://localhost:3000/api/v1) for local-API testing against an unreleased backend. Default: active profile.

Examples:
```bash

<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> ./apps/api/flui.yaml
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --repo acme/my-app --branch main
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --detach
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --env DATABASE_URL=postgres://... --env API_KEY=secret
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --env-file .env --secret DATABASE_URL --secret API_KEY
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --validate-only
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --cluster my-cluster
```

### `flui app backup create`

Back up an application volume to S3-compatible object storage. With --destination (a registered destination) the volume becomes a kopia snapshot: encrypted, deduplicated, kept until you delete it, and restorable whole or file by file with `flui app backup restore`. With --bucket a full plaintext copy is archived instead; when both are omitted the cluster provider auto-provisions a bucket (Scaleway: full-auto using your compute key; Hetzner: requires Object Storage credentials connected). Otherwise pass an explicit endpoint + --bucket and S3 credentials via flags or FLUI_S3_ACCESS_KEY/FLUI_S3_SECRET_KEY env. The backup runs in the background: the command follows it to the end unless --no-wait is given.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-v, --volume` — Volume (PVC) name when the app has multiple volumes. Required if more than one PVC exists.
  - `-d, --description` — Optional human-friendly tag appended to the key prefix
  - `--pause` — Stop the workloads holding the volume, copy it at rest, then start them again. A deliberate outage for the length of the copy.
  - `--allow-inconsistent` — Copy even though the volume holds a database that is being written to. The copy may not restore cleanly.
  - `-D, --destination` — Registered backup destination id (see `flui backup destination list`). Preferred: the copy is recorded against it and shows up in `flui backup list`.
  - `-b, --bucket` — Destination S3 bucket name. Omit to auto-provision via the cluster provider.
  - `-e, --endpoint` — S3 endpoint URL (required when --bucket is set). Examples: https://s3.fr-par.scw.cloud, https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com
  - `-r, --region` (default: "auto") — S3 region
  - `--access-key` — S3 access key. Defaults to FLUI_S3_ACCESS_KEY env var.
  - `--secret-key` — S3 secret key. Defaults to FLUI_S3_SECRET_KEY env var.
  - `--no-wait` — Return once the backup is queued; follow it with `flui operation <id> --follow`.
  - `--key-prefix` — Override the destination key prefix (default: flui/<cluster>/<app>/<timestamp>/)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app --description nightly
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app -D <destId> --no-wait
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app -b external-bucket -e https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com -r eu-central-1
```

### `flui app backup restore`

Restore a volume backup. Whole: into a new volume beside the application (or --to another one), which it uses once you --swap. With --path: the named files or directories are written back into the volume, over the current ones unless --into keeps them apart.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Application the backup belongs to
  - `backup` (required) — Backup id, or its first characters (from `flui app backup list`)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `--to` — Restore into this application instead (same cluster; use its id for another cluster)
  - `-v, --volume` — Volume of the target application to restore for (default: the backed-up volume, or the only one)
  - `--swap` — Make the application use the restored volume right away (it restarts). The data it used before is kept as a separate volume.
  - `-p, --path` — Restore only this path (file or directory, relative to the volume root). Repeatable. kopia backups only.
  - `--into` — With --path: write under this directory of the volume instead of over the current files
  - `-y, --yes` — Do not ask before writing over files in the live volume

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app 3f2a91c0
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app 3f2a91c0 --swap
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app 3f2a91c0 --to my-app-copy --swap
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app 3f2a91c0 --path uploads/report.pdf --path config
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-app 3f2a91c0 --path uploads --into restored-uploads

### `flui app resources`

Show or change how much CPU and memory an application may use. Without a change flag it shows the current values. A container is stopped for crossing its memory limit, never its request — the request is what a machine keeps free for it. Changing either restarts the application.

  - `name` (required) — Application name or slug

  - `--memory-request` — Memory a machine keeps free for it, e.g. 256Mi
  - `--memory-limit` — Most memory it may use before it is stopped, e.g. 512Mi or 1Gi
  - `--dry-run` — Write nothing: show the values as they would be stored and where the replicas would run — on a node already there, on a machine the scaling group would buy or propose, or nowhere yet
  - `--apply-proposal` — Apply the memory change Flui proposes (shown with the current values), as it stands now. The application restarts.

  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

```bash

### `flui backup enable database`

  - `--retention-max-copies`
  - `--enabled`
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-database --destination <destId>
```

### `flui cluster create`

Create a workload cluster. Defaults to the control cluster's provider and region, and attaches to its environment VNet automatically when the provider needs one. Pass --provider to place it elsewhere: the API allows that only when the control cluster permits cross-provider workloads.

Arguments:
  - `name` (required) — Cluster name (must be unique)

Flags:
  - `--node-size` — Server type for cluster nodes. Defaults to the provider recommended size.
  - `--region` — Region/location code. Defaults to the control cluster's own region.
  - `--worker-count` (default: 0) — Number of worker nodes (0 = master-only)
  - `--provider` — Provider for the workload cluster. Defaults to the control cluster's own. A different one is only accepted when the control cluster permits cross-provider workloads (the API refuses it otherwise).
  - `--flui-network` — No-op: on a provider that offers no private network of its own, Flui builds one either way — every node gets an address on an encrypted mesh and K3s binds to it, so traffic between pods stops crossing the internet in the clear. On a provider that has one, Flui uses that.
  - `--network-cidr` — Range for the network Flui builds, if the default would collide with something you already run. Defaults to 10.250.0.0/16.
  - `--vnet` — Attach the cluster to an existing private network (see `flui network list`).
  - `--subnet` — Subnet within --vnet. Defaults to the network’s only subnet.
  - `--no-wait` — Return immediately after queuing creation

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-workload
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-workload --node-size d2-4 --worker-count 2
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> my-workload --no-wait
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> edge --provider hetzner --region hel1

A value passed as an argument is visible to every process on the machine through the process list, which is not acceptable for a credential on a shared or managed host. Examples:
```bash

### `flui db tunnel`

Open a local tunnel to a Flui database so you can connect a native client
(psql/pgAdmin for Postgres, mariadb/DBeaver for MariaDB, an ORM). Flui databases
are not exposed outside the
cluster network — this forwards through the control plane over SSH + in-cluster
port-forward, so no public endpoint is opened. Stay in foreground; CTRL-C to close.

Two reserved names reach the platform's own databases instead of an application:
platform-postgres and identity-provider. Both are closed to the web console on purpose;

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> postgresql-051f58
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> postgresql-051f58 --local-port 5544
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> platform-postgres

### `flui env create`

Create control cluster infrastructure on K3s

Flags:
  - `-p, --provider` [hetzner | scaleway | ovh] — Cloud provider for the control cluster (default: the profile's configured provider). On OVH the firewall is applied on the server itself at first boot.
  - `--node-size` — Server type for cluster nodes (run "flui server-types list --provider <provider>" to see available types). Defaults to the provider recommended size.
  - `-r, --region` — Region/location code. Defaults to the provider default region.
  - `--node-count` (default: 0) — Number of worker nodes (0 = master-only, default: 0)
  - `--disk-size` — Root disk size in GB. Network-storage instance types (Scaleway BASIC3, STANDARD3, PRO2) default to 40. Optional for local-SSD types — defaults to the included size of the instance type.
  - `-d, --detached` — Detached mode: start cluster creation and exit immediately
  - `--wait` — Wait for cluster to be ready before returning (polls operation status)
  - `--configure-firewall` — Automatically configure firewall after cluster creation
  - `--firewall-ip` — Source IP/CIDR for firewall (comma-separated, default: auto-detect)
  - `--non-interactive` — Never prompt. Any missing answer becomes an error instead of a question — required when driving the CLI from a script or a managed runner, where a prompt would hang forever holding cloud resources.
  - `--ssh-mode` [ca | ephemeral-key] (default: "ca") — How the cluster is reached while it is built. "ca" (default) enrols this machine's SSH certificate authority on every node and leaves it there. "ephemeral-key" creates no CA at all and uses a throwaway key that is revoked on the nodes and deleted at the provider before the run ends — the cluster is then unreachable over SSH until its owner runs "flui env adopt". Use it when provisioning on someone else's behalf.
  - `--auth-mode` (default: "oidc") — Authentication mode (only oidc is supported)
  - `--image-registry` [ghcr | flui] (default: "ghcr") — Where builds from GitHub push their images: "ghcr" keeps them on each owner's GitHub Container Registry; "flui" runs a registry on this installation, so connecting GitHub needs no container token. An installation on ghcr can switch later with `flui registry enable`
  - `--image-registry-storage` [volume | s3] (default: "volume") — With --image-registry flui, where the registry keeps images: "volume" on the control cluster, or "s3", a bucket you connect after the installation with `flui registry storage connect` (needed to run more than one copy of the registry)
  - `--acme-staging` — Use Let's Encrypt staging endpoint (untrusted cert, no rate limits) — useful while iterating to avoid burning prod quota
  - `--latest` — Install mobile dev tags instead of the pinned release: bootstrap scripts from `master` and `:latest` Docker images. Default: every component is pinned to the CLI release version.
  - `--allow-undersized` — Skip the confirmation when --node-size is below the documented minimum for a control cluster's own stack (Postgres, Redis, Zitadel, observability all run on this one node — an undersized node may never reach READY).
  - `--no-flui-network` — Leave the Flui network off: for a control no other cluster can reach (for example behind NAT) or a host without WireGuard. Clusters on another provider than the control then cannot be created. Switch it later with `flui env overlay enable|disable`.
  - `--no-shared-storage` — Disable Flui shared storage (NFS+fscache). Default: shared storage enabled — master gets a Volume hosting the NFS export, workers mount it. Disable to fall back to local-path on each node bundled disk.
  - `--shared-storage-size` (default: 20) — Size in GB of the master shared storage Volume (only when shared storage is enabled). Default: 20.
  - `--host` — BYOS: install onto an existing Linux host (IP or DNS) over SSH instead of provisioning via a cloud provider. Enables BYOS mode.
  - `--port` (default: 22) — BYOS: SSH port of --host (default: 22)
  - `--user` (default: "root") — BYOS: SSH user for --host (default: root)
  - `--ssh-key` — BYOS: SSH private key for --host. Optional — if omitted, Flui reuses an existing key that already works, otherwise it authorizes one (asking for the host password once) and never stores the password. A passphrase-protected key is supported only when loaded in your ssh-agent (run `ssh-add` first).

  - `--skip-precheck` — BYOS: skip the host readiness precheck
  - `--best-effort` — BYOS: continue even if the precheck reports problems
  - `--local-stub` — BYOS (dev): stop after bootstrap + CA check; skip observability/kubeconfig/secret patch. Use with BOOTSTRAP_SCRIPTS_URL=file://… for local Podman testing.

<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --node-size cx32

### `flui iam grant add`

Create an access grant: bind a principal to a role at a scope. Scope is one of everything (global), a cluster, a portal section, or a selector over app attributes (kind/project/provider/tags/slugs — AND-ed; tags match ALL).

Flags:
  - `-t, --type` [user | group | service_account] (default: "user") — Principal type
  - `-p, --principal` (required) — Principal reference (email, group name, or service-account id)
  - `-r, --role` [viewer | operator | maintainer | owner | platform_operator] (required) — Role to grant. `owner` is the top of the ladder and conferring it requires iam:manage-users at global scope — i.e. an owner makes an owner. `platform_operator` runs clusters, nodes, updates and backups without reaching any application data; grant it with --expires.
  - `-s, --scope` [global | cluster | section | selector] (default: "global") — Scope type
  - `--cluster` — Cluster id (scope=cluster)
  - `--section` — Portal section key (scope=section)
  - `--kind` — App kind, e.g. DATABASE (scope=selector)
  - `--project` — Project (scope=selector)
  - `--provider` — Provider (scope=selector)
  - `--cluster-id` — Cluster id (scope=selector)
  - `--cluster-name` — Cluster name (scope=selector)
  - `--app-type` [system | user] — App type (scope=selector)
  - `--app` — App slug — repeatable (scope=selector)
  - `--tag` — Tag — repeatable, app must carry ALL (scope=selector)
  - `--selector` — Raw selector JSON (overrides individual selector flags)
  - `--expires` — End the grant on its own: a duration from now (30m, 8h, 7d, 2w) or a date (2026-10-01). Without it the grant stands until removed.
  - `--dry-run` — Say what this grant would open — and what the same change closes — and create nothing
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -p alice@acme.com -r maintainer
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -t group -p platform -r viewer -s cluster --cluster c1
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -p bob@acme.com -r operator -s selector --kind DATABASE
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -p ci-deployer -t service_account -r operator -s selector --app acme-api --app acme-web
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -p support@partner.example -r maintainer --expires 8h
```

## mail

### `flui mail connect`

Connect a mail provider and set up everything that can be set up

Arguments:
  - `provider` (required) — One of: scaleway-tem, brevo, zeptomail, smtp

Flags:
  - `--scope` [transactional | bulk] (default: "transactional") — What this sender carries. Never the same account for both — a suspension caused by a mailing list would stop password resets too.
  - `--domain` — Sending domain. Flui registers it and publishes the records.
  - `--secret` — API key or relay password. Not needed for Scaleway, which reuses the compute key. Prefer leaving this out: the value is then prompted for and never enters your shell history or `ps` output.
  - `--stdin` — Read the credential from standard input rather than prompting.
  - `--label` — What you call it
  - `--region` — ZeptoMail only, and required: the regional API host.
  - `--host` — SMTP relay host
  - `--port` — SMTP relay port
  - `--username` — SMTP username
  - `--allow-bulk` — SMTP only: declare that this relay permits one-to-many mail. Never deduced.
  - `--activate` — Start sending through this one straight away. Without it a provider is stored and only takes the scope if nothing else holds it — switch later with `flui mail use`.
  - `--spf-include` — SMTP only: the include from the relay setup page
  - `--dkim-selector` — SMTP only: verbatim from the relay
  - `--dkim-value` — SMTP only: verbatim from the relay
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> brevo --scope bulk --domain news.example.com
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> scaleway-tem --domain mail.example.com

### `flui repo map apply`

Act on the map of a connected repository. Flui cuts its OWN branch `flui/deploy-<sha7>` at the commit it read, lands one commit on it with a rendered flui.yaml and a build workflow per unit, and creates one application per unit on that branch. Your branch is read and never written to. This writes to the real GitHub repository and spends its Actions minutes. ```bash

It is one way to get a manifest, not the only one — `flui deploy` takes a flui.yaml you wrote yourself, and an image you already have needs neither.

Arguments:

Flags:

  - `-c, --cluster` — Weigh the map against this cluster (name or id). Half the verdict is capacity, so one is always chosen.
  - `-u, --unit` — Show only this unit (its id, `.` for the repository root)
  - `-o, --output` [text | json] (default: "text") — Output format. `json` prints the whole response, untouched.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> acme/shop
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> acme/shop --branch develop

## scaling

### `flui scaling apply`

Write a scaling group from a file — what a cluster may buy for itself, and where it must stop.
The file is the whole group: a field left out is a field reset to its default, and the same file applied twice leaves the same group. Several groups may live in one file, separated by `---`.
Every bound counts the whole fleet, master included, and sits between 1 and 20.

Flags:
  - `-f, --file` (required) — Path to the ScalingGroup YAML/JSON file
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID, for a file that names none. Refused when the file names a different one.
  - `--dry-run` — Read and check the file, say what would be written, and write nothing.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -f scaling.yaml
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -f scaling.yaml --dry-run
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> -f scaling.yaml --cluster prod-eu
```

### `flui scaling approve`

Carry out, once, what a manual scaling group proposes: buy the machine it names (floor raised) or give back the node it names (floor lowered). Without --yes it only shows the proposal. Every limit an automatic group meets still holds; the group stays manual and does nothing else on its own.

Arguments:
  - `group` — Scaling group name or ID (default: the only group of the cluster)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-y, --yes` — Buy the proposed machine, or give back the named node, now

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> general --cluster prod-eu --yes
```

### `flui scaling delete`

Remove a scaling group and the decisions it took. No node is removed and no machine stops. The only group of a cluster Flui buys for cannot be removed: its nodes change through it.

Arguments:
  - `group` — Scaling group name or ID (default: the only group of the cluster)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-y, --yes` — Remove it without asking

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> heavy --cluster prod-eu --yes
```

### `flui scaling export`

Export a scaling group as a `kind: ScalingGroup` document — the file `flui scaling apply` reads back.
Only what somebody wrote is exported. What the provider can do, and what the market is doing, are read fresh every time and would be stale in a committed file.

Arguments:
  - `group` — Scaling group name or ID (default: the only group of the cluster)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `--all` — Every group of the cluster, as one file of `---` separated documents
  - `-o, --output` [yaml | json] (default: "yaml") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> > scaling.yaml
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> general --cluster prod-eu
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --all --cluster prod-eu > scaling.yaml
```

### `flui scaling floor`

Add or remove a node: move the scaling group's floor (fewest nodes, master included). The target moves with it. A manual group then proposes the machine to buy or the node to give back, and `flui scaling approve --yes` carries it out; an automatic group acts on its own within its maximum of nodes and its spending ceiling.

Arguments:
  - `min` (required) — The new floor, master included
  - `group` — Scaling group name or ID (default: the only group of the cluster)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> 3
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> 2 general --cluster prod-eu
```

### `flui scaling get`

Show a scaling group: its limits in nodes, what they cost with the provider prices (from the minimum to the maximum), where and what it may buy, and the spending ceiling underneath.

Arguments:
  - `group` — Scaling group name or ID (default: the only group of the cluster)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-o, --output` [table | json | yaml] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> general --cluster prod-eu
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output yaml
```

### `flui scaling list`

One line per cluster: what it may buy, what it is spending, and what is waiting.
Clusters with no scaling group are listed too, and so are the ones that can only raise an alarm — the two cases a filter would hide precisely when somebody is needed.

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Show the scaling groups of one cluster instead
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --cluster prod-eu
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

### `flui scaling preview`

What a scaling group would do if a node were needed right now — the same engine the reconciler runs, on demand, buying nothing.
Every rung of the ladder is shown with the reason it lost. `refused-by-limit` is this group’s own rules and not the market, which from the outside looks exactly like an outage.

Arguments:
  - `group` — Scaling group name or ID (default: the only group of the cluster)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> general --cluster prod-eu
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

### `flui scaling retry`

Let a scaling group buy again after a purchase failed. A failed purchase holds the group back so it is not retried every minute; run this once the cause is fixed. It buys nothing by itself — the next pass may, inside the same limits.

Arguments:
  - `group` — Scaling group name or ID (default: the only group of the cluster)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> general --cluster prod-eu
```

### `flui scaling set`

Change one or more settings of a scaling group and leave the rest as they are. Limits are in nodes (--min, --max); the cost follows and is shown as scenarios. The spending ceiling (--max-monthly) is the safety net underneath, required to buy automatically, and kept unless you name it. --dry-run shows each setting before and after, with what the limits would cost, and writes nothing.

Arguments:
  - `group` — Scaling group name or ID (default: the only group of the cluster)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `--max-monthly` — Spending ceiling in euros a month: the safety net the engine checks before every purchase. "none" removes it (only on a manual group: automatic needs one)
  - `--hourly-only` — Buy only machines billed by the hour
  - `--provision` [automatic | manual] — automatic: Flui buys on its own up to --max nodes, never past the spending ceiling (required); manual: Flui proposes and a person buys
  - `--shapes` — Machines the group may buy, comma separated
  - `--regions` — Regions it may buy in, comma separated
  - `--min` — Min nodes: fewest, master included (1-20)
  - `--desired` — Target: nodes it keeps without load
  - `--max` — Max nodes: most, master included (1-20)
  - `--strategy` [cheapest | closest | roomiest | uniform] — How it picks among machines that fit
  - `--settle` — Seconds an app must wait for room before the group acts
  - `--dry-run` — Show each setting before and after; write nothing

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> default --max-monthly 30
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> default --provision manual
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> default --provision automatic --max-monthly 40
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> default --shapes cx33,cx23 --regions fsn1,nbg1 --dry-run
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> default --max 4 --desired 2
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> default --max-monthly none
```

### `flui scaling why`

The last scaling decision and its reason — including the times it decided to do nothing, which are the interesting ones.
Answers about the whole cluster by default, naming the group each decision came from. Name a group to narrow it to that one.

Arguments:
  - `group` — Scaling group name or ID (default: every group of the cluster)

Flags:
  - `-c, --cluster` — Cluster name or ID (default: auto-detect)
  - `-n, --limit` (default: 1) — How many decisions back to show, newest first
  - `--outcome` — Only these outcomes, comma separated: added, replaced, removed, declined, alerted, changed, node-ordered, node-joined, purchase-failed, node-drained, node-removed — or nodes for every machine that came or went
  - `--force` — Only these forces, comma separated: urgency, opportunity, person, fleet (what happened to a machine)
  - `--since` — Leave out rows older than this time (ISO, e.g. 2026-09-25T08:00)
  - `--until` — Leave out rows newer than this time (ISO)
  - `--before` — Next page: the time of the last row already shown
  - `-o, --output` [table | json] (default: "table") — Output format

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --cluster prod-eu
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> general --cluster prod-eu
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --limit 10
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --output json
```

## server-types

### `flui server-types list`

List available server types for a provider, with the CPU architecture of each

Flags:
  - `-p, --provider` [hetzner | scaleway | ovh] (required) — Cloud provider
  - `-r, --region` — Filter by region/location
  - `-m, --memory` — Filter by RAM in GB: exact "16", range "8-32", min "8-", or max "-32"
  - `--fits` — Only the types to start Flui on: x86, billed by the hour, 2–16 vCPU, 4–32 GB, at most €100/month (see --max-price)
  - `--max-price` — Leave out types above this price, in € per month
  - `-s, --sort` [price | memory | cores | disk | name] (default: "price") — Sort by field
  - `--desc` — Sort in descending order
  - `--json` — Output as JSON
  - `--force-refresh` — Force refresh cache from API

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider hetzner
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider hetzner --region fsn1
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider ovh --region EU-SOUTH-MIL --fits
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider scaleway --memory 16
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider scaleway --memory 8-32
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider scaleway --memory -32
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider scaleway --sort memory
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider scaleway --sort price --desc
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider hetzner --json
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --provider hetzner --force-refresh
```

## showcase

### `flui showcase add`

Publish one application to the showcase

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application slug, name or id

Flags:
  - `--note` — The line shown next to it, stored as the application's description
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> umami-29491d --note "Measures flui.cloud. Real visitors."
```

### `flui showcase list`

Applications published to the showcase

Flags:
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
```

### `flui showcase remove`

Take one application out of the showcase (it keeps running)

Arguments:
  - `app` (required) — Application slug, name or id

Flags:
  - `--json`

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> umami-29491d
```

## template

### `flui template use`

Create a new GitHub repository from a Flui framework template and connect it to your account.

Arguments:
  - `framework` (required) — Framework template to use (e.g. astro, nextjs, nestjs)
  - `name` (required) — Name for the new GitHub repository

Flags:
  - `--org` — GitHub organisation or user to create the repo under (default: your account)
  - `-d, --description` — Repository description
  - `--public` — Create as a public repository (default: private)
  - `--no-import` — Skip auto-importing the repository into Flui

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> astro my-astro-site
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> nextjs my-app --public
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> nestjs my-api --org my-org
```

## vault

### `flui vault init`

Create the vault that protects stored credentials on this machine. Run this before configuring anything else.

Flags:
  - `--stdin` — Read the passphrase from standard input rather than prompting. For scripted setup; the value never appears in the process list.

Examples:
```bash
<%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %>
printf "my passphrase" | <%= config.bin %> <%= command.id %> --stdin
```

### `flui vault lock`

Close the vault now, without waiting for it to time out.

### `flui vault status`

Show whether the vault exists, whether it is unlocked, and how long it has left.

Flags:
  - `--format` [text | json] (default: "text")

### `flui vault unlock`

Unlock the vault for this session so commands can open stored credentials.

Flags:
  - `--stdin` — Read the passphrase from standard input rather than prompting.
  - `--idle-minutes` — How long the vault may sit unused before it locks itself again (default 30). Same effect as setting FLUI_VAULT_IDLE_MINUTES, offered here because that variable has no way to announce itself.
  - `--max-minutes` — Absolute lifetime of the unlock, regardless of activity (default 480) — the backstop against a long-running session holding the key open all day just by staying busy. Same effect as FLUI_VAULT_MAX_MINUTES.

sections.title: Alerts, audit and costs
sections.body:
These five topics cover the installation as a whole,
rather than one cluster or one application.

## Alerts

The dashboard bell and the administrators' email always
receive the installation's critical alerts. `flui alerts`
adds other places, and decides whether administrators
also hear about warnings. The alerts of one application
are on [`flui app alerts`](/cli/applications/).

### `flui alerts destination add`

Sends alerts to an email address or to a signed webhook.

```bash
flui alerts destination add --email oncall@example.com
flui alerts destination add --webhook https://hooks.example.com/flui --min-severity warning
flui alerts destination add --email oncall@example.com --scope all
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--email <address>` | none | Send alerts to this address. |
| `--webhook <url>` | none | A public `https` address that receives a signed JSON `POST` for every alert. Its host has to resolve, or the destination is refused. |
| `--min-severity <level>` | `critical` | The least severe alert it receives: `warning` or `critical`. |
| `--scope <scope>` | `infrastructure` | `infrastructure`: alerts no application owns (nodes, disks, certificates, platform backups). `all`: every application's alerts too, which needs the right to reach application data. |
| `-o, --output <format>` | `text` | `text` or `json`. |

The command prints the new destination's id.

### `flui alerts destination list` / `test` / `remove`

```bash
flui alerts destination list
flui alerts destination test <id>
flui alerts destination remove <id>
```

`list` shows each destination with its severity, scope and
whether anything has been delivered to it yet. `test` sends
a real test alert, named `FluiTestAlert`, and says whether
it arrived. `remove` stops sending there.

### `flui alerts warnings`

```bash
flui alerts warnings          # what is set
flui alerts warnings --on     # email administrators warnings too
flui alerts warnings --off    # critical alerts only (the default)
```

Covers warnings about nodes, disks and certificates.

## `flui audit list`

Who did what on this installation, newest first: every
change, every refusal, and every read of application data.

```bash
flui audit list
flui audit list --user support@example.com --since 7d
flui audit list --data
flui audit list --refused --since 24h
flui audit list --before <id>
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--user <email>` | none | Only what this person did. |
| `--since <when>` | none | From this far back (`30m`, `8h`, `7d`) or from a date. |
| `--data` | off | Only actions that reached application data. |
| `--refused` | off | Only what was refused. |
| `--before <id>` | none | Only records older than this one: the next page. When a page is full, the command prints the line for the next one. |
| `--limit <n>` | `50` | How many records. |
| `-o, --output <format>` | `text` | `text` or `json`. |

Actions the platform takes on its own are listed too, as
*platform (system)*. A short-lived SSH certificate issued
to reach a node is one example.

## `flui costs`

What your clusters cost: spent and forecast, month by month
and provider by provider, deleted clusters included.

```bash
flui costs
flui costs --months 12
flui costs --provider hetzner
flui costs --json
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--months <n>` | `6` | Calendar months to show, ending with the current one (1 to 24). |
| `--provider <name>` | none | Only this provider. |
| `--json` | off | Machine-readable output. |

Amounts are in euros. For each provider the output says how
it bills and whether VAT is included, and breaks the current
month down by cluster. Costs are the machines and volumes of
your clusters; applications cost nothing on their own.
Traffic above what each machine includes is not counted, and
the forecast assumes what runs now keeps running until the
end of the month. A machine that started before Flui kept
the price it was bought at is priced at today's list price,
and the output says how many.

## `flui inference usage`

What the assistant and the console copilots have spent, by
model and by person.

```bash
flui inference usage
flui inference usage --days 1
flui inference usage --days 0 --price 0.20
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--days <n>` | `7` | The window to report on. `0` means everything. |
| `--price <amount>` | none | Your price per million tokens, to turn the totals into money. Model prices differ, so you supply the number. |
| `--json` | off | Machine-readable output. |

## Showcase

The showcase is the short list of applications this
installation puts in front of other people.

```bash
flui showcase list
flui showcase add <app> --note "Measures our website. Real visitors."
flui showcase remove <app>
```

`<app>` is the application's slug, name or id. For an app
that came with a catalog bundle, use the component's slug, as
`flui app list` shows it. `--note` is the line shown next to
it. It is stored as the application's description, so it
stays after `remove`. `remove` takes the application out of
the showcase and leaves it running. All three take `--json`.

sections.title: Applications
sections.body:
The `app` topic groups every command that acts on an application
running in a cluster, both catalog installs (`kind: CatalogApp`)
and source-built apps (`kind: Application`). The behaviour is the
same for both: the application is the unit of operation, whatever
put its image in the registry.

Almost every verb under `app` takes an application name or slug as
its first positional argument, and accepts `-c, --cluster
<name|id>` to pick the cluster (auto-detected when the active
profile has only one). The output flags follow the rest of the
CLI: `-o, --output table|json` (or `text|json` on the streaming
commands), `-f, --force` to skip confirmations, `--no-wait` to
queue and exit.

Two verbs are the exception, because they run locally and do not
target a running application: `flui app init` and `flui app
manifest`. Both are under [Project setup](#project-setup).

This page is the reference for the verbs and their flags. The
task pages cover the same ground step by step:
[Watch and operate a running
application](/tasks/watch-and-operate-an-application/),
[Set an application's configuration and
secrets](/tasks/configuration-and-secrets/), and
[Remove an application and its
data](/tasks/remove-an-application/).

## Read this before you delete anything

`flui app delete` also deletes the application's persistent
volumes. The data is gone, and Flui cannot bring it back.

Because this is the most destructive thing you can do to an
application, the command reads the cluster first and prints what
it will delete before it asks. When it cannot read the cluster,
it says "unknown", never "none". Full detail in
[Deletion](#deletion).

## Project setup

### `flui app init [<framework>]`

Copies Flui's deploy files (a `Dockerfile` and a `flui.yaml`)
from an official framework template into the current directory,
turning an existing Git repository into something `flui deploy`
can build.

```bash
flui app init --list           # list supported frameworks
flui app init nextjs           # latest supported Next.js
flui app init nextjs@16        # pin a major version
flui app init fastapi --target ./api
flui app init nestjs --force   # overwrite existing files
flui app init nuxt --dry-run   # print the actions, write nothing
```

| Flag / Arg | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `<framework>` | Framework template, optionally with a major-version pin (`nextjs`, `nextjs@16`). Omit when using `--list`. |
| `--list` | Print the supported frameworks and versions, then exit. |
| `--force` | Overwrite existing files without prompting. |
| `--dry-run` | Print the actions that would be taken; write nothing. |
| `--target <dir>` | Target directory. Default: the current working directory. |

`app init` adds Flui files to a repository you already have. To
create a new repository from a template instead, use
`flui template use`; see [Templates](/cli/templates/).

### `flui app manifest`

Prints the authoring reference for `flui.yaml` (`kind:
Application`): every field, what it does, and which fields the
spec accepts but does not apply on source deploys. It runs fully
offline, with no cluster and no login, and the field list comes
from the published spec schema, so it always matches what
`flui deploy` validates.

```bash
flui app manifest                    # the field reference
flui app manifest --json             # the raw JSON Schema
flui app manifest --example          # an annotated example
flui app manifest --example nextjs   # port + healthcheck for a framework
```

This prints the shape of a manifest, not the manifest of a
particular application. Point an assistant at it when it needs to
write a valid `flui.yaml`.

## Inspection

### `flui app list`

Lists the applications in the cluster with their high-level
state. Catalog installs made of several parts show as one row;
`-x, --expanded` breaks them out into their components.

```bash
flui app list
flui app list --expanded
flui app list --output json
```

### `flui app status <name>`

Shows the live runtime status of one application: how many
replicas are ready against desired, the current release, and any
condition that needs attention.

```bash
flui app status my-api
flui app status my-api --output json
```

### `flui app logs <name>`

Fetches application logs from the cluster. By default it returns
the last 100 lines; you can filter by level, search the text, or
widen the window.

```bash
flui app logs my-api
flui app logs my-api --level error
flui app logs my-api --tail 500
flui app logs my-api --search "connection refused"
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-l, --level` | none | Filter by `error`, `warn`, `info`, `debug`. |
| `-n, --tail <n>` | `100` | Number of lines to return. |
| `-s, --search <q>` | none | Full-text search. |
| `-o, --output text\|json` | `text` | Output format. |

### `flui app metrics <name>`

Instant resource metrics for one application: CPU, memory,
network I/O, replica count, then the health checks of the last
hour and what to do: add a replica, add a node, or nothing. Use
it to spot-check a workload's footprint, to line a spike up
against a deploy, or to decide whether it needs another copy.
`--output json` carries the same advice as `capacity_advice`.

```bash
flui app metrics my-api
flui app metrics my-api --output json
```

## Configuration

The values an application runs with come from three places: the
manifest, what you pass at deploy time, and what is stored
against the app.
[Set an application's configuration and
secrets](/tasks/configuration-and-secrets/) explains which one
wins. These two verbs read and write the stored set.

### `flui app env list <app>`

Lists the application's variables in three states: plain values,
sensitive keys that are **set** (only the fact, never the value),
and keys still **awaiting a value**, declared by the manifest but
never supplied.

```bash
flui app env list my-api
```

"Awaiting a value" is a state, not an error: the command exits 0
either way. No sensitive value is printed, because the API
answers with a mask and none is available to print.

### `flui app env set <app> <KEY>`

Delivers the value of a sensitive variable. There is no `--value`
flag. A value passed as an argument lands in your shell history,
is visible to every other process on the machine while the
command runs, and, when an agent composed the command, is copied
into a model's context on the way.

So the command prompts for the value, or reads it from standard
input.

```bash
flui app env set my-api STRIPE_SECRET_KEY
pbpaste | flui app env set my-api STRIPE_SECRET_KEY --stdin
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--stdin` | Read the value from standard input rather than prompting. |
| `-c, --cluster` | Cluster name or ID. |

The command prints the key and whether it is now configured; the
value is never echoed and cannot be read back later. It takes
effect on the next rollout: `flui app redeploy <app>`.

Two cases are refused: a key linked to a building block's own
secret, and the display mask sent back as if it were a value. In
a non-interactive shell the command refuses to prompt and tells
you to use `--stdin`.

## Runtime diagnostics

### `flui app crashes <name>`

Lists recent **crash diagnoses** for the application: automatic
reports produced when a workload restarted unexpectedly,
summarising the exit code, the signals the runtime saw, and the
probable cause.

```bash
flui app crashes my-api
flui app crashes my-api --output json
```

### `flui app crash <name> <id>`

Shows one crash diagnosis in full, including the reasoning the
platform used to classify it. `--dismiss` marks it resolved so it
stops appearing as an active issue on the dashboard. `--apply`
makes the change the diagnosis proposes (a higher memory limit
after an out-of-memory kill), and the application restarts. Flui
never makes that change on its own.

```bash
flui app crash my-api 5d3f...                # show one diagnosis
flui app crash my-api 5d3f... --apply        # accept the change it proposes
flui app crash my-api 5d3f... --dismiss      # mark it resolved
```

Get `<id>` from `flui app crashes`.

### `flui app traffic <name>`

HTTP traffic for one application, measured at the edge where
requests enter the cluster rather than inside your code: request
rate, the split by status class, error percentages, latency, and
a breakdown by method and by status code.

```bash
flui app traffic my-api
flui app traffic my-api --window 1h
flui app traffic my-api --output json
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-w, --window <d>` | `5m` | Rate window. Longer is smoother on low traffic. |
| `-o, --output` | `table` | `table` or `json`. |
