An application that is not exposed has no edge traffic, and the
command says so instead of printing zeroes.

Latency percentiles come from a histogram with fixed buckets.
When those buckets are too coarse to separate this application's
responses, the command prints the boundaries it had and labels
the percentiles as estimates. The mean is measured, not
estimated.

### `flui app alerts <name>`

Alerts for the application, one row per episode, newest first.
Each row shows the alert name, its severity, a one-line summary
and its timing.

```bash
flui app alerts my-api
flui app alerts my-api --firing     # only what is still firing
flui app alerts my-api --output json
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--firing` | off | Only alerts still firing. |
| `-n, --limit <n>` | `20` | How many to show. |
| `-o, --output` | `table` | `table` or `json`. |

A resolved alert marked with `*` stopped reporting instead of
sending a resolution, so its end time is approximate. The mark
tells you the alert went quiet, which does not mean it recovered.

### `flui app build <name>`

Status of the latest build of a source-built application
(`kind: Application`). With `--watch` the command stays in the
foreground, polling until the build reaches a terminal status.

```bash
flui app build my-api
flui app build my-api --watch
flui app build my-api --refresh     # force the backend to re-poll the CI
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--refresh` | none | Force the backend to re-poll GitHub Actions now. |
| `-w, --watch` | none | Poll until the build reaches a terminal status. |
| `--interval <s>` | `5` | Polling interval in seconds. |

### `flui app builds <name>`

Recent build history (default: last 10; `releases` also defaults
to 10, `versions` to 20).

```bash
flui app builds my-api
flui app builds my-api --limit 50
```

## Release management

A release is one rollout of an image into the cluster: a deploy
or a rollback. An image can be released more than once, and not
every image gets released.

### `flui app releases <name>`

Release history.

```bash
flui app releases my-api
flui app releases my-api --current        # only the running release
flui app releases my-api --limit 50
```

### `flui app versions <name>`

Image versions in the container registry for this application,
each marked as the current deployment, a previous release, or
unreleased.

```bash
flui app versions my-api
flui app versions my-api --limit 50
flui app versions my-api --output json
```

### `flui app redeploy <name> [<target>]`

Re-deploys an existing image without rebuilding. The target is a
tag, a short digest (12+ hex chars), or a full
`sha256:<digest>`. Alternatively, `--build <id>` deploys the
image produced by a specific earlier build.

```bash
flui app redeploy my-api a1cac27
flui app redeploy my-api sha256:812bdfd0a833...
flui app redeploy my-api --build <build-id>
```

This is the rollback path: pick a known-good `app versions` entry
and redeploy it. It is also how a newly delivered variable
reaches a running application.

### `flui app auto-deploy <name>`

Shows or changes whether an application redeploys itself when its
branch moves. Off by default.

```bash
flui app auto-deploy my-api
flui app auto-deploy my-api --on
flui app auto-deploy my-api --off
```

## Lifecycle

### `flui app start` / `flui app stop` / `flui app restart`

The everyday lifecycle verbs. `stop` scales to 0 replicas
(workloads disappear but their configuration and volumes are
kept); `start` brings the application back at one replica;
`restart` performs a rolling restart, replacing one replica at a
time.

```bash
flui app start my-api
flui app stop my-api
flui app restart my-api
```

`flui app stop` is equivalent to `flui app scale my-api
--replicas 0`.

### `flui app scale <name>`

Sets how many replicas an application runs: a fixed count, or a
range the count follows with the CPU load. Replicas that find no
room wait for a node, which makes the cluster's scaling group buy
one. For an app deployed from `flui.yaml`, the range is its
`deploy.scaling`.

```bash
flui app scale my-api --replicas 3
flui app scale my-api --replicas 0       # same as `app stop`
flui app scale my-api --min 2 --max 6 --cpu 70
flui app scale my-api --no-autoscale     # back to a fixed count
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-r, --replicas <n>` | A fixed count, 0 to 20. |
| `--min <n>`, `--max <n>` | The range the count follows with the load, 1 to 20. |
| `--cpu <percent>` | CPU use per replica, as a share of what it reserves, above which one is added (10 to 95). |
| `--[no-]autoscale` | Let the count follow the load, or go back to a fixed count. |

`--replicas` cannot be combined with the range flags or
`--[no-]autoscale`.

What `scale` can do depends on the application's storage class
(see [Storage classes and dedicated
placement](/concepts/21-storage-classes-and-dedicated-placement/)
for the model):

- **Shared storage.** Every replica reads and writes the same
  network filesystem, so the platform can run as many replicas as
  you ask for, on any node. This applies to stateless apps and to
  anything using the default storage class.
- **Dedicated storage.** The application is pinned to the node
  that holds its local disk, and there is only one such disk.
  Raising replicas above `1` would mean several copies competing
  for the same on-disk state, which is unsafe. For these apps,
  the platform does not support horizontal scaling. Give the
  workload more capacity by resizing its host node instead (see
  [`flui env
  scale-master`/`scale-node`](/cli/environments/#flui-env-scale-master--flui-env-scale-node)).

### `flui app resources <name>`

Shows or changes the CPU and memory an application reserves and
the ceilings it may reach. Changing either restarts the
application.

```bash
flui app resources my-api
flui app resources my-api --memory-limit 1Gi --dry-run
flui app resources my-api --cpu-request 250m --memory-request 512Mi
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--cpu-request`, `--cpu-limit` | CPU reserved, and the ceiling. |
| `--memory-request`, `--memory-limit` | Memory reserved, and the ceiling. |
| `--dry-run` | Say what would change, change nothing. |
| `--apply-proposal` | Apply the memory change Flui proposes, as it stands now. Cannot be combined with the value flags or `--dry-run`. |
| `--at-next-window` | With `--apply-proposal`: hold the change for the maintenance window that governs the app. |
| `--container <name>` | Pick the container in an app that has more than one. Default: the first one. |
| `-o, --output` | `table` (default) or `json`. |

### `flui app maintenance get|set|cancel <name>`

Changes that restart something can wait for a maintenance
window. `get` shows which window applies to the application, when
it next opens and the changes held for it (`--json` for machine
output). `set` makes the application follow the cluster's window
(`--follow`), use its own (`--slot`, repeatable, with
`--timezone`, default UTC), or apply changes at any time
(`--anytime`). `cancel <id>` drops a held change before it runs.

```bash
flui app maintenance get my-api
flui app maintenance set my-api --slot "sun 04:00 1h" --timezone Europe/Rome
flui app maintenance set my-api --anytime
flui app maintenance cancel my-api <change-id>
```

## Scheduled jobs

A scheduled job runs a command on the application's own image and
configuration, on a cron schedule. Because it is the same
environment your app runs in, a job can reuse the app's code, its
database connection and its variables without a second deployment
to maintain.

### `flui app schedule create <app>`

```bash
flui app schedule create my-app \
  --name nightly-cleanup \
  --schedule "0 3 * * *" \
  --command "node dist/cleanup.js"

flui app schedule create my-app \
  -n report -s "*/15 * * * *" \
  -x "php artisan report:run" --timezone Europe/Rome
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-n, --name <s>` | required | Schedule name (lowercase alphanumeric and dashes). |
| `-s, --schedule <s>` | required | Cron expression, five fields. |
| `-x, --command <s>` | required | Shell command, run through `/bin/sh -c`. |
| `-t, --timezone <tz>` | cluster time | IANA timezone, e.g. `Europe/Rome`. |
| `--concurrency` | `Forbid` | Overlap policy: `Allow`, `Forbid` or `Replace`. |
| `--disabled` | off | Create it suspended, not running. |

The default overlap policy is `Forbid`: if a run is still going
when the next one is due, the next one is skipped. That is the
safe default for jobs that touch shared state. `Replace` stops
the running one and starts the new one; `Allow` lets them
overlap.

### `flui app schedule update <app> <name>`

Changes a schedule in place. Only the flags you pass change:
`-s, --schedule`, `-x, --command`, `-t, --timezone`,
`--concurrency`.

```bash
flui app schedule update my-app nightly-cleanup --schedule "0 4 * * *"
```

### `flui app schedule suspend|resume <app> <name>`

`suspend` stops new runs without deleting the schedule; a run
already in progress finishes. `resume` turns it back on.

```bash
flui app schedule suspend my-app nightly-cleanup
flui app schedule resume my-app nightly-cleanup
```

### `flui app schedule list <app>`

Lists the application's schedules with their cron expression,
whether they are enabled or suspended, the last time each one
was scheduled, and the command.

```bash
flui app schedule list my-app
flui app schedule list my-app --output json
```

### `flui app schedule runs <app> <name>`

Recent runs of one schedule with their status (`Succeeded`,
`Failed`, `Running`) and whether each was started by the schedule
or by hand. How far back the history goes depends on what the
cluster keeps.

```bash
flui app schedule runs my-app nightly-cleanup
```

### `flui app schedule logs <app> <name>`

Logs of one run. Defaults to the most recent run; `-r, --run`
targets a specific one, named as it appears in `schedule runs`.

```bash
flui app schedule logs my-app nightly-cleanup
flui app schedule logs my-app nightly-cleanup \
  --run my-app-nightly-cleanup-28912345
```

An old run whose workload has already been cleaned up has no logs
left, and the command says so instead of failing.

### `flui app schedule trigger <app> <name>`

Runs the schedule now, whatever its cron timing says. Use it to
check a job works without waiting until 3am.

```bash
flui app schedule trigger my-app nightly-cleanup
```

### `flui app schedule delete <app> <name>`

Removes the schedule.

```bash
flui app schedule delete my-app nightly-cleanup
```

## Data management

Two separate tools work on an application's persistent volumes:

- **Snapshots** live inside the cluster: a copy of a volume, kept
  beside it. Each one is a full volume of the same size, and you
  pay for it as one until you delete it. Restoring is a local
  volume-to-volume copy, faster than fetching from object storage
  but not instant. The cost adds up with retention, so keeping
  many around quickly reduces the cluster's free capacity.
- **Backups** are kept in S3-compatible object storage outside
  the cluster. They are much cheaper, slower to restore, and
  survive a cluster destroy. Sent to a registered destination,
  they are encrypted snapshots you can restore whole or file by
  file.

The two sets are independent; neither implies the other.

The difference matters when you remove an application. A backup
sits outside the cluster, and a removal does not reach it. A
snapshot is a volume on the same cluster, carrying the same
application's label, so a removal deletes it too. A snapshot
protects you against a bad upgrade, not against deleting the app.

### `flui app snapshot create <name>`

Creates a snapshot of an application's volume. If the application
has more than one volume, pass `-v, --volume <name>`.

```bash
flui app snapshot create my-app
flui app snapshot create my-app --description before-upgrade
flui app snapshot create my-app --volume data
flui app snapshot create my-app --pause
```

A volume a database is writing to is refused, because the copy
might not restore cleanly. `--pause` stops the workloads holding
the volume for the length of the copy; `--allow-inconsistent`
copies anyway.

### `flui app snapshot list`

Lists snapshots. Without filters, it lists every snapshot in the
cluster; filter by application with `--app`.

```bash
flui app snapshot list
flui app snapshot list --app my-app
flui app snapshot list --app my-app --output json
```

### `flui app snapshot restore <name> <snapshot-id>`

Restores a snapshot into a new side-by-side volume. The
application is left untouched: the new volume is created
alongside it and can be promoted later with `snapshot swap`. Pass
`--swap` to restore and promote in one step.

```bash
flui app snapshot restore my-app <snapshot-id>
flui app snapshot restore my-app <snapshot-id> --swap
flui app snapshot restore my-app <snapshot-id> --swap --volume <name>
```

With `--swap` the CLI also needs to know which application volume
to retarget. Without `--volume` it assumes the volume is named
`data`, the conventional default. Pass `--volume <name>` whenever
your app's primary volume has a different name, or whenever it
has more than one.

### `flui app snapshot swap <name> <restored-volume>`

Swaps the application's live volume for a different one, usually
the one `snapshot restore` just created. It triggers a rolling
restart, and the previous volume is kept until you delete it. The
CLI asks you to confirm before applying; `-y, --yes` (or
`--force`) skips the prompt.

```bash
flui app snapshot swap my-app my-app-data-restored-20260511
flui app snapshot swap my-app my-app-data-restored-20260511 --volume <name>
flui app snapshot swap my-app my-app-data-restored-20260511 --volume <name> --force
```

The same `--volume` rule applies as for `restore --swap`: without
it the CLI assumes `data`.

### `flui app snapshot delete <name> <snapshot-id>`

Deletes a snapshot. Asks you to confirm; skip with `-y, --yes`
(or `--force`).

```bash
flui app snapshot delete my-app <snapshot-id>
flui app snapshot delete my-app <snapshot-id> --force
```

### `flui app snapshot discard <name> <volume>`

Deletes a restored or previous volume the application does not
use, the kind `snapshot restore` and `snapshot swap` leave
behind.

```bash
flui app snapshot discard my-app my-app-data-restored-20260511
```

### `flui app backup create <name>`

Takes a backup of an application's volume now. With
`--destination` it is an encrypted snapshot recorded against a
registered destination, kept until you delete it, and restorable
whole or file by file. With `--bucket`, a full plaintext copy is
archived instead, to a bucket you name; with neither, the
cluster's provider auto-provisions one. The command follows the
backup to the end unless you pass `--no-wait`.

```bash
flui app backup create my-app --destination <dest-id>    # preferred
flui app backup create my-app                            # auto-provisioned bucket
flui app backup create my-app --description nightly
flui app backup create my-app --bucket my-archive \
                              --endpoint https://s3.example.com \
                              --access-key <key> --secret-key <secret>
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-D, --destination <id>` | A registered backup destination (see `flui backup destination list`). Cannot be combined with `--bucket`. |
| `-b, --bucket <name>` | Destination S3 bucket. Auto-provisioned when omitted. |
| `-e, --endpoint <url>` | S3 endpoint URL. Required when `--bucket` is set. |
| `-r, --region <code>` | S3 region (default: `auto`). |
| `-v, --volume <name>` | Volume name when the app has more than one. |
| `-d, --description <s>` | Human-friendly tag appended to the key prefix. |
| `--access-key <k>` | S3 access key. Required when `--bucket` is set. Default: `FLUI_S3_ACCESS_KEY`. |
| `--secret-key <s>` | S3 secret key. Required when `--bucket` is set. Default: `FLUI_S3_SECRET_KEY`. |
| `--key-prefix <s>` | Override the destination key prefix. Default: `flui/<cluster>/<app>/<timestamp>/`. |
| `--pause` / `--allow-inconsistent` | As for `snapshot create`. |
| `--no-wait` | Return once the backup is queued. |

When `--bucket` is set, all three of `--endpoint`, `--access-key`
and `--secret-key` are mandatory (the last two can come from the
matching environment variables). Pass them together or not at
all; passing the bucket without credentials fails up front.

How far auto-provisioning goes depends on the provider. Where
the compute key also reaches object storage, it is fully
automatic; elsewhere, object storage credentials must be
connected first (see [the providers integrated
today](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/#the-providers-integrated-today)).
There is also a top-level [`flui backup`](/cli/backups/) topic
for scheduled, policy-driven backups with their own destinations
and jobs. `app backup` is the ad-hoc, single-app variant.

### `flui app backup list|browse|restore <name>`

`list` shows the application's volume backups, newest first.
`browse <name> <backup> [path]` lists a folder inside one without
changing anything. `restore <name> <backup>` brings it back,
whole, into a new volume by default. `--swap` puts it in place of
the current data and keeps the previous data as a separate
volume; `-p, --path` (repeatable) restores only those files, over
the current ones or, with `--into`, into a folder beside them;
`--to` restores into another application.

```bash
flui app backup list my-app
flui app backup browse my-app <backup-id> uploads
flui app backup restore my-app <backup-id> --swap
flui app backup restore my-app <backup-id> --path uploads/avatar.png
```

### `flui app backup before-deploy <name>`

Takes a backup before each deploy. `--required` makes a deploy
wait for it; `--off` turns it off.

### `flui app backup skip <name>`

Marks the application as intentionally not backed up, so it stops
being listed as needing a decision. `-n, --note` says why;
`--undo` reverses it.

### `flui app backup delete <name> <backup>`

Removes a volume backup and its record; it cannot be restored
afterwards. `--yes` skips the question. See
[Backups](/cli/backups/#flui-app-backup-delete-name-backup).

```bash
flui app backup delete my-app <backup-id> --yes
```

## Volumes

### `flui app volume resize <app>`

Makes an application's volume bigger. Volumes only grow.

```bash
flui app volume resize my-app --size 20
flui app volume resize my-app --volume uploads --size 50
```

`-s, --size` is in GiB; without it the command shows what is
possible and changes nothing. `-v, --volume` picks the volume
when there is more than one.

## Deletion

### `flui app delete <name>`

Permanently removes the application and everything it was using
in the cluster, including its persistent volumes. The data is
deleted, not moved to a bin, and Flui cannot bring it back.

Before it asks, the command reads the cluster, works out which
storage belongs to this application, and prints it: one sentence
with the total, then each volume by name and size.

```
This also deletes 10 GiB of data in 1 volume.
It cannot be undone.
```

The platform writes that sentence once, so the CLI, the dashboard
and an agent all quote the same number.

If the cluster cannot be reached, or its credentials cannot be
read, the command says so and tells you to assume data will be
lost. An empty list means "none found" only when the reading
succeeded.

```
The volumes this would delete could not be read from the cluster.
Assume data will be lost — it is not known to be none.
```

The confirmation is not a yes/no. You type the application's name
exactly, which makes you read the list above it. `--force` skips
that question but not the listing: the preview is printed either
way.

```bash
flui app delete my-app
flui app delete my-app --force            # skip confirmation
flui app delete my-app --no-wait          # queue and exit
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-c, --cluster` | Cluster name or ID. |
| `-f, --force` | Skip the typed confirmation. Also the acknowledgement a system-protected app requires. |
| `--no-wait` | Return as soon as the removal is queued. |

If the application you name is one part of a catalog install, the
preview lists every part and the removal takes all of them, so no
bundle is left half-removed.

Some applications are **system-protected** (typically the
components Flui itself depends on inside the control cluster).
For those, `--force` is required as an explicit acknowledgement.

For a catalog install the CLI waits for the uninstall to finish,
up to five minutes, unless you pass `--no-wait`. For a
source-built application it queues the delete and returns; check
with `flui app list`.

For the full procedure, including how to take a backup first, see
[Remove an application and its
data](/tasks/remove-an-application/).

### Storage no application owns

A cluster can hold volumes that no application owns any more,
left by an older removal or by something removed outside Flui.
They are unattached, not listed anywhere else, and still billed.

```bash
flui cluster volumes
flui cluster volumes --output json
flui cluster volumes --remove user-a1b2c3/data-uptime-kuma-0
```

A volume is only reported when nothing mounts it and no existing
application owns it. When in doubt the scan leaves a volume out:
one it cannot attribute to a departed application is not offered
for deletion. Removing one is permanent.

### `flui app image delete <name> <version-id>`

Removes an image version from the container registry. Two guards
protect your ability to roll back:

- The version that is currently deployed can never be deleted.
  This guard cannot be bypassed.
- The version of the most recent release is also refused;
  `--force` overrides this second guard only.

```bash
flui app image delete my-api 845914920
flui app image delete my-api 845914920 --force
flui app image delete my-api 845914920 --yes     # skip the prompt
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--force` | Override the latest-release guard only. |
| `-y, --yes` | Skip the confirmation prompt. |
| `-c, --cluster` | Cluster name or ID. |

`--force` and `--yes` do different things: `--force` lifts a
guard, `--yes` skips the question.

Get `<version-id>` from `flui app versions <name> --output json`.
It is the numeric registry id, not the tag.

sections.title: Authentication
sections.body:
The CLI never holds your password. It holds an **API key**,
stored in the active profile, and every command that talks
to the Flui API sends it.

That is why this page has four commands. Your own terminal
needs a key that can do everything you can do. A build
pipeline or an agent needs a key that can do far less, and you
need to see what you have handed out and take it back.

A key only ever narrows what its issuer could already do. You
cannot mint a key with more permissions than you have.

## `flui auth login`

Use this on your own machine. The CLI opens a browser, runs an OIDC sign-in against the identity provider
inside your installation, then uses the resulting token to
mint an API key and saves it in the active profile.

`flui login` is the same command, shorter.

```bash
flui auth login              # opens a browser
flui auth login --headless   # prints the authorization URL instead
flui auth login --key-name my-laptop
```

| Flag | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--headless` | Print the authorization URL instead of opening a browser. Useful over SSH. |
| `--key-name <name>` | Name attached to the generated key, shown later in listings. Default: `cli`. |
| `--prompt <mode>` | How the identity provider greets you. `select_account` (the default) shows the account picker, so you confirm or switch user before a key is minted; `login` forces re-authentication; an empty value reuses the current session silently. |
| `--profile <name>` | Profile to save the key into. Default: the active profile. |

After login, every command uses the saved key with no further
prompts. The key is long-lived. To rotate it, run
`flui auth login` again, or mint a new one with
`flui auth generate-api-key`.

The key `login` mints is unscoped. It carries all of your
permissions, because it is you at your own terminal. Do not
hand it to anything else; for that, use the next command.

### About the OAuth callback

The CLI listens for the redirect on `http://localhost:8899`,
with fallbacks through `8900`, `8901`, `8902` and `8910`.
There is a 120-second window between opening the URL and
receiving the callback.

## `flui auth generate-api-key`

Use this for a key that is not you at a terminal: a build
pipeline, a script or an agent.

```bash
flui auth generate-api-key --name agent \
  --scope mcp:app:read --scope mcp:obs:read

flui auth generate-api-key --name ci-pipeline \
  --expires 365 --unscoped
```

### It refuses to guess

If you pass neither `--scope` nor `--unscoped`, the command is
refused before anything else happens, before it touches the
network or the profile and before you need a token. It prints:

```
Say what this key may do.
  --scope <mcp:...>   a limited key; repeat the flag for more than one
  --unscoped          a key carrying your full weight
Omitting both used to mean --unscoped, silently.
```

The widest credential the installation can issue has to be
asked for explicitly, with `--unscoped`.

### It needs a session token

This command mints a key from a browser session token, not
from an existing key. Pass it with `--token`, or set
`FLUI_SESSION_TOKEN`.

| Flag | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--token <jwt>` | `FLUI_SESSION_TOKEN` | Session bearer token to mint with. |
| `--name <name>` | `cli` | Human-readable name for the key. |
| `--expires <days>` | no expiry | Expiry in whole days from now. |
| `--scope <scope>` | none | A scope for the key. Repeat for more than one. Cannot be combined with `--unscoped`. |
| `--unscoped` | `false` | Issue a key with no scope ceiling, carrying your full weight. |
| `--profile <name>` | active profile | Profile to save the key into. |

### The key is shown once, and never again

The plaintext key is written straight into the profile. The
command prints the key's id, name, expiry and scopes, followed
by this line:

```
⚠  The plaintext key is not shown and cannot be retrieved again.
```

The installation stores a digest of the key, not the key
itself, so there is nothing to hand back later, to you or to
anyone else.

From the CLI you never see the value. It goes straight into the
profile, encrypted, and every later command reads it from
there. If you need the literal string, to paste into a CI
secret or an agent's configuration, mint the key in the
dashboard instead: the API returns the plaintext once to
whoever asked for it, and the dashboard shows it to you.

A key minted here replaces the key already in that profile.
Pass `--profile` to write it somewhere else if you do not want
to log out of the profile you are working in.

### Scopes

A scope is one permission a key carries, in the form
`mcp:<area>:<depth>`. The full set:

```
mcp:onboarding:read      mcp:catalog:read
mcp:app:read             mcp:app:write             mcp:app:destructive
mcp:obs:read             mcp:spec:validate
mcp:backup:read          mcp:backup:write
mcp:migration:read       mcp:migration:write       mcp:migration:destructive
mcp:mail:read
mcp:iam:read             mcp:iam:write
mcp:infra:read           mcp:infra:write           mcp:infra:destructive
mcp:platform:update
```

**A scope you do not hold yourself is refused.** The whole
request fails and names the scope that caused it, instead of
returning a smaller key than you asked for.

**Every scoped key also gets `mcp:onboarding:read`**, whether
you ask for it or not. That is the scope that lets an agent
read the "how this installation is operated" document
before it does anything. An unscoped key already reaches
everything, so nothing is added to it.

### There is no `--groups` flag

The API and the dashboard offer a friendlier unit than raw
scopes: permission groups. There are sixteen of them, on two
axes, each described in one sentence written for a person, and
each is granted or refused as a whole.

The CLI does not have them: from the terminal you mint by raw
scope or with `--unscoped`.

If you are deciding what an agent should be allowed to do, read
[Choose what your agent may
do](/tasks/choose-what-your-agent-may-do/) first, then come
back and name the scopes by hand, or mint the key from the
dashboard instead.

## `flui auth api-keys`

Lists the keys issued for the identity you are signed in as,
not everyone's keys.

```bash
flui auth api-keys
flui auth api-keys --output json
```

`-o, --output` is `text` (the default) or `json`; `--profile`
reads the credential from another profile.

Each row shows a name, a state, the scopes the key carries,
and its id. The state is one of:

- **active**: usable now.
- **expired**: past the expiry it was minted with.
- **revoked**: switched off, and still listed, so a key that
  once existed does not vanish from the record.

A key with no scopes prints as
`(unscoped — the full weight of the issuer)`.

## `flui auth revoke-api-key <id>`

Takes a key back. It stops working immediately.

```bash
flui auth revoke-api-key 6f1c2d34-...
```

The id is the one printed by `flui auth api-keys`; it is not
the key itself, which the installation never keeps. You can
only revoke keys you minted. An id that belongs to someone
else, is already revoked or matches no key answers as not
found. `--profile` acts with another profile's credential.

Revoking does not remove the row. It marks the key revoked, so
the listing still shows that the key existed and was turned
off.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `FLUI_API_KEY` | Overrides the key stored in the profile for this invocation. The API URL still comes from the profile. |
| `FLUI_SESSION_TOKEN` | Session bearer token used by `generate-api-key`, instead of `--token`. |
| `FLUI_PROFILE` | Active profile selector. See [Profiles and config](/cli/profiles-and-config/). |

The full inventory of `FLUI_*` variables is in
[Environment variables](/cli/environment-variables/).

sections.title: Backups
sections.body:
The `backup` topic is where you turn protection on, check it and undo it. You start with one of two commands, and use the rest of this page afterwards: - [`flui backup quick-setup`](#flui-backup-quick-setup) provisions storage with the provider you already have connected and protects every application on a cluster with it, in one step. - [`flui backup enable`](#flui-backup-enable) gives you more control: `enable cluster` for every application on a cluster, including the ones installed later, and one subcommand per kind of thing when you want to protect a single application. What `enable` creates is a policy: a scope, a schedule, and one or more S3-compatible [destinations](#flui-backup-destination). The API runs it as a [job](#flui-backup-job). The [`policy`](#flui-backup-policy) commands maintain what `enable` created (list, pause, delete). You do not create policies with them. [`flui backup status`](#flui-backup-status) tells you whether protection is set up, and [`flui backup list`](#flui-backup-list) tells you whether it actually ran. The volume snapshots of one application (taking one now, looking inside, restoring whole or file by file) are under [`flui app backup`](#flui-app-backup), near the end of this page. Commands that turn protection on or read it for a cluster take `-c, --cluster ` and auto-detect the cluster when it is omitted. The listing commands (`backup list`, `job list`, `policy list`) take a cluster ID, and the commands that read data accept `--json` for machine-readable output. The sections below follow the order you need them: getting started, turning protection on, checking it, then destinations, policies, jobs, restores and volume snapshots. Platform configuration comes last. It protects the installation itself rather than an application or a cluster. ## `flui backup quick-setup` Provisions backup storage using the provider already connected, and protects every application on a cluster with it, as [`enable cluster`](#flui-backup-enable-cluster) does. It replaces creating a destination, testing it and protecting the cluster by hand. ```bash flui backup quick-setup # auto-detects the cluster flui backup quick-setup -c production-eu --dry-run ``` | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `-c, --cluster ` | auto-detect | Which cluster to protect. | | `--dry-run` | off | Report what would be set up, and whether it can be, without doing it. | | `--schedule ` | per kind | One cron schedule in UTC for every policy. Without it, each kind of backup keeps its own nightly time. | | `--retention-days ` | 30 | How long database backups are kept. | | `--no-first-backup` | off | Do not run the first backups immediately. | | `--json` | off | Machine-readable output. | Run it with `--dry-run` first. It tells you whether the connected provider can give you storage before anything is created. ## `flui backup enable` | Command | Protects | Does not cover | | --- | --- | --- | | `enable cluster` | every application on a cluster, including the ones installed later, each with the engine that fits it | databases it does not recognise, which are listed as [needing a decision](#flui-backup-status) | | `enable database ` | one database: continuously where the image allows it, with scheduled dumps otherwise | anything else | | `enable volumes ` | one application's volumes, as nightly encrypted snapshots: uploads, media, generated files | a volume a database is writing to, which is refused and listed unless the app is stopped for the copy | | `enable platform` | Flui itself: the control-plane database, sealed to a recipient | applications | `enable cluster` is the usual starting point. Use the other three to protect one thing at a time. They create the same kind of policy `enable cluster` creates for each application. These flags are common to `database`, `volumes` and `platform`: | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `-D, --destination ` | required | `[:primary\|replica[:priority]]`. Repeatable: pass it once per target to mirror across destinations. | | `--name ` | descriptive | Name for this protection. | | `--schedule ` | per kind | e.g. `"0 2 * * *"` for 02:00 UTC daily. Without it: databases at 02:30 (continuous) or 03:00 (dumps), volumes at 03:30, the platform at 02:00, all UTC. | | `--retention-days ` | 30 | How long each copy is kept. Volume snapshots follow their own rule instead (see below). | | `--retention-max-copies ` | none | Cap on retained copies. | | `--[no-]enabled` | enabled | Create it paused with `--no-enabled`. | | `-c, --cluster ` | auto-detect | Which cluster. | ### `flui backup enable cluster` Every application on the cluster gets a policy of its own: - a recognised database (PostgreSQL, MariaDB) gets continuous backup, or dumps when its image cannot ship its changes, and a first base copy right away; - every other application with volumes gets nightly snapshots; - Flui's own components and applications that keep no data are skipped, and an application that already has a policy is left as it is; - applications installed later get theirs within minutes of their first successful deploy. ```bash flui backup enable cluster -c production-eu -D flui backup enable cluster -D -D :replica --before-deploy ``` It follows the work to the end and prints one line per application: what it got, or why it got nothing. | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `-D, --destination ` | none | `[:primary\|replica]`. One primary, and at most one replica, which receives a copy of the volume snapshots after each run. Required. | | `-c, --cluster ` | auto-detect | Which cluster. | | `--schedule ` | per kind | One cron schedule in UTC for every policy. | | `--retention-days ` | 30 | How long database backups are kept. | | `--before-deploy` | off | Also take a [backup before each deploy](#flui-app-backup-before-deploy-name) of every application. | | `--[no-]first-backup` | on | Take the first volume snapshot of each application now. | | `--no-wait` | off | Return once protection is recorded, without following it. | The policies it creates are ordinary policies, listed by `flui backup policy list` like any other. ### `flui backup disable cluster` Stops giving new applications on a cluster a policy. The policies already created keep running; remove one with [`flui backup policy delete`](#flui-backup-policy-delete-id). ```bash flui backup disable cluster -c production-eu ``` ### `flui backup enable database ` Every change is shipped off-cluster as it happens, so the database can be restored to any moment in the retained window rather than to the last nightly copy. A database whose image cannot do that (one inside another application's bundle, for instance) gets scheduled dumps instead, each restorable to the moment it was taken. ```bash flui backup enable database my-api-db -D ``` To restore to a moment, use [`flui db pitr-restore`](/cli/databases/#flui-db-pitr-restore-app). ### `flui backup enable volumes ` Use this for uploads, media and generated files. It takes nightly encrypted snapshots, each storing only what changed since the one before. Flui keeps the last 7 daily and 4 weekly snapshots, and always the most recent one. `--keep-monthly` adds 3 monthly ones, for about 30% more space. `--retention-days` does not apply to snapshots. ```bash flui backup enable volumes my-api -D --exclude cache ``` | Flag | Effect | | --- | --- | | `--exclude ` | Leave a volume out. Repeatable; everything else is included, including volumes the application grows later. | | `--pause` | Stop the application for the length of each copy, so every volume is copied at rest. Each run records how long it was stopped. | | `--[no-]keep-monthly` | Also keep 3 monthly snapshots, or stop keeping them. | A volume a database is writing to is refused and named in the run, because a file copy of a running database does not restore. Redis, Valkey and SQLite are copied consistently while they run; anything else is listed as needing a decision until you pass `--pause` or `--exclude` for it. When the application already has a volume policy (from `enable cluster`, for example), running this again with `--pause`, `--exclude` or `--[no-]keep-monthly` changes that policy instead of adding a second one. This is how you record a decision. ### `flui backup enable platform` Protects Flui's own control-plane database, sealed so only the holder of the matching identity can open it. A rebuild starts from this backup when the cluster running Flui is gone. ```bash flui backup platform init # on your machine, first flui backup enable platform -D ``` | Flag | Effect | | --- | --- | | `--recipient ` | The recipient the dump is sealed to. Defaults to the key `flui backup platform init` keeps in your vault. **Without the matching identity nobody, including Flui, can open it.** | | `--heartbeat-url ` | Pinged after each successful run, so you can detect when runs stop. | ## `flui backup status` Shows what is protected, and how. For the whole installation it also lists, per cluster, whether every application is protected and what needs a decision: databases Flui does not recognise, and volumes the last snapshot had to refuse. Each comes with the two commands that resolve it: copy with the application stopped (`enable volumes --pause`), or leave the volume out (`enable volumes --exclude `). ```bash flui backup status # the whole estate flui backup status -a my-api # everything protecting one application ``` | Flag | Effect | | --- | --- | | `-a, --app ` | Narrow to one application. | | `-c, --cluster ` | With `--app`: the cluster the application is on. Auto-detected when omitted. | | `--json` | Machine-readable output. | For a database this prints a recoverable window. The **up to** time it shows is the end of the last base copy. Continuous shipping usually reaches later than that, so treat the time as a minimum. ## `flui backup list` Lists the backups that actually exist, for every engine. ```bash flui backup list --app flui backup list --cluster ``` `status` tells you whether protection is set up; `list` tells you whether it ran. A policy can be enabled and correct and still have produced nothing. ## `flui backup destination` A destination is an S3-compatible storage target where backup artifacts are written. Supported providers are `hetzner_object_storage`, `scaleway_object_storage`, `ovh_object_storage`, `minio`, and `generic_s3`. ### `flui backup destination create` Registers a new destination. Provider, endpoint, region and bucket are required. When you leave out the access and secret keys, the command asks for them. That is safer, because a value typed at the prompt never enters your shell history or the process list. Encryption defaults to `flui_managed`; pass `--encryption-mode byo_passphrase` to supply your own passphrase, which is asked for the same way. ```bash flui backup destination create \ --name my-s3 --provider hetzner_object_storage \ --endpoint https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com \ --region fsn1 --bucket flui-backups flui backup destination create \ --name scw --provider scaleway_object_storage \ --endpoint https://s3.fr-par.scw.cloud \ --region fr-par --bucket flui-bkp ``` | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `--name ` | none | Display name (≤120 chars). Required. | | `--provider

` | none | Storage backend: `hetzner_object_storage`, `scaleway_object_storage`, `ovh_object_storage`, `minio`, `generic_s3`. Required. | | `--endpoint ` | none | S3 endpoint URL (e.g. `https://s3.fr-par.scw.cloud`). Required. | | `--region ` | none | S3 region. Required. | | `--bucket ` | none | Target bucket. Required. | | `--access-key ` | prompted | S3 access key. | | `--secret-key ` | prompted | S3 secret key. | | `--prefix ` | none | Optional path prefix inside the bucket. | | `--encryption-mode ` | `flui_managed` | `flui_managed`, `byo_passphrase`, or `none`. | | `--encryption-passphrase ` | prompted | Passphrase to use with `--encryption-mode=byo_passphrase`. | | `--force-path-style` | off | Force path-style S3 URLs (needed for MinIO and some providers). | | `--use-sse` | off | Use server-side encryption (SSE-S3) at the provider. | | `--cost-per-gb-month-cents ` | none | What the storage costs, in euro cents per GB per month (e.g. `1.606`), used for estimates. | ### `flui backup destination list` Lists the destinations configured in the API, with provider, region and bucket, usage, and health when available. ```bash flui backup destination list flui backup destination list --json ``` ### `flui backup destination show ` Shows one destination in full, including endpoint, prefix, encryption mode, health, and reported usage. ```bash flui backup destination show flui backup destination show --json ``` ### `flui backup destination test ` Checks that a destination is reachable by running a real S3 PUT, GET and DELETE against the bucket. Use it right after `create` to confirm the credentials and endpoint work. ```bash flui backup destination test ``` ### `flui backup destination set-cost []` Sets what a destination costs, in euro cents per GB per month, so backup cost estimates use your price. `--list-price` goes back to the published price Flui knows for the provider. ```bash flui backup destination set-cost 1.606 flui backup destination set-cost --list-price ``` ### `flui backup destination delete ` Removes a destination from the API. **Artifacts already in the bucket are not removed**; only the registration is deleted. It asks you to confirm; skip that with `-y, --yes`. ```bash flui backup destination delete flui backup destination delete --yes ``` ## `flui backup policy` A policy is what [`flui backup enable`](#flui-backup-enable) creates: a scope, a schedule and one or more destinations. The API runs it on that schedule (and on demand via [`backup job run`](#flui-backup-job-run)), producing artifacts subject to its retention. The commands in this section list, inspect, pause and remove policies that already exist. > **`flui backup policy create` does not create a policy.** It > prints which command to use and exits. Create policies with > [`flui backup enable`](#flui-backup-enable), where the subcommand > says which kind you mean. ### `flui backup policy list` Lists policies, optionally filtered to one cluster. Each row shows the name, the engine and profile or scope, cluster, cron schedule, and whether it is disabled. ```bash flui backup policy list flui backup policy list --cluster flui backup policy list --json ``` ### `flui backup policy show ` Shows one policy: its schedule in words and the next run, its health and last good run, the applications it covers, retention, its destination list (each with role and priority), and the last five runs. ```bash flui backup policy show flui backup policy show --json ``` ### `flui backup policy delete ` Deletes a policy. **Existing backups are kept**; only the policy and its schedule are removed. It asks you to confirm; skip that with `-y, --yes`. ```bash flui backup policy delete flui backup policy delete --yes ``` ### `flui backup policy pause ` Turns a policy's schedule off. The policy's scope, schedule, retention and destinations stay as configured; the API stops queueing new runs from it until someone resumes it. `flui backup job run` still works on a paused policy, so you can still take an on-demand backup. Only the cron schedule stops. One exception: a database-class policy ships every change continuously, and pausing it does not stop that stream, because stopping it would leave a gap in the recovery window. Deleting the policy is the only way to stop it. ```bash flui backup policy pause ``` ### `flui backup policy resume ` Turns a paused policy's schedule back on. ```bash flui backup policy resume ``` ## `flui backup job` A job is one run of a policy, either scheduled or on demand. A job shows a backup's status, timing, bytes transferred, and any error. ### `flui backup job run` Triggers an on-demand backup for a given policy, outside its normal schedule. Returns the queued job's ID so you can track it with `backup job show`. ```bash flui backup job run --policy ``` ### `flui backup job list` Lists the backup jobs for a cluster. `--cluster` (cluster ID) is required. ```bash flui backup job list --cluster flui backup job list --cluster --json ``` ### `flui backup job show ` Shows one job: its policy, status, start and completion times, bytes transferred, and error message if it failed. ```bash flui backup job show flui backup job show --json ``` ## `flui backup restore` Shows the history of restores. You start a restore with the command that fits what you are restoring: - a database, to a moment, into a new database: [`flui db pitr-restore`](/cli/databases/#flui-db-pitr-restore-app); - a volume, whole or file by file: [`flui app backup restore`](#flui-app-backup-restore-name-backup); - the applications of a lost cluster: [`flui cluster rebuild`](/tasks/rebuild-a-lost-cluster/), and those of a lost control cluster [`flui cluster rebuild-control`](/tasks/rebuild-the-control-plane/). ### `flui backup restore list` Lists restore jobs, with status, target kind, and target cluster. ```bash flui backup restore list flui backup restore list --json ``` ### `flui backup restore show ` Shows one restore job: status, source artifact and destination, target, timing, and error message if it failed. ```bash flui backup restore show flui backup restore show --json ``` ### `flui backup restore preview` Shows what a backup holds in its storage (objects and bytes) before you restore it. Both flags are required. ```bash flui backup restore preview --artifact --source-destination ``` ## `flui app backup` The volume snapshots of one application. The nightly ones come from its policy; these commands take one now, look inside, restore and delete. Each takes the application's name or slug, and `-c, --cluster `. ### `flui app backup create ` Takes a snapshot now. A snapshot you take yourself stays until you delete it, and does not replace a nightly one. ```bash flui app backup create my-app -D flui app backup create my-app -D --volume uploads --no-wait ``` | Flag | Effect | | --- | --- | | `-D, --destination ` | A registered destination: the copy becomes an encrypted snapshot in the application's own repository there. | | `-v, --volume ` | Which volume, when the application has more than one. | | `--pause` | Stop the application for the length of the copy, so a volume a database is writing to is copied at rest. | | `--allow-inconsistent` | Copy it while a database writes anyway. The copy may not restore cleanly. | | `--no-wait` | Return once the backup is queued instead of following it. | The backup runs in the background. Without `--no-wait`, the command follows it to the end. Without `--destination` the copy is a full, unencrypted copy instead of a snapshot. It goes to a bucket passed with `-b, --bucket` and `-e, --endpoint`, or to one the cluster's provider creates. Use a destination when you can. ### `flui app backup list ` The application's volume backups, newest first. **SIZE** is what a restore writes back; **ADDED** is what the backup added to the destination. ```bash flui app backup list my-app flui app backup list my-app -o json ``` ### `flui app backup browse [path]` Lists a folder inside a snapshot, read-only. Use it to find the paths to give `restore --path`. ```bash flui app backup browse my-app 3f2a91c0 flui app backup browse my-app 3f2a91c0 uploads/2026 ``` ### `flui app backup restore ` A whole snapshot is written into a new volume beside the application, which keeps running on its current data until you switch. With `--path`, only the named files or folders are written back into the live volume. ```bash flui app backup restore my-app 3f2a91c0 flui app backup restore my-app 3f2a91c0 --swap flui app backup restore my-app 3f2a91c0 --to my-app-copy --swap flui app backup restore my-app 3f2a91c0 --path uploads/report.pdf --path config flui app backup restore my-app 3f2a91c0 --path uploads --into restored-uploads ``` | Flag | Effect | | --- | --- | | `--swap` | Switch the application to the restored volume right away. It restarts; the data it used before is kept as a separate volume. | | `--to ` | Restore into another application instead. | | `-v, --volume ` | The target application's volume, when it has more than one. | | `-p, --path ` | Restore only this file or folder, relative to the volume root. Repeatable. | | `--into

` | With `--path`: write under this folder instead of over the current files. | | `-y, --yes` | Do not ask before writing over files in the live volume. | ### `flui app backup delete ` Removes a snapshot and its record from the destination. It cannot be restored afterwards. The command asks first; `--yes` skips the question. ```bash flui app backup delete my-app 3f2a91c0 flui app backup delete my-app 3f2a91c0 --yes ``` ### `flui app backup before-deploy ` Takes a backup before each deploy of the application. For a database with continuous backup this is a restore point, and the deploy waits the few seconds it takes. For everything else it is a dump or a volume snapshot, which is started and not waited for. It uses the policies that already protect the application. ```bash flui app backup before-deploy my-app flui app backup before-deploy my-app --required flui app backup before-deploy my-app --off ``` | Flag | Effect | | --- | --- | | `--required` | Fail the deploy when the backup before it cannot be taken. Without it the deploy goes ahead and the failure is logged. | | `--off` | Stop taking a backup before each deploy. | ### `flui app backup skip ` Records that the application is not to be backed up, so `flui backup status` stops listing it as needing a decision. `-n, --note` says why; `--undo` reverses it. ```bash flui app backup skip my-app --note "rebuilt from source, nothing to keep" flui app backup skip my-app --undo ``` ## `flui backup platform` Everything above protects an application or a cluster. A platform-class policy protects this installation's own control plane: the database holding every user, API key, provider token and application record Flui has. That backup cannot be sealed with a key the control plane holds itself, because if the master is lost, a key stored on the master is lost with it. So a platform backup is encrypted to an age key pair you generate on your own laptop. Only the public half, the recipient, is registered on the policy. The private identity never touches the master. ### `flui backup platform init` Generates that identity entirely on your machine and keeps it sealed in your [vault](/cli/profiles-and-config/#the-vault) next to the rest of the profile's secrets, so the vault passphrase is the only one you need to remember. Needs the vault unlocked. Prints the public recipient. Because the vault lives on one machine, `init` also writes a **recovery copy** (default `~/flui--platform-recovery.age`) sealed with the same vault passphrase. A rebuild starts from it if this machine is lost too. Run `init` again at any time to write a fresh copy; the key in the vault is kept. **Move the recovery copy off this machine and off the master.** Flui does not hold one. Lose both the vault and the copy, or the passphrase, and every platform backup becomes permanently unrecoverable. ```bash flui backup platform init flui backup platform init --out /Volumes/usb/flui-recovery.age ``` | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `--policy ` | none | Platform backup policy to register the recipient on. | | `--heartbeat-url ` | none | Dead-man's-switch URL the master pings while its last platform backup stays fresh. Only takes effect together with `--policy`. | | `--out ` | `~/flui--platform-recovery.age` | Where to write the recovery copy. | | `--passphrase ` | none | Your vault passphrase, checked against the vault. Prompted if omitted. | | `--rotate` | off | Replace the key in the vault. The previous one is kept, so older backups still open, and goes into the recovery copy too. Register the new recipient on your policies afterwards with `--policy`. | | `--force` | off | Overwrite an existing file at `--out`. | | `--json` | off | Print `{recipient, out, outcome, keys}` as JSON. Requires `--passphrase`, since it cannot prompt. | [`flui backup enable platform`](#flui-backup-enable-platform) creates the policy and seals it to the key `init` put in your vault. Run `init` first, on your own machine, or pass `--policy` here to register the recipient on a policy that already exists. ### `flui backup platform download` Fetches the two files of a platform backup, the key bundle and the dump of Flui's own state, so `flui backup platform restore` can open them. The API hands out short-lived links, so the storage credentials never leave it, and the files stay sealed to your key. ```bash flui backup platform download flui backup platform download --job --out ./rebuild-input ``` | Flag | Effect | | --- | --- | | `--job ` | The backup to fetch. Defaults to the newest. | | `--out ` | Where to write. Defaults to `./flui-platform-backup-`. | | `--force` | Overwrite files already in `--out`. | | `--json` | Print the job, its date and the files written as JSON. | ### `flui backup platform restore` Opens a platform backup. It decrypts the sealed key bundle and the dump of Flui's own state with the key in your vault (or, when this machine is gone, the recovery copy) and writes out everything a fresh installation needs to become this one again. It runs on your machine and sends nothing anywhere. ```bash flui backup platform restore --bundle keybundle.age --dump flui-pg.dump.gz.enc flui backup platform restore --bundle keybundle.age --dump flui-pg.dump.gz.enc \ --identity ~/flui-default-platform-recovery.age ``` | Flag | Effect | | --- | --- | | `--bundle ` | The sealed key bundle. Required. | | `--dump ` | The encrypted dump from the same run. Required. | | `--identity ` | Open with the recovery copy instead of the vault. | | `--passphrase ` | The recovery copy's passphrase. Prompted if omitted. | | `--out ` | Where to write. Defaults to `./flui-rebuild`. | | `--force` | Overwrite an existing output directory. | [Rebuild the control plane](/tasks/rebuild-the-control-plane/) explains what to do with the files it writes. ### `flui backup platform status` Lists every platform-class policy: its recipient, whether a dead-man's-switch URL is set, its schedule and next run, its health, the last good run and the last run. A paused platform policy is marked `[disabled]`. ```bash flui backup platform status flui backup platform status --json ``` ## `flui backup velero uninstall []` Removes Velero, a cluster backup engine, from a cluster where Flui installed it: its controller, node agent, bucket credentials and the rest of what Flui set up for it. Only what Flui installed is removed. The backups it wrote stay in their destination, and Flui cannot restore them. Running it again continues where it stopped. ```bash flui backup velero uninstall --plan flui backup velero uninstall production --yes ``` | Flag | Effect | | --- | --- | | `--plan` | Show what would be removed and change nothing. | | `-y, --yes` | Do not ask for confirmation. | | `--no-wait` | Start the removal and return its operation id. |

sections.title: Clusters and nodes
sections.body:
This page covers the commands that act on a cluster as a whole, or on the machines inside it: `cluster`, `node`, `server-types` and `ssh`. ## Which cluster a command is talking to An installation has one **control cluster**, which runs Flui itself, and any number of **workload clusters**, which run only your applications. The two kinds are stored in different places, and that decides which commands can see them. The CLI keeps a local record of the cluster it created on this machine, which is the control cluster. Workload clusters are created from the dashboard, with `flui cluster create`, or by an agent. They live only in the installation's database, so the CLI has to ask the API for them. Some commands read both, and some read only the local record: - `flui cluster list`, `flui cluster volumes`, `flui cluster destroy`, the `flui scaling` commands and `flui ssh` read the API too, so they see every cluster. - `flui node list` and `flui node remove` read the local record only, and `flui node connect` always joins the control cluster. Point the first two at a workload cluster and they answer that it does not exist. The commands that take `-c, --cluster ` auto-detect the target when there is only one cluster to choose from, and refuse to guess when there is more than one. For the control cluster's own lifecycle (create, status, resize, destroy), use the [`env`](/cli/environments/) topic. It is the only surface that always targets the control cluster and has the operations specific to it. ## `flui cluster list` Lists every cluster of the installation: name, type (`control` or `workload`), provider, region, node count, status and id. The control cluster is printed first, since it is the one a bare `flui ssh master` addresses. ```bash flui cluster list flui cluster list --output json ``` | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `-o, --output table\|json` | `table` | Output format. | If the API cannot be reached (you are not logged in, or the installation is down), the command still prints the clusters it holds locally and says that the workload clusters could not be listed. It does not show an empty list as if there were nothing there. The JSON form prints only an allow-list of fields. The local record also holds cluster credentials, which must not reach standard output, where they could be redirected into a file or pasted into a chat. ## `flui cluster create ` Creates a workload cluster. It starts from the control cluster's provider and region and joins its private network on its own when the provider needs one. `--provider` places it elsewhere, which the installation accepts only when the control cluster permits workloads on another provider. ```bash flui cluster create edge flui cluster create edge --worker-count 2 flui cluster create edge --provider hetzner --region hel1 flui cluster create edge --vnet --subnet flui cluster create edge --no-wait ``` | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `--provider

` | the control cluster's | Where the cluster runs. | | `--region ` | the control cluster's, on the same provider | Region of the cluster. | | `--node-size ` | the provider's recommended type | Server type of every node. | | `--worker-count ` | `0` | Workers beside the master; 0 is master-only. | | `--vnet ` | none | Join a private network that already exists (see `flui network list`). Cannot be combined with `--network-cidr`. | | `--subnet ` | the network's only subnet | Subnet within `--vnet`; needs `--vnet`. | | `--network-cidr ` | `10.250.0.0/16` | Address range of the Flui network. | | `--no-wait` | off | Return once the creation is queued. | Without `--no-wait` it follows the creation, for up to half an hour. ## `flui cluster destroy` Permanently destroys a workload cluster and all its nodes. The command asks you to retype the cluster name before it proceeds, then waits up to ten minutes for it to go. ```bash flui cluster destroy flui cluster destroy --force # skip confirmation flui cluster destroy --force --no-wait # queue and exit ``` | Argument / Flag | Effect | | --- | --- | | `` | Cluster name or ID (required). | | `-f, --force` | Skip the typed confirmation prompt. | | `--no-wait` | Queue the destroy operation and return immediately. | > The command refuses the control cluster by name. To destroy > the control cluster, use > [`flui env destroy`](/cli/environments/#flui-env-destroy). ## `flui cluster volumes` Removing an application takes its storage with it. A cluster can still carry storage that belongs to no living application. That storage keeps costing money, and this command is the only place that lists it. ```bash flui cluster volumes flui cluster volumes --output json flui cluster volumes --remove user-a1b2c3/data-uptime-kuma-0 ``` | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `-c, --cluster ` | auto-detect | Target cluster. | | `--remove ` | none | Delete one abandoned volume, given exactly as the listing printed it. Permanent. | | `-f, --force` | off | Skip the typed confirmation of `--remove`. | | `-o, --output table\|json` | `table` | Output format. | The listing is cautious, because a false positive here is someone's data. A volume is only called abandoned when it sits in a place Flui made for applications, nothing is using it, nothing that could re-create it still exists, no living application is attributed to it, and it has been sitting there for at least fifteen minutes. Each entry prints the reason it qualified. So a volume missing from the listing is not proof that nothing is left: the command errs on the side of leaving things alone. When the cluster's credentials cannot be read at all, it says so instead of printing an empty list. `--remove` takes one entry, exactly as the listing printed it, and asks you to type the volume's name to confirm. The platform then re-runs the whole check on its side before it deletes anything, so a volume that has come back into use in the meantime is refused rather than removed. A deleted volume cannot be recovered. Listing is read-only and needs access to the infrastructure area. Removing needs authority over the cluster's machines, which is a level above reading them, so someone who can see the list may not be able to act on it. ## Nodes On a provider Flui buys from, a cluster's machines change through its scaling group: `flui scaling floor ` raises or lowers the number of nodes, and `flui scaling approve --yes` carries out what a manual group proposes (see [Let a cluster buy its own machines](/tasks/let-a-cluster-buy-its-own-machines/)). The `node` topic lists the machines, and attaches or detaches machines of your own. The master is created with the cluster and goes away only with `cluster destroy` or `env destroy`. ### `flui node list` Lists every node in the target cluster, master and workers, with its id, role, status, address and name. When the master of the control cluster is reserved for the control plane, the listing says so on the master's row. ```bash flui node list flui node list --cluster my-cluster flui node list --output json ``` | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `-c, --cluster ` | auto-detect | Target cluster. | | `-o, --output table\|json` | `table` | Output format. | ### `flui node remove` Detaches a machine you attached yourself with `node connect`. The platform always works in this order: stop giving the node new work, move the work already on it to the other nodes, then remove it from the cluster. A machine Flui bought goes back through the scaling group instead (`flui scaling floor`). `node remove` refuses the master; to get rid of it, destroy the whole cluster. ```bash flui node remove flui node remove --cluster my-cluster flui node remove --no-wait ``` Take `` from `flui node list`. The CLI checks the id against the cluster's current nodes before queuing anything, so an unknown id fails immediately and points you back to `node list` instead of queuing an operation that cannot work. The CLI waits five minutes. If the removal takes longer (the work is slow to move, or an application is slow to release its node), it returns and tells you the operation is still running; `flui node list` shows the final state. `--no-wait` skips the wait. | Argument / Flag | Effect | | --- | --- | | `` | Node ID to remove (required, the master is rejected). | | `-c, --cluster ` | Target cluster (auto-detect when only one). | | `--no-wait` | Queue and return immediately. | ### `flui node connect` Flui buys machines through the scaling group. This command is for a machine you already have: it joins a Linux host to the cluster as a worker over SSH, and provisions nothing. It applies to an installation running on your own servers. The command joins the control cluster. If that cluster was created at a cloud provider, it joins nothing and points you at `flui scaling floor`. ```bash flui node connect --host 203.0.113.10 flui node connect --host 198.51.100.12 --master-ip 198.51.100.11 --node-network 198.51.100.0/24 ``` | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `--host ` | required | Address or DNS name of the host to join. | | `--port ` | `22` | SSH port of the host. | | `--user ` | `root` | SSH user on the host. | | `--ssh-key ` | `~/.ssh/id_rsa` | Private key that already authenticates to the host. | | `--master-ip ` | the cluster's master address | The address the new machine uses to reach the master. | | `--node-network ` | the `/24` of the detected private address | The private network the nodes share. | | `--skip-precheck` | off | Do not inspect the host first. | | `--best-effort` | off | Continue even when the inspection reports problems. | Before it starts, the command lists the three conditions the host must meet: you can reach it over SSH with the key you named, it can reach the cluster's master on the shared private network, and it is a clean machine with no cluster software on it. It then inspects the host and reports what it found: operating system, architecture, memory and processors. An unsupported architecture, less than about 2 GB of memory, or a cluster runtime already installed each count as a problem, and the command stops instead of joining a host that would misbehave later. `--best-effort` proceeds anyway, and `--skip-precheck` skips the inspection. Neither is meant for normal use. When it finishes, it prints the new node's name and private address. Run `flui node list` to confirm. ### `flui node logs ` Prints the install log of a node an operation is creating (a new cluster's first node, or one added node), and with `-f, --follow` keeps printing until the operation ends. The operation id comes from the command that added the node, `flui operation`, or `flui scaling why`. ```bash flui node logs flui node logs --follow ``` | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `-f, --follow` | off | Keep printing until the operation has finished. | | `--interval ` | `3` | Seconds between reads while following. | ## Recovery and maintenance ### `flui cluster rebuild --to ` Re-creates the applications of a cluster that is gone, onto one that is alive, from Flui's records and the backups. `--plan` shows what would happen and stops. See [Rebuild a lost cluster](/tasks/rebuild-a-lost-cluster/) for the full procedure. ### `flui cluster rebuild-control` Brings back the applications of the old control cluster after a platform backup has been restored into a new installation. See [Rebuild the control plane](/tasks/rebuild-the-control-plane/). ### `flui cluster recover-access []` Gets you back into a node whose SSH is closed, through its provider rather than its network. `` is a server name or id, and defaults to the master. Without `--yes` the command only says what it would do. On OVHcloud the node is rebooted into a rescue system, the Flui firewall is reset on its disk, and it boots again with the firewall re-applied. On Hetzner and Scaleway, port 22 is opened on the provider firewall to one address (yours by default, or the one you give with `--source-ip`) until you remove it. A machine you brought yourself is recovered from its own console. ```bash flui cluster recover-access hz-cluster worker-1 --yes ``` ### `flui cluster host-firewall ` Shows, or turns on or off (`--on`, `--off`), the Flui firewall on the nodes of a workload cluster; `--json` prints the state as JSON. It applies where the provider's own firewall filters in front of the nodes (see [the providers table](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/#the-providers-integrated-today)): this adds the same rules on each node, so one left outside the provider firewall still exposes only SSH, HTTP, HTTPS and the Flui network. Flui turns it on when it creates the cluster; a cluster that does not have it stays off until you turn it on. ### `flui cluster enrol-overlay` Brings an existing cluster onto Flui's private management tunnel. It restarts the cluster software on the cluster's first node to reissue its certificate, and puts the node back exactly as it was if it does not come up. It asks first; `--yes` skips the confirmation. ```bash flui cluster enrol-overlay --cluster workload-1 ``` ## Private networks A cluster's nodes talk to each other over a private network. Most providers get one when the first cluster is created; on a provider that needs one before a cluster can exist, you create it first. ### `flui network list` ```bash flui network list flui network list --provider hetzner flui network list -o json ``` Lists each network with its range, the provider it lives on (or *built by Flui*), its state and id. Under each network are the subnets a cluster can be attached to, with the ids that `flui cluster create --vnet` and `--subnet` take. ### `flui network create` ```bash flui network create --provider ovh --zone GRA flui network create --provider hetzner --zone eu-central --ip-range 10.60.0.0/16 ``` | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `--provider ` | none | Required. The provider to create the network on. | | `--zone ` | the provider's only zone | The network zone. Left out where there are several, you are shown the choices. | | `--ip-range ` | `10.60.0.0/16` | The network's range. | | `--subnet-range ` | the whole range | The range of its first subnet. | | `--name ` | `--` | The network's name. The suffix is there because providers refuse a duplicate name and an installation may want more than one network in a zone. | It creates a resource on the provider's account. ## Server types ### `flui server-types list` Lists the machines a provider sells, with CPU, memory, disk and monthly price. Read it before you pick a size, for a new installation or before resizing an existing node, so that the size you ask for exists. ```bash flui server-types list --provider hetzner flui server-types list --provider hetzner --region fsn1 flui server-types list --provider scaleway --memory 8-32 flui server-types list --provider scaleway --sort memory flui server-types list --provider ovh --region GRA flui server-types list --provider hetzner --json flui server-types list --provider hetzner --force-refresh ``` | Flag | Default | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `-p, --provider hetzner\|scaleway\|ovh` | required | Which provider's catalogue to read. | | `-r, --region ` | none | Filter by region or location code. | | `-m, --memory ` | none | Filter by memory in GB: `16` exactly, `8-32` a range, `8-` a minimum, `-32` a maximum. | | `-s, --sort price\|memory\|cores\|disk\|name` | `price` | Sort key. | | `--desc` | off | Sort descending. | | `--json` | off | Machine-readable output. | | `--force-refresh` | off | Skip the local cache and re-read from the provider. | Results are cached locally and the command says when the cache expires. `--force-refresh` goes back to the provider. ## SSH access ### `flui ssh /` Opens a shell on a node. You do not set up a key: for each connection the CLI makes a throwaway key pair, has it signed for five minutes by the certificate authority the active profile manages, uses it, and cleans up afterwards. Nothing long-lived is left on the machine you connected from. The argument names a node, and it takes two forms: ```bash flui ssh master # the control cluster flui ssh worker-1 # the control cluster flui ssh workload-cluster-1/master # any cluster, by name flui ssh workload-cluster-1/worker-2 ``` A bare node name means the control cluster. Put a cluster name in front of it, separated by a slash, and you can reach any cluster of the installation, including the workload clusters that only exist in the installation's database. | Argument | Effect | | --- | --- | | `/` | Node of a named cluster. | | `` | Node of the control cluster. | The node part accepts `master`, `worker-N`, or a node's own server name as shown by `flui node list`. If you name a cluster that does not exist, the error lists the available clusters and their nodes. If you name an unknown node, it lists that cluster's nodes. On an installation running on your own server, the address, port and user recorded when it was installed are used; otherwise the connection is `root` on port 22. SSH is the lowest-level surface Flui exposes. Use it for direct shell work such as debugging, looking at system processes or one-off inspection. For everyday operations (metrics, logs, restarts, deploys), use the higher-level commands; you should not need a shell for them. ## Where to go from here - [Add a cluster and give it capacity](/tasks/add-a-cluster/): the same ground as a task, with the dashboard and agent paths alongside the CLI. - [Nodes and cluster topology](/concepts/06-nodes-and-cluster-topology/): what a node is, and what stays constant when a cluster changes shape. - [Remove an application and its data](/tasks/remove-an-application/): the removal that takes the storage with it. - [CLI: Environments](/cli/environments/): the control cluster's own lifecycle.

sections.title: Databases
sections.body:
The `db` topic covers working with a Flui database building
block from your own machine: with `psql` or pgAdmin for
Postgres, `mariadb` or DBeaver for MariaDB, `redis-cli` for
Valkey/Redis, or your application's ORM. A Flui database is an
application running in the cluster, so it is identified the
same way as any other.

Flui databases are not exposed outside the cluster network, so
there is no public endpoint to point a client at. The commands
on this page work around that, and fall into three jobs:

- **Connect.** [`flui db credentials`](#flui-db-credentials-app)
  prints the in-cluster address and credentials, which another
  app running on Flui uses.
  [`flui db tunnel`](#flui-db-tunnel-app) opens a temporary
  local tunnel so a client on your machine can connect.
- **Copy the data out, and back.**
  [`flui db dump`](#flui-db-dump-app) streams a dump to a file
  or to a backup destination;
  [`flui db restore`](#flui-db-restore-app-file) runs one back
  into the live database.
- **Check it is still healthy.**
  [`flui db disk`](#flui-db-disk-app) shows how full the storage
  is, [`flui db backup-status`](#flui-db-backup-status-app) shows
  how far back you can recover, and
  [`flui db pitr-restore`](#flui-db-pitr-restore-app) rebuilds
  a Postgres database as of a moment in time.
- **See who is connected to a managed PostgreSQL.**
  [`flui db pooler`](#flui-db-pooler-app) shows its connection
  pooler and the two addresses applications use;
  [`flui db sessions`](#flui-db-sessions-db) lists the sessions and
  stops one.

If you would rather not install a local client, the dashboard
has an in-browser console for the same databases; see
[The database console](/concepts/25-the-database-console/).
For the steps rather than the flags, read
[Open a database from your
machine](/tasks/open-a-database/).

## Two shapes of command

The `db` commands are not all addressed the same way, and
knowing which is which saves you a confusing error.

`credentials` and `tunnel` resolve the database by name, slug or
id, and take `-c, --cluster <name|id>` to say where to look
(auto-detected when the active profile has only one cluster).
Both read the password straight from the cluster over SSH, never
from the API.

`dump`, `restore`, `disk`, `backup-status` and `pitr-restore`
go straight to the API with the application's id, which
`flui app list` prints. They have no `-c, --cluster` flag,
because the id already says which cluster the database is on
(`pitr-restore` has a `--cluster` of its own, for where the
copy goes).

`pooler` and `sessions` sit in between. They take the database's
name or id, find it, and then ask the API. Neither reads a
password. `pooler` looks a name up on every cluster unless you
pass `-c, --cluster`. `sessions` looks it up on one cluster: the
one you pass with `-c, --cluster`, or the only one your profile
has.

Every one of them checks access first. Owning the database is
not enough by itself: you need a grant that reaches it, and an
agent key is held to its own limits before the database is even
looked up. See
[Who is allowed to open
one](/tasks/open-a-database/#who-is-allowed-to-open-one).

## `flui db credentials <app>`

Shows how to connect to a Flui database: the in-cluster service
address and its credentials, plus a ready-to-copy
`DATABASE_URL`. This is the connection information for another
app running on Flui in the same cluster. The host is the
in-cluster address, not a public one.

The password is read from the cluster over SSH and is hidden by
default. Pass `--show` to print it in plaintext.

```bash
flui db credentials postgresql-051f58
flui db credentials postgresql-051f58 --show
flui db credentials postgresql-051f58 --show --hide-after 30
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-c, --cluster <name\|id>` | auto-detect | Cluster to resolve the database in. |
| `--show` | off | Print the password in plaintext (hidden otherwise). |
| `--hide-after <seconds>` | `0` | Opt-in optical wipe: hold the terminal for N seconds with a countdown, then erase the password from the screen. Only takes effect together with `--show` on a TTY; `0` returns immediately. |

To connect a native client from your own machine, use
`flui db tunnel` instead. The in-cluster host shown here is not
reachable from outside the cluster.

## `flui db tunnel <app>`

Opens a local tunnel to a Flui database so you can connect a
native client. Because Flui databases are not exposed outside
the cluster, the command forwards the connection through the
