One workstation can drive several installations, and the worst
mistake that allows is a command that works perfectly on the wrong
one.

So the commands that act on an installation as a whole print a line
before their output, naming where they are about to act:

```
┌─ context production · api https://api.example.com/api/v1
```

`context` is the active profile. `api` is the installation that
profile points at, or a yellow `(not set)`, which is normal for a
profile you have just created and not yet pointed at anything. Some
commands add the target cluster's provider and region on the same
line.

Not every command prints it. The banner appears on the families whose
reach is the installation itself: `env`, `backup`, `migrate`, `dns`,
`catalog` and a few more. Elsewhere, `flui context show` names the
active profile.

## Profiles on disk

A profile is one installation as this machine sees it: its API
address, its credentials, and its local view of what that
installation holds. Everything the CLI keeps lives under `~/.flui`:

```
~/.flui/
├── context              # the name of the active profile
├── vault.json           # the vault header, one per machine
└── profiles/
    ├── default/
    └── production/
```

Each profile directory holds:

- `config.json`: your preferences in plain text, plus the sealed
  values (the provider credentials you stored and the API key
  `auth login` saved).
- `ca/`: the trust material this profile uses to reach cluster
  nodes.
- `clusters.json`, `nodes.json`, `firewalls.json`, `vnets.json`,
  `operations.json`: a local copy of what the installation last told
  the CLI. You can delete these; the next command that needs them
  fetches them again.

The directories and files are created readable by their owner only.

Switching profiles is local and instant. Nothing in any cluster
notices; the CLI reads a different directory from then on.

```bash
flui context list                    # every profile, active marked *
flui context show                    # just the active name
flui context create staging --switch # create it and switch
flui context use default             # switch back
flui context delete staging          # warns only; -f deletes
```

`default` is created on first run and cannot be deleted, and neither
can the active profile. Names accept letters, digits, hyphens and
underscores. `FLUI_PROFILE` overrides the active profile for one
command without switching.

Nothing operational crosses between profiles. A provider token saved
in one is not visible from another, and the keys that seal them are
different. A command typed in the wrong profile cannot reach another
installation, because it does not hold the credentials.

If you only run one installation from this machine, the auto-created
`default` profile is enough and you can skip this section.

## Where to go next

- [Get Flui running](/tasks/get-flui-running/): the first
  installation, step by step, including the case where you are taking
  over one somebody else provisioned.
- [Deploy an application](/tasks/deploy-an-application/): including
  the one-off GitHub and registry connections the first source-built
  deploy needs.
- [Multi-context](/concepts/07-multi-context-cli/): why one
  workstation driving several installations is a different problem
  from one installation driving several clusters.
- [Profiles and config](/cli/profiles-and-config/): the layered
  configuration, provider credentials, and the full profile
  reference.
- [Authentication](/cli/authentication/): the login flags and the
  environment variables that override the active key.
- [Connect an agent](/tasks/connect-an-agent/): what to do with a
  scoped key once you have minted one.

sections.title: CLI Reference
sections.body:
A Flui installation has three surfaces: this CLI, the
dashboard, and the API both of them call. The CLI comes
first. When you create the control cluster there is no
dashboard yet, since the dashboard runs on the control
cluster, so the first command is typed here or run for you
by [app.flui.cloud](https://app.flui.cloud).

After that the three surfaces mostly do the same work, and
which one you use is a matter of taste. The overlap is not
complete, though, in either direction:

- **Only the CLI** creates and destroys the control cluster
  (`flui env create`, `flui env destroy`; app.flui.cloud
  creates one by running that same command), holds the vault
  that protects credentials on your own machine
  (`flui vault`), takes over an installation someone else
  provisioned (`flui env adopt`), and clears the provider
  resources an abandoned provisioning run left behind
  (`flui env scrub`). Those last three work from what is
  stored on your own machine (the vault, the profile, the
  provider credentials), which a browser cannot reach.
  `flui env scrub` does not call the API at all: it goes
  straight to the provider, because the installation it would
  have asked was never finished.
- **Only the dashboard and the API** answer an agent's paused
  write. When an agent asks for something that stops to ask a
  person, the person answers in the dashboard or through the
  API; there is no `flui` command for it. The same goes for
  minting an agent key by permission group:
  `flui auth generate-api-key` takes raw scopes or
  `--unscoped`, and has no group flag.

This page is a map of what exists. For how to do a
particular job (deploy an app, open a database, connect an
agent), see the [task pages](/tasks/), which show the same
job on each surface that can do it.

## How the CLI is organised

Commands are grouped into topics such as `app`, `env`,
`backup` and `iam`. Each topic owns a set of verbs
that act on the same kind of thing: `flui app logs`,
`flui env create`, `flui iam grant add`.

Some topics group their verbs one level deeper, when the
topic covers more than one kind of object:
`flui backup policy list`, `flui migrate db create`,
`flui gateway routes add`.

Every command has `--help`, which prints its usage, its
flags and its examples. `flui <topic> --help` lists the verbs
in that topic, and `flui --help` lists every topic. That
built-in help is generated from the CLI itself, so it is
never out of date. When this page and `--help` disagree,
`--help` is right.

## Topics

| Topic | What it does | Read more |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `alerts` | Where this installation sends its alerts besides the dashboard (an email address or a signed webhook), and whether administrators also get warnings. | [Alerts, audit and costs](/cli/alerts-audit-and-costs/#alerts) |
| `app` | Everything about a running application: status, logs, metrics, HTTP traffic, alerts and crash reports; scale, restart, stop and start; releases, image versions and redeploys; volume snapshots and backups; scheduled jobs; variables; delete. | [Applications](/cli/applications/) |
| `audit` | Who did what on this installation: every change, every refusal and every read of application data. | [Alerts, audit and costs](/cli/alerts-audit-and-costs/#flui-audit-list) |
| `auth` | Sign in through the browser, mint and revoke API keys, and list the keys you hold. | [Authentication](/cli/authentication/) |
| `backup` | Protect a whole cluster or one application, answer what needs a decision, manage destinations, policies and jobs, plus the platform's own backup setup. The `app backup` volume snapshots are documented on the same page. | [Backups](/cli/backups/) |
| `catalog` | List what this installation can install, install it, check how an install is going, and validate a manifest. | [Deploy](/cli/deploy/) |
| `cluster` | Create a workload cluster, list every cluster, rebuild one, recover access to it, manage the Flui firewall on its machines, destroy a workload cluster, and list storage left behind by applications that no longer exist. | [Clusters and nodes](/cli/clusters-and-nodes/) |
| `config` | Layered configuration: preferences, and the provider credentials the CLI keeps encrypted. | [Profiles and config](/cli/profiles-and-config/) |
| `context` | Profiles: create, list, switch and delete the installations this workstation talks to. | [Profiles and config](/cli/profiles-and-config/) |
| `db` | Reach a Flui database from your machine: credentials, a local tunnel, dumps and restores, disk usage, continuous-backup state, point-in-time restore. | [Databases](/cli/databases/) |
| `demo` | The self-running cross-provider migration demonstration an installation can perform on itself. | `flui demo --help` |
| `dev` | Helpers for people working on Flui itself, not for operating an installation. | [Dev tools](/cli/dev-tools/) |
| `dns` | The zones a cluster publishes under, the single wildcard record that covers all of its applications, and second-provider replicas. | `flui dns --help` |
| `env` | The control cluster's whole life: create, status, capacity, storage, scale, firewall, stop and restart, reinstall, upgrade, adopt, scrub, destroy. | [Environments](/cli/environments/) |
| `gateway` | Named routes at the edge of an application, and the policies on them: sign-in, rate limits, IP allowlists. | `flui gateway --help` |
| `iam` | Who can reach what: grants, groups, the built-in roles, your own effective permissions, and the policy file. | `flui iam --help` |
| `inference` | What the assistant and the console copilots have spent, by model and by person. | [Alerts, audit and costs](/cli/alerts-audit-and-costs/#flui-inference-usage) |
| `integration` | Connect GitHub for the installation and for your own account, and manage the token used to pull images. | [Integrations](/cli/integrations/) |
| `mail` | Connect mail providers, register sending domains, check what still blocks a message, send, and read delivery outcomes and suppressions. | `flui mail --help` |
| `migrate` | Move a database, an application, or both together, to another cluster: create, cut over, abort, destroy the source. | `flui migrate --help` |
| `network` | The private networks of this installation, and creating one on a provider that needs it before a cluster. | [Clusters and nodes](/cli/clusters-and-nodes/#flui-network-create) |
| `node` | Join a machine you already own, list nodes, read a node's logs, remove a machine you joined. | [Clusters and nodes](/cli/clusters-and-nodes/) |
| `operating-context` | Write down how this installation is run, so people and agents read it before acting. | `flui operating-context --help` |
| `repo` | Connect, list and disconnect the repositories this installation can deploy from. | [Integrations](/cli/integrations/) |
| `sandbox` | The guest areas of a demonstration installation: what is being held, and ending one now. | `flui sandbox --help` |
| `scaling` | What a cluster may buy for itself and where it must stop, what it decided, and what it would decide right now. | `flui scaling --help` |
| `server-types` | The machine sizes a provider offers. | [Clusters and nodes](/cli/clusters-and-nodes/) |
| `showcase` | Publish an application to the showcase (the short list this installation puts in front of other people), or take it back out. | [Alerts, audit and costs](/cli/alerts-audit-and-costs/#showcase) |
| `template` | Start a new repository from a Flui framework template. | [Templates](/cli/templates/) |
| `vault` | The passphrase that protects the credentials this CLI stores on your machine. | [Profiles and config](/cli/profiles-and-config/) |

Seven commands sit at the top level, outside any topic:

| Command | What it does | Read more |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `flui costs` | What your clusters cost, spent and forecast, month by month and provider by provider. | `flui costs --help` |
| `flui deploy` | Deploy an application from a `flui.yaml` manifest. | [Deploy](/cli/deploy/) |
| `flui operation <id>` | Show an infrastructure operation, such as a cluster being created or a node being added, and follow it to the end. | `flui operation --help` |
| `flui reconcile` | Bring the CLI's local DNS state back in line with the API. | [Utilities](/cli/utilities/) |
| `flui ssh` | Open a shell on a cluster node. | [Clusters and nodes](/cli/clusters-and-nodes/) |
| `flui update` | Update the CLI itself. | [Utilities](/cli/utilities/) |
| `flui version` | The CLI version, and the platform release it pins. | [Utilities](/cli/utilities/) |

Where the "read more" column says `--help`, there is no
hand-written page for that topic, and the command's own help
is the reference.

## Common conventions

A few flags recur across the CLI:

- **`-c, --cluster <name|id>`**: pick the target cluster on
  the commands that act on one. When the installation has a
  single cluster, it is detected for you.
- **`-o, --output <format>`**: switch between human and
  machine-readable output. The exact set varies by command,
  but `json` is there for scripting; the human format is
  `table` or `text` depending on the command's shape.
- **`--no-wait` / `--detach` / `-d, --detached`**: on
  commands that start long work, return as soon as the job
  is queued instead of blocking until it finishes.
- **`-f, --force` / `-y, --yes`**: skip the confirmation on
  a destructive command.
- **`--dry-run`**: on a subset of commands, print what
  would happen and change nothing.

Commands that talk to the API first print a short context
banner with the active profile and the API URL, so you always
know which installation you are operating on.

## Profiles on disk

The CLI keeps each installation's state under
`~/.flui/profiles/<name>/`. A profile holds the API key, the
provider credentials, the SSH trust root used to reach
cluster nodes, and the local view of clusters, nodes,
firewalls and operations that installation knows about.
The active profile is named in `~/.flui/context`, and
`FLUI_PROFILE` overrides it for one command.

Credentials in a profile are protected by a vault at
`~/.flui/vault.json`. One vault covers every profile: you
choose the passphrase once with `flui vault init`, open it
for a session with `flui vault unlock`, and close it with
`flui vault lock`. Profiles still get their own derived
keys, so two accounts stay apart behind one passphrase.

To switch installations, run `flui context use <name>`.
Every command after that targets the new profile.

sections.title: Integrations and repositories
sections.body:
Source-built applications (`kind: Application`) need three things on a
fresh installation before the first deploy:

1. The **GitHub integration**, configured once on the installation by
   the operator. Two modes are supported: a **Personal Access Token**
   (recommended) or a **GitHub App**.
2. Your own **user connection** to GitHub, once per Flui user. In PAT
   mode you paste your own classic PAT. In App mode you install the App
   on your account or organisation.
3. The **repository** itself, imported into your Flui account.

Two CLI topics cover this, and they answer different questions.

**`flui integration …`: is Flui connected to GitHub?**
[`setup github`](#flui-integration-setup-github) and
[`reset github`](#flui-integration-reset-github) are the operator's
once-per-installation commands.
[`connect github`](#flui-integration-connect-github) is the
once-per-user one.
[`status github`](#flui-integration-status-github) and
[`list`](#flui-integration-list) show where you stand, and
[`ghcr-pat set|status|revoke`](#ghcr-pat-app-mode-only) manages the
credential that pulls the images Flui builds.

**`flui repo connect | list | disconnect`: which repositories may be
deployed?** This is a separate step, and the one people forget.
Connecting GitHub lets Flui see your repositories but does not import
any of them. A repository has to be connected before `flui deploy`
touches it, and disconnecting it stops future deploys without changing
anything on GitHub. See [Repositories](#repositories).

The dashboard has the same flows under
*Apps → Repositories → GitHub setup*. CatalogApps (`kind: CatalogApp`)
skip every step: they pull a pre-built image from a public registry,
with no source repository on the install side.

## Choosing a mode

| | Personal Access Token | GitHub App |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identity used to talk to GitHub | Your own user | Bot identity owned by the App |
| Per-user setup | Paste a classic PAT | Install the App on your account / org |
| Can register webhooks | Yes, the PAT grants `admin:repo_hook` | Yes, with the App |
| Org policies that block PATs | May block the PAT entirely | Unaffected |
| Container registry (GHCR) | The same PAT covers cloning *and* pulling images | Needs a separate per-user PAT (see [GHCR PAT](#ghcr-pat-app-mode-only)) |
| Recommended for | Most installations, including your own | Teams that want one shared bot identity |

On an installation that keeps images in its own registry (see
[Where the image is kept](/concepts/20-build-pipeline-today-and-tomorrow/#where-the-image-is-kept)),
neither mode needs a token for images. The GitHub App then needs
nothing beyond the one-click install, and `flui integration list`
shows the GHCR token as not needed.

A Personal Access Token is the recommended path: nothing has to be
registered on GitHub, one token covers repositories and images, and
each person connects in a minute. Choose a GitHub App when a team wants
one shared identity instead of personal tokens, or when an
organisation's policy blocks personal access tokens.

Registering webhooks does not by itself make a push go live. See
[A push does not redeploy on its own](#a-push-does-not-redeploy-on-its-own).

## A push does not redeploy on its own

GitHub calls Flui back when a build finishes, in both App mode and PAT
mode. What Flui does with that call depends on the application.

An application's first deploy always goes live once the build
succeeds.

For an application that is already running, a later push redeploys
automatically only if that application has **auto-deploy on push**
turned on, and by default it does not. Otherwise the finished build is
recorded as an available image and nothing rolls out.
`flui app versions <app>` marks that image `unreleased`, and you
deploy it yourself with `flui app redeploy <app> <target>` (a tag, a
digest, or `--build <id>`). See
[Release management](/cli/applications/#release-management) in the
applications reference.

The setting is per application, not installation-wide.
`flui app auto-deploy <app>` shows it, and `--on` or `--off` changes
it; see
[`flui app auto-deploy`](/cli/applications/#flui-app-auto-deploy-name).
If a push did not roll out, check `flui app versions` for an
unreleased build waiting for you.

## Setup (operator, once per installation)

### `flui integration setup github`

Interactive setup that walks the operator through either mode.
Admin only.

```bash
flui integration setup github
flui integration setup github --headless     # print URLs instead of opening a browser
```

If the integration is already configured, the command asks before
overwriting. Run `flui integration reset github` first if you want a
clean slate.

#### Personal Access Token branch (recommended)

The command opens GitHub's token-creation page with the required
scopes pre-filled, then validates the token against GitHub before
saving it. Missing scopes are reported inline, so you know what to
fix.

Scopes requested:

- `repo`: clone and push private repositories
- `workflow`: commit `.github/workflows/flui.yml` on first deploy
- `user:email`: identify the user
- `admin:repo_hook`: register webhooks
- `write:packages`, `read:packages`, `delete:packages`: push, pull
  and clean up images on GHCR

The same token covers the repository side and the GHCR side, so PAT
mode has no separate GHCR step.

A fine-grained token works too, and can be limited to the
repositories you choose. Give it, on those repositories: Contents
and Workflows *Read and write*, Secrets *Read and write*, Actions
*Read-only*. It cannot reach GitHub's container registry, so it is
enough only on an installation that keeps images in its own
registry (see
[Where the image is kept](/concepts/20-build-pipeline-today-and-tomorrow/#where-the-image-is-kept)).
Elsewhere use a classic token with the scopes above.

#### GitHub App branch

The command builds a [GitHub App manifest](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/sharing-github-apps/registering-a-github-app-from-a-manifest),
opens GitHub with the App name and all permissions pre-filled, and
waits for you to confirm. When you click *Create*, GitHub redirects
back to the API, which exchanges the temporary code for the final App
credentials and stores them.

The command asks for:

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| App name | Must be unique across GitHub. Defaults to `flui-<hostname>`. |
| Flui public URL | Base URL of this Flui API as reachable from `github.com`. Callback, manifest redirect and (if enabled) webhook URL are all derived from this. For local development behind a tunnel, use the tunnel URL. |
| Enable webhooks for deploy-on-push? | Off by default. Whether a push redeploys a running application is decided per application; see [A push does not redeploy on its own](#a-push-does-not-redeploy-on-its-own). |
| Allow install on other accounts / organizations? | Off by default (only the owner account can install). Turn on if Flui needs repos under multiple accounts or orgs. |

After you confirm, the credentials (App ID, slug, Client ID, Client
Secret, Webhook Secret, private-key PEM) are stored in Flui, with
nothing to copy and paste.

### Equivalent dashboard flow

Open *Apps → Repositories → GitHub setup* in the dashboard for the
same choice of two cards (PAT, or App via manifest). The dashboard
polls the API the same way and the resulting configuration is
identical. Under the App card, an "I already have a GitHub App"
disclosure lets you enter existing App credentials instead of running
the manifest flow.

## User connection

### `flui integration connect github`

The command asks the installation which mode it uses and follows it.

In PAT mode it opens GitHub's token page with the required scopes,
asks for your classic PAT, validates it and connects it. In a script,
pipe the token in with `--stdin` instead of typing it, so it never
appears on the command line. If you are already connected it says so,
and `--stdin` replaces the token.

In App mode it opens the browser so you can install the Flui GitHub
App on your account or organisation, and waits for the local callback.
The same round trip also performs the OAuth grant your user needs to
commit `.github/workflows/flui.yml` on first deploy.

```bash
flui integration connect github
printf %s "$GITHUB_TOKEN" | flui integration connect github --stdin   # PAT mode, scripted
flui integration connect github --headless     # print URLs instead of opening a browser
```

If the integration is not configured, the command exits with a hint
that an administrator must run `flui integration setup github` first,
instead of showing the raw API error.

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--stdin` | PAT mode: read the token from standard input rather than prompting. |
| `--headless` | Print the URL instead of opening one. Useful over SSH. |

The callback uses the same ports as `flui auth login`: 8899, then
8900, 8901, 8902 and 8910.

### `flui integration list`

Lists the third-party integrations configured for your account,
whether each is connected, and the state of the GHCR PAT.

```bash
flui integration list
```

`github` is the only provider the topic accepts.

## Status and health

### `flui integration status github`

Shows the active mode (App or PAT), runs a live health check against
GitHub (administrators see the result) and, in PAT mode, prints your
own user connection state.

```bash
flui integration status github
```

Sample output (App mode):

```
  Instance configuration
    Mode:          github_app
    App slug:      flui-acme
    Health:        ✔ App auth ok — 2 installations
```

Sample output (PAT mode):

```
  Instance configuration
    Mode:          pat
    Health:        ✔ PAT mode enabled (per-user credentials)

  Your connection
    Authenticated: @acme-dev
    Scopes:        repo user:email admin:repo_hook write:packages …
```

When the health check fails (App deleted on GitHub, credentials
revoked, network unreachable), the output flags it and the dashboard
shows a banner with the same information.

## Reset

### `flui integration reset github`

Removes the instance-wide GitHub configuration and every per-user
token and App installation Flui has on file. Use it to switch modes
(from App to PAT or back) or to start over after a bad registration.
Admin only.

```bash
flui integration reset github             # type "reset" to confirm
flui integration reset github --yes       # skip the confirmation (CI / scripts)
```

The App on `github.com` is not uninstalled. Uninstall it there if you
want to clean up the GitHub side too.

After a reset, run `flui integration setup github` to configure a new
integration. Every user then reconnects.

## GHCR PAT (App mode only)

In App mode, the App's bot token cannot pull container packages from
`ghcr.io` (see
[community discussion #34084](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/34084)),
so each user stores a small classic PAT scoped only for packages. PAT
mode skips this step, because the main PAT already grants the package
scopes.

### `flui integration ghcr-pat set`

Saves or replaces the GHCR PAT for your user.

```bash
flui integration ghcr-pat set
flui integration ghcr-pat set --headless     # print the token-creation URL
```

The command opens GitHub's token-creation page with `read:packages`
and `delete:packages` pre-filled. The first is required (or
`write:packages` instead); the second lets Flui clean up old images.
Paste the token at the masked prompt and pick an expiry, 90 days by
default. Flui warns you 14 days before it expires.

### `flui integration ghcr-pat status`

Shows the stored token's login, scopes, days until expiry, when it
was rotated and when it was last verified. Status values: `VALID`,
`EXPIRING_SOON`, `EXPIRED`, `INVALID`, `UNKNOWN_EXPIRY`. With no
token stored it says *not configured*.

```bash
flui integration ghcr-pat status
```

### `flui integration ghcr-pat revoke`

Deletes the stored PAT from Flui. It does not revoke the token on
GitHub; do that at `https://github.com/settings/tokens`. After
revoking, `flui deploy` refuses to run until a new PAT is set.

```bash
flui integration ghcr-pat revoke
flui integration ghcr-pat revoke --yes
```

## The installation's image registry

These commands apply to an installation created with
`--image-registry flui`, which keeps built images in a registry of
its own. They need the permission to manage integrations.

### `flui registry storage status`

Shows where the registry keeps images, the space they take and the
applications that take the most, and the bucket it is connected to.

```bash
flui registry storage status
flui registry storage status --measure    # measure now instead of showing the last measurement
flui registry storage status --json
```

The space is measured every 30 minutes. The total counts each layer
once, however many applications share it; the size shown for an
application counts its shared layers too. Administrators get an
alert when the space passes a threshold: 80% of the volume, or 50 GiB
on a bucket, which never fills but is paid by the GiB.

### `flui registry storage connect`

Connects the registry to a bucket. On an installation created with
`--image-registry-storage s3`, the registry moves to it right away.

```bash
flui registry storage connect scaleway --region fr-par
flui registry storage connect s3 --provider ovh_object_storage \
  --endpoint https://s3.gra.io.cloud.ovh.net --region gra \
  --bucket flui-registry --access-key <access key id>
```

`scaleway` needs nothing else: Flui uses the Scaleway connection the
installation already has to create a project for the registry, a
bucket in it, and a key whose only permission is object storage in
that project, so it cannot open your backup buckets. It can take a
few minutes, while Scaleway applies the new permissions.

`s3` connects a bucket of your own. Give it a key that reaches only
that bucket. The secret key is asked at a masked prompt, or read
from standard input with `--stdin`. Flui writes and deletes a test
file before it accepts the bucket.

Images already in the registry are not copied to the new bucket. An
application whose image is not there anymore needs a new build
before it can start somewhere else.

### `flui registry storage list`

Lists the buckets the registry has been connected to: the one in use
and the ones it replaced.

### `flui registry storage remove <id>`

Removes a bucket the registry no longer uses. A bucket Flui created
is deleted with the images in it, together with the project and the
key made for it. A bucket of your own is only forgotten, and what it
holds stays. The bucket in use cannot be removed.

```bash
flui registry storage remove 3f2c9a1e-…
flui registry storage remove 3f2c9a1e-… --yes
```

## Admin diagnostics

### `flui integration installations`

Lists every GitHub App installation Flui tracks, which helps when
diagnosing a stale or duplicated record. It shows the numeric
`installationId` that `remove-installation` needs.

```bash
flui integration installations
```

### `flui integration remove-installation <installationId>`

Removes an installation record from the Flui database. It does not
uninstall the App on GitHub. Uninstall it there first, otherwise the
next webhook creates the record again.

```bash
flui integration remove-installation 12345678
flui integration remove-installation 12345678 --yes
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-y, --yes` | Skip the confirmation prompt. |

Get the ID from `flui integration installations`.

## Repositories

### `flui repo connect [<owner/repo>]`

Imports a repository into your Flui account so `flui deploy` can
deploy it. Pass the full `owner/repo` slug, or leave it out for an
interactive picker over the repositories the connected integration
can reach.

```bash
flui repo connect acme/my-app
flui repo connect                              # interactive picker
```

The repository must be visible to whichever side is connected: the
GitHub App installation in App mode, or the PAT's permissions in PAT
mode. If the picker does not show it, run
`flui integration connect github` again and add the repository on the
GitHub install page (App mode), or issue the PAT again with broader
access (PAT mode). `flui deploy` on a repository that is not imported
is refused with
`Repository "<owner>/<repo>" is not connected to your account`. In a
terminal, if your credential reaches the repository, it offers to
connect it on the spot and retries. Otherwise it tells you to run this
command.

### `flui repo list`

Lists the repositories already connected to your Flui account.

```bash
flui repo list
flui repo list --output json
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-o, --output text\|json` | `text` | Output format. |

### `flui repo disconnect <owner/repo>`

Removes the repository from your Flui account. It requires admin
privileges and asks for confirmation; pass `-y, --yes` to skip the
prompt. The repository on GitHub is not touched.

```bash
flui repo disconnect acme/my-app
flui repo disconnect acme/my-app --yes
```

A disconnected repository cannot be deployed until you connect it
again with `flui repo connect`.

## Reading and deploying from the map

Two more commands answer a different question from the three above.
Instead of whether a repository is connected, they show what it says
about itself and whether it can be deployed as it stands. The full
model is in
[How Flui reads a repository](/concepts/30-how-flui-reads-a-repository/).

### `flui repo map show <repository>`

Reads a connected repository without cloning it, refuses symlinks,
and reports the limits it applied to the read. It prints the
deployable units, the services they want, the variables they need,
blockers, caveats, open questions, a verdict, and the `flui.yaml` Flui
would render for each unit. Every fact comes with its own `file:line`
and how confident Flui is in it. The command is read-only: nothing is
deployed, provisioned, written or committed.

```bash
flui repo map show acme/shop
flui repo map show acme/shop --branch develop
flui repo map show acme/shop --unit api
flui repo map show acme/shop --output json
```

`<repository>` takes `owner/repo`, a full GitHub URL, or the
repository's own id.

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-b, --branch <ref>` | Git ref to read. Defaults to the repository's default branch. |
| `-c, --cluster <name\|id>` | Weigh the map against this cluster. Half the verdict is capacity, so a cluster is always chosen, automatically when there is only one. |
| `-u, --unit <id>` | Show only this unit (its id, `.` for the repository root). |
| `-o, --output text\|json` | `json` prints the whole response, untouched. |

The command has no client-side timeout. A large repository takes a
while to read, and a client that gave up before the server did would
report a failure that never happened.

### `flui repo map apply <repository>`

Acts on the map. Flui creates its own branch, `flui/deploy-<sha7>`, at
the exact commit the map was read from, and adds one commit to it with
a rendered `flui.yaml` and a build workflow per unit. That commit
starts the builds. Flui reads your branch and branches from it, but
never writes to it.

```bash
flui repo map apply acme/shop
flui repo map apply acme/shop --unit api --unit web
flui repo map apply acme/shop --branch develop --yes
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-b, --branch <ref>` | The branch to read and cut from. Defaults to the repository's default branch. Never written to. |
| `-c, --cluster <name\|id>` | Cluster the applications are created on. |
| `-u, --unit <id>` | Apply only this unit; repeat for several. Without it, every rendered unit is applied. |
| `-y, --yes` | Skip the confirmation prompt. |
| `-o, --output text\|json` | Output format. |

Run `flui repo map show` first. An apply is refused when the verdict
is `blocked`, `insufficient_capacity` or `not_assessed`. Read what the
map objected to instead of spending your repository's Actions minutes
to reach the same conclusion.

If a unit's manifest declares `deploy.services`, that service is
installed from the catalog and Flui waits for it to reach `RUNNING`
before anything is committed to GitHub. The wait takes minutes, which
is why this command, like `flui repo map show`, sets no client-side
timeout of its own.

## First-deploy flow, end to end

For an `Application` repository on a fresh installation, the operator
runs:

```bash
flui auth login                              # OIDC against the installation
flui integration setup github                # one-time: configure App or PAT
```

Then every user runs, in PAT mode (the recommended one):

```bash
flui auth login                              # OIDC, once per machine
flui integration connect github              # paste your classic PAT
flui repo connect acme/my-app            # import the repo
flui deploy                                  # build via GitHub Actions, roll out
```

The same PAT covers cloning and GHCR pulls, so there is no separate
image-registry step. On a single-user install the operator already
connected their PAT during setup, so only the last two lines remain.

In App mode, every user runs instead:

```bash
flui auth login                              # OIDC, once per machine
flui integration connect github              # install the Flui App on your account
flui integration ghcr-pat set                # required for the cluster to pull built images
flui repo connect acme/my-app            # import the repo
flui deploy                                  # build via GitHub Actions, roll out
```

After the first deploy of a repository, later rollouts need only
`flui deploy`. Replace your PAT before it expires by piping the new
one to `flui integration connect github --stdin` (PAT mode), or rotate
the GHCR PAT with another `flui integration ghcr-pat set` (App mode).

sections.title: Profiles and config
sections.body:
The CLI keeps all its local state under `~/.flui/` and has three
related topics for it:

- **Profiles** (`context` topic). Each profile is one isolated
  Flui installation on this machine, with its own API URL,
  credentials and local inventory of clusters, nodes and firewalls.
- **The vault** (`vault` topic). One passphrase per machine that
  seals every stored credential, in every profile.
- **Configuration** (`config` topic). A layered resolver that
  decides the value of each preference and stores provider
  credentials, always inside the active profile.

If you only run one installation from this machine, the
auto-created `default` profile is enough and you can ignore the
`context` topic. You use `config` whenever you change an email, add
a provider credential, or want to know why a preference has the
value it has. You use the vault once to create it, then once per
session to open it.

## Profiles

A profile is a directory `~/.flui/profiles/<name>/`. The CLI creates
`default` on first run and remembers the active one in
`~/.flui/context`. Switching profile only changes local state. The
cluster is not involved; the CLI points every following command at
a different installation.

### Commands

```bash
flui context list                    # all profiles, active one marked
flui context show                    # name of the active profile
flui context create staging          # create a new profile
flui context create staging --switch # create and switch in one go
flui context use prod                # switch to an existing profile
flui context delete staging          # warns, deletes nothing
flui context delete staging --force  # deletes it
```

Profile names accept alphanumeric characters, hyphens, and
underscores. The `default` profile and the active one cannot be
deleted.

## The vault

Stored credentials are encrypted. A key kept in the profile
directory, next to the data it protects, would give anyone who can
read the folder both halves, so the key comes from a passphrase
you know and this machine does not keep. That is the vault. There
is one per workstation, and it covers every profile.

```bash
flui vault init      # once per machine, before storing anything
flui vault unlock    # once per session
flui vault status    # is it open, and for how long
flui vault lock      # close it now
```

`flui vault init` creates the vault and asks for a passphrase
twice. It suggests a five-word one. The passphrase is never stored,
cannot be derived from anything and cannot be reset, so losing it
means losing every credential this machine has sealed. Write it
down when you create it. If a vault already exists, `init` refuses
to overwrite it, because that would make every sealed credential
unreadable.

`flui vault unlock` asks for the passphrase once and then leaves a
small background helper holding the key for the session. That
helper is `flui vault agent`. It is a command only because that is
how the CLI starts a copy of itself; it is hidden from help and you
never run it by hand. It receives the passphrase through a pipe
rather than as an argument, so the passphrase never appears in the
process list.

Each profile has its own key, derived from the passphrase and the
profile's name. A command working in `staging` cannot open
`prod`'s stored credentials.

The session closes on its own after thirty minutes of inactivity,
and after eight hours in any case. Both limits are in minutes and
can be changed:

| Variable | Default |
| --- | --- |
| `FLUI_VAULT_IDLE_MINUTES` | `30` |
| `FLUI_VAULT_MAX_MINUTES` | `480` |

Any value that is not a positive whole number falls back to the
default, so a typo cannot make a session permanent. `flui vault
unlock --idle-minutes <n> --max-minutes <n>` sets them for one
session.

`flui vault status` tells you whether a vault exists, whether it is
open, and how long each of those two clocks has left. `--format
json` prints the same answer as `{ initialised, unlocked, location,
idleRemainingMs, lifeRemainingMs }`. It also warns you if other
users on this machine can reach the helper's socket. Keeping that
socket private is the only thing that keeps them away from the key.

`flui vault lock` overwrites the key in memory and stops the
helper. On a machine where nothing is open, it says so and does
nothing.

A locked vault does not make every command fail. Most commands
read a preference or an API URL, both plain text, and never ask for
the passphrase. Only a command that opens a stored credential
stops. It then says the vault is locked and names
`flui vault unlock`, instead of reporting a decryption failure that
would send you looking for corrupt data.

### An upgrade locks nobody out

A profile that still holds the older `.key` file keeps working
as before, so updating the CLI does not strand credentials you
already have. The first `flui vault unlock` re-seals those
profiles under the vault and deletes the old key file. Each entry
is rewritten under the new key before the old one is removed, so an
interrupted move loses nothing, and it reports how many secrets it
moved. A profile it cannot move is left as it is, with a warning
naming it.

### Without a terminal

Both `flui vault init` and `flui vault unlock` take `--stdin` and
read the passphrase from standard input instead of prompting. Use
it in scripts. Without a terminal, both commands refuse to prompt
and tell you to use `--stdin`.

```bash
printf 'my passphrase' | flui vault init --stdin
printf 'my passphrase' | flui vault unlock --stdin
```

Some callers have no terminal and no home directory that outlives
the run, such as a provisioning worker. For them, setting
`FLUI_PROFILE_KEY` to 32 bytes of base64 gives the CLI a profile
key directly, and no vault is used:

```bash
export FLUI_PROFILE_KEY="$(openssl rand -base64 32)"
```

The key then lives only in whatever started the CLI. Anything the
run sealed can no longer be opened once that caller forgets the
key. A value that is present but malformed is an error; the CLI
does not fall back to anything else.

## Layered configuration

`flui config` reads and writes preferences and credentials. Every
value goes through a cascade, and the first layer that has a value
wins:

```
explicit CLI input  >  env var  >  ./flui.config.json  >  user-global config.json (active profile)  >  schema default
```

`./flui.config.json` is an optional file in the directory you run
the command from, for preferences that belong to one project.

`flui config show` prints every preference with the layer its
current value came from. Use it to debug an unexpected value:

```bash
flui config show
```

### Preferences

Four preferences are declared in the schema:

| Key | Env var | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `email` | `FLUI_EMAIL` | *(required)* | Contact email for Let's Encrypt and operational notifications. |
| `certificateMode` | `FLUI_CERTIFICATE_MODE` | `production` | Certificate issuance mode written into the dashboard config. One of `production`, `staging`, `preflight`. See [TLS and certificates](/concepts/14-tls-and-certificates/). |
| `apiPath` | `FLUI_API_PATH` | `.` | Path to the `flui-core` repo. Only relevant to Flui contributors using `env export-config` / `dev creds`. |
| `dashboardPath` | `FLUI_DASHBOARD_PATH` | `../flui-dashboard` | Path to the `flui-dashboard` repo. Same scope as `apiPath`. |

```bash
flui config set email you@example.com
flui config set certificateMode preflight
flui config get email                       # resolved value + source
```

Preferences are not secrets and are stored in plain text, so
reading or writing one never asks for the vault.

### Provider credentials

`flui config set <provider>` stores the credentials needed to talk
to a cloud provider's API. The command works the same way for every
provider. What differs is whether the credential is a single token
or a key and secret pair. A single token can be passed inline; a
pair goes through the interactive prompt, or a JSON object on
`--stdin`:

| Provider | Credential | Input |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hetzner` | Single API token (`apiKey`) | Inline accepted: `flui config set hetzner <TOKEN>` |
| `scaleway` | Access Key ID + Secret Key | Not inline: `flui config set scaleway` prompts for both fields, or reads them as JSON with `--stdin`, and live-validates them against the Scaleway IAM API before saving |
| `ovh` | OpenStack username + password | Not inline: `flui config set ovh` prompts for both fields, or reads them as JSON with `--stdin`, and live-validates them against OVHcloud's Keystone endpoint before saving |

OVHcloud is addressed through OpenStack, so the credential is the
username and password of a Public Cloud user (OVH Manager → Public
Cloud → Users & Roles), not an OVH API application key. The password
is shown once, at the moment the user is created. The user must have
access to exactly one OpenStack project: Flui resolves the project
from the credential itself, and stops if the credential reaches none
or several.

These are the keys `flui config` accepts as providers. What each
provider can do is in [the providers
table](/concepts/01-flui-vs-provider-layer/#the-providers-integrated-today).

Storing a credential writes to the vault, so the vault must be
unlocked. The exception is a profile that still holds the old key
file, where that file's key is used.
A value passed as an argument is visible to every process on the
machine through the process list, so `--stdin` is the safer way to
pass one. For a provider with a credential pair, it is also the
only way to configure it without a terminal, as a JSON object of
its fields:

```bash
printf '%s' "$TOKEN" | flui config set hetzner --stdin
printf '{"accessKey":"…","secretKey":"…"}' | flui config set scaleway --stdin
printf '{"accessKey":"…","secretKey":"…"}' | flui config set ovh --stdin
```

For `ovh`, `accessKey` is the OpenStack username and `secretKey` the
OpenStack password. The field names are the generic ones for a
credential pair, shared with Scaleway.

Credentials are never printed back. `flui config list` shows which
providers have credentials stored but not their values; `flui config
get` works on preferences only, and says so if you ask it for a
provider.

```bash
flui config set hetzner <YOUR_API_TOKEN>
flui config set scaleway                    # interactive prompt
flui config list                            # everything in the active profile
flui config list --tokens                   # provider credentials only
flui config list --preferences              # preferences only
flui config list --verbose                  # with created/updated times
flui config test hetzner                    # read-only API call with the stored credentials
flui config remove hetzner                  # asks to confirm by retyping the key
flui config remove scaleway --force         # skip the confirmation
```

`flui config test <provider>` checks the stored credentials with a
real, read-only call to the provider and lists the servers,
Flui-managed volumes and networks it finds on the account. It
creates and changes nothing.

### System keys

`api-url` is the only system-level key: the URL of the Flui API the
active profile talks to. `flui env create` sets it, and
`flui env adopt`, `env sync` and `env status` refresh it. You rarely
need to edit it by hand; when you do, use `flui config set
api-url <url>`. `flui config remove api-url` clears it.

## What lives in a profile, and how it is stored

One file sits above the profiles:

- `~/.flui/vault.json`: the vault header, with the salt and a value
  that proves a passphrase is right. It holds no credential, and
  nothing in it helps anyone who does not know the passphrase.

A profile directory contains:

- `config.json`: preferences (plain) and provider credentials
  (sealed under the vault).
- `.key`: the pre-vault key file. Present only on a profile that
  has not been moved to the vault yet; the first
  `flui vault unlock` removes it.
- `ca/`: the SSH CA used to authenticate to cluster nodes
  (sealed under the vault).
- `clusters.json`, `nodes.json`, `firewalls.json`, `vnets.json`,
  `operations.json`: local inventory cached from the API. You can
  delete them; the next command that needs them fetches them again.

## Examples

```bash
# Set the machine up once
flui vault init
flui vault unlock

# Create a staging workspace on Hetzner
flui context create staging --switch
flui config set email staging@example.com
flui config set hetzner <staging-token>
flui config set certificateMode staging
flui env create

# Same on Scaleway: interactive prompt for the key pair
flui context create staging-scw --switch
flui config set email staging@example.com
flui config set scaleway
flui env create --provider scaleway

# Same on OVHcloud: OpenStack username and password
flui context create staging-ovh --switch
flui config set email staging@example.com
flui config set ovh
flui env create --provider ovh --region GRA

# Debug where a preference is coming from
flui config show
flui config get certificateMode

# Remove a provider's credentials
flui config remove scaleway --force

# Finish for the day
flui vault lock
```

[Multi-context CLI](/concepts/07-multi-context-cli/) explains why
the vault works this way: one passphrase over many installations,
and what it does and does not defend against.

sections.title: Templates
sections.body:
The `template` topic takes you from "I want to start a new
application in framework X" to a repository the platform can build
and deploy. One command creates a new repository that already has
the Dockerfile, `flui.yaml` and healthcheck Flui needs. See
[Framework templates](/concepts/19-framework-templates/) for the
concepts.

## `flui template use <framework> <name>`

Creates a new repository copied from the framework's template and, by
default, imports it into Flui so the application appears in the
dashboard right away. If a repository with that name
already exists and was made from the same template, it is reused.

```bash
flui template use <framework> my-app                   # private repo, default owner
flui template use <framework> my-app --public          # public repo
flui template use <framework> my-api --org my-org      # under a specific org
flui template use <framework> my-svc -d "Internal microservice"
flui template use <framework> my-app --no-import       # skip the Flui-side import
```

| Argument / Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `<framework>` | Template name: `nextjs`, `nuxt`, `angular`, `sveltekit`, `astro`, `vue-vite`, `vitepress`, `nestjs`, `spring-boot`, `django`, `fastapi`, `aspnet-core` or `generic`. |
| `<name>` | Name for the new repository (required). |
| `--org <name>` | Organisation or user to create the repo under. Default: your linked GitHub account, or, with the Flui GitHub App, an account it is installed on that you can reach. |
| `-d, --description <s>` | Repository description. |
| `--public` | Create as public. Default: private. |
| `--no-import` | Create the repository on GitHub but skip the Flui-side import. |

## Prerequisites

- You have run `flui auth login`. The command uses the active
  profile's API key.
- Your linked GitHub account needs permission to create a repository
  in the destination organisation. If the target is your personal
  account this is implicit; for an org, you (or the linked
  installation) must have repository-create rights there.

sections.title: Utilities
sections.body:
These commands do not belong to a single operational topic and sit at
the top level of the CLI.

## `flui version`

Prints the CLI version and the platform release it pins: the
component image tags and the bootstrap revision a fresh
`flui env create` would install. Use it when debugging an install or
checking which release a machine is on.

```bash
flui version
flui version --latest   # show what `env create --latest` would resolve to
flui version --json
```

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--latest` | Show the rolling development tags (bootstrap `master`, `:latest` images) that `flui env create --latest` resolves to, instead of the pinned release. |
| `--json` | Machine-readable output. |

## `flui update`

Checks `npm` for a newer published version of `@flui-cloud/cli` and,
if there is one, asks for confirmation and reinstalls the CLI
globally.

```bash
flui update
```

The reinstall runs `npm install -g @flui-cloud/cli@<latest>`. If you
installed the CLI with `pnpm` or `yarn`, the command still works but
leaves a mixed install in your local Node setup. If that matters,
reinstall with your own package manager.

## `flui reconcile`

Reconciles the CLI's local state with what the API knows. It covers
only the DNS configuration, and helps after manual edits to DNS
records or to the provider zone, to bring the two views back in line.

```bash
flui reconcile
flui reconcile --type dns
flui reconcile --dry-run
```

| Flag | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-t, --type <kind>` | `all` | Reconciliation kind. One of `dns`, `all`. Repeatable. |
| `--api-url <url>` | from the profile, else `http://localhost:3000/api/v1` | Override the API URL for this run. |
| `--dry-run` | none | Show what would be reconciled without applying changes. |

## DNS

The `dns` topic has more commands than this page covers. This page
documents the low-level ones: checking resolvers and cleaning up
leftover records. For everyday DNS work (assigning a zone to a
cluster, publishing the wildcard record that covers every application
on it, and adding a second provider for redundancy), see
[Put an application on the internet](/tasks/put-an-application-on-the-internet/),
which covers `flui dns zone`, `flui dns wildcard` and
`flui dns replica` end to end, in the CLI and the dashboard.

### `flui dns resolvers`

Shows whether certificates are checked through public resolvers
before Flui asks for one. Without public resolvers, a name published
a moment ago can look missing for up to an hour.

```bash
flui dns resolvers
flui dns resolvers --cluster production --pin
```

`--pin` sets public resolvers when they are missing, and the
certificate service restarts once. `--json` gives output for scripts.

### `flui dns cleanup`

Deletes every `A` record in the named zone on Hetzner DNS. Use it
after destroying a batch of test clusters that left their hostnames
behind.

```bash
flui dns cleanup --domain example.com --dry-run    # preview first
flui dns cleanup --domain example.com
flui dns cleanup --domain example.com --force      # skip confirmation
```

| Flag | Required | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--domain <name>` | yes | Zone name on Hetzner DNS. |
| `-f, --force` | no | Skip confirmation. |
| `--dry-run` | no | Preview the records that would be deleted. |

> **Destructive and irreversible.** Always run `--dry-run` first. The
> command does not check which records belong to active clusters; it
> removes every `A` record in the zone.
